citations.quote: Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.2 allows XSS via a crafted directory name because notebook/static/tree/js/notebooklist.js handles certain URLs unsafely.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the breadcrumb rendering in the file browser so the link element is created through jQuery constructors, the link target is set as an attribute, and the directory name is set as plain text instead of being concatenated into an HTML string. The root folder link and click handlers were restructured the same way, while URL encoding of path components was already present and is unchanged.

patterns.title: lxml HTML cleaner misses escaped javascript: URLs, enabling XSS
patterns.cause: In lxml before 4.2.5, the link-cleaning logic in lxml.html.clean stripped whitespace from a URL and then tested for the javascript scheme, but it never percent-decoded the URL first. A link whose scheme was written with percent-encoded characters or encoded whitespace therefore did not match the check and was left in the output. A browser that decodes such a link, such as Internet Explorer, could then treat it as a script URL.
preconditions: The application uses the lxml.html.clean module to sanitize untrusted HTML.
The installed lxml version is older than 4.2.5.
The cleaned HTML is rendered in a browser that decodes percent-encoded characters in the scheme and runs the resulting javascript: URL.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade lxml to version 4.2.5 or later. When filtering URLs, normalize the value the way a browser would before judging it: percent-decode it, then remove whitespace and control characters, and only then compare the scheme against the blocked list. Prefer an allow-list of safe schemes over a block-list. Test the cleaner with percent-encoded, whitespace-split and mixed-case scheme variants as well as the plain form.
patterns.limitations: The fix applies a single round of URL decoding, so other obfuscations such as HTML entity tricks, double encoding or control characters inside the scheme are not shown to be covered by this change. The advisory demonstrates only Internet Explorer. Other XSS vectors in the cleaner are out of scope.

fixtures.scenario: A comment form passes user HTML through the lxml cleaner on lxml 4.2.4. A link whose address is written as j a v a s c r i p t: with a payload survives cleaning and is shown to Internet Explorer users.
The same form runs on lxml 4.2.5 or later. The escaped javascript: link is removed during cleaning, and a test with escaped scheme variants confirms none remain in the output.

citations.quote: does not remove javascript: URLs that use escaping, allowing a remote attacker to conduct XSS attacks
This is a similar issue to CVE-2014-3146.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the javascript link check percent-decode the URL (including turning plus signs into spaces) before whitespace is removed and the scheme is tested. This closes the gap where encoded characters in the scheme hid a script URL from the check. The card's cause and its prevention advice (decode first, then strip whitespace, then compare the scheme) match this change.

patterns.title: Stored XSS from edited metadata database objects in Apache Airflow page views
patterns.cause: Apache Airflow before 1.10.2 rendered certain page views from object state held in its metadata database in a way that let script content in that state run in the browser. A malicious admin user could edit that state to plant the script. The sources do not name the specific pages, fields, or templates involved.
preconditions: Apache Airflow older than 1.10.2 is in use.
An attacker holds admin-level access and can edit the state of objects in the metadata database.
Another user opens one of the affected page views, which displays the edited state.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 1.10.2 or later. In any similar application, treat values read from the metadata database as untrusted, even when only privileged users can write them. Encode or escape them for the HTML context where they are displayed, and avoid inserting them into pages as raw markup or script.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which page views or object fields were affected, nor how the fix works, so the output-encoding guidance is general direction rather than a description of the upstream change. The issue is limited to a malicious admin user, so it does not cover unauthenticated or low-privilege attackers. The sources give no workaround other than the fixed version.

fixtures.scenario: A malicious admin user edits the state of an object in the metadata database so it contains script content. A colleague later opens a page view that displays that object, and the browser runs the script in the context of the Airflow web interface.
The deployment runs Airflow 1.10.2 or later. An admin edits the same object state to include script-like text, and the page view shows it as inert text rather than running it in the viewer's browser.

citations.quote: a malicious admin user could edit the state of objects in the Airflow metadata database to execute arbitrary javascript on certain page views

patch_review.observation: The fix escapes database-sourced values (DAG run id, chart label, pool name) before they are placed into HTML link markup in the list-view formatter functions of both the classic and RBAC web UIs. A test adds a pool whose name contains script tags and checks that the list page shows them HTML-encoded. This matches the card's cause (unescaped stored object state rendered as HTML) and its prevention (encode values for the HTML context instead of inserting raw markup).

patterns.title: Serve user files under a CSP header so they are treated as a separate origin (Jupyter Notebook XSS via SVG)
patterns.cause: Jupyter Notebook before 5.5.0 did not send a CSP header that makes the browser treat served files as belonging to a separate origin. A file such as an SVG document could therefore carry an XSS payload and be handled as part of the application's own origin.
preconditions: The application serves user-supplied or user-editable files, such as SVG documents, over HTTP.
The responses for those files carry no CSP header that isolates them from the application origin.
The deployment runs Jupyter Notebook before version 5.5.0.
patterns.prevention: Attach a Content-Security-Policy header to every response that serves a user file, so the browser treats those files as a separate origin from the application and not as trusted application content. Apply it in the shared file-serving path, so file types that can embed active content, such as SVG, are covered along with the rest. Upgrade to Jupyter Notebook 5.5.0 or later, which the advisories identify as the first version past this issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the exact CSP directives, the affected URL paths or handlers, or how the fix is implemented. They do not describe other file types beyond the SVG example. They do not say whether a CSP header alone is enough, or whether other mitigations such as a separate serving domain are needed.

fixtures.scenario: A notebook server of a version before 5.5.0 serves a user-uploaded SVG document with no CSP header. The SVG contains an XSS payload, and the browser treats the file as part of the application's origin.

A notebook server at version 5.5.0 or later serves the same SVG document with a CSP header that makes the browser treat served files as a separate origin from the application. The embedded payload does not run with the application's origin.

citations.quote: Jupyter Notebook before 5.5.0 does not use a CSP header to treat served files as belonging to a separate origin.
an XSS payload can be placed in an SVG document.

patch_review.observation: The fix overrides the content security policy for the two file-serving handlers, the authenticated static file handler and the files handler. It appends a sandbox directive that permits scripts, so any HTML or SVG served from user files runs in a unique opaque origin and cannot interact with the notebook server. This matches the card's cause and prevention of isolating served files from the application origin through CSP in the shared file-serving path.

patterns.title: Browsable API templates with autoescaping disabled allow XSS in Django REST framework
patterns.cause: In Django REST framework versions before 3.9.1, the default Browsable API view templates disable autoescaping. Content rendered through those templates is therefore not HTML-escaped by default, so attacker-influenced data shown in the browsable interface can be interpreted as markup or script by the browser.
preconditions: The application uses django-rest-framework before version 3.9.1
The default Browsable API view templates are in use
Data that an attacker can influence is rendered through those templates and viewed by another user in a browser
patterns.prevention: Upgrade django-rest-framework to version 3.9.1 or later, where the default Browsable API templates no longer disable autoescaping. In any custom or overridden Browsable API templates, keep the template engine's autoescaping enabled so that dynamic values are HTML-escaped on output, and avoid turning escaping off for values that may carry user-controlled content.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that the default Browsable API templates disable autoescaping before 3.9.1. They do not identify which template fields or inputs are exploitable, give attack payloads, or describe the exact upstream change. Whether the Browsable API renderer is enabled in a given deployment, and whether custom templates are affected, is not covered and must be checked separately.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs django-rest-framework 3.9.0 with the default Browsable API renderer enabled. A user-controlled value reaches the default templates, where autoescaping is disabled, and a second user who opens the browsable page in a browser has the unescaped content treated as markup.

An application runs django-rest-framework 3.9.1 or later, and any customized Browsable API templates leave autoescaping on. The same user-controlled value is HTML-escaped on output and displayed as plain text.

citations.quote: allows XSS because the default DRF Browsable API view templates disable autoescaping.
Django REST framework (aka django-rest-framework) before 3.9.1 allows XSS

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the autoescape-off block around the response headers and content in the Browsable API base template, so the output is escaped by default again. It also reworks the urlize_quoted_links filter so every text fragment and link part is escaped when autoescape is active, and the filter now honors the autoescape flag. New tests check that script markup in content is escaped while URLs are still linkified.

patterns.title: Authorization header forwarded on cross-origin redirect in urllib3
patterns.cause: urllib3 before 1.24.2 did not remove the authorization HTTP header when following a redirect that differs in host, port, or scheme. The issue exists because an earlier fix for CVE-2018-20060 was incomplete: it was case-sensitive.
preconditions: The application uses urllib3 before version 1.24.2
A request carries an authorization HTTP header
The server answers with a redirect to a different host, port, or scheme
The client follows the redirect automatically
patterns.prevention: Upgrade urllib3 to 1.24.2 or later. In any redirect-following code, compare the origin (host, port, and scheme) of the original request with the redirect target. If they differ, drop the authorization header before resending. Match the header name case-insensitively, because the earlier case-sensitive fix was incomplete.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how the 1.24.2 fix is implemented. They do not cover other sensitive headers such as cookies, or how same-origin redirects are handled. They also give no detail on which header spellings bypassed the earlier fix.

fixtures.scenario: A client on urllib3 1.24.1 sends a request with an authorization header. The server redirects to a different host, port, or scheme, and the header is forwarded to that unintended destination, exposing the credentials.
A client on urllib3 1.24.2 or later follows the same cross-origin redirect, but the authorization header is removed before the request is resent, so the other host never receives the credentials.

citations.quote: does not remove the authorization HTTP header when following a cross-origin redirect
this issue exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2018-20060 (which was case-sensitive)

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the removal of sensitive headers on cross-host redirects case-insensitive. The retry settings now store the header names to strip in lowercase, and the redirect handling in the pool manager compares each request header name in lowercase before dropping it. Tests confirm that a lowercase authorization header, or a custom lowercase secret header, is no longer forwarded.

patterns.title: Unsafe pickle deserialization in Superset before 0.23 allows remote code execution
patterns.cause: Superset versions prior to 0.23 used an unsafe load method from the pickle library to deserialize data. Deserializing untrusted data this way can lead to possible remote code execution.
preconditions: The deployment runs a Superset version prior to 0.23.
A code path deserializes data with the pickle library's unsafe load method.
The data being deserialized can come from an untrusted source, as the advisory title Deserialization of Untrusted Data indicates.
patterns.prevention: Run Superset 0.23 or later. In any code that handles data crossing a trust boundary, do not pass that data to the pickle library's unsafe load method. Review other code paths that deserialize data in the same way.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which Superset features or data paths used the unsafe load, how an attacker could supply the data, or what replaced it in the fix. They also do not describe any mitigation short of upgrading. They note only that 0.23 was released before any Apache Software Foundation release of Superset, so version numbering may be confusing when checking affected installs.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs a Superset release older than 0.23. A component deserializes stored or received data with the pickle library's unsafe load method, so a crafted payload could trigger remote code execution.
A deployment runs Superset 0.23 or later. A review of the code finds no use of the pickle library's unsafe load method on data that an untrusted party could influence.

citations.quote: Versions of Superset prior to 0.23 used an unsafe load method from the pickle library to deserialize data leading to possible remote code execution.
Deserialization of Untrusted Data in superset
Note Superset 0.23 was released prior to any Superset release under the Apache Software Foundation.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes pickle from the dashboard export and import feature. Export now writes JSON through a custom encoder, and the import view parses the uploaded file as JSON with a custom decoder that rebuilds only a fixed set of model classes, instead of unpickling it. This matches the card's cause (unsafe pickle loading of untrusted data) and its prevention (stop feeding untrusted data to the unsafe pickle load).

patterns.title: Stored XSS from admin-editable metadata database state shown in Airflow page views
patterns.cause: The pagination helper used by the list views built its HTML by plain string formatting. It put query parameters, such as the search text, into link targets without URL-encoding or HTML-escaping them. It then returned the result as markup that is trusted as safe. A value containing quotes and tag characters could break out of the link attribute and run script in the viewer's browser.
preconditions: A list view passes a value that someone else can influence, such as a search term, into the pagination helper.
The helper output is rendered as trusted HTML without further escaping.
A victim opens a page whose pagination links carry the crafted value.
patterns.prevention: Build query strings with a proper URL-encoding routine and never by concatenating raw values. Build HTML fragments from templates that are aware of HTML escaping, so every interpolated value is escaped automatically, and mark only the static template text as safe. Do not return plain-string HTML from helpers and then mark it safe. Add tests that feed a hostile value through every helper that emits links or markup and check that the raw text never appears in the output. Apply the same fix to every parallel UI code path, and upgrade to an Airflow release that includes the fix.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows the unescaped input as the search parameter of the pagination links. It does not show how that value relates to the admin-edited database state named in the advisory. Other views that render stored object fields without escaping are not covered by this change.

fixtures.scenario: An admin user changes the stored state of an object in the metadata database so that it contains script content. A second user opens a page view that displays that object, and the script runs in the second user's browser session.
The same modified object state is displayed on the page view only after being encoded for HTML output. The browser shows the content as inert text and no script runs for the second user.

citations.quote: A malicious admin user could edit the state of objects in the Airflow metadata database to execute arbitrary javascript on certain page views.
Apache Airflow vulnerable to Stored XSS

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the query-string helper to use proper URL encoding, so values such as the search text can no longer break out of link targets. It also turns the pagination node templates into escaping-aware markup objects, so interpolated values are HTML-escaped and only the static template text is trusted. The same change is applied to both the classic and role-based UI code paths, with tests that feed a hostile search value and check that the raw text is absent.

patterns.title: SQL injection through a crafted password in the Salt MySQL module user_chpass function
patterns.cause: In the Salt MySQL module, user_chpass built the ALTER USER statement for MySQL 8.0.11 and later by joining the user name, host and password directly into the SQL string. A crafted password (or user or host value) containing quote characters could break out of the string literal and alter the statement. The older UPDATE path for earlier servers already bound the user and host as parameters, so the unsafe concatenation was specific to the newer-server branch.
preconditions: Salt 2018.3 or 2019.2 earlier than the fixed release is in use
The connected MySQL server is version 8.0.11 or later, so the ALTER USER branch is taken
The mysql.user_chpass function is called with a password, user or host value that an attacker can influence
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Salt to a release containing the fix (2018.3.4 or later). In code that changes database account credentials, never concatenate the password, user name or host into the statement text. Pass them as bound parameters through the database driver so they are always treated as data, including in the passwordless unix socket variant. Also limit who can supply values to this function.
patterns.limitations: Parameter binding works here because the driver can quote account names and password literals in ALTER USER. Identifiers such as column names still need separate validation if they are ever built dynamically. Servers older than 8.0.11 used a different branch that was already partly parameterized, so exposure on those versions is less clear from this diff.

fixtures.scenario: A Salt 2018.3 master runs mysql.user_chpass with a password string from an untrusted source. The string is crafted so the MySQL server runs attacker-chosen SQL, which can escalate privileges.
A Salt release at or above 2018.3.4 runs mysql.user_chpass with the same crafted password. The password is handled purely as a value, so it is stored as the password and no extra SQL runs.

citations.quote: The component is: The mysql.user_chpass function from the MySQL module for Salt. The attack vector is: specially crafted password string.
An attacker could escalate privileges on MySQL server deployed by cloud provider. It leads to RCE.
The fixed version is: 2018.3.4.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes user_chpass so the ALTER USER statement for MySQL 8.0.11 and later no longer concatenates the user, host and password into the SQL text. It uses named placeholders with values passed to the driver. The passwordless unix socket variant, which also concatenated values, now uses bound user and host values with the auth_socket plugin. The older UPDATE branch already bound user and host, as the card says.

patterns.title: Open redirect after login via crafted links to the login page
patterns.cause: The login handler's redirect-safety check judged the post-login next target with a plain string prefix test against the server base URL. With no base URL prefix the base URL is just a slash, so a protocol-relative target such as a double slash followed by an attacker host passed the check and the browser was sent off-site after login. The check also left backslashes unescaped, and some browsers, notably Chrome, treat a double backslash like a double slash, which gave another way to smuggle in a host.
preconditions: Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.8 or JupyterHub before 0.9.6, which use the weak redirect check after login
The server runs at the root path with no base URL prefix, so a target starting with a double slash still satisfies the prefix test
The user is lured to a login link whose next parameter holds an off-site or protocol-relative target, and then logs in successfully
For the backslash variant, the user's browser treats backslashes in URLs as slashes, as Chrome does
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Notebook 5.7.8 or later and JupyterHub 0.9.6 or later. When validating a post-login redirect, parse the target with a real URL parser instead of comparing string prefixes. Reject any target that carries a host component unless it passes an explicit origin allow check, compare only the parsed path to the base URL, and escape backslashes before parsing so that browser quirks cannot turn them into slashes. Fall back to the base URL when validation fails, and add tests for protocol-relative, absolute and backslash-style targets.
patterns.limitations: This describes the Notebook fix in the supplied diffs. The JupyterHub change was not shown, so its details are assumed to be similar. The advisory and the CVE record give different fixed version numbers, so check the release notes. A deployment with a base URL prefix makes the simple double slash target fail the prefix test, but that is a side effect of the weak check and not a dependable mitigation.

fixtures.scenario: An unprefixed Jupyter Notebook server older than the fixed release receives a login link crafted by an attacker. The user logs in with valid credentials and the browser is then redirected to an attacker-controlled site.

The server runs a fixed release, or checks that the post-login destination stays on the same server. The same crafted link leads to a normal on-server landing page after login, and the user is not sent to an external site.

citations.quote: allows crafted links to the login page, which will redirect to a malicious site after successful login.
Servers running on a base_url prefix are not affected.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the plain prefix test on the post-login redirect target with real URL parsing. A target with a host component is rejected unless it passes the explicit origin check, and only the parsed path is compared to the base URL. A second change escapes backslashes before parsing so that browsers treating a double backslash like a double slash cannot sneak in a host. The new tests cover protocol-relative, absolute and off-base-path targets.

patterns.title: Open redirect in Jupyter Notebook via empty netloc in redirect target validation
patterns.cause: Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.8 could be made to issue an open redirect when the redirect target had an empty netloc. The sources say this was an incomplete fix for CVE-2019-10255, meaning the earlier redirect validation did not cover this case.
preconditions: The application is Jupyter Notebook before version 5.7.8.
A redirect target is taken from a request-supplied value and checked before redirecting.
The supplied target has an empty netloc, a case the earlier check for CVE-2019-10255 did not handle.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Jupyter Notebook to 5.7.8 or later. In code that redirects to a user-supplied target, make the validation handle a target whose parsed netloc is empty explicitly, rather than assuming an empty netloc is safe. Only allow redirects that are clearly local to the application. After fixing one bypass, re-check the whole validation path for similar variants, since this CVE exists because an earlier fix was incomplete.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the exact request format that triggers the redirect, the affected endpoints, or how the upstream check was changed. They also do not say whether other malformed targets bypass validation. This card describes the direction only and does not claim the full set of unsafe inputs.

fixtures.scenario: A Notebook server older than 5.7.8 receives a login or similar request carrying a redirect target that parses with an empty netloc. The earlier validation for CVE-2019-10255 lets it through, and the server redirects the user to a location the attacker chose.

A Notebook server at 5.7.8 or later receives the same request. Validation handles the empty netloc case, so the target is not treated as a safe local redirect and the user is not sent to an attacker-chosen location.

citations.quote: In Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.8, an open redirect can occur via an empty netloc.
This issue exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2019-10255.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops relying on the parsed netloc being non-empty to decide whether a redirect target is local. It rebuilds a path-only form of the target with scheme and netloc stripped and rejects anything that differs from the original, which catches inputs such as a triple-slash host or a backslash-prefixed host that parse with an empty netloc. It also allows full URLs that match the request's own origin, and adds tests for the bypass inputs.

patterns.title: Object.prototype pollution through jQuery deep extend in versions before 3.4.0
patterns.cause: In jQuery before 3.4.0, the deep-copy mode of the extend function mishandles a source object that has an enumerable __proto__ property. The copy can then extend the native Object.prototype, which pollutes the prototype shared by all objects.
preconditions: The application uses a jQuery version before 3.4.0, for example one bundled with a product such as Drupal or Backdrop CMS.
Client code calls jQuery extend in deep mode, with true as the first argument, to merge a source object into a target.
The source object is unsanitized and contains an enumerable __proto__ property.
patterns.prevention: Use jQuery 3.4.0 or later, and check that any copy of jQuery bundled with a product or framework is also upgraded. Do not feed unsanitized objects into a deep merge. Treat a __proto__ key in untrusted data as hostile and reject or strip it before merging.
patterns.limitations: The sources only describe the prototype pollution flaw in jQuery. They do not say how the pollution leads to cross-site scripting, and they do not state which Django components bundle jQuery or how Django changed. The upstream fix is not described here, and the sources give no other mitigation.

fixtures.scenario: A page runs on jQuery 3.3.1 and deep-merges a parsed request object into its defaults. The object has an enumerable __proto__ property, so the merge extends Object.prototype for all objects.
The page runs on jQuery 3.4.0 or later and removes any __proto__ key from untrusted objects before a deep merge, so Object.prototype is not extended.

citations.quote: If an unsanitized source object contained an enumerable __proto__ property, it could extend the native Object.prototype.
jQuery before 3.4.0, as used in Drupal, Backdrop CMS, and other products, mishandles

patch_review.observation: The diff patches the copy of jQuery 3.3.1 bundled in Django admin static files, in the deep-copy loop of the extend function. It now skips the special prototype-link key, alongside the existing self-reference check, so merged untrusted objects can no longer modify the shared Object prototype. This matches the card's cause, and its advice to upgrade jQuery or reject that key agrees with the fix. Django patched the vendored file in place rather than upgrading it.

patterns.title: Unvalidated Current URL link in Django AdminURLFieldWidget enables clickable JavaScript links
patterns.cause: The AdminURLFieldWidget shows a clickable Current URL value and displays the provided value without validating it as a safe URL. A value that carries a JavaScript link therefore becomes a clickable script link in the admin page (CWE-79).
preconditions: Django 1.11 before 1.11.21, 2.1 before 2.1.9, or 2.2 before 2.2.2 is in use.
The admin renders a URL field through AdminURLFieldWidget, which shows the clickable Current URL value.
The displayed value is unvalidated, either stored in the database or supplied as a URL query parameter payload.
A user must interact with the rendered link for the script to run.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a patched Django release (1.11.21, 2.1.9, 2.2.2 or later). In general, an implementation that shows a value as a clickable link should first validate that the value is a safe URL. A value that fails validation should be shown as plain, escaped text and not as a link. This applies to values read from the database and to values taken from URL query parameters.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the flaw and the affected versions but not the exact validation rules, the permitted URL schemes, or how the upstream fix works. They do not say which users or pages are exposed beyond the admin widget, or whether other widgets are affected. Treat the safe-URL check described here as a direction, not a full specification.

fixtures.scenario: An admin change form for a model with a URL field renders the Current URL link from a stored value that uses a JavaScript URL scheme, or from a query parameter payload with the same content. The link is clickable and runs script when an administrator clicks it.

The same admin change form runs on a patched Django release, or the value is checked as a safe URL before being linked. A value using a JavaScript URL scheme is not turned into a clickable link and is displayed only as escaped text.

citations.quote: The clickable Current URL value displayed by the AdminURLFieldWidget displays the provided value without validating it as a safe URL.
an unvalidated value stored in the database, or a value provided as a URL query parameter payload, could result in an clickable JavaScript link.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the admin URL widget run Django's standard URL validator on the value when building its context, and the template only renders the clickable Current link block when that check passes. Values such as a JavaScript link or a relative path no longer become links and appear only in the ordinary input field. This matches the card's cause (unvalidated value shown as a link) and its prevention (validate before linking, upgrade to a patched release).

patterns.title: Stored XSS via editable metadata database object state in Airflow page views
patterns.cause: The RBAC web UI exposed an edit action on the DAG model view. An admin user could use it to change DAG records in the metadata database, including fields the scheduler manages, such as the file location. Those edited values were later shown in page views and used to find files, which allowed stored script injection and disclosure of files readable by the webserver. The upstream fix removes the edit capability instead of changing how values are rendered.
preconditions: The attacker holds an admin role that can reach the edit form of the DAG model view
Edited DAG record fields are stored in the metadata database and later shown to other users or used by the webserver
The webserver process can read local files, which bounds what the file disclosure can reach
patterns.prevention: Make model views that mirror scheduler-managed metadata read-only. Grant only list and show permissions and remove the edit route, so users cannot change fields such as the file location through the web UI. Apply the same least-privilege review to every auto-generated admin view, and allow editing only for fields that truly need it. As defense in depth, also encode stored values for their output context and avoid using stored paths to choose files to read.
patterns.limitations: The diff only removes the edit permission and its tests. It does not show how the script injection or file disclosure worked in detail, and it does not show any output encoding change. It covers the RBAC UI only, and the sources give no affected or fixed version ranges. Other views that allow editing of stored state would need a separate review.

fixtures.scenario: An admin edits a stored object state in the metadata database so it contains script content. Another user opens a page view that displays that object, and the script runs in that user's browser.
The same edited state is displayed on the page view, but the value is treated as untrusted data and encoded for its output context. It appears as plain text and no script runs.

citations.quote: A malicious admin user could edit the state of objects in the Airflow metadata database to execute arbitrary javascript on certain page views.
This also presented a Local File Disclosure vulnerability to any file readable by the webserver process.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the edit permission from the DAG model view in the RBAC web UI, leaving only list and show. It also deletes the tests for the edit page and edit URL. This closes the route by which an admin could alter scheduler-managed DAG records, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Archive extraction path traversal in NLTK Downloader packages
patterns.cause: The NLTK Downloader before version 3.4.5 mishandled entries in a downloaded NLTK package, which is a ZIP archive, during extraction. An entry name containing dot dot slash sequences could place files outside the intended location, so an attacker who controls the package contents could write arbitrary files.
preconditions: The NLTK Downloader of a version before 3.4.5 is used to fetch and extract a package.
The package is a ZIP archive that contains an entry name with a dot dot slash sequence.
The attacker can influence the package content that the downloader extracts.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NLTK to version 3.4.5 or later. In any code that extracts archives, do not trust entry names from the archive. Before writing each entry, resolve its final destination path and confirm it stays inside the intended extraction directory. Reject or skip any entry whose resolved path falls outside that directory, rather than writing it.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that extraction mishandled dot dot slash in ZIP entries and that versions before 3.4.5 are affected. They do not describe the exact upstream change, other traversal forms such as absolute paths or symlinks, or what the downloader does with untrusted package sources. Those points are not covered here.

fixtures.scenario: A user on NLTK 3.4.4 downloads a package whose ZIP archive contains an entry named with leading dot dot slash components. During extraction the entry is written outside the data directory, overwriting a file elsewhere in the user's file system.
A user on NLTK 3.4.5 or later downloads the same package. Each entry is checked against the extraction directory, and the entry with dot dot slash components is not written outside it.

citations.quote: NLTK Downloader before 3.4.5 is vulnerable to a directory traversal, allowing attackers to write arbitrary files
in an NLTK package (ZIP archive) that is mishandled during extraction

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the hand-written extraction loop in the unzip helper, which joined raw archive entry names onto the target directory and so let dot dot slash names escape it. It now calls the standard library extractall, which sanitizes member names by dropping parent-directory and absolute-path components, so files stay under the target directory. The card's cause and its direction of confining writes to the extraction directory match this, though the real fix neutralizes bad names instead of rejecting them.

patterns.title: Untrusted zone name used in a remote ps check allows command injection in solaris_zone
patterns.cause: The solaris_zone module checks the zone name by listing processes with the ps command on the remote Solaris host. The zone name is attacker-influenced input, and a crafted name can lead to arbitrary commands running on that host. The advisory title lists OS command injection and improper input validation as the weaknesses.
preconditions: The solaris_zone module from the Ansible Community modules is used to set a zone name on a Solaris host.
An attacker can influence the zone name value that is passed to the module.
The Ansible Engine version is 2.7.15, 2.8.7, 2.9.2 or an earlier version.
patterns.prevention: Treat the zone name as untrusted data. Validate it against a strict allow-list of characters and length before use. Do not let it be interpreted as shell syntax when the remote process check runs. Pass it as a plain argument or compare it against process output inside the module, instead of building a command line from it. Update to a release that contains the fix referenced for this CVE.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact vulnerable code, the specific characters that trigger the injection, or how the upstream fix works. The validation and argument-handling guidance above is general direction for this weakness class, not a description of the upstream change. The sources do not say which releases are fixed beyond naming 2.7.15, 2.8.7 and 2.9.2 and earlier as affected.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook takes a zone name from an external or untrusted variable and passes it to solaris_zone on an affected Ansible version. The module checks the name with a bare ps command on the remote host, and a crafted name causes extra commands to run there.

A playbook restricts the zone name to a short allow-list of plain characters before calling solaris_zone. It runs a patched Ansible version, so the name is never interpreted as shell syntax by the remote process check.

citations.quote: the zone name is checked by listing the process with the 'ps' bare command on the remote machine
An attacker could take advantage of this flaw by crafting the name of the zone and executing arbitrary commands in the remote host.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the zone class constructor that rejects any zone name not matching a strict allow-list. Names must start with an alphanumeric character, may contain only letters, digits, underscores, hyphens and periods, and are capped at 64 characters. The module fails early on anything else, and the changelog describes the cause as missing validation of the zone name before it is used in actions that can run commands.

patterns.title: Path traversal via Content-Disposition filename in pip URL installs
patterns.cause: When pip installed from a URL, it took the download filename from the Content-Disposition response header. That header can contain ../ sequences, so the saved file could land outside the intended download location and overwrite files such as an SSH authorized_keys file. The sources place the flaw in _download_http_url in _internal/download.py. It was fixed in pip 19.2.
preconditions: A tool or installer is given a URL and downloads the file itself
The local filename is taken from the server-supplied Content-Disposition header
The header filename is joined to a destination directory without removing directory components
The process has write access to sensitive paths outside the download directory
patterns.prevention: Treat the filename from a Content-Disposition header as untrusted input. Reduce it to a bare file name with no directory parts or ../ sequences before building the destination path. Then resolve the final path, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it still lies inside the intended download directory, rejecting the download otherwise. Upgrade pip to version 19.2 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so the checks above are general hardening direction rather than a description of that change. They also do not cover other filename sources, such as the URL path, or other attack vectors. Platform-specific separators and encodings are not discussed.

fixtures.scenario: A user runs an install command with a URL. The server replies with a Content-Disposition filename containing ../ segments. The client joins it to the download directory unchecked and writes outside it, overwriting a file in the home directory.

The same server reply arrives, but the client keeps only the final name component and confirms the resolved path stays inside the download directory. The file is saved safely there, or the download is rejected.

citations.quote: a Content-Disposition header can have ../ in a filename, as demonstrated by overwriting the /root/.ssh/authorized_keys file
This occurs in _download_http_url in _internal/download.py.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that parses the Content-Disposition header and reduces its filename to the final path component with a basename operation. It falls back to the URL-derived default name when the result is empty, and _download_http_url now uses this helper. The card's cause and its main prevention step (strip directory parts from the header filename) match. The extra resolved-path containment check it suggests goes beyond the patch but does not contradict it.

patterns.title: Ansible fetch module writes outside the destination when an absolute path is not restricted
patterns.cause: The helper that expands a tilde path on the remote host trusted the home directory text returned by the remote host. It did not reject parent-directory components in the result. A malicious or compromised managed host could return a home directory with relative traversal, and modules such as fetch then built file paths from it that escaped the intended location, so files could be written or overwritten outside the intended destination on the controller.
preconditions: The controller runs an Ansible version before 2.5.15, 2.6.14 or 2.7.8 (depending on the release line).
A task uses a module such as fetch, whose action plugin expands a tilde path by running a command on the remote host.
The remote host is untrusted or compromised and returns a home directory path containing parent-directory components.
The expanded path is used without further validation to build a file location.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Ansible 2.5.15, 2.6.14, 2.7.8 or later. In similar code, treat any path text produced by a remote host as untrusted input. After expanding it, reject results whose directory part contains parent-directory components, and where possible normalize the final path and confirm it stays inside the intended base directory before reading or writing.
patterns.limitations: The check only looks at the directory portion of the expanded path for parent-directory segments. It does not cover other ways a remote value could redirect a local write, such as a crafted source path or symlinks. The diff does not show any change inside the fetch module itself.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook on an affected Ansible version runs the fetch module with a specified local destination directory. The path in use is absolute and unrestricted, so the file is written to a location outside that directory on the controller host and overwrites an existing file there.

The controller runs a fixed release, or the fetch logic restricts absolute paths. The file is written only inside the specified destination directory, and a path that would resolve outside it is rejected or confined.

citations.quote: Ansible fetch module before versions 2.5.15, 2.6.14, 2.7.8 has a path traversal vulnerability
allows copying and overwriting files outside of the specified destination in the local ansible controller host, by not restricting an absolute path.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the remote tilde-expansion helper of the action base class. After the home directory is expanded, it raises an error if the directory portion contains a parent-directory component, so a malicious managed host cannot return a traversing home path. The card's cause and prevention both match this, and its note that the fetch module itself is unchanged is also correct.

patterns.title: SQL injection through the order_by parameter in SQLAlchemy before 1.3.0b3
patterns.cause: Before 1.3.0b3, SQLAlchemy accepted plain strings in many SQL construction positions and treated them as trusted raw SQL, emitting at most a warning. For order_by and group_by, a string that did not match any label or column was converted to literal text and placed into the statement unescaped. If an application passed user-controlled input there, an attacker could inject arbitrary SQL. Related spots such as filter, where, having, select_from, foreign key action keywords, the PostgreSQL index method and function names had the same unvalidated pass-through.
preconditions: The application runs SQLAlchemy 1.2.x or 1.3.0 beta releases before 1.3.0b3.
A string built from or influenced by external input is passed to order_by or group_by (for example a sort column name from a request).
The string does not match a label or column already present in the statement, so it falls through to raw text rendering.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a release that contains the fix (1.3.0b3 or later), where an unresolvable string in order_by or group_by raises a compile error and plain strings elsewhere raise an argument error unless explicitly wrapped as text. Regardless of version, never pass external input directly into order_by or group_by. Map user choices to an allowlist of known column objects or labels and build the ordering from those objects. Where raw text is truly needed, declare it explicitly with text() and only with trusted, fixed content.
patterns.limitations: The fix is a hardening change rather than a narrow patch, so applications that relied on implicit string-to-text conversion will now see errors and need code changes. It was not backported to the 1.2.x line, so that line stays exposed. Explicit text() or literal_column() with untrusted data remains the caller's responsibility and is still unsafe. The affected-version wording in the sources is inconsistent, so exact boundaries should be checked against release notes.

fixtures.scenario: A web service runs SQLAlchemy 1.2.x and builds a listing query whose order_by parameter is influenced by a request value chosen by the client. A crafted value could inject SQL, and no 1.2.x release has the fix.
The service runs SQLAlchemy 1.3.0b3 or later, which contains the upstream fix. Request values do not control the order_by parameter directly.

citations.quote: SQLAlchemy through 1.2.17 and 1.3.x through 1.3.0b2 allows SQL Injection via the order_by parameter.
all 1.2.x versions remain vulnerable.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops treating plain strings as trusted SQL. An unresolvable label string in ORDER BY or GROUP BY now raises a compile error, and plain strings in filter, where, having, select_from and similar positions raise an argument error unless explicitly declared as text. It also validates foreign key action phrases and the PostgreSQL index method against strict patterns, and quotes unusual function names. This matches the card's cause, prevention and listed related spots.

patterns.title: Archive member names must be sanitized when extracting ansible-galaxy collection tarballs
patterns.cause: When ansible-galaxy installs a collection from a .tar.gz file, it creates a directory from a name stored in the archive without sanitizing that name. A crafted archive can therefore make the extraction step write outside the intended location.
preconditions: ansible-engine 2.9.x prior to 2.9.7 is in use
A collection is installed with the ansible-galaxy collection install command
The collection .tar.gz file is attacker-controlled or comes from an untrusted source
patterns.prevention: Treat every filename inside an archive as untrusted input. Before creating a directory or file for an archive member, sanitize the name and confirm that the final destination stays inside the intended extraction directory. Reject or skip members whose names would escape it. Upgrading to ansible-engine 2.9.7 or later is the vendor-side remedy implied by the affected version range.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a brief description. They do not say which sanitization method the fix uses, whether other member types such as links are affected, or which platforms are affected. The advice to confirm the destination stays inside the extraction directory is a general direction, not a description of the upstream change. Versions outside the 2.9.x range are not addressed.

fixtures.scenario: An installer on an affected 2.9.x version is given a collection tarball whose member names contain parent-directory components. It creates the directory from the unsanitized name, so extraction writes outside the collection install path and can overwrite an existing file on the system.

An installer sanitizes each member name and checks that the destination stays inside the collection install directory. When given the same tarball, it rejects the offending members and leaves files outside the install path untouched.

citations.quote: When extracting a collection .tar.gz file, the directory is created without sanitizing the filename.
An attacker could take advantage to overwrite any file within the system.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the tar extraction helper so the destination path is normalized to an absolute path and its parent directory must lie inside the collection install directory. Otherwise an error is raised and the entry is not extracted. The install routine also removes the partly created collection directory when any error occurs. The card's cause (archive member names used unsanitized to build paths) and its prevention (confirm the final destination stays inside the extraction directory and reject escaping members) match this.

patterns.title: Stored XSS in the Wagtail admin page revision comparison view
patterns.cause: The Wagtail admin revision comparison view displays StreamField block content by rendering each block to HTML and inserting that into the page without escaping. This applies to blocks that were changed, added or removed between revisions. An editor can store script in a block value such as a text, raw HTML or rich text block, and it runs in the browser of a higher-privileged user who opens the comparison. Text blocks and raw HTML blocks had no dedicated comparison handling, which left their values unescaped.
preconditions: The attacker has an editor account that can save page revisions containing StreamField content.
The page model uses a StreamField with text, raw HTML, rich text or similar blocks that the comparison view renders.
A user with higher privileges opens the revision comparison view for a revision pair containing the crafted block content.
The deployment runs Wagtail before 2.7.2 on the 2.7 branch or before 2.8.1 on the 2.8 branch.
patterns.prevention: In comparison views, never insert a block's rendered HTML directly. Escape the values of plain text and raw HTML blocks so any markup is shown as visible text. For rich text and other blocks, extract only the text content from the rendered output, then escape it for display, and build the diff from that text. Apply this to every path: changed blocks, added blocks and deleted blocks. Upgrade to Wagtail 2.7.2 or 2.8.1. As a stopgap, the advisory suggests disabling the comparison view by redirecting its URL to the admin home page.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the comparison view in the admin. Custom blocks that define their own comparison class are outside this change and must escape their own output. Rich text comparison now shows text only, so formatting differences are no longer visible. The redirect workaround disables the view and does not fix the underlying rendering.

fixtures.scenario: A low-privilege editor saves a page revision whose content includes script-bearing markup. A superuser later opens the comparison view for that page on Wagtail 2.8.0, and the script runs with the superuser's credentials.

The same editor saves the same revision, but the site runs Wagtail 2.8.1 or 2.7.2, or the comparison route is redirected to the admin home page. When the superuser views the comparison, no attacker script runs and the content cannot act with the superuser's credentials.

citations.quote: A cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability exists on the page revision comparison view within the Wagtail admin interface.
could potentially craft a page revision history that, when viewed by a user with higher privileges, could perform actions with that user's credentials.
The vulnerability is not exploitable by an ordinary site visitor without access to the Wagtail admin.
Patched versions have been released as Wagtail 2.7.2 (for the LTS 2.7 branch) and Wagtail 2.8.1 (for the current 2.8 branch).

patch_review.observation: The fix stops the comparison view from inserting a block's rendered HTML directly. Plain text, char and raw HTML blocks now use the character comparison class, which escapes values for changed, added and deleted blocks. The base block comparison and rich text blocks now extract text from the rendered HTML and escape it. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Command injection in an example DAG shipped with Apache Airflow
patterns.cause: The bundled example_trigger_target_dag in Apache Airflow 1.10.10 and below used a BashOperator whose command text embedded the message field of the DAG run configuration through a Jinja template. That value can be supplied by a user who triggers a run from the web UI. BashOperator does no escaping, so the rendered text was parsed by the shell and a crafted message could run arbitrary commands as the worker user.
preconditions: Apache Airflow 1.10.10 or below is deployed with the example DAGs loaded, which is the default.
The attacker is an authenticated user who can trigger a DAG run and supply its configuration.
The command text of a BashOperator task interpolates a value from the DAG run configuration through a template.
patterns.prevention: Never render user-controlled values, such as DAG run configuration, directly into BashOperator command text. Pass them through the operator's environment dictionary and reference them as shell variables inside double quotes, so the shell treats them as data and not as syntax. Upgrade to a release that contains the corrected example DAG and the documentation warning, and disable example DAG loading on deployments that serve real users.
patterns.limitations: The fix only corrects the example DAG and adds documentation. The BashOperator itself still performs no escaping, so custom DAGs that template user-influenced values into command text remain exposed. Quoting inside the command is fragile, and the environment variable approach depends on the command using the variable safely, for example inside double quotes.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 1.10.10 deployment keeps example loading enabled. An authenticated low-privilege user triggers the vulnerable example DAG and gets arbitrary commands executed as the worker or scheduler user.

An Airflow deployment has example loading disabled in its configuration, or runs a release newer than 1.10.10. The vulnerable example DAG is not available, so an authenticated user cannot use it to run commands.

citations.quote: A remote code/command injection vulnerability was discovered in one of the example DAGs shipped with Airflow
would allow any authenticated user to run arbitrary commands as the user running airflow worker/scheduler

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the example trigger target DAG so the user-supplied message from the DAG run configuration is no longer rendered into the shell command text. It is passed through the operator's environment dictionary and read as a shell variable inside double quotes. The fix also adds a docstring warning to the bash operator that it does no escaping or sanitization, and that DAG run configuration submitted through the web UI is the main risk.

patterns.title: Command injection through a directly reachable Celery broker in Apache Airflow
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow 1.10.10 and below, the Celery worker task that executes commands took the command list from the broker message and passed it to a subprocess without checking what it was. Validation, if any, happened only on the sending side. Anyone able to publish to the broker (Redis or RabbitMQ) could therefore enqueue an arbitrary command and have the worker run it.
preconditions: Apache Airflow 1.10.10 or below is deployed.
The deployment uses CeleryExecutor, where workers execute commands received from a message broker.
An attacker can publish messages to the broker directly, for example because it is reachable without authentication or with weak credentials.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a release that includes the fix, which validates the command on the receiving side. The worker's execution task and the other executors must refuse any command that does not begin with the airflow tasks run subcommand, and raise an error before starting any subprocess. Treat all broker content as untrusted and enforce an allowlist at the point of execution, not only where tasks are queued. As defense in depth, restrict network access to the broker and require authentication.
patterns.limitations: The allowlist only limits which airflow subcommand is run. It does not stop an attacker who can publish to the broker from triggering arbitrary task runs or passing unexpected arguments to the permitted subcommand. Broker access control is still needed. The exact first fixed release is not stated in the diff.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 1.10.10 deployment uses CeleryExecutor with a Redis broker that other hosts on the network can reach. An attacker connects to the broker directly and injects a command, and a Celery worker runs it.
An Airflow deployment runs a release newer than 1.10.10. Its broker accepts connections only from the scheduler and worker hosts, so an outside party cannot connect to the broker to inject commands.

citations.quote: When using CeleryExecutor, if an attacker can connect to the broker (Redis, RabbitMQ) directly, it is possible to inject commands
resulting in the celery worker running arbitrary commands.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds receiving-side validation in the Celery worker's execute_command task, which now raises an error before any subprocess runs unless the command begins with the airflow tasks run subcommand. The Dask, Local and Sequential executors get the same check, and the Kubernetes executor only requires the first element to be the airflow program. The second diff, an output-escaping change in the web UI paging, is a separate XSS fix and does not bear on this CVE.

patterns.title: Celery worker deserializes malicious broker payloads in Apache Airflow CeleryExecutor (CVE-2020-11982)
patterns.cause: The default Celery configuration shipped with Airflow let workers accept both json and pickle as message content types. Pickle deserialization can run arbitrary code, so anyone able to put a crafted message into the broker could get code executed on a worker.
preconditions: Apache Airflow 1.10.10 or earlier using CeleryExecutor with the default Celery configuration
The worker accepts pickle as a content type
An attacker can write messages directly to the broker, for example an exposed or unauthenticated Redis or RabbitMQ instance
patterns.prevention: Restrict the Celery accepted content types so workers only deserialize json, and never allow pickle for data that crosses a broker. Upgrade to an Airflow release that ships this safer default, and check any custom Celery configuration that overrides it. As defense in depth, require authentication on the broker and limit network access to trusted Airflow components.
patterns.limitations: The fix changes only the shipped default, so deployments with a custom Celery configuration that still permits pickle remain vulnerable. Restricting content types does not protect against an attacker who can already submit legitimate json tasks through the broker. Broker authentication and network controls reduce exposure but do not replace the safer serializer setting.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 1.10.10 deployment uses CeleryExecutor with a Redis broker reachable by an attacker. The attacker inserts a crafted payload into the broker and the worker deserializes it, which leads to code execution.

A patched Airflow deployment uses CeleryExecutor with a broker reachable only by trusted Airflow components. Workers do not deserialize arbitrary payloads, so a crafted broker message is not executed.

citations.quote: Insecure default config of Celery worker in Apache Airflow
if an attack can connect to the broker (Redis, RabbitMQ) directly, it was possible to insert a malicious payload directly to the broker

patch_review.observation: The relevant change in the second diff narrows the default Celery accepted content types from json plus pickle to json only. That removes pickle deserialization of broker messages by default, which is what the card describes. The other changes in the diffs (worker concurrency, broker and result backend URLs) are unrelated defaults and test setup.

patterns.title: Unencoded query parameters in Django admin ForeignKeyRawIdWidget enable XSS
patterns.cause: The Django admin ForeignKeyRawIdWidget generated query parameters that were not properly URL encoded. This created a possibility of cross-site scripting (CWE-79).
preconditions: The application runs Django 2.2 before 2.2.13 or Django 3.0 before 3.0.7.
The Django admin is used with a field rendered by ForeignKeyRawIdWidget, which generates query parameters.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 2.2.13, Django 3.0.7, or a later release, where the generated query parameters are properly URL encoded. In custom code that builds URLs or query strings, encode every parameter name and value with a standard URL-encoding routine at the point where the query string is assembled. Do not concatenate raw values into URLs that are rendered in pages.
patterns.limitations: The advisories give no detail on which inputs reach the widget, where the injection occurs, or how an attack would be carried out. They do not say whether Django versions outside the listed ranges are affected, or whether other widgets share the problem. This card therefore stays at the level of the stated cause and the fixed versions.

fixtures.scenario: An admin site runs Django 3.0.6 and a model form uses the raw ID widget for a foreign key. The widget builds query parameters that are not properly URL encoded, so the page is exposed to XSS.
The same admin site runs Django 3.0.7 or later. The query parameters generated by the raw ID widget are properly URL encoded, so the XSS exposure described in the advisory does not apply.

citations.quote: Query parameters generated by the Django admin ForeignKeyRawIdWidget were not properly URL encoded, leading to a possibility of an XSS attack.
An issue was discovered in Django 2.2 before 2.2.13 and 3.0 before 3.0.7.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the lookup link in ForeignKeyRawIdWidget so that the query string is built with the standard urlencode helper instead of joining raw keys and values by hand. It also drops the mark_safe call on the resulting URL, so template autoescaping applies. A new test uses a limit_choices_to value containing quote, ampersand and angle-bracket characters and expects them to be percent-encoded.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS through the origin parameter on Airflow endpoints such as /trigger
patterns.cause: Several Airflow web views took the origin parameter straight from the request and used it as a return link, for example in the cancel button of the trigger form, without checking what it contained. An attacker could supply a value with a script scheme or an external address, which then ran in the victim's browser or sent them off-site when rendered or followed. This is reflected cross-site scripting through an unvalidated URL.
preconditions: Apache Airflow earlier than 1.10.12 is deployed.
A view such as trigger, clear, run, delete, failed or success reads an origin value from the request.
The origin value is placed into the response, for example in a button handler or redirect target, without validation.
A victim can be lured into opening a crafted link or submitting a crafted form.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 1.10.12 or later. In your own code, never reuse a request-supplied return URL directly. Parse it and allow only web schemes (http, https, or none) with a host that is the current server or empty, and fall back to a known safe page such as the home page otherwise. Apply this check consistently in every handler that accepts such a parameter, rather than only the one reported.
patterns.limitations: The fix is an allowlist on scheme and host for the return URL, not general output encoding. Relative paths on the same host are passed through unchanged. Other parameters that are rendered into pages need their own escaping or validation.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment running a version earlier than 1.10.12 receives a request to the /trigger endpoint. The origin parameter holds attacker-chosen content instead of a normal return location.
The same request is sent to a deployment running Airflow 1.10.12 or later, where the origin parameter is no longer reported as vulnerable to XSS.

citations.quote: In Apache Airflow < 1.10.12
was vulnerable to XSS exploit.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that parses the user-supplied origin value and accepts it only if the scheme is http, https or empty and the host is the current server or empty. Otherwise it falls back to the Airflow home page. The helper is applied to the origin handling in the run, delete, trigger, clear, dagrun clear, dagrun failed, dagrun success, failed and success views, and a test checks that script and external URLs are replaced in the trigger form's cancel button.

patterns.title: Unescaped form field help text in Wagtail form pages enables editor-driven XSS
patterns.cause: When a form page type is exposed to editors through the wagtail.contrib.forms app and its template uses Django's standard form rendering helpers such as form.as_p, HTML tags in a form field's help text are rendered unescaped. Django allows this by design, but Wagtail policy does not let editors insert arbitrary HTML, so editors could inject script, including for privilege escalation.
preconditions: A form page type is made available to editors through the wagtail.contrib.forms app.
The page template renders the form with Django's standard helpers such as form.as_p.
An editor can author the help text of form fields.
Wagtail version is before 2.7.4 on the 2.7 branch or before 2.9.3 on the 2.9 branch.
patterns.prevention: Treat editor-authored help text as untrusted and escape it on output so HTML tags are not interpreted. Upgrade to Wagtail 2.7.4 or 2.9.3 or later, which escape help text by default. If an upgrade is not possible, render the form field by field in the template and do not apply the safe filter to the help text. Enable the opt-in setting that allows HTML in help text only if editors are fully trusted with that risk.
patterns.limitations: The sources say the flaw is not exploitable by ordinary visitors without Wagtail admin access, so the threat is limited to editor-level users. They do not describe the exact code change in the fix. Sites that re-enable HTML in help text through the opt-in setting accept the risk again. Behavior in other releases is not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A site uses an older Wagtail with a form page whose template calls form.as_p. An editor puts a script tag in a field's help text. Visitors, including administrators, load the page and the markup is output unescaped.
The site runs a patched Wagtail release, or renders fields one by one without the safe filter on help text. The same script tag appears as visible escaped text and is not executed by the browser.

citations.quote: any HTML tags used within a form field's help text will be rendered unescaped in the page.
In these versions, help text will be escaped to prevent the inclusion of HTML tags.
as a matter of policy Wagtail does not allow editors to insert arbitrary HTML by default
omitting the |safe filter when outputting the help text.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the form builder's field option generation so a form field's help text is passed through conditional escaping by default, which stops editor-entered HTML from being rendered. An opt-in Django setting restores the old unescaped behavior for sites that trust their editors, and tests cover both modes. This matches the card's cause (unescaped help text in form pages) and its prevention (escape by default, with an opt-in to allow HTML).

patterns.title: Stored XSS through SVG attachments uploaded to a MoinMoin wiki
patterns.cause: MoinMoin before 1.9.11 did not treat SVG as an active-content type. Its default XSS-protection list covered HTML, Flash and XHTML but not image/svg+xml. An uploaded SVG attachment containing script could therefore be served inline with its original type, and the script ran in the wiki origin for any viewer.
preconditions: The wiki runs MoinMoin before 1.9.11 with the default XSS-protection mimetype list, or a custom list that omits image/svg+xml.
The attacker can upload attachments, which requires write permission.
A victim opens the uploaded SVG attachment directly in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to MoinMoin 1.9.11 or later, which adds image/svg+xml to the default list of mimetypes protected against XSS, so the attachment is not rendered inline in the wiki origin. If the wiki uses a custom list for this option, add the SVG mimetype to it by hand. Treat any user-supplied SVG as executable content: serve it as a forced download or from a separate origin, and restrict upload rights to trusted users.
patterns.limitations: The fix is a configuration default, so wikis that override the XSS-protection mimetype list keep the flaw until they update their own list. It covers only mimetypes on that list, so other active-content types would need their own entries. This review looked only at the two configuration changes in the diff, so the exact serving behaviour for protected types is not confirmed here.

fixtures.scenario: A wiki runs a MoinMoin version older than 1.9.11 and gives write access to many contributors. One contributor uploads an SVG attachment containing javascript. When another user opens that SVG on the wiki, the script runs in their browser.

The wiki is upgraded to MoinMoin 1.9.11 or later, and write permissions are limited to trusted users. An SVG attachment containing javascript is no longer exploitable against viewers, and a Content Security Policy in the web server adds a further layer.

citations.quote: In MoinMoin before version 1.9.11, an attacker with write permissions can upload an SVG file that contains malicious javascript.
This javascript will be executed in a user's browser when the user is viewing that SVG file on the wiki.
a work around via a Content Security Policy in the web server might be possible.
MoinMoin Wiki 1.9.11 has the necessary fixes and also contains other important fixes.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds the SVG mimetype to the default list of mimetypes that are protected against XSS, so SVG attachments are no longer served inline in the wiki origin. It also adds SVG to the list of image types the browser is treated as supporting, which keeps SVG usable as an image. The card's cause and prevention match the main change.

patterns.title: Unescaped Ansible facts reaching the pipe lookup plugin shell command
patterns.cause: The pipe lookup plugin runs its command through the subprocess Popen call with the shell option enabled. If a variable placed in that command is not escaped by the quote plugin, an attacker who can overwrite ansible facts can control what the shell executes. This is OS command injection (CWE-78).
preconditions: A playbook or template uses the pipe lookup plugin.
The command string given to the plugin includes a variable or fact value.
That variable is not escaped by the quote plugin.
An attacker is able to overwrite the ansible facts that supply the value.
patterns.prevention: Treat every fact or variable that reaches the pipe lookup command as untrusted data. Escape each interpolated value with the quote plugin before the command string is built, so the shell reads it as one literal argument and not as shell syntax. Where possible, avoid building shell command strings from variable data at all. Review existing uses of the pipe lookup plugin and check that each interpolated value is escaped. Also upgrade to an ansible release that contains the fixes referenced for this CVE.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how facts get overwritten in practice, which ansible versions are affected, or what the upstream change does internally. The advice above is a direction drawn from the stated cause (a missing quote escape with the shell enabled), not a description of the upstream fix. Escaping with the quote plugin may not cover every other plugin or module that handles untrusted facts, and the sources do not address those.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook uses the pipe lookup plugin with a command that embeds a fact value directly and does not pass it through the quote plugin. An attacker overwrites that fact with text containing shell metacharacters and a second command. The shell runs the injected command on the controller.

A playbook uses the pipe lookup plugin, and every fact or variable in the command string is first escaped with the quote plugin. When an attacker overwrites the fact with shell metacharacters, the shell treats the whole value as one literal argument and no extra command runs.

citations.quote: A flaw was found in the pipe lookup plugin of ansible.
the variable is not escaped by quote plugin
An attacker could take advantage and run arbitrary commands by overwriting the ansible facts.

patch_review.observation: The upstream change only updates documentation and examples for the pipe lookup plugin. It states that the plugin intentionally runs its command through a shell, warns that unsanitized user or variable input is a security risk, and recommends passing such input through the quote filter, with the example updated to match. This is the same cause (shell enabled, unescaped values) and the same prevention (escape with the quote filter) that the card describes.

patterns.title: Fetch module lets an intercepted or injected path choose the destination on the controller
patterns.cause: When the Ansible Engine fetch module is used, an attacker who intercepts the module can inject a new path and choose a new destination path on the controller node. The advisory text does not say which value is trusted wrongly, so the exact mechanism is not described in the sources.
preconditions: The fetch module is used to copy files from a managed host to the controller node.
An attacker is able to intercept the module and inject a new path.
The Ansible Engine version is in the 2.7.x, 2.8.x or 2.9.x branches, which are believed to be vulnerable.
patterns.prevention: Do not let a path that comes back from the module or the remote side decide where a file is written on the controller. Derive the controller destination from values the controller itself controls. Before writing, resolve the final destination to its canonical form and confirm it stays inside the intended destination directory, rejecting anything that falls outside. Also move to an Ansible release that includes the upstream fix for CVE-2020-1735.
patterns.limitations: The sources are short and do not describe the vulnerable code path, the exact injected field, the fixed versions, or the upstream fix. The prevention direction here is general path-confinement guidance and is not a description of the actual patch. The sources also do not say how an attacker gains the ability to intercept the module.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook runs the fetch module against a managed host. An attacker who intercepts the module injects a new path, and the file is written to a destination of the attacker's choosing on the controller node, outside the directory the playbook author intended.

A playbook runs the fetch module and the controller computes the destination from its own configured destination directory. It resolves the final path and refuses to write if the result is outside that directory, so an injected path cannot redirect the file.

citations.quote: An attacker could intercept the module, inject a new path, and then choose a new destination path on the controller node.
All versions in 2.7.x, 2.8.x and 2.9.x branches are believed to be vulnerable.

patterns.title: Zip extraction in win_unzip writing outside the destination folder
patterns.cause: The Extract-Zip function in the Ansible win_unzip module joined each archive entry name onto the destination folder without normalizing the result or checking containment. Entry names containing relative parent-directory segments could therefore resolve to locations outside the destination, and the module would create directories and write files there.
preconditions: Ansible 2.7.17 and prior, 2.8.9 and prior, or 2.9.6 and prior is in use.
A zip archive is extracted on a Windows host with the win_unzip module.
The archive is attacker-crafted and contains entry names with relative parent-directory segments that resolve outside the destination.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a release containing the fix. In extraction code, combine the destination with each entry name, convert the result to a full normalized path, and compare it with the full normalized destination path that ends with a directory separator. If the target does not begin with the destination prefix, fail the operation instead of writing. Do this before creating directories or files, and treat entry names as untrusted input.
patterns.limitations: The check is a prefix comparison on normalized paths, so it depends on correct normalization and on the separator being appended to the destination, and a case-sensitive comparison may behave differently from the file system. It covers zip extraction in win_unzip only and does not address other archive formats or modules.
