fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user sends the S3 API an XML document containing an external entity declaration that points to a local file on the Swift host, and the service returns that file content in its response.
The same authenticated user sends the same crafted XML to a patched Swift release, and the service does not resolve the external entity, so no host file contents are returned.

citations.quote: By supplying crafted XML files, an authenticated user may coerce the S3 API into returning arbitrary file contents from the host server
This impacts both s3api deployments (Rocky or later), and swift3 deployments (Queens and earlier, no longer actively developed).
An issue was discovered in OpenStack Swift before 2.28.1, 2.29.x before 2.29.2, and 2.30.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the shared lxml-based XML parser in the s3api etree module so it no longer expands entities and no longer fetches resources over the network. Tests send a document type declaration with an external entity pointing at a local file in several S3 operations (multi-delete, bucket ACL, bucket creation, versioning, multipart completion) and check that file contents never appear in responses. This matches the card's description of XXE leading to host file disclosure and its direction of not letting client XML resolve external resources.

patterns.title: Stored cross-site scripting in pyload-ng before 0.5.0b3.dev42
patterns.cause: The web UI package view in pyload-ng builds HTML strings in browser-side scripts and inserts stored link data, such as the link URL and name, directly into an anchor element's href and text without validation or encoding. An attacker who can add a package or link with a script-scheme URL or markup in the fields gets script execution in another user's session when that user opens the package and clicks the link.
preconditions: The deployment runs pyload-ng earlier than 0.5.0b3.dev42 with the modern or pyplex theme.
An attacker can add a package or link whose URL or name contains attacker-controlled content, and the application stores it.
A victim opens the package list and activates the rendered link, so the stored URL is used for navigation.
patterns.prevention: Never place stored link fields into HTML by string concatenation. Build elements with safe DOM APIs or HTML-encode the name and URL, and only allow safe URL schemes such as http and https for href values. The upstream change adds a click handler on the link that cancels default navigation in both themes, which stops a script-scheme URL from running on click. Upgrade to 0.5.0b3.dev42 or later.
patterns.limitations: The upstream patch only blocks the click navigation path in the package link list for two themes. It does not encode the name, error or other concatenated fields, so other injection points in the same templates may remain. The card relies on the diff alone and does not confirm which attacker privileges are needed to create the stored entry.

fixtures.scenario: A pyload-ng instance runs a release older than 0.5.0b3.dev42 and is therefore within the affected range for the stored XSS issue.
A pyload-ng instance runs version 0.5.0b3.dev42 or newer, outside the affected range named in the advisories.

citations.quote: Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Stored in GitHub repository pyload/pyload prior to 0.5.0b3.dev42.
Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Stored in GitHub repository pyload/pyload prior to 0.5.0b3.dev42.

patch_review.observation: The fix touches the package link rendering in the modern and pyplex themes. It adds an inline click handler on the generated anchor that cancels default navigation, so a stored script-scheme URL no longer runs when the link is clicked. Encoding of the name and URL is not changed, which the card's limitations section already states.

patterns.title: Remote file existence check via absolute path traversal in mlflow server and mlflow ui
patterns.cause: The file-based model registry store uses the caller-supplied registered model name as a path component under its storage root. Name validation did not reject path separators, so a remote caller could pass an absolute path as the model name. The store then resolved a location outside its own data directory, and the response revealed whether that path existed (CWE-36).
preconditions: The MLflow server or UI runs a version older than the patched release.
The Model Registry uses the file-based store backend, which maps model names to directories.
Remote callers can reach the registry endpoints without authentication or network restriction.
patterns.prevention: Validate registered model names in the file store and reject any name containing the platform path separator or the alternate separator, so a name can never be treated as a path. Apply this check on every entry point that turns a model name into a filesystem location, including lookups of existing models. Also upgrade to a patched MLflow release, and as defense in depth limit who can reach the server and scope its file and cloud credentials to MLflow data only.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the file-based registry store; other backends and other user-supplied identifiers that become path components need their own review. Separator rejection does not replace resolving the final path and confirming it stays under the storage root. Access restriction and credential scoping only reduce exposure and do not remove the flaw. The fixed version differs between sources, so choose the later one.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs mlflow server on an older version with the Model Registry reachable by any host on a broad network. There is no authentication, and the server uses cloud credentials that can read many buckets. A remote caller can learn whether arbitrary local or remote files exist.

The team runs a patched MLflow release, places the server behind a VPC with an IP allowlist and authentication middleware, and scopes the server's cloud credentials to MLflow artifact locations only. Unrelated files cannot be probed by outsiders.

citations.quote: enables an actor to check the existence of arbitrary files unrelated to MLflow from the host server
Absolute Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.2.2.
This vulnerability has been patched in MLflow 2.2.1, which was released to PyPI on March 2nd, 2023.
restrict the scope of your server's cloud credentials such that it can only access files and directories related to MLflow

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a file-store-specific model name check that runs the original validation and then rejects any name containing the platform path separator or the alternate separator, using a new helper in the file utilities. Because the wrapper replaces the imported validator inside the file store, every entry point that maps a name to a path is covered. The added test confirms that looking up a model by an absolute path name now fails with an invalid-name error.

patterns.title: Path traversal in MLflow server and UI lets remote callers read files outside MLflow storage
patterns.cause: In MLflow versions before 2.2.1, the server handlers for downloading and uploading artifacts through the mlflow-artifacts endpoints were meant to validate the caller-supplied artifact path. A coding mistake passed the validator function itself as its own argument instead of the path, so the check never inspected the request path. Traversal sequences, including backslash-style ones, therefore reached the artifact repository, letting a remote caller read (and potentially write) files outside the intended artifact root.
preconditions: The deployment runs the mlflow server or mlflow ui command with an MLflow version older than 2.2.1.
The artifact serving endpoints for downloading or uploading artifacts are reachable by the caller.
Untrusted parties can reach the server because there is no VPC, IP allowlist, or authentication or authorization middleware.
The server process can access files beyond MLflow data, such as local host files or remote storage reachable with its credentials.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to MLflow 2.2.1 or later, where both artifact handlers pass the request's artifact path to the path safety validator. When writing validation code, make sure the check is applied to the untrusted input itself, and add tests that send traversal payloads, including backslash and encoded forms, to every handler that accepts a path. Until upgrading, limit who can reach the server with a VPC, an IP allowlist, or authentication and authorization middleware, and scope the server's storage credentials to MLflow-related locations only.
patterns.limitations: The fix only corrects the argument passed to the existing validator in the download and upload handlers. How robust the validator is against all traversal encodings is not shown in this diff. Network restrictions and credential scoping reduce exposure but do not remove the flaw in unpatched versions. Integrations that do not use mlflow server or mlflow ui, such as Databricks Managed MLflow and MLflow on Azure Machine Learning, are reported as unaffected.

fixtures.scenario: An MLflow 2.2.0 instance started with mlflow server is exposed to a wide network with no authentication. A remote caller sends a request whose path value uses backslash and two-dot traversal elements to name a file outside MLflow storage, and the server returns that file.

The same deployment runs MLflow 2.2.1 or later. The server sits inside a VPC with an inbound IP allowlist and uses cloud credentials scoped to MLflow artifact locations only, so a traversal-style request cannot reach unrelated files.

citations.quote: enables an actor to download arbitrary files unrelated to MLflow from the host server, including any files stored in remote locations
Path Traversal: '\..\filename' in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.2.1.
This vulnerability has been patched in MLflow 2.2.1, which was released to PyPI on March 2nd, 2023.
limiting who can access your MLflow Model Registry and MLflow Tracking servers using a cloud VPC, an IP allowlist for inbound requests

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the artifact download and upload handlers in the server so the safety validator receives the caller-supplied artifact path. Before, each handler passed the validator function to itself, so the request path was never checked. This matches the card's cause and its prevention of upgrading and validating the untrusted input directly.

patterns.title: Command injection from improper neutralization in Apache Airflow and the Airflow MySQL Provider
patterns.cause: The MySQL hook read the local file loading setting from the connection extra field, for both the mysqlclient driver and the mysql-connector driver. Anyone able to create or edit a connection, or supply connection settings, could therefore turn on the LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE capability for a MySQL connection. That let a malicious or compromised server read files from the Airflow host. The feature was controlled by untrusted configuration data instead of by trusted code.
preconditions: The deployment runs Apache Airflow before 2.5.1 or the Apache Airflow MySQL Provider before 4.0.0.
An attacker can create or modify a MySQL connection, or influence its extra settings, or can make a task connect to a MySQL server they control.
The connection extra enables local file loading, or the attacker is able to add that setting.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Airflow 2.5.1 or later and the MySQL Provider 4.0.0 or later. In the fixed design the local file loading feature is off by default and is no longer read from connection extras. It is enabled only through an explicit hook parameter, which the transfer operators set only when bulk load is requested. Also restrict who can edit connections, and do not enable local file loading on connections to servers that are not fully trusted.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the MySQL hook and the Hive and Vertica transfer operators shown in the diff. Existing DAGs that relied on the connection extra setting for bulk loading must now pass the hook parameter or use an operator that does. Other code that builds commands from untrusted input is outside the scope of this change.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs Apache Airflow 2.5.0 together with an Apache Airflow MySQL Provider release older than 4.0.0, so both components fall in the affected ranges.
A deployment runs Apache Airflow 2.5.1 or later together with the Apache Airflow MySQL Provider 4.0.0 or later, so neither component is in an affected range.

citations.quote: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in a Command ('Command Injection') vulnerability in Apache Software Foundation Apache Airflow
This issue affects Apache Airflow: before 2.5.1; Apache Airflow MySQL Provider: before 4.0.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops the MySQL hook from reading the local file loading setting out of connection extras for both the mysqlclient and mysql-connector drivers. Local file loading is now off by default and is enabled only by an explicit hook parameter, which the Hive-to-MySQL and Vertica-to-MySQL operators set only when bulk load is requested. This matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Path traversal through the run_id parameter in Apache Airflow before 2.6.3
patterns.cause: Airflow accepted arbitrary user-supplied run_id values when a DAG run was triggered. Characters such as path separators were only met with a deprecation warning and were still allowed. A crafted run_id could therefore carry path-like content into places that use the run identifier, enabling path traversal. The missing control was input validation of run_id against a strict allowlist.
preconditions: The deployment runs apache-airflow in a version before 2.6.3.
The attacker is an authenticated user who is allowed to trigger DAG runs.
The attacker can choose the run_id when triggering a run, for example through the trigger form or an equivalent request.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to 2.6.3 or later. The fix validates user-provided run_id values against a configurable allowlist pattern, and the default pattern allows only letters, digits and a small set of safe punctuation characters. The check runs in the trigger view, in DAG run creation and in a model-level validator, and invalid values are rejected. Internally generated run IDs for scheduled, manual and dataset-triggered runs are matched by a separate built-in format so they keep working. In general, validate identifiers that may reach file paths with a strict allowlist at every entry point, and do not loosen the configured pattern to allow path separators.
patterns.limitations: The diff does not show which file operation consumed the run_id, so the exact impact of the traversal is not confirmed here. The validation applies to newly created runs and does not clean up run IDs that already exist. An administrator who sets a permissive custom pattern can weaken the protection, because the configured pattern is accepted as an alternative to the default.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user submits a run_id value crafted to point outside the directory the application intends to use. The application is an Airflow release before 2.6.3, and the resulting file access lands outside the intended directory structure.
The same authenticated user submits the same crafted run_id to an Airflow 2.6.3 or later deployment. Access derived from run_id remains confined to the intended directory structure.

citations.quote: allows an attacker to perform unauthorized file access outside the intended directory structure by manipulating the run_id parameter
it requires an authenticated user to exploit it
It is recommended to upgrade to a version that is not affected

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a configurable allowlist pattern for user-supplied run IDs, with a default that permits only letters, digits and a few safe punctuation characters. It replaces the old warning about forward slashes with a hard rejection in the trigger view, in DAG run creation and in a model-level validator on the run_id field. Internally generated run IDs for scheduled, manual and dataset-triggered runs are matched by a separate built-in format so they are not affected.

patterns.title: Relative path traversal in mlflow versions prior to 2.3.1
patterns.cause: When creating a model version, the tracking server accepted a user-supplied source URI that was not local, such as http, https, ftp, object store, or mlflow-artifacts schemes, without checking its path for relative segments. A source containing parent-directory references could therefore be crafted to point outside the intended artifact location and reach local file system paths on the tracking server.
preconditions: The deployment runs an mlflow tracking server older than 2.3.1 with the model registry enabled.
An attacker can call the model version creation endpoint and control the source field.
The source uses a non-local scheme or path whose path component contains relative segments.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mlflow to version 2.3.1 or later. In general, validate the model version source on the server by taking the path component of the URI, normalizing it, and rejecting the request when the normalized path differs from the supplied one, so that relative segments cannot lead outside the intended artifact root. Apply this check to all source schemes, not only local paths.
patterns.limitations: The check compares the path to its normalized form and rejects any source with relative references, so legitimate sources that use such segments must be rewritten as absolute paths. It covers the model version creation source only, and other endpoints that take paths or URIs need their own validation. Encoded or unusual path forms may deserve extra review.

fixtures.scenario: An mlflow deployment older than 2.3.1 is exposed to untrusted users, and a path containing relative segments is supplied to it, which falls under the reported relative path traversal weakness.
The deployment runs mlflow 2.3.1 or later, so it is outside the affected range stated in the advisories.

citations.quote: Relative Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.3.1.
Relative path traversal in mlflow

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a validation step to the model version source check. It takes the path component of the source URI, resolves it to a canonical form, and rejects the request with an invalid-parameter error if the result differs from the supplied path, which blocks parent-directory references. The check runs for http, https, ftp, object store and mlflow-artifacts sources, and the new tests confirm that such sources with relative segments are refused while absolute ones are accepted.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through the watch URL field in changedetection.io
patterns.cause: The watch URL was accepted if it looked like a generic URL, with no check on its scheme. A value using a script scheme such as javascript: passed validation, was stored, and was later used as the link target for the watch on the main page. When a user clicked the link, the script ran in the application origin. Escaping the text for HTML does not stop this, because the dangerous part is the scheme of the link target, not markup characters.
preconditions: The application accepts a watch URL through the web form, quick add, edit page, or API without restricting its scheme.
The stored URL is used as the target of a link on the main page or other pages.
A victim with access to the interface clicks the link built from the attacker-supplied value.
The attacker can add or edit a watch, or can trick a user into adding one.
patterns.prevention: Enforce an allowlist of permitted URL schemes (web and file-transfer schemes only) and reject everything else, including script schemes. Apply it centrally and at every entry point: form validation, quick add, clone, edit, API creation, and the datastore add function. Handle prefixes that wrap another scheme, such as the source: prefix, by stripping them before the check so they cannot hide a script scheme, and trim whitespace before matching. Also check the scheme when building the link for display, and show a disabled placeholder if it is unsafe, so that previously stored bad values stay harmless. Make add paths report an error when a URL is refused instead of queuing a watch. Keep normal output encoding as defense in depth. Upgrade to a release containing the fix.
patterns.limitations: The allowlist still permits the file scheme by default, which depends on a separate setting that gates local file access. Operators can change the allowlist through configuration, which could weaken the protection. Existing stored watches are only protected by the display-time check. The affected version range differs between sources, so confirm the fixed release in the project notes.

fixtures.scenario: A user adds a new watch and enters a URL value containing a crafted script or HTML payload. The value is stored. When anyone opens the main page, the payload is rendered as active content and runs in their browser.

A user adds a new watch and enters the same crafted payload. The application rejects it as an invalid URL, or stores it and encodes it on output. The main page shows it as inert text and no script runs.

citations.quote: Changedetection.io before 0.40.2 was discovered to contain a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the main page.
execute arbitrary web scripts or HTML via a crafted payload injected into the URL parameter
Changedetection.io before v0.40.1.1 was discovered to contain a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the main page.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a central scheme allowlist check (http, https, ftp, file, overridable by an environment setting) that also strips the source: prefix and trims whitespace before matching. It is applied in form validation, the datastore add function, quick add, clone and the API, which now report an error instead of queuing a watch. The watch link property also returns a disabled placeholder for unsafe stored URLs, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Shell command injection through the terminal title helper in IPython on Windows without ctypes
patterns.cause: The IPython terminal title helper, set_term_title in IPython.utils.terminal, can let text passed as the title be run as shell commands. This happens on Windows when ctypes is unavailable. Untrusted text such as a directory name can then become commands executed with the privileges of the current process.
preconditions: The code runs on Windows in a Python environment where ctypes is not available.

set_term_title is called directly, for example by a tool that uses IPython as a library. The ipython binary itself does not reach the vulnerable code, because the ctypes dependency in IPython.utils._process_win32 blocks it.
Attacker-influenced text, such as a directory name the user is induced to enter, reaches the title argument.
An affected IPython release is installed.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade IPython to a patched release. Until then, make sure every call to set_term_title uses only trusted or filtered input. Do not pass attacker-influenced strings such as folder names, paths or user-supplied labels as the title. Library authors who call this helper should treat the title as untrusted data and must not rely on the ctypes dependency to make the vulnerable path unreachable.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch changes the code, so this card does not either. They also do not say exactly how the shell command is built. The advisories disagree on the fixed version: the CVE and PYSEC text say prior to 8.1.0, while the GitHub advisory says prior to 8.10.0. Check the installed version against the GitHub advisory. The sources do not say what filtering is sufficient. The impact is limited to the scope of the current process.

fixtures.scenario: A Windows tool built on IPython as a library runs in an environment without ctypes. It calls set_term_title with the current working directory, and an attacker has created a folder whose name contains shell command text. When the user changes into that folder, the text can run as commands.

The same tool runs on a patched IPython release, or it only calls set_term_title with a fixed trusted title or a value filtered against shell metacharacters. A folder name containing command text is not executed.

citations.quote: Should an attacker get untrusted input to an instance of this function they would be able to inject shell commands as current process
Users are only vulnerable when calling this function in Windows in a Python environment where
Users of ipython as a library are advised to upgrade.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the Windows fallback that built a shell command string from the title and ran it through the system shell when ctypes could not be imported. Windows now always imports ctypes and sets the console title through the Win32 API, so title text never reaches a shell. The card's cause, preconditions and upgrade-first prevention agree with this.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from URL payloads rendered as-is in hosted Streamlit apps
patterns.cause: In Streamlit 0.63.0 through 0.80.0, the 404 error responses from the custom component file route and the media file route echoed the requested URL path (and, for component read errors, the exception text) straight into the response body. Because the body was served as HTML, a crafted URL containing script content was reflected unescaped and ran in the victim's browser.
preconditions: The app runs a Streamlit version from 0.63.0 through 0.80.0 inclusive.
The server is reachable by other users over a network.
An attacker can craft a link to a component or media path that does not exist or cannot be read, with script content in the path.
A user is tricked into opening the crafted link in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Streamlit 0.81.0 or later. The fix returns fixed generic messages for not-found and read-error responses and logs the detailed path and exception on the server only. In custom handlers, never reflect request-controlled values such as paths or exception text into a response body. If a value must be shown, escape it for HTML and send a non-HTML content type for error text.
patterns.limitations: The fix only covers the error paths in the component file handler and the media file handler. Other places that reflect request data would need separate review. The advisory rates severity as moderate, with a maximum CVSSv3 base score of 5.9. Versions before 0.63.0 and after 0.80.0 are stated to need no action.

fixtures.scenario: A team hosts an internal dashboard on a Streamlit release between 0.63.0 and 0.80.0. An attacker sends a colleague a link to the dashboard with a Javascript payload in the URL. The colleague opens it and the server renders the payload as-is, so the script executes in the colleague's browser.

The same dashboard runs Streamlit 0.81.0 or later. The same crafted link is opened, but the patched version does not render the payload as executable script, so nothing runs in the colleague's browser.

citations.quote: An attacker could craft a malicious URL with Javascript payloads to a Streamlit app.
the server would render the malicious javascript payload as-is, leading to XSS.
Version 0.81.0 contains a patch for this vulnerability.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the 404 bodies in the component file handler and the media file route with fixed generic text (not found, read error) instead of echoing the requested path or the exception text. The detailed path and exception are now only logged on the server. This matches the card's cause (request-controlled data reflected into the response body) and its prevention.

patterns.title: Open redirect in Tornado 6.3.1 and earlier via a crafted URL
patterns.cause: The static file handler's path validation issues a permanent redirect that appends a trailing slash when a request maps to a directory. It built the redirect target from the raw request path without checking for two leading slashes. A path like that becomes a protocol-relative URL, so browsers treat the first segment as an external host and send the user to an attacker-chosen site.
preconditions: The application runs Tornado 6.3.1 or earlier and serves files through the static file handler.
The handler is configured so that the request path reaches validation with a prefix already trimmed by routing, and the path resolves to a directory without a trailing slash.
An attacker can craft a link whose path begins with two slashes followed by an external hostname, and a user is induced to open it.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Tornado 6.3.2 or later, which refuses to redirect any request path that starts with two slashes and returns a 403 error instead. As a general rule, when building a redirect from request path data, reject or normalize paths with multiple leading slashes so the result is always a same-site relative path. Also review custom handlers that redirect using the incoming path.
patterns.limitations: The behavior is only reachable under certain routing configurations of the static file handler, so not every Tornado application is exposed. The fix covers the trailing-slash redirect in that handler only. Other redirects built from user input in application code are not changed by it.

fixtures.scenario: An application on Tornado 6.3.1 receives a link with a crafted URL, sent by an attacker in a phishing message. A user opens it and is redirected to an attacker-chosen web site.

An application on a Tornado release newer than 6.3.1 receives the same crafted URL. Any redirect destination derived from request input is confirmed to be a trusted site, so the user is never sent to the attacker's site.

citations.quote: Open redirect vulnerability in Tornado versions 6.3.1 and earlier allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to redirect a user to an arbitrary web site
conduct a phishing attack by having user access a specially crafted URL.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the static file handler's path validation so that, when it would redirect a directory request to a trailing-slash URL, a request path starting with two slashes is rejected with a 403 error. Such a path would otherwise become a protocol-relative URL and cause an open redirect. The card describes this cause, the narrow configuration needed, and the fix direction correctly.

patterns.title: Stored XSS in Wagtail ModelAdmin parent chooser and document inspect views
patterns.cause: Two Wagtail ModelAdmin admin views displayed attacker-influenced page and document data without safe HTML escaping. The sources describe the workaround as patched HTML escaping, using plain-text breadcrumbs for pages and escaped link markup for documents. A low-privilege editor could store content that ran script when a higher-privileged admin opened these views.
preconditions: Wagtail ModelAdmin is enabled, with Wagtail from version 1.5 and before 4.1.4 or 4.2.2
For pages, ChooseParentView is reachable because pages are managed through ModelAdmin
For documents, the ModelAdmin InspectView is enabled and shows document fields
A limited-permission editor can create pages or documents that a higher-privileged user later views
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Wagtail 4.1.4 or 4.2.2 or later. If upgrade is not possible, disable ModelAdmin for page models, or use a custom ChooseParentView that shows page breadcrumbs as plain text. For documents, disable InspectView, exclude document fields from it, or use a custom view that builds document link markup with escaped values. Treat content written by editors as untrusted in every admin view.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the exact fields that carry the payload, nor describe the upstream fix in detail. They cover only ChooseParentView and InspectView, so other admin views are not assessed. Ordinary site visitors without admin access are stated as not affected. The workaround must be applied to each ModelAdmin class concerned.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs an affected Wagtail with ModelAdmin managing a page model. A limited editor saves a page with script-bearing content. An administrator opens the Choose a parent page view, and the script runs with the administrator's credentials.
The site runs Wagtail 4.1.4 or 4.2.2 or later. The same editor content is shown in the Choose a parent page view and the document Inspect view as inert text, and no script runs for the administrator.

citations.quote: could potentially craft pages and documents that, when viewed by a user with higher privileges, could perform actions with that user's credentials
The vulnerability is not exploitable by an ordinary site visitor without access to the Wagtail admin, and only affects sites with ModelAdmin enabled.
Site owners who are unable to upgrade to the new versions can disable or override the corresponding functionality.
Patched versions have been released as Wagtail 4.1.4 and Wagtail 4.2.2.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the parent chooser form's label method for pages so it no longer marks the joined ancestor titles as safe HTML. It now joins the titles as plain text with a text separator, so the template escapes them, and a test confirms a script in a page title is escaped. This matches the card's page-side cause and its plain-text breadcrumb prevention. The document inspect view fix is not in this diff, so that half of the card cannot be checked here.

patterns.title: Starlette StaticFiles path traversal via character-wise prefix check
patterns.cause: The static file handler decided whether a requested file was inside the served directory by calling os.path.commonprefix(). That function compares paths one character at a time and does not treat its arguments as paths. A dot-dot request that resolves to a sibling whose name begins with the served directory name (for example static1.txt next to static) therefore passes the containment check.
preconditions: The application serves files with StaticFiles from a directory such as static.
A sibling file or directory exists whose name starts with the same characters as the served directory name.
An attacker can send a request path containing dot-dot segments unchanged, for example with curl --path-as-is.
patterns.prevention: Check containment by comparing whole path components, not characters. Resolve the requested path to a normalized absolute form, then use os.path.commonpath() against the served directory, as the advisory recommends, and reject the request if the common path is not the served directory itself. Upgrade Starlette to 0.27.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the fixed version handles symbolic links, Windows path forms, or other normalization edge cases. They do not say whether the check alone is sufficient for every deployment. Only the dot-dot sibling-prefix case is documented. The affected range is stated as 0.13.5 up to, but not including, 0.27.0.

fixtures.scenario: A service mounts a static files handler on a directory named static. A sibling file named static1.txt and a sibling directory named static_disallow exist. A request using a dot-dot path, sent as-is, reaches the sibling and its content is returned.

Same layout, but the containment check compares whole path components after resolving the request path. The dot-dot request resolves outside the static directory and is rejected as not found, while files inside static are still served.

citations.quote: it does not treat the arguments as paths.
Confidentiality is breached: An attacker may obtain files that should not be open to the public.
allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to view files in a web service which was built using Starlette.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the character-wise prefix comparison in the static file lookup with a component-wise common path comparison against the resolved served directory. New tests confirm that dot-dot requests reaching a sibling file or directory whose name begins with the served directory name now return not found.

patterns.title: Stored XSS on the Airflow task instance details page (CVE-2023-29247)
patterns.cause: A script on the task instance details page reads each displayed task attribute and rewrites it into richer markup. For timestamp-like values it builds a time element, and for values containing http it builds a link. It does this by concatenating the raw attribute text into an HTML string and assigning that string through the HTML-parsing property of the element. The link target was also left unquoted. Attacker-influenced task attribute values were therefore parsed as markup and could inject script or break out of the attribute context. The URL check was only a substring match for http, so almost any string with that text became a link.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version is earlier than 2.6.0.
An attacker can influence a task instance attribute value that is rendered on the task instance details page, for example through DAG or task definition content.
A user opens the task instance details page so the client-side script runs and rewrites the attribute into markup.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Apache Airflow to 2.6.0 or later. When transforming displayed values in client-side code, do not build HTML by string concatenation. Create elements with the DOM creation API, set attributes through the attribute setter, and insert the value as a text node so the browser never parses it as markup. Validate that a value is a real URL with a proper validator before turning it into a link, instead of using a substring test, and consider restricting allowed URL schemes.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the timestamp and link formatting in the task details script only. Other pages or templates that insert stored values into the page as markup would need their own review. A URL validator accepts a broad range of strings, so scheme restrictions may still be needed to block unsafe link targets. The exact privileges needed to write the malicious attribute value depend on the deployment.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment running a version earlier than 2.6.0 shows the task instance details page to operators. Attacker-influenced stored content appears on that page, and the browser treats it as active content when an operator views it.
An Airflow deployment runs version 2.6.0 or later. Stored values on the task instance details page are displayed as plain text, so an operator viewing the page does not trigger script execution.

citations.quote: Task instance details page in the UI is vulnerable to stored cross-site scripting.
This issue affects Apache Airflow before 2.6.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces string-built markup in the task details script with DOM element creation. Attributes are set through the attribute setter and the displayed value is inserted as a text node, for both the time element and the link. A follow-up change swaps the substring test for http with a proper URL validator from the validator package. This matches the card's cause (raw values parsed as HTML, unquoted link target, weak URL check) and its prevention.

patterns.title: Directory traversal through the path parameter of the mlflow get-artifact endpoint
patterns.cause: Several artifact endpoints (get-artifact, artifact listing, and model-version get-artifact) took the path parameter from the request and passed it to the artifact repository, or joined it to the artifact root, with no check on its form. Absolute paths or parent-directory sequences could therefore point outside the intended artifact directory and read arbitrary files on the server.
preconditions: The mlflow tracking server exposes the get-artifact, artifact listing, or model-version get-artifact endpoints to callers who are not fully trusted.
The server runs an affected mlflow version, before the release that adds path validation.
The request path is used as a relative location under a trusted artifact root, such as a local or proxied artifact store.
patterns.prevention: Validate every client-supplied artifact path before it is used or joined to a trusted prefix. Normalize it as a POSIX-style relative path, then reject it with an invalid-parameter error if it is absolute, contains an operating-system-specific alternate separator, or still begins with a parent-directory reference after normalization. Apply the same check in every endpoint that accepts an artifact path, not only get-artifact. Do not rely on filesystem canonicalization alone, because artifact roots may be remote or proxied stores. Upgrade to an mlflow release that contains this validation.
patterns.limitations: The check is purely lexical. It does not follow symbolic links or inspect the real storage location, so it protects only if the artifact repositories treat the validated relative path as confined to their root. Other endpoints that accept paths need the same validator. The advisories also disagree on the affected range, so confirm the fixed version in the project release notes.

fixtures.scenario: A client calls the /get-artifact endpoint with a path value that points outside the artifact store, and the server returns the contents of an arbitrary file from its filesystem.

A client calls the /get-artifact endpoint with a path value. The server resolves it to a canonical location and confirms it is inside the artifact root. A value that points elsewhere is rejected and no file content is returned.

citations.quote: A directory traversal vulnerability in the /get-artifact API method of the mlflow platform up to v2.0.1
allows attackers to read arbitrary files on the server via the path parameter.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a shared path validator that normalizes the client-supplied path as a POSIX path and rejects it with an invalid-parameter error if it contains OS-specific alternate separators, is absolute, or escapes upward via a parent-directory reference. It is called in the get-artifact handler, the artifact listing handler, and the model-version get-artifact handler before the path is used or joined to the artifact root.

patterns.title: Prompt-injected arbitrary URL retrieval (SSRF) in Langchain before 0.0.329
patterns.cause: The APIChain component in Langchain before 0.0.329 asks the language model to produce an API URL from the user question and then fetches that URL with no check on its destination. Because a prompt-injected question can steer the model's output, an attacker can make the server request arbitrary URLs, including internal services, and feed the response into later steps.
preconditions: The application uses the APIChain component from a Langchain version before 0.0.329.
Attacker-influenced text reaches the question that the model turns into an API URL.
The server can reach internal or otherwise sensitive hosts that the attacker cannot reach directly.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to 0.0.329 or later and give the chain an explicit allowlist of permitted domains when creating it. The fixed version compares the scheme and host of the model-generated URL with the allowlist before any request and raises an error on a mismatch. Creation fails if no allowlist is given, and allowing all domains must be chosen deliberately and is discouraged. Keep the list narrow, use full scheme-and-host entries, and treat fetched content as untrusted.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers only the API chain's request path, not other Langchain components that fetch URLs. The check matches the scheme and host of the URL only, so path-level restrictions are not enforced. It does not address redirects from an allowed host or DNS tricks, so network egress controls are still worthwhile. Passing None for the allowlist turns the protection off. The CVE record and the advisories also give different affected version ranges.

fixtures.scenario: A service built on a Langchain version before 0.0.329 accepts user text. An attacker embeds an instruction in that text that makes the service retrieve data from an attacker-chosen URL, and the fetched content then flows into later processing steps.
The service runs Langchain 0.0.329 or later. The destination of any retrieval is not decided by prompt text alone, and fetched content is handled as untrusted data before it reaches downstream tasks.

citations.quote: In Langchain before 0.0.329, prompt injection allows an attacker to force the service to retrieve data from an arbitrary URL
potentially injecting content into downstream tasks.
prompt injection allows an attacker to force the service to retrieve data from an arbitrary URL, essentially providing SSRF

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a domain allowlist option to the API chain. Creation now fails if no allowlist is given (an explicit None opts out). Both the sync and async request paths compare the scheme and host of the model-generated URL against the allowlist and raise an error on a mismatch before any request is made.

patterns.title: Crafted input to the LangChain JIRA API wrapper can lead to OS command injection and remote code execution
patterns.cause: In langchain before v0.0.225, the other action of JiraAPIWrapper took the query string and ran it as Python code through dynamic execution, with the wrapper object in scope. Anything that could shape that string, including text generated by a language model from untrusted user prompts, could run arbitrary Python and so arbitrary commands on the host. The tool prompt even told the model to write Python code as the input.
preconditions: The application uses langchain before v0.0.225 with the JIRA toolkit or JiraAPIWrapper.
The generic other action of the wrapper is reachable, for example through the agent tool for other Jira API calls.
An attacker can influence the query text, directly or through prompts to an agent that fills in the tool input.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade langchain to v0.0.225 or later. Never pass tool or user supplied text to dynamic code execution. Accept structured input instead, such as a JSON object naming an allowed function with arguments, and parse it as data. Hardening that goes beyond the patch: check the requested function name against an explicit allowlist of safe Jira operations, and run agents with a Jira account that has the least privilege needed.
patterns.limitations: The fix removes dynamic code execution but still resolves the function name from the input by attribute lookup on the Jira client. A caller can therefore still invoke any public client method with chosen arguments, which can read or change Jira data within the account's permissions. This is a smaller issue than code execution, but it is not blocked by the patch. The tool prompt change only guides the model and is not a security control.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs langchain at a version before v0.0.225 and exposes the JIRA API wrapper to requests that carry attacker-controlled text. The attacker submits crafted input and arbitrary code runs on the host.

A service runs langchain v0.0.225 or later. Input to the JIRA API wrapper is still treated as untrusted, and the wrapper is only reachable by trusted callers, so crafted input does not lead to code execution.

citations.quote: Langchain before v0.0.225 was discovered to contain a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in the component JiraAPIWrapper (aka the JIRA API wrapper).
This vulnerability allows attackers to execute arbitrary code via crafted input.
Langchain OS Command Injection vulnerability
Langchain 0.0.171 is vulnerable to Arbitrary Code Execution.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the dynamic execution of the query string in the other action of JiraAPIWrapper. It now parses the input as JSON and calls a named method on the Jira client with the supplied positional and keyword arguments. The tool prompt is also changed to ask for a dictionary instead of Python code. The card's cause, prevention and the remaining risk from attribute-based method lookup all match this.

patterns.title: ReDoS in Django EmailValidator and URLValidator via many domain name labels
patterns.cause: The URL and email validators ran their regular expressions on input of any length. A value with a very large number of domain name labels made the matching take excessive time, which allowed regular expression denial of service. Upstream fixed this by capping input length before matching rather than by rewriting the patterns.
preconditions: The application runs Django 3.2 before 3.2.20, Django 4.1 before 4.1.10, or Django 4.2 before 4.2.3.
URLValidator or EmailValidator is applied to attacker-controlled text, for example through email or URL form fields, model fields, or direct calls to the validators.
No length limit is enforced on the value before it reaches the validator, so a very long string with many labels is accepted for matching.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 3.2.20, 4.1.10, 4.2.3 or later, which reject over-long values up front: URLs longer than 2048 characters and emails longer than 320 characters fail validation before any regular expression runs, and the forms email field defaults to a maximum length of 320. As defense in depth, enforce request size and field length limits at the web server or form layer, and keep validators from running on unbounded input.
patterns.limitations: The length caps reduce the cost of matching but do not remove the underlying regular expression structure. Custom validators that subclass or copy these patterns, or other regular expressions applied to unbounded input, need their own length limits. Legitimate URLs longer than 2048 characters are now rejected unless the maximum length attribute is overridden. Django series not listed as affected are not covered by this assessment.

fixtures.scenario: A public signup form validates the email field with EmailValidator on Django 4.2.2. An attacker submits an address whose domain part has a very large number of labels, and the validation work ties up the worker handling the request.
The same signup form runs on Django 4.2.3 or later, which is outside the affected range, so an email with a very large number of domain labels is not subject to this ReDoS.

citations.quote: potential ReDoS (regular expression denial of service) attack via a very large number of domain name labels of emails and URLs.
In Django 3.2 before 3.2.20, 4 before 4.1.10, and 4.2 before 4.2.3

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a length cap before any regular expression runs: the URL validator rejects non-string values and values over 2048 characters, and the email validator rejects values over 320 characters. The forms email field now defaults its maximum length to 320. The regular expressions are left unchanged, and new tests cover a long run of domain labels, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: SQL injection via SQLDatabaseChain in langchain before v0.0.247
patterns.cause: SQLDatabaseChain asked a language model to turn a natural language question into SQL and then ran the result directly on the connected database with no inspection. Because the question is attacker-influenced, an attacker can use prompt injection to make the model emit arbitrary statements (not just selects), so the SQL layer executes attacker-chosen queries and can expose or modify sensitive data (CWE-89). The weakness is missing validation of generated SQL before execution, not unsafe string building in a fixed query.
preconditions: The application uses langchain before v0.0.247 with SQLDatabaseChain or its sequential variant.
Untrusted users can supply the natural language question that is turned into SQL.
The generated SQL is executed on a database connection that has broad read or write rights.
No separate validation of the generated SQL is performed before it runs.
patterns.prevention: Never execute model-generated SQL without checking it first. Parse each generated statement before running it, reject anything that fails to parse, and by default allow only plain select statements. Optionally forbid select-all queries and refuse to run when the SQL dialect cannot be validated. Combine this with a database account that has read-only access to only the required tables, since parsing checks cannot catch every harmful select. Upgrade to a langchain release that includes the validation step and note that the chain was later moved to the experimental package, so treat it as unsafe for untrusted input and review how it is used.
patterns.limitations: The validation is a parser-based allow check on statement type and wildcards. It does not stop a permitted select from reading data the connection should not expose, and it is skipped by default for unsupported dialects. It also does not address prompt injection itself. Least-privilege database credentials and limits on who can reach the chain remain necessary. Exact affected version ranges differ between advisories, so confirm them with the vendor.

fixtures.scenario: A public web service runs langchain v0.0.64 and passes user-submitted text to SQLDatabaseChain over a database that holds customer records. A remote attacker crafts input that triggers SQL injection and reads data the service was never meant to return.
The service runs langchain v0.0.247 or later, and SQLDatabaseChain uses a database account limited to the minimum data needed. The same crafted input does not expose the sensitive records.

citations.quote: SQL injection vulnerability in langchain before v0.0.247 allows a remote attacker to obtain sensitive information via the SQLDatabaseChain component.
SQL injection vulnerability in langchain v.0.0.64 allows a remote attacker to obtain sensitive information via the SQLDatabaseChain component.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a validation step that parses the model-generated SQL with a SQL parsing library before it is run. By default it rejects anything that fails to parse or is not a select statement, and it offers opt-in switches to forbid wildcard selects and to refuse unsupported dialects. A later commit moves the SQL chain into the experimental package, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Low-privilege role can test database connections through default REST API permission
patterns.cause: The default permission set in Apache Superset up to and including 2.1.0 let the Gamma role use the REST API function that tests database connections. This function was not limited to roles meant to manage databases, so an authorization gap left an outbound-connection feature open to low-privilege users.
preconditions: Apache Superset version 2.1.0 or earlier is deployed.
The attacker holds an authenticated account with the Gamma role.
The default REST API permissions for the Gamma role have not been tightened.
patterns.prevention: Grant any API function that makes the server connect to a configurable database target only to roles that are meant to manage database connections. Do not include it in the default permissions of low-privilege roles such as Gamma. Audit role-to-permission mappings after install and after upgrade, and move to a Superset release newer than 2.1.0 that corrects the default permission. Keep an authorization check on the connection-test endpoint itself, so it does not rely on the user being logged in.
patterns.limitations: The advisories give only a one-sentence description. They do not name the endpoint, the permission name, the fixed release, or the exact network behavior. The server-side request forgery classification comes from the CWE metadata, not from the source text. This card therefore cannot say which internal targets are reachable or what a tester can learn from the responses.

fixtures.scenario: A Superset 2.1.0 instance runs with default role permissions. A user logged in with only the Gamma role calls the REST API to test a database connection, and the request is accepted although the user has no database management duties.

The same instance has the connection-test permission removed from the Gamma role, or runs a release newer than 2.1.0 that corrects the default. The Gamma user's request to test a database connection is denied as unauthorized, and only database-management roles can run it.

citations.quote: An improper default REST API permission for Gamma users in Apache Superset up to and including 2.1.0
allows for an authenticated Gamma user to test database connections.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the route-to-permission mapping so the connection-test and parameter-validation API methods need the write permission on the database resource instead of the read permission. Gamma holds only read access there, so it can no longer reach these outbound-connection functions. This matches the card's account of an authorization gap, where a low-privilege role could use a function meant for roles that manage databases.

patterns.title: Apache Airflow before 2.6.3: crafted input from an authenticated user makes a request hang
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow before 2.6.3, the DAG partial_subset logic accepts a task id pattern from an authenticated user and matches it against each task id with Python's backtracking regular expression engine. A crafted pattern can trigger catastrophic backtracking, which makes the request hang and burns CPU (regular expression denial of service).
preconditions: The deployment runs Apache Airflow at a version before 2.6.3.
The attacker is an authenticated user who can supply a regular expression that reaches the DAG subset or task selection logic.
The DAG has task ids that the pattern is matched against, so a pathological pattern or input pairing can trigger heavy backtracking.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Apache Airflow to 2.6.3 or later. The fix evaluates user-supplied task id patterns with the RE2 engine (google-re2 package), which matches in linear time and has no catastrophic backtracking. More generally, never run untrusted patterns through a backtracking engine; use a linear-time engine, or cap pattern length and execution time.
patterns.limitations: The fix only changes the regex engine used in the DAG model module. Other places in the code base or in plugins that compile user-supplied patterns with the standard library engine are not covered by this change. RE2 does not support some features such as backreferences and lookarounds, so patterns that relied on them may behave differently or be rejected.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment on a version before 2.6.3 accepts input from an authenticated user. That user submits crafted input and the current request hangs.
An Airflow deployment runs version 2.6.3 or later. The same crafted input from an authenticated user does not cause the request to hang.

citations.quote: an authenticated user can use crafted input to make the current request hang
It is recommended to upgrade to a version that is not affected

patch_review.observation: The fix swaps the standard library regex module for the RE2 binding in the DAG model module, so the task id pattern used in partial_subset is matched with a linear-time engine. It also adds the google-re2 package as a required dependency in the packaging configuration.

patterns.title: Airflow test connection feature abused by users with Connection edit privileges
patterns.cause: Before Apache Airflow 2.7.0, the connection test feature was always available through the UI, REST API and CLI. A user with Connection edit privileges could make the server build a hook from attacker-chosen connection settings and open outbound connections, which allowed server-side request abuse, probing of internal services, and resource exhaustion from repeated tests. No deployment-level switch existed to turn the capability off.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version earlier than 2.7.0 is deployed
The attacker is authenticated and can create or edit Connections
The test connection endpoint or button is reachable and enabled, as it was always on before 2.7.0
The Airflow server can reach internal or external hosts that the attacker wants to contact
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 2.7.0 or newer, where connection testing is controlled by the core test_connection setting, which defaults to disabled. The API, CLI and UI all enforce it: the API refuses with a forbidden status, the CLI exits with an error, and the UI button is disabled or hidden. Leave it disabled unless connection testing is needed. Enable it only after reviewing which users can add or edit Connections and confirming they are trusted. Also restrict Connection edit permissions to administrators.
patterns.limitations: The fix is an opt-in gate and not a validation of destinations. When an admin enables the setting, trusted editors can still make the server connect to arbitrary hosts, and the fix adds no rate limiting or destination filtering. Versions before 2.7.0 have no such switch, so permission reduction is the only mitigation there.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 2.6 deployment grants Connection edit rights to many users. One user repeatedly submits test connection requests with chosen settings, exhausting the server and making it open unwanted connections.
Airflow 2.7.0 or newer is deployed, and Connection edit rights are limited to a few trusted administrators who have reviewed their access to sensitive functions.

citations.quote: can be exploited by an authenticated user possessing Connection edit privileges
exploit the test connection feature by sending many requests, leading to a denial of service (DoS) condition on the server
administrators are encouraged to review and adjust user permissions to restrict access to sensitive functionalities, reducing the attack surface.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a core configuration option for connection testing that defaults to Disabled. The REST API refuses test requests with a forbidden status, the CLI test command prints a message and exits with an error, and the UI button is disabled or hidden depending on the option value. It is an opt-in gate with a warning to review who can edit Connections, and it adds no destination validation.

patterns.title: Absolute path traversal in mlflow before 2.5.0 (CVE-2023-3765)
patterns.cause: The advisories classify the flaw as an absolute path traversal in the mlflow project. In this class of bug, a caller-supplied path that is already absolute is used to reach files directly, instead of being kept inside an intended base location. The sources do not name the affected function, endpoint, or parameter.
preconditions: The deployment runs mlflow at a version earlier than 2.5.0.
A path value comes from an untrusted party and is used for file access.
The path is not confined to an intended base directory before it is used.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mlflow to version 2.5.0 or later. In any code that accepts file locations from untrusted input, refuse absolute paths. Resolve the final path with a canonicalizing call such as os.path.realpath(). Then confirm the resolved result is still inside the intended base directory before any read or write. Reject the request if it is not.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that this is an absolute path traversal in mlflow prior to 2.5.0. They do not identify the vulnerable component, the entry point, the impact (read, write, or both), or the exact fix. The generic hardening steps above are the standard defense for this weakness class, not a description of the upstream change. Check the mlflow release notes and advisory details before treating any specific code path as affected or fixed.

fixtures.scenario: A service running an mlflow version older than 2.5.0 accepts a file location from a remote user. The user supplies an absolute path that points outside the intended storage area, and the service uses it as given.

A service runs mlflow 2.5.0 or later. Any custom code that handles user-supplied locations rejects absolute paths, resolves the final path, and verifies it lies under the intended base directory before accessing the file.

citations.quote: Absolute Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.5.0.
Absolute Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.5.0.

patterns.title: Command injection in PaddlePaddle fs.py before version 2.5.0
patterns.cause: In PaddlePaddle before 2.5.0, the local filesystem mkdirs method in the fleet utils fs.py module built a shell command string containing the caller-supplied path and ran it through the operating system shell. The distributed launch utilities did the same with the log directory option. Shell metacharacters in a path could therefore be interpreted as extra commands, giving arbitrary command execution.
preconditions: A PaddlePaddle release earlier than 2.5.0 is installed.
An attacker can influence a directory path passed to the local filesystem mkdirs method or to the launch log directory setting.
The path reaches a shell invocation without quoting or validation.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to PaddlePaddle 2.5.0 or later. The upstream fix creates directories with the standard library's recursive directory-creation function, so the path is never parsed by a shell. In general, use native library calls or an argument-list process invocation without a shell for file operations, and never interpolate untrusted values into shell command strings.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows the replacement of shell calls for directory creation. Other places in the code base that call the shell with interpolated values, such as a remaining file-removal call in the launch utilities, are not changed by this diff. How an attacker would supply the path depends on how the application exposes these APIs and options.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs PaddlePaddle older than 2.5.0 and uses its fs.py functionality with values that an outside party can influence, so an attacker may be able to run arbitrary commands on the host.
The same service runs PaddlePaddle 2.5.0 or later, and any custom code that invokes operating system commands keeps untrusted data out of command interpretation.

citations.quote: PaddlePaddle before 2.5.0 has a command injection in fs.py.
This resulted in the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the operating system.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces shell-based directory creation (os.system with an interpolated path) with the standard library recursive directory-creation call in the local filesystem mkdirs method and in several launch utilities that handle the log directory. The path is no longer parsed by a shell, which removes the injection. A shell call that removes the endpoints log file is left unchanged.

patterns.title: Open redirect after login in Jupyter Server via crafted login links
patterns.cause: The post-login redirect safety check parsed the requested next URL with a server-side parser that disagrees with browsers. A URL with a scheme followed by extra slashes was seen by the server as having no host and a path, so it passed as a local path. Browsers instead took the first path segment as the host and navigated to an external site, giving an open redirect.
preconditions: The attacker knows the address of a Jupyter Server and can craft a login link with a next-URL value.
The victim follows the crafted link and logs in, or already has a session, so the server issues the redirect.
The next-URL value uses a scheme followed by three or more slashes, which the server-side parser and browsers interpret differently.
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on a single parse of an untrusted redirect target when the browser may parse it differently. Normalize the URL before validation, for example by collapsing any run of slashes after the scheme separator to exactly two, and replacing backslashes. Treat a URL as non-local if it has either a scheme or a host, and send it through the same-origin or allowed-origin check, falling back to a safe default page on the server. Add regression tests for malformed forms such as a scheme with an extra slash and an encoded userinfo part. Upgrade jupyter-server to 2.7.2 or later.
patterns.limitations: The diff covers only the redirect helper in the login handler and its tests. It does not show other redirect paths, and other parser differences beyond the slash and backslash cases handled here may exist.

fixtures.scenario: A user receives a login link for a known Jupyter Server that carries a destination pointing to an external site. The user logs in, or is already logged in, and the server sends the browser to that external site.
A user receives the same kind of login link, but the server accepts only destinations served by the Jupyter Server. The external destination is rejected and the browser lands on a page on the server.

citations.quote: Maliciously crafted login links to known Jupyter Servers can cause successful login or an already logged-in session to be redirected to arbitrary sites
which should be restricted to Jupyter Server-served URLs
There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

patch_review.observation: The fix normalizes the next URL before parsing, collapsing any run of slashes after the scheme separator to exactly two, because the server-side parser and browsers disagree on a scheme followed by three slashes. It also treats a URL as non-local when it has either a scheme or a host, so such URLs go through the cross-origin check. A regression test was added using a scheme with an extra slash and an encoded at-sign in the host part.

patterns.title: Incomplete cross-site credential checks on the jupyter-server files endpoint
patterns.cause: The handler serving the /files/ URLs did not apply proper cross-site credential checks. The earlier upstream patch for CVE-2019-9644 was not applied completely, so part of that vulnerability stayed open. As a result, certain file contents could be exposed to cross-site requests, or files could be accessed when a user opened untrusted files via Open image in new tab.
preconditions: jupyter-server older than release 2.7.2 is in use
The /files/ URLs are served by the default files handler, not the alternative handler the advisory says implements the correct checks
A user can be induced to open untrusted content or an attacker-controlled page while having access to the server
patterns.prevention: Upgrade jupyter-server to 2.7.2 or later. If an upgrade is not possible, set the ContentsManager files handler class option to the FilesHandler class in jupyter_server.files.handlers. It is slower but implements the correct checks. In general, any handler that serves user files, including a performance-oriented replacement for a standard handler, should enforce the same cross-site credential checks as the reference handler. A security patch should also be applied to every handler path that serves the same data, so no variant is left unprotected.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which checks are missing, which request properties are validated, or how the faster default handler differs from FilesHandler. They do not describe a concrete exploit chain or the exact file types affected. This card gives only the general direction and the documented workaround, and it does not cover other endpoints.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs a jupyter-server version older than 2.7.2 with the default files handler. A user opens an untrusted file or a cross-site page, and a request to a /files/ URL is served without the proper cross-site credential check, exposing file contents.
A deployment runs jupyter-server 2.7.2 or later, or sets the files handler class option to the FilesHandler class. Cross-site requests to /files/ URLs are subject to the correct credential checks.

citations.quote: Upstream patch for CVE-2019-9644 was not applied completely, leaving part of the vulnerability open.
Improper cross-site credential checks on
which implements the correct checks.
Jupyter Server 2.7.2

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a cross-site request forgery token check at the start of the get method in the authenticated static file handler in base/handlers.py. This is the default handler behind the files URLs, so it had been missing the check that the alternative FilesHandler already enforced. This matches the card's account of an incomplete earlier patch and its advice to upgrade, to use the stricter handler as a workaround, and to protect every handler path that serves the same data.

patterns.title: Unblocked non-multi options in GitPython clone and clone_from allow command injection
patterns.cause: GitPython before 3.1.32 did not block insecure non-multi options in clone and clone_from. The library makes external calls to git without sufficient sanitization of input arguments, so attacker-influenced input such as a crafted remote URL can reach the git command line and lead to remote code execution. The advisory describes this as an incomplete fix for CVE-2022-24439.
preconditions: The application uses GitPython older than 3.1.32.
The application calls clone or clone_from.
An attacker can influence the remote URL or the options passed to the clone call.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade GitPython to 3.1.32 or later. Treat any remote URL or clone option that comes from users or other untrusted input as hostile. Do not let such input choose which git options are passed to clone or clone_from. Allow only a fixed, reviewed set of options and validate the repository URL against an expected form (for example, permitted schemes and hosts) before calling the library.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not list which options are considered insecure, do not describe the exact validation the fixed release performs, and do not give the precise exploit payload. This card therefore cannot say whether an input filter alone is sufficient, and it does not replace upgrading. The sources also do not cover other GitPython entry points beyond clone and clone_from.

fixtures.scenario: A web service lets users submit a repository address and optional clone settings. It passes them straight to clone_from on GitPython 3.1.31. A crafted remote URL or option value is forwarded to git and executes attacker-chosen commands on the server.

The same service runs GitPython 3.1.32 or later. It accepts only a repository URL that matches an allowlist of expected hosts and schemes, and it ignores any user-supplied clone options, so untrusted input cannot add options to the git invocation.

citations.quote: GitPython before 3.1.32 does not block insecure non-multi options in clone and clone_from.
the library makes external calls to git without sufficient sanitization of input arguments
which makes it possible to inject a maliciously crafted remote URL into the clone command

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the clone path check the keyword arguments passed to clone and clone_from against the list of unsafe git clone options, such as upload-pack and config, unless unsafe options are explicitly allowed. Before this, only the multi-options list was checked, so these options could be passed unchecked as plain keyword arguments. The new tests confirm that both clone and clone_from now raise an error for these options.

patterns.title: OS command injection in mlflow versions prior to 2.6.0 (CVE-2023-4033)
patterns.cause: In mlflow's pyfunc backend, the predict operation (used by the models predict command when the environment manager is not local) assembled a shell command string by formatting the model URI, input path, output path and content type into inline Python code run through a shell. The scoring server command builder likewise placed the host and address values into a shell command line without escaping. Shell metacharacters such as quotes, semicolons or ampersands in these values could end the intended argument and run attacker-chosen commands.
preconditions: The mlflow version is older than 2.6.0.

An attacker can influence the input path, output path, content type or serve host value passed to the models predict or models serve commands, for example through a wrapper service or automation that forwards untrusted parameters.
The command runs through a non-local environment manager, such as conda or virtualenv, so the command string is executed by a shell.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mlflow to 2.6.0 or later. The fix stops building inline Python code from user values: predict now runs a small dedicated script that receives its inputs as named command-line arguments, and user-controlled values are shell-quoted before being joined into the command. The serve command builder also quotes the host and address. When writing similar code, pass arguments as a list to a process API without a shell, or quote every untrusted value, and never embed values in code strings. Validate content type against known values and treat paths and hosts as data.
patterns.limitations: The fix relies on quoting plus a joined command string, so any new code that adds unquoted values to the same command would reintroduce the problem. Quoting rules differ between POSIX shells and Windows, and the Windows branch of the serve command builder only has the host quoted. This analysis is based on the single diff shown and does not cover other mlflow components that may build shell commands.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs an mlflow installation whose version is older than 2.6.0, and it is within the range the advisories list as affected by OS command injection.
A team runs mlflow 2.6.0 or later, which is outside the affected range stated in the advisories.

citations.quote: OS Command Injection in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.6.0.
OS Command Injection in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.6.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops the predict path from embedding the model URI, input path, output path and content type in an inline Python code string run through a shell. It adds a small dedicated script that takes these as named command-line arguments, and the user-controlled values are shell-quoted before the command is joined. The scoring server command builder also shell-quotes the host and the host-and-port address, including the Windows branch for the host. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Static view path traversal up one directory through null-byte handling in Python 3.11 path normalization
patterns.cause: On affected Python 3.11 and 3.12 pre-release versions, the path normalization function os.path.normpath truncates its input at the first null byte. A Pyramid static view that serves files from a full filesystem path can then resolve a request to a location one directory above the static root. The only file the sources say could be exposed this way is index.html in the parent directory. The sources do not describe the exact request form that triggers this.
preconditions: Pyramid 2.0.0 or 2.0.1 is in use.
The runtime is an affected Python version: 3.11.0 to 3.11.4, or 3.12.0a1 to 3.12.0rc1.
A static view is configured with a full filesystem path.
An index.html file sits exactly one directory above the static view's filesystem path.
patterns.prevention: Reject any requested path that contains a null byte before it is normalized or joined to the static root, so that truncation during normalization cannot change the resolved location. Run a Python version in which normalization no longer truncates at the first null byte, such as 3.11.5 or later in the 3.11 series, or temporarily use the 3.10 series. Use a Pyramid release that rejects null-byte paths, which is 2.0.2 per the advisory. Treat null bytes in file and directory names as invalid for static serving.
