patterns.limitations: The fix covers the link extraction helper only. It does not address redirects that leave the allowed host after a fetch, DNS rebinding, or links to internal addresses on the allowed host itself. The fixed release number is not stated in the diff.

fixtures.scenario: A crawler starts at a trusted site with outside links prevented. A page there links to a different host whose name looks similar. The crawler downloads that file anyway.
The same crawl runs on a fixed langchain version. The link to the different host is rejected before any request is sent, and only pages on the intended site are fetched.

citations.quote: the crawler would proceed to download that file as well even though
langchain Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability

patch_review.observation: The fix to the link extraction helper parses the base URL and each candidate link, and when outside links are prevented it requires the network location (host and port) to match before also requiring the link to start with the full base URL, which keeps the scheme and path restriction. The new test rejects lookalike hosts, other ports and a changed scheme, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Path traversal via remote filename when loading HTTP dataset sources
patterns.cause: When a dataset is loaded from an HTTP source, the filename in the server's Content-Disposition header was used to build the local destination path without checking that it was a plain file name. A malicious server could return a name with parent-directory sequences, a relative directory, or an absolute path, so the download was written outside the intended directory. The fallback that takes the last segment of the URL path was not the problem, because it already yields only a base name.
preconditions: The application loads a dataset from a source URL with an HTTP or HTTPS scheme
The remote server controls the response headers and returns a Content-Disposition filename that contains path separators, dot-segments, or an absolute path
The header filename is joined to the local download directory without being checked to be a bare file name
patterns.prevention: Treat the Content-Disposition filename as untrusted input. Validate that it is a bare file name, meaning it is equal to its own base name, and reject the download with an invalid-parameter error if it contains any directory component, dot-segment, or absolute path. As defense in depth, resolve the final destination path and confirm it stays inside the intended download directory before writing. Upgrade mlflow to a release that includes this validation.
patterns.limitations: The check only covers the Content-Disposition branch and relies on a base-name comparison that follows the host operating system's path rules. It does not address other dataset source types, and it does not by itself protect against an unsafe destination directory chosen by the caller. The diff does not show how a file write could escalate to code execution.

fixtures.scenario: A dataset is loaded from an HTTP URL whose server sends a Content-Disposition filename containing parent-directory sequences or an absolute path. The file is written outside the download directory.
The same dataset load reduces the remote filename to a bare base name, then checks the resolved destination is inside the download directory. A traversal filename is rejected or neutralized.

citations.quote: the filename extracted from the `Content-Disposition` header or the URL path is used to generate the final file path without proper sanitization
This flaw enables an attacker to control the file path fully by utilizing path traversal or absolute path techniques
The issue is fixed in version 2.9.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that treats a name as a path when it differs from its own base name. The load method now uses it on the Content-Disposition filename and raises an invalid-parameter error for absolute paths, relative directories, and parent-directory sequences. The URL-path fallback is left alone, and tests cover the rejected cases.

patterns.title: Filter bypass leads to command injection in the PaddlePaddle wget download helper
patterns.cause: The download helper paddle.utils.download._wget_download in paddlepaddle 2.6.0 was affected by command injection (CWE-78). The advisory describes it as a bypass of a filter, so a filter was present but could be circumvented. The sources do not say what the filter checked or how it was bypassed.
preconditions: The application uses paddlepaddle 2.6.0, the version named in the advisories.
Execution reaches the wget-based download helper paddle.utils.download._wget_download.
The sources do not say which input is attacker-controlled, so whether outside data reaches the helper must be checked per deployment.
patterns.prevention: Do not treat a filter or blocklist as sufficient protection for data that ends up in an operating system command, because this issue was a bypass of such a filter. Keep outside-influenced values out of any command line that a shell interprets. Prefer a native download facility, or pass each argument as a separate element to the process launcher without a shell. Also validate the value strictly against an allow-list of expected forms before use. Upgrade to a release that contains the upstream fix for this CVE.
patterns.limitations: The sources only give the affected function, the version, the weakness class and the fact that a filter was bypassed. They do not describe the vulnerable input, the bypass technique, the first fixed version or the upstream change. The prevention direction is general guidance for this weakness class, not a description of what the maintainers changed.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs paddlepaddle 2.6.0 and passes a value supplied by an outside party to the wget-based download helper. It relies only on the built-in filter to make that value safe.

A service never passes outside-influenced values to the wget-based download helper unchecked. It validates them against a strict allow-list, and its downloads do not go through a shell-interpreted command line.

citations.quote: Command injection in paddle.utils.download._wget_download (bypass filter) in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0
Command injection in paddle.utils.download._wget_download (bypass filter) in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0

patch_review.observation: The fix deletes the wget download helper entirely. That helper built a command string, quoted the URL and file name, and ran it through a shell. The hub caller no longer selects wget for gitee, and only the native httpx-based download method remains. This matches the card's advice to avoid shell-interpreted commands and prefer a native download facility.

patterns.title: Command injection in the IrGraph.draw method of PaddlePaddle 2.6.0
patterns.cause: IrGraph.draw converts the generated dot file to a pdf with the Graphviz dot tool. The helper built the command by concatenating the file paths, which come from the save path and name arguments, into a single string and ran it with shell execution enabled. Shell metacharacters in those values were therefore interpreted by the shell, which allowed arbitrary command injection.
preconditions: The application uses paddlepaddle 2.6.0 or another build that still has the shell-based pdf conversion.
The application calls IrGraph.draw with a save path or name that an outside party can influence.
The code path that converts the dot file to pdf is reached, and the shell parses the combined string.
patterns.prevention: Run external programs without a shell and pass the program name and each argument as separate list items, so path values are never parsed as command text. The upstream fix does this for the dot invocation in the pdf conversion helper. Upgrade to a PaddlePaddle release that contains this change. Until then, do not pass untrusted values as the save path or name for IrGraph.draw, and restrict them to a fixed, safe set of characters.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers only the dot-to-pdf call in IrGraph.draw. Other places that build shell command strings are not addressed by this change. The diff does not show which release first contains the fix, so confirm the patched version from the vendor advisory. Passing arguments as a list prevents shell injection but does not stop a value that starts with a dash from being read as an option by dot.

fixtures.scenario: A service running paddlepaddle 2.6.0 calls IrGraph.draw, and a value that an outside party can influence ends up in that call.
A service calls IrGraph.draw only with fixed, developer-chosen values, or runs a release confirmed to contain the vendor fix, and does not build command text from external input.

citations.quote: Command injection in IrGraph.draw in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0
Command injection in IrGraph.draw in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the pdf conversion helper in IrGraph.draw so the dot tool is launched with an argument list and without shell execution. The file paths derived from the save path and name are no longer parsed by a shell, which removes the command injection.

patterns.title: Arbitrary file overwrite via path traversal in PaddlePaddle before 2.6
patterns.cause: The download helper in the paddle dataset common module builds its target directory and file name from the caller-supplied module name and optional save name without validating them. Values containing parent-directory segments could move the downloaded file outside the intended data home directory and overwrite an arbitrary file.
preconditions: The deployment uses paddlepaddle at a version earlier than 2.6.
An untrusted party can influence the module name or the save name passed to the dataset download helper.
The process has write permission to the file that the traversal reaches.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade paddlepaddle to version 2.6 or later. In code that calls the download helper, accept only module names and save names that match a strict allowlist of letters, digits, underscore, hyphen and limited separators, and reject any name containing parent-directory sequences. As defense in depth, resolve the final path to its canonical absolute form and confirm it stays inside the data home directory before writing. Run the process with the least write access it needs.
patterns.limitations: The patch uses a pattern match that raises an unhandled error on non-matching input instead of giving a clean rejection. The patterns still allow forward slashes, so an absolute-looking module name may not be fully blocked, and no canonical path containment check is added. Only the download helper is changed in this diff, so other file-writing code paths are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs paddlepaddle 2.5. An externally supplied name containing parent-directory segments is joined to an output directory and used for a write, so a file outside that directory is overwritten.

An application runs paddlepaddle 2.6 or later. Any externally supplied name is resolved to a canonical absolute path and rejected unless it lies inside the intended output directory, so no file outside it is written.

citations.quote: Arbitrary File Overwrite Via Path Traversal in paddlepaddle/paddle before 2.6

patch_review.observation: The fix adds regular-expression checks at the start of the download helper. The module name may only contain letters, digits, underscore, hyphen and slash, so it cannot hold dots or parent-directory segments. The save name may also contain dots but not two in a row. Non-matching input causes an unhandled error, and slashes are still allowed, so absolute-looking values are not fully blocked. The card's cause, prevention and limitations match this.

patterns.title: Gradio path traversal: local file include via user-supplied JSON in an API request
patterns.cause: A JSON value supplied by a remote user in an API request was not safely handled, so it could trigger a local file include on the server. The sources do not say which field or code path was affected.
preconditions: A vulnerable version of the gradio package is exposed to remote API requests.
The server accepts a user-supplied JSON value in an API request.
That value can influence which local file the server reads or includes.
patterns.prevention: Treat every JSON value from an API request as untrusted. Do not let such a value choose a local file location directly. Where a request value must refer to a file, resolve it to a canonical absolute path (for example with os.path.realpath()) and accept it only if it falls inside an explicitly allowed directory. Reject anything else. Also upgrade to a gradio release that includes the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that a local file include could be triggered remotely through a user-supplied JSON value. They do not name the vulnerable endpoint, the JSON field, the affected or fixed versions, or the exact validation the fix applies. The canonicalize-and-confine approach above is a general direction, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A remote client sends an API request whose JSON value points at a local file path outside the intended content area, and the server reads or includes that file because it trusts the value.

A remote client sends the same kind of API request, but the server canonicalizes the path from the JSON value, finds it outside the allowed directory, and rejects the request without reading the file.

citations.quote: A local file include could be remotely triggered in Gradio due to a vulnerable user-supplied JSON value in an API request.
Gradio Path Traversal vulnerability

patterns.title: Unneutralized input in generated pages in django CMS (CVE-2024-11319)
patterns.cause: The page_attribute template tag in django CMS sanitized the page title with tag stripping instead of HTML escaping. Stripping does not neutralize quotes or unclosed tag fragments, so a crafted title could inject attributes or script when the value was rendered in a page, causing cross-site scripting (CWE-79).
preconditions: The site runs an affected django-cms release (3.11.7, 3.11.8, 4.1.2 or 4.1.3, per the advisory).
A template renders the page title through the page_attribute tag.
An attacker, such as a user with permission to edit page titles, can store markup-bearing text in a page title that is later shown to other users.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a django-cms release that includes the upstream fix. The fix escapes every value returned by the page_attribute tag, except dates, with standard HTML escaping rather than stripping tags. When rendering untrusted text, use context-appropriate output escaping instead of tag removal, and add regression tests with payloads that contain quotes and unclosed tags. Review custom templates and tags that mark title values as safe or strip them manually.
patterns.limitations: The diff does not show which release first contains the fix, so confirm the fixed version in the project's release notes. Escaping at this tag does not protect other places where titles or other user-controlled fields are output without escaping. Titles already stored in the database are not changed, so the protection relies on escaping at output time.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs django-cms 4.1.3. Input that a visitor or editor can influence ends up in a generated page without proper neutralization, so a script supplied by an attacker can run in another user's browser.
A site runs a django-cms release that is not in the affected list. Custom page-generation code neutralizes externally influenced input for its output context before it appears in the page.

citations.quote: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS or 'Cross-site Scripting') vulnerability in django CMS Association django-cms allows Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).
This issue affects django-cms: 3.11.7, 3.11.8, 4.1.2, 4.1.3.

patch_review.observation: In the page_attribute tag's value lookup, the page title was handled with tag stripping while other attributes were escaped. The fix removes that special case so every non-date value gets standard HTML escaping. The tests now check that a script payload, an ampersand and a quote-plus-unclosed-tag payload all come out escaped. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Untrusted configuration files deserialized without validation in MobileViTV2 handling (CVE-2024-11392)
patterns.cause: Hugging Face Transformers shipped model conversion scripts, including the one for MobileViTV2, inside its release packages. These scripts read legacy checkpoint and configuration files with unsafe deserialization, so a crafted file can run arbitrary code as the user who runs the script. Nothing in the library needed these scripts at runtime, yet they were distributed and reachable.
preconditions: A user has a Transformers release that still contains the MobileViTV2 or another conversion script.
The user runs a conversion script on a configuration or checkpoint file that comes from an untrusted party.
The script loads that file with an unsafe deserializer such as pickle-based loading, without restricting what can be instantiated.
patterns.prevention: Do not ship one-off conversion tooling in release artifacts. Strip the conversion scripts from the models directory during the pre-release step so wheels no longer contain code that opens pickle or Torch bin files. Upgrade to a release built after this change. When a conversion must be run, use the repository source in an isolated environment, only on files from trusted sources, and prefer safe formats and safe loading modes.
patterns.limitations: The fix removes the scripts from release packages only. Source checkouts and older releases still contain them, and the scripts themselves are not made safe. The diff does not show the exact unsafe call in the MobileViTV2 script, and it does not change how the library loads configurations at runtime.

fixtures.scenario: A user downloads a MobileViTV2 configuration file from an untrusted source and loads it with Transformers. The configuration handling deserializes its contents without validating them, so a crafted file can run attacker-chosen code as the current user.

A user loads a MobileViTV2 configuration only from a trusted source, using a Transformers release that includes the fix. Content from any untrusted origin is validated as plain data before it is used, so no unvalidated content is deserialized.

citations.quote: The specific flaw exists within the handling of configuration files.
The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data.
User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a step to the pre-release process that deletes every model conversion script under the models directory, so release wheels no longer include code that opens pickle or Torch bin files. The scripts are not made safe and the library's runtime loading is unchanged, which is what the card describes.

patterns.title: Deserialization of untrusted model files in Hugging Face Transformers MaskFormer
patterns.cause: Transformers release packages shipped legacy checkpoint conversion scripts, including the one for MaskFormer. These scripts load old-format model files (pickle-based or Torch bin checkpoints) with unsafe deserialization. A crafted checkpoint passed to one of them can run attacker code as the current user. The weakness is the unsafe loader exposed in the distributed package, not missing validation in the core loading path.
preconditions: An affected Transformers release that still includes the model conversion scripts in the installed package.
A user runs a conversion script, such as the MaskFormer one, on a checkpoint file from an untrusted party.
The checkpoint is in an unsafe serialization format such as pickle or a Torch bin file that executes code on load.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a Transformers release built after the upstream change, which strips the conversion scripts from release wheels so the unsafe loaders are no longer shipped. Do not run conversion scripts, from a source checkout or elsewhere, on checkpoints you do not trust. Prefer safe tensor-only formats such as safetensors, and where legacy formats cannot be avoided, load them only in an isolated, low-privilege environment. Release engineers should keep a packaging step that excludes legacy conversion tooling that opens insecure file types.
patterns.limitations: The fix removes the scripts only from release artifacts. Source checkouts and older releases still contain them, and the scripts still load unsafe formats if run by hand. It does not harden the loaders themselves or change how the main model loading path treats untrusted files.

fixtures.scenario: A service lets users submit a MaskFormer model file and parses it with an affected Transformers installation without validating its contents. A crafted file leads to deserialization of untrusted data and code execution as the service user.

A service loads MaskFormer model files only from a source the team trusts and controls, on an updated Transformers release. It rejects user-submitted model files and runs the loader with minimal privileges.

citations.quote: The specific flaw exists within the parsing of model files.
The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data.
User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a step to the release preparation script that deletes every model conversion script (files whose names start with convert) under the models directory when a release or patch is prepared. This keeps the legacy loaders, which open pickle and Torch bin files, out of release wheels. It does not change the loaders or the core model loading path, which matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Untrusted Trax model files deserialized without validation in Transformers
patterns.cause: Legacy model conversion scripts shipped inside the Transformers release package, including one that converts Trax checkpoints. These scripts deserialize checkpoint files with unsafe mechanisms such as pickle, with no check on where the file came from. A crafted Trax model file passed to such a script can run arbitrary code as the current user.
preconditions: A Transformers release package that still contains the conversion scripts for older model formats is installed.
A user runs a conversion script, or code that imports it, on a Trax model file supplied by an untrusted party.
The file is deserialized with an unsafe format loader, so its contents can trigger code execution.
patterns.prevention: Do not ship conversion code that opens unsafe serialization formats in release packages. The upstream fix adds a step to the release process that deletes the conversion scripts under the models directory, so installed packages no longer contain them. Users should upgrade to a release built after this change, convert old checkpoints only from trusted sources and in an isolated environment, and prefer safe tensor formats over pickle based ones.
patterns.limitations: The fix removes the scripts from release builds only. The scripts remain in the source repository and in older releases, so anyone installing from source or running an old version stays exposed. It does not make the unsafe loading code safe, and the diff does not show the exact vulnerable function or the affected version range.

fixtures.scenario: An application downloads a Trax model file from an unknown third party and loads it with an affected Transformers version. The file contains attacker-crafted data, so loading it deserializes untrusted content and runs the attacker's code with the current user's privileges.

An application loads Trax model files only from a trusted, verified source, and the loading path validates the file data before deserializing it. The same application runs a Transformers version that includes the maintainers' fix, so a crafted file does not lead to code execution.

citations.quote: The specific flaw exists within the handling of model files.
The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data.
An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current user.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a pre-release step that deletes the model conversion scripts under the models directory, so release wheels no longer contain scripts that open unsafe formats such as pickle or Torch bin files. The card's cause, its prevention (strip the scripts from release builds), and its limitations (source and older releases remain affected) all match this change.

patterns.title: Gradio file parameter lets attackers probe internal ports through distinguishable responses
patterns.cause: The file route in gradio decided whether a path was a URL by calling a validation helper that sent a real network request from the server to the attacker-supplied address. If that request succeeded, the route returned a redirect with a Location header. Otherwise it fell through to a File not allowed error. The two outcomes let an attacker tell which internal hosts and ports were reachable, which is a blind SSRF port-scanning oracle. The redirect to an arbitrary URL is the open redirect side of the weakness.
preconditions: The gradio server is reachable by the attacker, who can send GET requests to the file route with an arbitrary value in the path.
The server can reach internal hosts or ports that the attacker cannot reach directly.
The attacker can observe whether the response is a redirect or a File not allowed error.
patterns.prevention: Never perform a network request from the server just to validate a client-supplied URL. Classify the value with a local, string-based check, such as whether it looks like an http or https URL, so that response behavior does not depend on whether the target is reachable. Keep any redirect or file-serving decision independent of remote reachability. If redirecting to external URLs is not required, restrict it to an allowlist or drop it. Upgrade gradio to a release that includes the fix for CVE-2024-1183.
patterns.limitations: The fix removes the reachability-dependent behavior, so the port-probing oracle is gone. A URL-like value still produces a redirect, so a plain open redirect to an attacker-chosen site may remain unless the route is restricted further. The exact affected version range is not shown in the diff.

fixtures.scenario: An attacker sends repeated GET requests to a gradio app, changing the file parameter to point at different internal addresses and ports. Some responses carry a Location header and others return a File not allowed error, so the attacker maps which internal ports are open.

The same requests are made, but the app checks the file parameter against what it is meant to serve and refuses all other values. Every refused request gets the same response whether or not the internal port is open, so the attacker learns nothing about the internal network.

citations.quote: By manipulating the 'file' parameter in a GET request, an attacker can discern the status of internal ports
based on the presence of a 'Location' header or a 'File not allowed' error in the response.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the call to a validation helper that made a real network request from the server with a local, string-based check on whether the value looks like an http or https URL. The redirect branch no longer depends on whether the target host or port is reachable, which removes the SSRF probing oracle.

patterns.title: Open redirect via unvalidated next parameter in login flow
patterns.cause: The login functionality of pyload-ng handles the next parameter improperly, so an attacker-supplied value can send users to an arbitrary external site after they interact with the login page.
preconditions: The application exposes a login endpoint that accepts a next parameter indicating where to send the user afterward
The affected version is pyload 0.5.0, before the fix in pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev79
A victim can be induced to follow an attacker-crafted login link containing a malicious next value
patterns.prevention: Treat the next parameter as untrusted input. Before redirecting, check that the target is a local path on the same site and not an absolute URL or a URL naming another host. Reject or ignore any value that fails the check and fall back to a fixed default page. Alternatively, map allowed destinations to server-side identifiers instead of accepting raw URLs. Upgrade to pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev79 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation the upstream fix applies, which URL forms were accepted by the vulnerable code, or whether other endpoints share the same weakness. The guidance above is general redirect-handling direction and not a description of the upstream change. Whether the redirect happens before or after authentication is not stated.

fixtures.scenario: A phishing email links to the pyload login page with a next parameter pointing to an attacker-controlled external site. The user logs in and the application redirects the browser to that external site, which imitates the real interface.

The login page receives a next parameter pointing to an external site. The application detects that the target is not a local path on the same site, discards it, and redirects the user to the default home page after login.

citations.quote: The vulnerability is due to improper handling of the 'next' parameter in the login functionality.
An attacker can exploit this vulnerability to redirect users to malicious sites, which can be used for phishing or other malicious activities.
The issue is fixed in pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev79.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops accepting a raw URL for the post-login destination. The next value is now treated as an application route name, resolved through the router, and any unknown value falls back to the dashboard. The login-required decorator now passes only the endpoint name, and the Referer header is no longer used as a redirect source. The older same-host URL check is dropped, since it could be bypassed.

patterns.title: ReDoS in the Nougat fast tokenizer post-processing of transformers
patterns.cause: In the huggingface/transformers file tokenization_nougat_fast.py, the post_process_single() function runs a regular expression over specially crafted input. The regex can show exponential time complexity under certain conditions, which causes excessive backtracking and very high CPU usage.
preconditions: The application uses transformers version 4.46.3, the affected version named in the advisories.
The application uses the Nougat fast tokenizer code in tokenization_nougat_fast.py.
post_process_single() is called on text that an attacker can craft or influence.
patterns.prevention: Do not run a regular expression that can backtrack exponentially over untrusted or model-generated text. Review the patterns used in post-processing and rewrite any that can backtrack heavily so their running time stays predictable. Upgrade to a transformers release that includes the upstream fix once it is available for your environment. Where possible, keep untrusted text from reaching this post-processing step without checks, and keep a CPU or time limit around it so one request cannot stall the service.
patterns.limitations: The sources name the affected file, function and version, but do not describe the exact regex, the triggering input shape, or how the upstream fix changes the pattern. They also do not list fixed versions or say how the crafted input reaches the function in a given deployment. The mitigations here are general directions, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A service uses transformers 4.46.3 and passes externally supplied text to the Nougat fast tokenizer post-processing. A crafted input makes the regex in post_process_single() backtrack excessively, so CPU stays pinned and the service becomes unresponsive.

A service uses a transformers release that includes the upstream fix, or a patched post-processing step whose pattern cannot backtrack exponentially. The same crafted input finishes in normal time, and the service keeps handling other requests.

citations.quote: The vulnerability occurs in the post_process_single() function, where a regular expression processes specially crafted input.
The issue stems from the regex exhibiting exponential time complexity under certain conditions, leading to excessive backtracking.
This can result in significantly high CPU usage and potential application downtime

patch_review.observation: The diff changes only the heading-removal pattern in post_process_single in the Nougat fast tokenizer. The old pattern repeated a group that itself contained a repeated alternative, a nested quantifier that backtracks exponentially on long digit or numeral runs. The new pattern removes that nesting by using simple, non-nested repeats, so matching time stays predictable.

patterns.title: SQL injection via prompt injection in the LlamaIndex JSON query engine
patterns.cause: The JSON query engine in llama-index core took SQL written by an LLM from prompt content an attacker could influence and ran it on an in-process SQLite database with no sandboxing or validation. Prompt injection could therefore steer the executed SQL, which allows arbitrary file creation on the host and resource exhaustion. The upstream fix does not harden the SQL path. It removes the engine from core, replaces it with a stub that raises a deprecation error, and relocates the unchanged logic to the experimental package with an explicit warning that it is unsafe outside a sandbox.
preconditions: The application builds the JSON query engine from llama-index core, in a version before the one that removed it.
An untrusted party can influence the natural language question or the data that the LLM turns into SQL.
The generated SQL is executed directly against SQLite on a host where the process may write files and use resources freely.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade llama-index core to a release that no longer ships a working JSON query engine, at least 0.12.3, and treat the experimental package at 0.5.1 or later as the only home of this feature. Do not expose the engine to untrusted users or untrusted prompts. If you must use the experimental version, run it only inside a sandbox or virtual machine with no sensitive files, restrict filesystem write access and resource limits for the process, and do not rely on the library to validate generated SQL. For production use, prefer a design that never executes model-written SQL, or that executes it only against a read-only, isolated in-memory store with an allow-list of statements.
patterns.limitations: The fix relocates and deprecates the engine rather than making it safe, so the experimental package keeps the same risk by design. Code that imported the engine from core will now fail until it is migrated. The sources disagree on the fixed version: the GitHub advisory names 0.12.3 for core and the CVE record names 0.5.1, which matches the experimental package bump. Use the higher core version and confirm against the release notes. Other query engines that execute generated SQL were not examined.

fixtures.scenario: A chat application passes user questions to JSONalyzeQueryEngine on an unpatched llama-index. A user embeds instructions in the question, and the generated SQL is altered to create files or exhaust resources on the host.

The application runs a llama-index version that includes the fix, at least 0.12.3. It treats user-derived query text as untrusted and runs the engine in a process with restricted file and resource permissions. The same malicious question does not result in file creation or denial of service.

citations.quote: allows for SQL injection via prompt injection. This can lead to arbitrary file creation and Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks.
The vulnerability affects the latest version and is fixed in version 0.12.3.
The vulnerability affects the latest version and is fixed in version 0.5.1.
LlamaIndex vulnerable to Creation of Temporary File in Directory with Insecure Permissions

patch_review.observation: The fix does not harden the SQL path. It replaces the core JSON query engine with a stub whose constructor raises a deprecation warning, and moves the original logic essentially unchanged (97 percent similarity) into the experimental package. The moved module gets a warning that LLM-generated SQL run on SQLite can create arbitrary files and needs heavy sandboxing, and the experimental package version is bumped to 0.5.1. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Unvalidated file paths in Gradio upload requests allow arbitrary file read
patterns.cause: The UploadButton handling of file upload paths did not properly validate user-supplied input. An attacker who intercepts and modifies the network request to the queue join endpoint can change the file path and make the server read or place files in unintended locations, such as private SSH keys.
preconditions: The Gradio application runs a version older than 4.19.2
The application is reachable by untrusted users, for example through a public link or Hugging Face Spaces
The attacker can intercept and modify the requests the Gradio front end sends to the server
patterns.prevention: Treat every file path that arrives in a client request as untrusted. Do not let the client choose which server-side file is read or where an upload lands. Check the path on the server against the directories the application is meant to expose, and reject anything outside them before any file access. Upgrade Gradio to version 4.19.2 or higher, which contains the fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation flaw, the request fields involved, or how the patch works. They give no detail on which directories are safe or how the check should be written. The claim that remote code execution is possible is stated only as a potential outcome.

fixtures.scenario: A public Gradio app uses an upload button. An attacker edits the request sent to the queue join endpoint so the file path points to a private SSH key on the host, and the server accepts the path and returns the file.
The server treats the submitted path as untrusted and checks it against the allowed locations. A path pointing outside them is rejected, and the app runs Gradio 4.19.2 or higher.

citations.quote: access files on the machine hosting the Gradio application
improper validation of user-supplied input in the UploadButton component
allowing attackers to redirect file uploads to unintended locations on the server
Yes, the problem has been patched in Gradio version 4.19.2 or higher.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the input preprocessing path. When a request comes from the network rather than a direct call to the Blocks function, any non-URL file path in the payload must lie inside the configured upload folder, or a ValueError is raised before the file is copied into the cache. A shared helper now provides the upload folder, and an explicit-call flag lets internal calls skip the check. This matches the card's cause (unvalidated client-supplied paths) and its prevention (server-side check against allowed directories, reject anything outside).

patterns.title: ReDoS in Scrapy XML node iteration and open_in_browser from regex-based parsing of untrusted responses
patterns.cause: Scrapy used vulnerable regular expressions to parse response content in two places: the default iternodes node iterator (used by XMLFeedSpider and its subclasses, and by direct calls to scrapy.utils.iterators.xmliter), and, in Scrapy 2.6.0 to 2.11.0, open_in_browser for a response with no base tag. A crafted response makes the regular expression engine do inefficient work, which causes extreme CPU and memory usage and can hang the process.
preconditions: The application uses XMLFeedSpider or a subclass with the default iternodes iterator, or calls scrapy.utils.iterators.xmliter directly.
Alternatively, on Scrapy 2.6.0 to 2.11.0, the application calls open_in_browser on a response that has no base tag.
An attacker can influence the response content that is parsed, for example through a malicious or compromised site or feed being crawled.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Scrapy 2.11.1, or to Scrapy 1.8.4 if on 1.8 or lower and the upgrade to 2.11.1 is not possible. As an interim workaround for XMLFeedSpider, switch the node iterator from the default to the xml or html iterator. For open_in_browser, either review the response content before calling it or define the base tag manually so that the automatic definition is not triggered. In general, avoid parsing untrusted markup with regular expressions that can backtrack heavily, and prefer a real parser or bounded patterns.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the exact vulnerable patterns, the input shapes that trigger them, or the size at which the slowdown becomes severe, so this card cannot describe attack payloads. They do not say whether the xml and html iterators are free of every similar issue, only that switching to them is a listed workaround. The manual review workaround for open_in_browser is vague about what to look for. The sources do not say whether other Scrapy parsing code is affected, nor whether open_in_browser is affected in versions older than 2.6.0 (the advisory only lists 2.6.0 to 2.11.0).

fixtures.scenario: A crawler uses an XMLFeedSpider subclass with the default iternodes iterator to process feeds fetched from third-party servers. One server returns a specially crafted XML body, and the worker spends extreme CPU and memory in node iteration and stops serving other requests.

The same crawler runs Scrapy 2.11.1 or later (or 1.8.4 on the 1.8 line). If it must stay on an older release, the spider is configured to use the xml or html node iterator instead of the default, so the crafted body does not cause runaway resource use.

citations.quote: Handling a malicious response could cause extreme CPU and memory usage during the parsing of its content
Upgrade to Scrapy 2.11.1.
either manually review the response content to discard a ReDos attack or manually define the base tag
By crafting malicious XML content that exploits inefficient regular expression complexity used in the parsing process, an attacker can cause a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the default node iterator used by XMLFeedSpider from the regex-based xmliter to the lxml-based xmliter_lxml. It also deprecates xmliter with a ReDoS warning, and backports this to the 1.8 line. For open_in_browser, it replaces the backtracking comment-stripping and head-tag regexes with a plain string-search comment remover and a tighter, single-substitution head pattern, with timing tests for both inputs.

patterns.title: Server-side request forgery in TFIDFRetriever load_local (langchain-community 0.0.26)
patterns.cause: The load_local function of TFIDFRetriever loads a vectorizer and documents from joblib and pickle files in a local folder without any safeguard. These formats can execute arbitrary code during loading, so a crafted or modified file leads to code execution on the host. The CVE title calls this server-side request forgery, but the upstream fix addresses unsafe deserialization of untrusted files.
preconditions: The application uses langchain-community 0.0.26 or an earlier version without the opt-in flag.
The application calls load_local on TFIDFRetriever with a folder path.
An attacker can place or modify the saved joblib or pickle files that load_local reads, for example through a shared, uploaded or otherwise untrusted storage location.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade langchain-community to 0.0.27 or later, where load_local raises an error unless the caller sets the allow_dangerous_deserialization argument to true. Only set that argument when the saved files come from a trusted source that attackers cannot write to, and consider verifying file integrity before loading. Never load retriever files that come from users or untrusted storage.
patterns.limitations: The fix is an explicit opt-in guard and does not make the loading of pickle or joblib files safe. Callers who enable the flag still face code execution if the files are untrusted. Existing callers must update their code to pass the flag, and the fix does not validate file contents or provenance.

fixtures.scenario: A service pins langchain-community 0.0.26 and uses TFIDFRetriever load_local in a way that remote users can influence. The service is exposed to server-side request forgery.
The same service is upgraded to langchain-community 0.0.27 or later, and the dependency lock file and deployed image are checked to confirm the old version is gone.

citations.quote: Affected is the function load_local in the library libs/community/langchain_community/retrievers/tfidf.py of the component TFIDFRetriever.
The manipulation leads to server-side request forgery.
Upgrading to version 0.0.27 is able to address this issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the load_local method of TFIDFRetriever so it takes a keyword-only opt-in flag that defaults to false. Unless the caller sets it, the method raises an error before reading the joblib and pickle files, because those formats can run arbitrary code on load. The card's cause (unsafe deserialization of untrusted local files) and its prevention (upgrade, opt in only for trusted files) match this change, even though the CVE title says server-side request forgery.

patterns.title: Stored XSS via attacker-controlled href on anchor elements in Dash apps
patterns.cause: Dash HTML and core components put user- or data-controlled URL values straight into the DOM without checking the URL scheme. An attacker-supplied value with a script-executing scheme (such as a javascript URL) in href on anchors and dcc.Link, action on forms, formAction on buttons, src on iframes and embeds, or data on objects runs in the victim's browser. If the value is stored in app state or a saved view, other users who reload it are affected.
preconditions: The app runs an affected Dash release (before 2.15.0) or older dash-html-components and dash-core-components.
An attacker can influence the value of a URL-type property such as href, action, formAction, src, or data on a rendered component.
The app stores or echoes that value so another user's browser later renders it, for example through a saved view.
The victim clicks the link or submits the form, or the element loads automatically as with iframes, embeds and objects.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade dash to 2.15.0 or later and use the matching fixed dash-html-components and dash-core-components releases. The fix sanitizes these URL properties on the client, replacing dangerous schemes with a blank page URL and reporting an error. As defense in depth, validate or allow-list URL schemes on the server for any value that reaches these properties, and do not build these properties from untrusted stored data.
patterns.limitations: The client-side sanitizer depends on a third-party URL sanitizing library and covers only the listed components and properties. Other components or custom components that take URLs are not protected by this change. Server-side validation of stored values is still advisable. Affected version ranges differ slightly between advisories.

fixtures.scenario: A Dash app lets signed-in users save a view and share it. The saved state sets the href of an anchor tag from user input. The app runs dash 2.14. Another user opens the shared view and the attacker's script runs in that user's session.
The app runs dash 2.15.0 or later with fixed component packages, and saved view data is never used to set an anchor href. A user opening a shared view only sees content the app itself controls.

citations.quote: are vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting (XSS) when the href of the a tag is controlled by an adversary.
This is only exploitable in Dash apps that include some mechanism to store user input to be reloaded by a different user.
versions of the package dash before 2.15.0

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a URL sanitizing library to the generated html components (anchor, form, button, iframe, object, embed) and to the core Link component, so dangerous schemes like javascript are replaced with a blank page URL and a front-end error is reported through the renderer. An integration test confirms the affected properties become a blank page URL.

patterns.title: XSS in djangorestframework via the break_long_headers template filter
patterns.cause: The break_long_headers template filter splits a header value and joins the pieces with line break tags, but the input is not properly sanitized before this step. Untrusted header content can therefore end up in rendered HTML as active markup.
preconditions: The application uses a djangorestframework version before 3.15.2.
A template renders content through the break_long_headers template filter.
The value passed to the filter can be influenced by an attacker, for example a request header value.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade djangorestframework to version 3.15.2 or later. In any custom filter that inserts line break tags into text, neutralize the untrusted input first by escaping it for HTML output, and only then split and join the pieces, so that only the intended break tags are treated as markup. Avoid marking the combined result as safe before the input has been escaped.
patterns.limitations: The sources only name the break_long_headers filter, the improper sanitization before splitting and joining with line break tags, and the fixed version 3.15.2. They do not describe which inputs reach the filter in practice, how exploitation is carried out, or what the exact upstream change is, so the escaping direction above is general guidance rather than a description of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs djangorestframework 3.15.1 and renders a page that passes a header value containing markup through the break_long_headers filter. The value is split and joined with line break tags without proper sanitization, so the markup reaches the page unescaped.

An application runs djangorestframework 3.15.2 or later, or uses a custom filter that escapes the header value for HTML before splitting and joining it with line break tags. Markup in the header value is shown as text and not interpreted by the browser.

citations.quote: Versions of the package djangorestframework before 3.15.2 are vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting (XSS) via the break_long_headers template filter

due to improper input sanitization before splitting and joining with
tags.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the break_long_headers filter so the header value is HTML-escaped before it is split on commas and rejoined with line break tags. Previously the raw value was split and joined and then marked safe, so attacker-controlled markup in a long header was rendered as active HTML. Escaping first leaves only the intended break tags as markup, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Unvalidated client-supplied URLs added to proxy target set enable SSRF in gradio
patterns.cause: The root and config routes derived the application's root URL from the client-controlled X-Direct-Url header and stored it in the shared app config. File and proxy URLs were then built from that attacker-influenced root, so a crafted header could steer later server-side proxy requests toward arbitrary hosts. The root was also rewritten on every request instead of being fixed once.
preconditions: The application serves the root and config routes and trusts the X-Direct-Url request header when computing its root URL.
The computed root is saved in shared configuration that later influences which URLs the proxy or file routes will fetch.
An unauthenticated client can send arbitrary request headers to these routes.
patterns.prevention: Never take the application root or any proxy target base from a client request header. Derive it from the server's own request URL or fixed configuration, and set it once instead of overwriting shared config per request. Build file and proxy URLs on the server side and hand finished URLs to clients, rather than letting client code assemble them from a root value. Treat forwarding-style headers as trusted only when they come from a known reverse proxy.
patterns.limitations: The shown diff does not include the proxy route itself, so any extra destination validation there cannot be confirmed from it. Affected and fixed version ranges are not stated. The change is also a broad refactor of URL handling across components, so it is not a minimal patch for this one weakness.

fixtures.scenario: A client sends a request to the config route with a header naming an internal address. The server adds it to its trusted replica URL set. The client then calls the proxy route with that address, and the server fetches the internal endpoint.

The trusted proxy target set is fixed by server configuration and ignores client headers. A request naming an internal address is rejected when the proxy request is built, because the address is not on the allowlist.

citations.quote: An SSRF vulnerability exists in the gradio-app/gradio due to insufficient validation of user-supplied URLs
allowing the addition of arbitrary URLs for proxying
potential access to internal endpoints within the Hugging Face space

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the use of the client-controlled X-Direct-Url header when computing the app root in the root and config routes. It now derives the root from the request URL and sets it only once in the shared config. It also moves file and proxy URL construction to the server by adding URLs during file caching and prefixing the root on outputs, and it drops the client-side function that assembled these URLs from a root value.

patterns.title: HTML attribute injection through user-controlled keys in the Jinja xmlattr filter
patterns.cause: The xmlattr filter in affected Jinja versions accepts attribute keys that contain spaces. Each space-separated part is then read by the browser as a separate attribute. When keys come from user input, an attacker can inject arbitrary attributes and keys, which bypasses autoescaping and can lead to XSS.
preconditions: The application uses the xmlattr filter on a mapping rendered into HTML or XML.
Attribute keys, not only values, come from user input.
The rendered page is viewed by other users.
A vulnerable Jinja version is in use.
patterns.prevention: Do not let untrusted input choose attribute keys passed to the xmlattr filter. Check each key against a fixed allowlist of known attribute names before rendering, and reject keys with spaces or other unexpected characters. Do not rely on a blacklist of dangerous attributes, since blacklist-based checks may be bypassed. Upgrade Jinja to a release that includes the upstream fix as defense in depth, and keep validating keys anyway.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the fixed Jinja version or describe the exact characters the fix rejects. They do not detail how blacklist checks are bypassed. Attribute values and other contexts are not covered. Accepting user keys is described as an uncommon use of the filter.

fixtures.scenario: A profile page builds an attribute mapping from user-submitted names and values and renders it with the xmlattr filter. A key containing a space adds a second attribute, such as an event handler, which runs for other viewers.
The page accepts only keys from a fixed allowlist, and user input supplies values only. A submitted key with a space or an unknown name is rejected before rendering, so no extra attribute is created.

citations.quote: XML/HTML attributes cannot contain spaces, as each would then be interpreted as a separate attribute.
an application doing so should already be verifying what keys are provided regardless of this fix.
It may also be possible to bypass attribute validation checks if they are blacklist-based.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the xmlattr filter raise a ValueError when any attribute key contains ASCII whitespace, so a key cannot be split into several injected attributes. It was released in 3.1.3 with a regression test, and values are still escaped as before. This matches the card's cause (keys with spaces are accepted) and its prevention (validate keys and upgrade).

patterns.title: Directory traversal in Salt syndic cache directory creation
patterns.cause: Syndic cache directory creation in Salt is vulnerable to a directory traversal attack. The path used to create the cache directory is not confined to its intended location, so a malicious user can cause an arbitrary directory to be created on a Salt master.
preconditions: A Salt master creates syndic cache directories.
A malicious user or attacker can influence the path used for syndic cache directory creation.
The directory creation step does not keep the final path inside the intended cache location.
patterns.prevention: Before creating a cache directory, resolve the final path and confirm it is still inside the intended cache root. Reject any value that would escape that root, such as one containing parent-directory components or path separators. Prefer treating externally supplied identifiers as a single plain name rather than as a path. Upgrade to a Salt release that contains the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief. They do not say which input carries the traversal sequence, which Salt component supplies it, or whether authentication is needed. They do not list affected or fixed versions, and they do not describe how the upstream fix works. The prevention guidance is the general approach for directory traversal, not a description of the upstream change. The sources only describe arbitrary directory creation, not file read or write.

fixtures.scenario: A Salt master builds a syndic cache directory path from a name supplied by a malicious user. The name contains parent-directory components, so the directory is created outside the cache area at a location the attacker chose.

A Salt master builds the syndic cache directory path from a supplied name, resolves the full path, and checks that it stays inside the cache root. A name that would escape the root is rejected and no directory is created.

citations.quote: Syndic cache directory creation is vulnerable to a directory traversal attack in salt project
create an arbitrary directory on a Salt master

patch_review.observation: In the master's syndic return handler, the cache path is built from the syndic id supplied by the caller. The fix now checks that this path stays inside the syndics cache root, using the clean_path verification helper, before creating any directory. The same commit also adds root-confinement checks to the roots fileserver, which is a separate traversal issue, but the syndic change matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Directory traversal through a crafted url in the Salt file server
patterns.cause: The fileserver validated the requested path for absolute paths and parent-directory sequences before the escaped-url prefix was removed. A crafted escaped url could therefore slip past the check and, once unescaped, resolve outside the served root. The roots backend then joined the path to the root and opened it without confirming it stayed inside the root, and the serving step trusted the located path. The master also built a syndic cache path from a requester-supplied id without containment checking.
preconditions: A Salt master serves files through the roots fileserver backend and accepts file requests whose path is chosen by the requester.
The requester can send a path using the escaped-url form that hides parent-directory sequences or an absolute path until after the early validation has run.
Requester-supplied identifiers such as a syndic id are joined into filesystem paths without a containment check.
patterns.prevention: Normalize and unescape untrusted request paths first, and only then apply rejection rules for absolute paths and parent-directory sequences. Enforce containment at the point of use: in both the file lookup and the file serving steps, verify that the final joined path lies under one of the configured file roots using a path-containment helper, and skip or refuse anything outside. Apply the same containment check to any path built from requester-supplied identifiers, such as a syndic id used for a cache directory. Do not rely on a single early text check of the raw request.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the roots backend and the syndic cache path; other fileserver backends rely on their own handling and are not changed here. Path-containment checks based on normalization do not by themselves address symbolic links that point outside a root. Exact affected and fixed versions are not shown in this diff.

fixtures.scenario: A user sends the Salt file server a crafted url, and the server maps it to a file outside the served directories. The user reads an arbitrary file from the master filesystem.
The file server resolves each requested url to a canonical path, checks that it is under the configured file server root, and refuses any request that resolves elsewhere.

citations.quote: A specially crafted url can be created which leads to a directory traversal in the salt file server.
A malicious user can read an arbitrary file from a Salt master

patch_review.observation: The fix moves the absolute-path and parent-directory rejection in the fileserver lookup to after the escaped-url prefix is removed, so a crafted escaped url no longer slips past it. It also adds a containment check in the roots backend for both file lookup and file serving, and a containment check on the syndic cache path built from the requester-supplied id in the master.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through Markdown preview in JupyterLab (CVE-2024-22420)
patterns.cause: The table of contents code in JupyterLab derived heading anchor IDs by asking the Markdown parser for HTML and inserting that unsanitized HTML into a DOM element. The derived ID was also interpolated into a CSS attribute selector without escaping. A crafted heading in a Markdown cell or Markdown file could therefore run script or break out of the selector when the table of contents or heading navigation processed it, giving the attacker the victim's privileges in the session.
preconditions: The victim runs a JupyterLab release older than 4.0.11 (or the matching notebook release line that bundles the same code).
The victim opens a malicious notebook with Markdown cells, or a malicious Markdown file, so its headings are processed by the table of contents.
The table of contents extension is active, or heading navigation in the notebook is used, so the heading ID computation runs on attacker-controlled text.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to JupyterLab 4.0.11 or later, or disable the table of contents extension as a stopgap. In code, never treat the output of a Markdown parser as safe HTML: render it through the sanitizing renderer with the content marked untrusted before reading anything from it, and pass the application sanitizer to every component that derives IDs or text from Markdown. Escape any value taken from document content before placing it in a CSS selector, using the standard escape helper. Open notebooks and Markdown files from untrusted sources only after the fix or workaround is in place.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows the fix in the heading ID helper and the selector construction for notebooks and Markdown files. It does not show the exact exploit payload, and it does not show whether other rendering paths outside the table of contents were affected. Fixed release numbers for the notebook package are not visible in the diff.

fixtures.scenario: A user on JupyterLab 4.0.10 with the table of contents extension enabled opens a notebook from an untrusted source. One Markdown cell contains attacker-written content. Viewing it in the preview feature lets the attacker read data the user can access and send requests as the user.

A user on JupyterLab 4.0.11 or later opens the same notebook in the preview feature. Alternatively, a user who cannot upgrade has disabled the table of contents extension first. The Markdown content does not run as attacker-controlled active content, and the user's data and session stay protected.

citations.quote: The vulnerability depends on user interaction by opening a malicious notebook with Markdown cells, or Markdown file using JupyterLab preview feature.
A malicious user can access any data that the attacked user has access to as well as perform arbitrary requests acting as the attacked user.
JupyterLab version 4.0.11 has been patched. Users are advised to upgrade. Users unable to upgrade should disable the table of contents extension.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the heading ID helper so it no longer inserts raw parser HTML into a DOM element. It now renders through the sanitizing markdown renderer with content marked untrusted and a sanitizer passed in by the callers (markdown viewer, notebook table of contents, notebook widget). It also escapes the derived ID before using it in CSS attribute selectors in all three places.

patterns.title: Token exposure through a malicious link in JupyterLab running with an older jupyter-server
patterns.cause: JupyterLab client code built request URLs by joining a fixed API base with an identifier that could be attacker-influenced, such as a workspace id, setting id, session id, terminal name, locale or hub server name, without checking the result. A dot-dot segment in the identifier let the final URL climb out of the intended API path and point at a different server endpoint. Combined with an older jupyter-server that has a redirect weakness, a crafted link could make authenticated requests reach an endpoint that sends the user's Authorization and XSRF tokens to a third party. The root weakness in JupyterLab is path traversal in client-side URL construction.
preconditions: The deployment runs a JupyterLab release older than the patched versions (4.1.0b2, 4.0.11 or 3.6.7).

An attacker can influence an identifier that JupyterLab places into a URL path, for example through a crafted link that opens a workspace or addresses a settings, session, terminal or translation resource.
The jupyter-server in use is older than 2.7.2 and has the redirect weakness, so the escaped request can lead to token exposure.
A user follows the malicious link while authenticated.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade JupyterLab to a patched release and upgrade jupyter-server to 2.7.2 or newer. In code that builds URLs, treat identifiers as untrusted path segments: join the fixed base first, then add the identifier, and reject the request if the normalized result is not still inside the base. Prefer validating or encoding each identifier so it cannot contain path separators or dot-dot segments, and apply the same check at every call site that builds API URLs.
patterns.limitations: The fix is a containment check on the joined URL string at several call sites, so any call site that builds URLs another way is not covered. Parts of the patch look imperfect: the workspace navigation check compares the base against the full URL in the opposite direction, and the hub extension restart URL logic overrides the server-name branch. The server-side redirect weakness is fixed separately in jupyter-server, so this change alone does not remove the exposure. The sources do not state a patched notebook version.

fixtures.scenario: An administrator runs a JupyterLab release older than 4.0.11 on a jupyter-server older than 2.7.2. A user clicks a link crafted by an attacker, and the user's Authorization and XSRF tokens may be exposed to a third party.

An administrator runs JupyterLab 4.0.11 or a later patched release on jupyter-server 2.7.2 or newer. The same malicious link does not expose the user's tokens, because both the JupyterLab patch and the redirect fix are present.

citations.quote: JupyterLab versions 4.1.0b2, 4.0.11, and 3.6.7 are patched.
to version 2.7.2 or newer which includes a redirect vulnerability fix.
Users of JupyterLab who click on a malicious link may get their

patch_review.observation: The fix changes each client-side URL builder so it first joins the fixed API base, then appends the identifier, and throws if the resulting URL no longer starts with the base. This covers the workspace, settings, session, terminal, translation, workspace navigation and hub spawn call sites, and the tests check that a dot-dot identifier is rejected. The card describes this cause and prevention correctly, including the flaws in the workspace navigation check and the hub restart logic.

patterns.title: Directory traversal in aiohttp static routes when symlink following is enabled
patterns.cause: With follow_symlinks enabled, the static route skipped the check that the requested path stays under the static root. The joined path was resolved on the filesystem with no containment check, so a request containing parent-directory segments could reach files outside the root, even with no symlinks present. The fix collapses those segments lexically before resolving and requires the result to be under the root.
preconditions: aiohttp serves a static route with a configured root directory
The follow_symlinks option on that route is set to true
The aiohttp version is older than 3.9.2
The server accepts raw requests from remote users that contain parent-directory segments
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to aiohttp 3.9.2 or later. When building a file path from user input, normalize it lexically first, collapsing parent-directory segments, and confirm the normalized path is still under the static root before resolving symlinks or opening the file. Do not rely only on checking the symlink-resolved path against the root, because that would also reject legitimate symlinks that leave the root. Avoid enabling follow_symlinks on internet-facing servers, and prefer serving static files from a reverse proxy such as nginx in production.
patterns.limitations: Symlinks that point outside the root remain reachable by design when follow_symlinks is on, so a misplaced symlink in the static tree still exposes its target. The lexical check does not remove the risk from a symlink that points outside the root. Setups that leave follow_symlinks disabled were not affected by this issue.

fixtures.scenario: A public aiohttp application registers a static route for a static directory with follow_symlinks set to true and runs a version older than 3.9.2. A remote client requests a path that resolves outside the static root, and the server returns the contents of an unrelated file on the host.

The application registers the static route without enabling follow_symlinks, runs aiohttp 3.9.2 or later, and has a reverse proxy serve static assets in production. Requests for paths outside the static root are not served.

citations.quote: When 'follow_symlinks' is set to True, there is no validation to check if a given file path is within the root directory.
This option is NOT needed to follow symlinks which point to a location _within_ the static root directory
Disabling follow_symlinks and using a reverse proxy are encouraged mitigations.
Version 3.9.2 fixes this issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes both the file-serving handler and the URL-building helper in the static route. When symlink following is on, it now collapses parent-directory segments lexically, requires the result to be under the static root, and only then resolves the path. Previously no containment check ran in that mode. The new tests use raw requests with parent-directory segments, with and without a symlink inside the root, and expect a not-found response.

patterns.title: Open redirect after login via URL that the parser treats as relative but the client normalizes to an external host
patterns.cause: After login, pyload-ng checks the next value with a safe-URL check inside the redirect helper before redirecting the user. The check relies on urlparse. For an unusual URL such as https:///example.com, urlparse treats it as a relative path, so it passes. The actual request then normalizes it to https://example.com, so the user is sent to an arbitrary domain. The parser and the client disagree about what the URL means.
preconditions: The application redirects the user after login to a destination taken from a user-controlled next parameter.
The safe-URL check decides whether the target is local based on how urlparse classifies it.
An attacker can get a victim to follow a login link carrying a crafted next value.
patterns.prevention: Do not trust the parser's classification of a redirect target alone. Validate it the way the client will interpret it. Treat malformed or unusual absolute-URL forms, such as a scheme followed by an empty host and extra slashes, as untrusted instead of as relative paths. Either normalize the value first and then compare its host with the application's own host, or reject anything that is not a plain local path. Fall back to a fixed default page when the check fails.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the contents of the upstream patch, the affected version range, or any bypass forms beyond the one example. This card does not claim that blocking that single form is sufficient. The sources say only that validation of the next value was incorrect.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens a login link whose next value is https:///example.com. The safe-URL check parses it as a relative path and accepts it. After login the browser normalizes it to https://example.com and lands on the attacker's site, which can be used for phishing.

A user opens a login link with the same next value. The validator rejects the malformed absolute-URL form, or normalizes it and sees that the host is not the application's own. The user is sent to the default page after login instead of the external site.

citations.quote: Open redirect vulnerability due to incorrect validation of input values when redirecting users after login.
The documentation in the urllib library shows that improper URLs are recognized as relative paths when using the
interprets it as a relative path, but in the actual request it is converted to

patch_review.observation: The fix stops treating the next value as a free-form URL. The login redirect now accepts only a route name, resolves it to a server-side path, and falls back to the dashboard otherwise. The safe-URL helper also rejects scheme-style values with an empty host that do not start with a slash, which blocks the triple-slash form the card describes.

patterns.title: Unsanitized imported task data rendered in Choices or Labels tags enables stored XSS
patterns.cause: Data imported through the file upload feature is not properly sanitized before it is rendered within a Choices or Labels tag. Markup supplied in an imported task field is therefore treated as active page content instead of inert text, so script can run in the browser of whoever opens the task.
preconditions: Label Studio version earlier than 1.11.0 is in use
The attacker has permission to use the data import function
The project labeling config renders imported values through a Choices or Labels tag
A user opens a task whose imported data contains attacker-supplied markup
patterns.prevention: Treat every value in imported task data as untrusted, whatever the file source. Sanitize or escape it for the HTML context before it is rendered in Choices or Labels output, so markup and event handler attributes are never interpreted as live content. Apply the protection at render time as well as at import. Upgrade to Label Studio 1.11.0 or later, since the advisory names earlier versions as affected.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so the exact sanitization method and library are unknown. They do not say whether other tags or import paths are affected, or whether any mitigation exists besides upgrading. The proof of concept was reproduced only on version 1.10.1 with one template.

fixtures.scenario: A user with data import permission uploads a task file whose image field holds HTML with an event handler attribute. A labeling config using Choices or Labels renders it unsanitized, and the script runs when another user opens the task.

The same task file is uploaded, but imported values are sanitized before rendering in Choices or Labels. The markup appears as inert text or is stripped of active content, and no script runs when the task is opened.

citations.quote: On all Label Studio versions prior to 1.11.0, data imported via file upload feature is not properly sanitized prior to being rendered
Malicious scripts can be injected into the code, and when linked with vulnerabilities such as CSRF, it can cause even greater damage.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS on the Flask-AppBuilder OAuth login page via crafted URL
patterns.cause: In Flask-AppBuilder 4.1.4 through 4.2.0, the OAuth login template placed the next query parameter from the request into an inline JavaScript string and marked it as safe. That disabled automatic escaping, so a crafted next value could close the string and run attacker script in the victim's browser. This is a reflected XSS issue (CWE-79).
preconditions: The application runs Flask-AppBuilder 4.1.4 up to and including 4.2.0 with OAuth login enabled.
The OAuth login page is reachable and renders the default login template.
An attacker can get a user to open a login URL with a crafted next parameter.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Flask-AppBuilder to 4.2.1 or later, where the template no longer disables escaping for the next value. More generally, never mark request-derived values as safe, especially inside script blocks. Pass such values through the template engine's normal escaping, or serialize them as JSON for script contexts. Also validate the redirect target against local paths.
patterns.limitations: The fix relies on default autoescaping inside a quoted script string. That is adequate for this case but is not a full defense for every script context. Deployments that override the login template or copy the old template into their own code remain vulnerable until they make the same change. This fix does not add validation of the redirect target.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs Flask-AppBuilder 4.2.0 with OAuth login enabled. An attacker sends a user a specially crafted link to the OAuth login page, and script code embedded in the URL runs in the user's browser.
The application runs Flask-AppBuilder 4.2.1 or newer. The same crafted link to the OAuth login page does not result in injected JavaScript executing in the user's browser.

citations.quote: An attacker could trick a user to follow a specially crafted URL to the OAuth login page.
This issue was introduced on 4.1.4 and patched on 4.2.1, user's should upgrade to 4.2.1 or newer versions.

patch_review.observation: The fix edits the OAuth login template so the next query parameter is no longer passed through the filter that marks it as safe.
