With the default autoescaping restored, a crafted value can no longer break out of the quoted script string. This matches the card's cause (request-derived value marked safe inside an inline script) and its prevention (stop disabling escaping for it).

patterns.title: Template variable XSS in MLflow recipe output escalating to client-side RCE in Jupyter
patterns.cause: MLflow did not sufficiently sanitize template variables when rendering content for a recipe. Values controlled by an untrusted recipe could therefore be emitted as active markup or script in the rendered output, producing cross-site scripting.
preconditions: A user runs an untrusted recipe with an affected MLflow version
Recipe-controlled values are inserted into a template without sanitization
For the client-side RCE impact, the recipe is run and its output rendered in a Jupyter Notebook
patterns.prevention: Treat every template variable as untrusted data and neutralize it for the output context before it is placed into rendered content, for example by relying on the template engine's automatic escaping or by explicitly escaping each value. Do not run recipes from untrusted sources, particularly in Jupyter Notebook, and upgrade to a MLflow release that contains the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that sanitization of template variables was insufficient. They do not name the affected template, the exact output context, the affected version range, or the specific escaping method used by the fix, so this card does not cover those details.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens an untrusted recipe in a Jupyter Notebook. A value defined by the recipe is placed into a template without sanitization, and the rendered output runs attacker-chosen script in the notebook's browser context.
The same untrusted recipe is processed, but every template variable is escaped for its output context before rendering. The value is displayed as inert text and no script runs in the notebook.

citations.quote: Insufficient sanitization in MLflow leads to XSS when running an untrusted recipe.
This issue leads to a client-side RCE when running an untrusted recipe in Jupyter Notebook.
The vulnerability stems from lack of sanitization over template variables.

patch_review.observation: The fix applies the template engine's escape filter to two template variables in recipe HTML cards, the failure stacktrace tab and the ingest step data schema tab. Values that could be controlled by an untrusted recipe are now HTML-escaped when the card is rendered, instead of being emitted as raw markup.

patterns.title: Unsanitized dataset table fields in MLflow recipes enable XSS and client-side RCE in Jupyter
patterns.cause: MLflow did not sufficiently sanitize dataset table fields. When a recipe ran on an untrusted dataset, content from those fields reached the rendered output as active content, which caused cross-site scripting.
preconditions: A recipe is run on a dataset that comes from an untrusted source.
Dataset table fields are included in the output the recipe produces without sufficient sanitization.
For the client-side RCE impact, the recipe is run inside a Jupyter Notebook.
patterns.prevention: Treat every value in a dataset table as untrusted data. Sanitize or neutralize all dataset table fields before they are rendered in any output the recipe produces, so that field content is displayed as plain text and never interpreted as active content. Apply this to every field, not only fields assumed to hold free text. Also treat datasets from outside parties as untrusted input and avoid running recipes on them in a notebook session you trust.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief. They do not name the exact fields or rendering code paths involved, the specific sanitization method used, or the first fixed MLflow version. They also do not describe how the script reaches code execution in Jupyter beyond stating that it does. Review the referenced fix commits and advisory before relying on this card for version decisions.

fixtures.scenario: A user runs an MLflow recipe on a dataset received from a third party. One table field holds markup that includes script content. The recipe output is shown in a Jupyter Notebook with the field passed through unsanitized, so the script runs in the user's browser session.

A user runs the same recipe on the same dataset. Every dataset table field is sanitized before it is rendered, so the markup in the field appears as inert text in the Jupyter Notebook output and no script runs.

citations.quote: Insufficient sanitization in MLflow leads to XSS when running a recipe that uses an untrusted dataset.
This issue leads to a client-side RCE when running the recipe in Jupyter Notebook.
The vulnerability stems from lack of sanitization over dataset table fields.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the table rendering helper so every cell value in the dataframe is converted to a string and HTML-escaped before styling, so dataset content is shown as text instead of active markup. It also adjusts the stacktrace and data schema card templates so escaping is applied once, in the right place. A separate commit in the diff set only changes permission checks for artifact proxy deletion and is not part of this weakness.

patterns.title: Unescaped file names in aiohttp static index pages enable XSS
patterns.cause: When the static file handler is configured to show directory indexes, the generated index page does not escape file names. A file name containing markup is placed into the HTML as written, so the browser can run attacker-chosen script.
preconditions: aiohttp earlier than 3.9.4 serves static files directly, with the directory index option enabled
Users can place files with arbitrary names in the served static directory, for example through uploads
A victim opens the generated index page in a browser
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to aiohttp 3.9.4 or later. If upgrading is not possible, disable the directory index option on the static route. Serve static files through a reverse proxy such as nginx, as the maintainers recommend. In any code that builds directory listings, treat file names as untrusted and HTML-escape them before inserting them into the page.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which characters or HTML contexts the fix escapes, and they do not describe the patch internals. They also do not cover other output paths, or whether restricting upload file names is a sufficient defense on its own.

fixtures.scenario: An aiohttp 3.9.3 app serves an upload directory as a static route with index display enabled. An uploader saves a file whose name contains script markup. A visitor opens the index page and the unescaped name runs as script in the site origin.

The same app runs aiohttp 3.9.4 or later, or has the index option disabled, or sits behind nginx serving the files. The markup-bearing file name is escaped or never listed, so it shows as plain text or not at all and no script runs.

citations.quote: the resulting index pages do not escape file names.
If users can upload files with arbitrary filenames to the static directory, the server is vulnerable to XSS attacks.
This vulnerability is fixed in 3.9.4.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the directory index generator in the static file handler so file names and the relative directory path in the heading are HTML-escaped, and link targets are URL-quoted instead of inserted raw. Tests use file and directory names containing an image tag with an error handler and check that the output is escaped. This matches the card's cause (unescaped file names in the index page) and its prevention (upgrade, or escape file names).

patterns.title: Regular expression denial of service in Django HTML-aware word truncation
patterns.cause: Word truncation in HTML mode (the Truncator words method and the truncatewords_html filter) used a regular expression that tries to match a whole tag from every open angle bracket, scanning ahead for a closing bracket. On input made of many open brackets with no closing bracket, each position rescans the rest of the text, so run time grows far faster than the input size. Earlier fixes for CVE-2019-14232 and CVE-2023-43665 did not remove this edge case.
preconditions: The application runs Django 3.2 before 3.2.25, 4.2 before 4.2.11, or 5.0 before 5.0.3.
The application truncates text by words with HTML awareness, through the Truncator words method with HTML enabled or the truncatewords_html template filter.
An attacker can supply a long string containing many unclosed open angle brackets that reaches the truncation code.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 3.2.25, 4.2.11, 5.0.3 or later. The upstream fix removes the backtracking pattern and uses a helper that locates an open bracket or word first and then looks for the closing bracket with a plain string search, falling back to word matching when none exists. When writing similar scanners, avoid lazy patterns that restart at every opener, prefer linear scanning, cap the input length, and keep a regression test with very long runs of open brackets.
patterns.limitations: The diffs only change the word-splitting pattern; other patterns in the same module, such as the character-based and tag patterns, are left as they were. The existing input length cap for HTML truncation is not changed and no timing figures are given. No workaround other than upgrading or limiting untrusted input is described.

fixtures.scenario: A site on Django 4.2.10 renders user-submitted HTML comments through the truncatewords_html template filter for list previews. An attacker posts a crafted string, and the regular expression work keeps a worker busy long enough to degrade the service.
The same site runs Django 4.2.11 or later, which contains the fix for this issue. The same crafted comment passes through the truncatewords_html filter without causing a denial of service.

citations.quote: are subject to a potential regular expression denial-of-service attack via a crafted string.
this issue exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2019-14232 and CVE-2023-43665.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the single tag-or-word regular expression used for HTML-aware word splitting with a small helper. The helper first finds an open bracket or a plain word, then uses a plain string search for the closing bracket, and falls back to word matching when none exists. This removes the quadratic rescanning on long runs of unclosed open brackets, and the tests add a case with 60,000 open brackets.

patterns.title: Cookie tossing from a sibling subdomain turns self-XSS into session XSS in JupyterHub
patterns.cause: JupyterHub is deployed on a single origin, or next to user-controlled applications on subdomains or peer subdomains of the Hub or a single-user server. An attacker who tricks a user into visiting a malicious subdomain can use cookie tossing to leverage a self-XSS into XSS in the victim's session. That gives access to the Hub API and the user's single-user server.
preconditions: Single-origin JupyterHub deployment, or user-controlled applications on subdomains or peer subdomains of the Hub or a single-user server
The victim can be tricked into visiting a malicious subdomain
JupyterHub older than 4.1.0, or the hardening options below not enabled
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to JupyterHub 4.1 or later in both the hub and the user environment. Enable per-user domains by setting the Hub subdomain_host option to a dedicated domain. Enable the cookie_host_prefix_enabled option so cookies are domain-locked. On earlier versions, run the Hub on its own domain that is not shared with other services, and also enable per-user domains.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain the self-XSS entry point or how cookie tossing is carried out. They do not describe the code change in the fix. They do not say whether other cookie or origin settings matter. Per-user domains and a dedicated Hub domain are deployment choices that the sources do not walk through in detail.

fixtures.scenario: The Hub and single-user servers share one origin, or sit beside user-run web apps on peer subdomains. A user opens a malicious subdomain, and the attacker's XSS in the session can create an API token and read the user's notebooks.

JupyterHub is 4.1 or later in both hub and user environments. It has its own domain with per-user domains enabled and domain-locked cookies turned on, so a sibling subdomain app cannot toss cookies into the session.

citations.quote: By tricking a user into visiting a malicious subdomain, the attacker can achieve an XSS directly affecting the former's session.
to enable domain-locked cookies
deploy jupyterhub on its own domain, not shared with any other services

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the XSRF token a signed value tied to the login session and user, and applies XSRF checks to cookie-authenticated requests on the Hub and single-user servers. It also adds an opt-in prefix mode for authentication cookies that blocks cookie tossing from sibling subdomains, plus tighter framing, websocket cookie and URL token defaults. The card's cause (cookie tossing turning self-XSS into session XSS) and its prevention (upgrade to 4.1, per-user domains, host-prefixed cookies) agree with this.

patterns.title: XSS from untrusted snapshot response data in a webcam snapshot test feature
patterns.cause: In OctoPrint up to and including 1.9.3, the Classic Webcam plugin settings have a Test button for the snapshot URL. When the interface renders the returned snapshot image, a crafted response runs JavaScript in the administrator's browser. The proof of concept uses a response content type header with quote characters and an event handler attribute, which suggests that remote response metadata reaches the rendered markup without safe handling.
preconditions: OctoPrint version 1.9.3 or earlier with the Classic Webcam plugin settings available
An attacker controls a snapshot URL, either as a malicious admin or by persuading an administrator to enter it
A victim with administrator rights clicks the Test button for that snapshot URL
The remote server answers with a crafted content type that the interface uses when rendering the snapshot image
patterns.prevention: Treat everything returned by the tested URL, including the content type header, as untrusted data. Do not place it into markup or attributes without context-appropriate encoding. Accept only a strict set of expected image media types and reject or ignore any other value. Build the preview through safe DOM APIs rather than string-built HTML. Upgrade to a patched release, which the advisories say is 1.10.0rc3 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code path or the exact upstream fix, so the encoding and allowlist guidance is a general direction and not a statement of what the patch does. The attack needs administrator interaction. The advisory workaround is to vet who has admin access and which settings they change on the advice of strangers.

fixtures.scenario: An admin is told to enter a snapshot URL on an attacker server. The server replies with a content type containing a quote and an event handler attribute. The Test button renders the preview and the script runs in the admin's session.

The same Test action runs, but the response content type is checked against expected image types and anything else is rejected. Any value shown is encoded or set through safe DOM properties, so no script runs.

citations.quote: will execute JavaScript code in the victims browser when attempting to render the snapshot image
Create a URL that responds with a malicious content type.
The vulnerability is patched in version 1.10.0rc3.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops building the snapshot test dialog from a concatenated HTML string. The content type from the remote response and the image data were inserted directly into markup. The dialog now creates the paragraph and image elements through jQuery, sets the text as plain text, and sets the image source as an attribute value, so a crafted content type can no longer break out of the attribute and add an event handler.

patterns.title: Validate every URI component, including the fragment, for directory traversal
patterns.cause: The application checked for directory traversal sequences such as '../' in the query string of a URI but did not validate the fragment. This bypassed an earlier patch that covered only the query string. An attacker could put traversal sequences in the fragment and read arbitrary local files such as /etc/passwd.
preconditions: The application accepts a URI from an untrusted party
Traversal validation covers only some URI parts, such as the query string, and not the fragment
The affected mlflow version is 2.9.2, fixed in 2.11.3
patterns.prevention: Treat every part of an untrusted URI as attacker-controlled: scheme, path, query and fragment. Apply the same traversal checks to all of them, so a patch for one component cannot be bypassed through another. Reject any value containing parent-directory sequences before it influences a local file location. Upgrade mlflow to 2.11.3 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the affected endpoints or code paths. They do not say how encoded or alternate traversal forms are handled, or how the fix is implemented. They give only 2.9.2 as the affected version and 2.11.3 as the fixed one, so other affected versions are unknown. This card gives general direction only.

fixtures.scenario: A service validates the query string of a user-supplied URI for parent-directory sequences but ignores the fragment. A request with traversal sequences in the fragment makes it read a file outside the intended directory.
A service applies the same traversal check to the path, query and fragment of a user-supplied URI. A request with traversal sequences in any part is rejected before any local file is accessed.

citations.quote: failure to properly validate URI fragments for directory traversal sequences such as '../'
a bypass to a previous patch that only addressed similar manipulation within the URI's query string

patch_review.observation: The fix makes experiment creation reject any artifact location that has a URL fragment, closing the gap left by the earlier patch that only checked the query string. It also hardens model version source validation so the run artifact directory is used as an allowed base only when the run's artifact location is a local URI. The card's fragment-bypass cause and its direction of covering every URI component match the main fix, though the fix rejects fragments outright instead of scanning them for traversal sequences.

patterns.title: SSRF through unrestricted fetching in the Web Research Retriever
patterns.cause: The Web Research Retriever does not restrict requests to remote internet addresses, so it can reach local addresses. The host running it can then be used to reach internal services and read their responses.
preconditions: The application uses the WebResearchRetriever component from langchain-community to fetch web content.
The host running the retriever can reach local or internal network addresses, including cloud instance metadata services.
patterns.prevention: Require an explicit opt-in before the retriever is allowed to fetch remote content, so it is never enabled by default. Send the retriever's outbound requests through a proxy that blocks requests to local addresses. Treat network-level egress control as the main barrier, because the retriever itself does not limit destinations to remote internet addresses.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact opt-in mechanism, how an attacker supplies the target addresses, or the full range of affected versions. The CVE text names only version 0.1.5 of langchain-ai/langchain. The patch as described suggests a proxy rather than blocking local addresses itself. The issue is limited to GET requests.

fixtures.scenario: A service offers a research feature built on the Web Research Retriever with default settings. A crafted request makes it fetch a local address or a cloud instance metadata endpoint, and the response data is read back.
The retriever is enabled only through explicit opt-in, and its outbound requests pass through a proxy that blocks local addresses, so local services and metadata endpoints are unreachable from it.

citations.quote: the Web Research Retriever does not restrict requests to remote internet addresses, allowing it to reach local addresses.
Requires users to opt-in
Suggests using a proxy to prevent requests to local addresses
The vulnerability is limited to GET requests, as POST requests are not possible

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a boolean opt-in setting to the Web Research Retriever that defaults to off. The constructor raises an error unless the user turns it on, and the message warns about SSRF toward internal machines and recommends routing requests through a proxy. It does not filter destinations itself, which matches the card's cause and its advice to rely on opt-in plus proxy or egress control.

patterns.title: NiceGUI leaflet resources route allows reading arbitrary local files
patterns.cause: The NiceGUI leaflet component serves resource files through a route whose final path portion is chosen by the requester. In affected versions, a request to this resources route could reach files beyond the component's own resources. The sources call this a local file inclusion but do not describe the exact request form or the missing check.
preconditions: The application runs a NiceGUI version earlier than 1.4.21.
The leaflet component is present in the application.
An attacker can reach the application's website and request the resources route.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NiceGUI to version 1.4.21 or later, which the advisory says addresses the issue. The sources report no known workarounds. For similar resource-serving routes, an implementation should ensure that a requester-supplied path can only resolve to files belonging to the intended resource set, and not to any file the web server process can read.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain the root mechanism, such as which path sequences or encodings were accepted. They also do not describe the code change. The advice to confine resolved paths to the intended resource set is a general direction inferred from the impact, not a description of the upstream fix. Components other than leaflet are not discussed. The sources do not say how reading arbitrary files could be detected.

fixtures.scenario: An application on NiceGUI 1.4.20 shows a leaflet map and is exposed to untrusted users. A user sends a crafted request to the resources route with a path chosen to reach a file outside the component resources. The server returns a backend file that the web server account can read.

The same application runs NiceGUI 1.4.21 or later. A request to the resources route with an attacker-chosen path no longer returns arbitrary backend files, and only the component's intended resource files are served.

citations.quote: A local file inclusion is present in the NiceUI leaflet component when requesting resource files
any file on the backend filesystem which the web server has access to can be read by an attacker
This vulnerability has been addressed in version 1.4.21. Users are advised to upgrade.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the generic resource-serving handler so the requested path is joined to the resource directory, fully resolved, and checked to lie inside that directory. If it escapes, the handler returns a 403 forbidden response instead of serving the file. This matches the card's account of a requester-chosen path reaching files outside the intended resource set, and its prevention of confining resolved paths.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through injected task instance log data in Apache Airflow 2.9.0
patterns.cause: The Task Instance Log views convert ANSI and terminal escape sequences in log text into HTML with the AnsiUp library. Its hyperlink support let log content, which an authenticated user can influence, produce attacker-controlled anchor elements in the page. The advisory calls this stored XSS. The log renderer trusted escape sequences in log data and turned them into active links instead of treating the data as plain text.
preconditions: The deployment runs Apache Airflow 2.9.0 with the web UI log viewers enabled.
The attacker is authenticated and can get crafted terminal hyperlink escape sequences written into task logs, for example through task output.
A victim opens the Task Instance Log or Log Details view, where the log text is converted to HTML and the generated link is displayed.
The victim interacts with the rendered link or content so that the injected markup runs in the browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 2.9.1 or later. The fix configures every AnsiUp instance, in both the legacy log script and the React log parser, with an empty URL allowlist. As a result, hyperlink sequences from logs are no longer turned into anchors. When rendering untrusted log text, disable or strictly limit any feature that produces links or markup from escape sequences, and escape output by default. Log-group click handling was also changed so that default browser behavior is cancelled only for fold and unfold controls, not for every click.
patterns.limitations: The diff does not show the exact payload form or which URL schemes were abusable. Disabling all log hyperlinks removes that capability for legitimate log content too. Only the two front-end log renderers shown are covered. Other places that render task output were not examined.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs Apache Airflow 2.9.0. An authenticated user causes malicious data to be written into a task instance's logs. When another user opens the Log or Log Details view for that task instance, the injected data can lead to cross-site scripting.
A team runs Apache Airflow 2.9.1 or later. An authenticated user tries to get malicious data into a task instance's logs, and the fixed release addresses the issue described in the advisory.

citations.quote: Apache Airflow version 2.9.0 has a vulnerability that allows an authenticated attacker to inject malicious data into the task instance logs.
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.9.1, which fixes this issue.
XSS vulnerability in Task Instance Log/Log Details

patch_review.observation: The fix sets an empty URL allowlist on the AnsiUp converter in both the legacy log script and the React log parser. As a result, hyperlink escape sequences in task logs are no longer turned into anchors. It also narrows the log-group click handler so default browser behavior is cancelled only for the fold and unfold controls, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from unescaped notification URL values in changedetection.io validation errors
patterns.cause: The shared template helper files that render form fields and their validation errors used an extension that the Flask/Jinja2 autoescape setting does not recognize, so autoescaping was silently off for them. Submitted values, including rejected notification URLs, titles and bodies, were echoed into the settings page without HTML encoding, and markup in them ran in the viewer's browser. The weakness is in how the templates were loaded, not in how the validator builds its message.
preconditions: An affected changedetection.io version, such as 0.45.21, is running.
An attacker can get a crafted value into a settings form field, such as the notification URLs, title or body.
The page is rendered through the macros in the helper templates that lacked autoescaping, so the value or its validation error is output as raw HTML.
patterns.prevention: Make sure every template that outputs user-controlled data is rendered with autoescaping on. Give template and macro files an extension covered by the framework autoescape rules (or enable autoescape explicitly for all templates), and update all import references. Add a regression test that submits markup in the settings form and asserts it appears encoded in the response. Upgrade to version 0.45.22 or later.
patterns.limitations: The fix addresses autoescaping for the helper templates; it does not review other places where values might be marked safe or built into HTML outside the templates. The test covers only the notification settings fields. Other template files with unusual extensions or manual escaping bypasses were not assessed.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens the settings page and adds a notification URL whose text contains an HTML tag with an event handler attribute. Apprise rejects it, the validator echoes the raw text in the error message, and the browser runs the script in the application origin.
The same invalid notification URL is submitted. The page shows a generic invalid-URL error, or shows the submitted text encoded as plain text. No markup is interpreted and no script runs.

citations.quote: Input in parameter notification_urls is not processed resulting in javascript execution in the application.
is not a valid AppRise URL
A reflected XSS vulnerability happens when the user input from a URL or POST data is reflected on the page without being stored
This issue has been addressed in version 0.45.22. Users are advised to upgrade.

patch_review.observation: The fix renames the shared helper templates from the .jinja extension to .html and updates every import reference. Flask autoescape only applies to certain extensions, so these helpers had been rendering submitted values such as notification URLs, titles and bodies without encoding. A new regression test submits markup in the settings form and checks that it comes back HTML-encoded.

patterns.title: Attribute injection through user-controlled keys in the Jinja xmlattr filter
patterns.cause: The xmlattr filter in affected Jinja versions accepts keys containing characters that cannot appear in an attribute name, such as spaces, slash, greater-than and equals sign. Each of these would be read as the start of a separate attribute. The earlier fix for CVE-2024-22195 only handled spaces, not the other characters.
preconditions: The application uses Jinja and renders attributes with the xmlattr filter.
Attribute keys, not only values, come from user input.
The keys are not otherwise validated.
The rendered page is seen by other users.
patterns.prevention: Never let untrusted input choose attribute names passed to xmlattr. Take keys from fixed, application-controlled names, and treat user input as values only. If keys must vary, validate them against a strict set of known-good names before rendering. Upgrade to Jinja 3.1.4 or later, but do not rely on the upgrade alone, because accepting keys as user input is now an unintended use case of the filter regardless of version.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the 3.1.4 fix works or which characters it rejects. They do not say what key validation is sufficient. They only state that values from users remain safe with this filter, and they say nothing about other template contexts or filters.

fixtures.scenario: A profile page builds an attribute dictionary from user-submitted name and value pairs and renders it with xmlattr. An attacker submits a key with a slash or equals sign that adds an event handler attribute, running script for other visitors.

A profile page uses a fixed set of attribute names chosen by the developer and passes only user-supplied text as the values to xmlattr. Users cannot add or rename attributes, and Jinja is at version 3.1.4 or later.

citations.quote: The fix for CVE-2024-22195 only addressed spaces but not other characters.
If an application accepts keys (as opposed to only values) as user input
Accepting _values_ as user input continues to be safe.
This vulnerability is fixed in 3.1.4.

patch_review.observation: The fix widens the attribute key check in the xmlattr filter from whitespace only to whitespace, slash, greater-than and equals sign, and raises a ValueError for such keys. The docs now state that user input should never be used as keys, or must be validated separately. This matches the card's cause (the earlier CVE-2024-22195 fix covered only spaces) and its prevention (keep keys application-controlled and upgrade to 3.1.4 or later).

patterns.title: Pickle deserialization of untrusted checkpoint data in TFPreTrainedModel repo checkpoint loading
patterns.cause: The load_repo_checkpoint function of the TFPreTrainedModel class in huggingface/transformers reads serialized checkpoint data with pickle loading. The data may come from an untrusted source. Pickle can run attacker-chosen behavior while it reads data, so a crafted payload can execute arbitrary code on the machine doing the load.
preconditions: The application reaches load_repo_checkpoint on a TFPreTrainedModel instance.
The checkpoint data being loaded comes from a source an attacker can influence.
The attacker has crafted a malicious serialized payload that looks like a harmless checkpoint.
A victim loads that checkpoint, for example during a normal training process.
patterns.prevention: Treat any checkpoint or serialized artifact from outside your trust boundary as hostile input. Do not pass it to a general-purpose object deserializer such as pickle. Only load checkpoints from sources you control or can verify, and prefer a loading path that does not run code from the data. Upgrade to a transformers release that contains the fix for CVE-2024-3568. Treat checkpoint loading as a code-execution boundary when reviewing training and fine-tuning workflows.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, the affected or patched version ranges, or which serialization formats are safe replacements. They do not say whether other loading paths in the library are affected. This card gives general direction only and should be checked against the release notes and the fix commit.

fixtures.scenario: A training job resumes from a checkpoint pulled from a repository that a third party can modify. The loader reads it with pickle, and a crafted payload runs attacker commands on the training machine.

A training job resumes only from checkpoints produced and stored inside the team's own controlled environment, on a transformers version that includes the fix. The loading path does not run code embedded in the data, and externally sourced checkpoints are not loaded this way.

citations.quote: Attackers can execute arbitrary code and commands by crafting a malicious serialized payload
deceiving victims into loading a seemingly harmless checkpoint during a normal training process

patch_review.observation: The patch deletes the load_repo_checkpoint method from TFPreTrainedModel in its entirety, along with the now-unused Repository and list_repo_files imports. That method fetched a checkpoint from a repo and read its extra data file with pickle loading, so removing it eliminates the code-execution path from untrusted checkpoint data.

patterns.title: Path traversal in LocalFileStore key handling (CVE-2024-3571)
patterns.cause: The LocalFileStore in langchain builds file paths from caller-supplied keys in its mset and mget methods without adequately sanitizing them. Directory traversal sequences in a key can therefore resolve to locations outside the intended store directory.
preconditions: An application uses the LocalFileStore functionality of langchain.
Attacker-influenced input is passed as keys to the mset or mget methods.
Keys containing directory traversal sequences are not rejected or neutralized before the path is built.
patterns.prevention: Treat every key as untrusted. Before touching the filesystem, resolve the combined root directory and key to a canonical absolute path, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm the result is still inside the canonical store root. Reject the request if it is not. Also reject keys that contain traversal sequences or absolute path components. Apply the same check on both the read path and the write path. Upgrade to a langchain release that includes the upstream fix for this issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the affected or fixed versions, the exact traversal sequences involved, or how the upstream fix works, so this card does not describe them. They also do not say whether other langchain components are affected. The advice to canonicalize and check containment is a general mitigation direction, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A service exposes a LocalFileStore and passes user-supplied identifiers straight to mset and mget as keys. A user submits a key with parent-directory sequences. The store resolves it outside its root directory and reads or overwrites an arbitrary file on the filesystem.

A service passes user-supplied identifiers to a LocalFileStore that canonicalizes the joined path and verifies it stays under the store root. A key with parent-directory sequences is rejected before any file is read or written, so only files inside the store directory are reachable.

citations.quote: An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to read or write files anywhere on the filesystem, potentially leading to information disclosure or remote code execution.
The issue lies in the handling of file paths in the mset and mget methods, where user-supplied input is not adequately sanitized

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the store root an absolute path and, in the key-to-path helper, normalizes the joined path and checks that it still lies under the root. If it does not, an invalid-key exception is raised. This closes the gap left by the existing character whitelist, which still allowed dots and slashes, so parent-directory and absolute-path keys got through. The new tests cover absolute and parent-relative keys on the read, write and key-listing paths.

patterns.title: Unvalidated URL fragment lets artifact URLs bypass path checks and read arbitrary local files
patterns.cause: The experiment creation handler checked only the query string of a user-supplied artifact location and let a fragment through. A location such as a remote-scheme URL with a path in the fragment was stored, and the run artifact URI inherited that fragment. The model version source validator then converted the run artifact URI into a local path without checking the scheme, so the scheme was ignored and the fragment path became the trusted artifact directory. A local source path inside that directory passed the containment check, which allowed arbitrary local file read or write. This bypassed the earlier fix for CVE-2023-6909.
preconditions: The server accepts an artifact location for a new experiment from an untrusted client.
The server later converts a run artifact URI into a local filesystem path without first confirming that it is a local URI.
The model version source check trusts a local source path if it lies inside the converted artifact directory.
patterns.prevention: Reject artifact locations that contain a fragment at creation time, in addition to validating the query string. In the source validator, apply the local-path containment check only when the run artifact URI really is a local path, and fail closed for any other scheme. Do not use a scheme-agnostic URI-to-path conversion on values that came from users. Add regression tests for fragment variants of artifact locations and for runs with non-local artifact URIs.
patterns.limitations: The fix rejects fragments outright instead of normalizing them, so legitimate locations with a fragment are no longer accepted. Other URL components or other handlers that convert URIs to paths may need similar checks, and this diff does not show them. Affected and fixed version ranges are not shown in the diff.

fixtures.scenario: An attacker submits an artifact URL with a '#' character, followed by a path to a sensitive local file such as an SSH or cloud key. The validator checks the main part of the URL and accepts it. The path conversion then uses the fragment path, and the server reads and returns the file.

The same artifact URL with a path in the fragment is checked as a whole, including the fragment. The request is rejected before any filesystem access. A normal artifact URL with no unexpected fragment content is still accepted and resolved only within the expected artifact location.

citations.quote: a '#' character can be used to insert a path into the fragment, effectively skipping validation
The issue stems from insufficient validation of the fragment portion of the URL, leading to arbitrary file read through path traversal.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the experiment creation handler reject any artifact location that has a URL fragment, in addition to the existing query string check. It also changes the model version source validator so the containment check runs only when the run artifact URI is a local URI. Otherwise validation falls through to the error. The added tests cover both a fragment location and a non-local run artifact URI.

patterns.title: Directory traversal in Salt recv_file method allows writes into the master cache directory
patterns.cause: The master's file receive handler (_file_recv) joins a minion-supplied path list onto the minion's files directory. Its final guard only checked that the normalized result began with the top-level cache directory, using a plain string prefix test. That boundary is far too wide. Dot-dot components in the path could climb out of the per-minion files directory and overwrite other files under the master cache, such as the master key file.
preconditions: The attacker can send a file receive request to the master, for example as an authenticated minion that can obtain a valid token.
The request carries a path list with parent-directory components that is not fully confined by earlier checks.
The guard compares against the whole cache directory instead of the directory reserved for that minion's received files.
patterns.prevention: Confine each write to the narrowest directory the feature is meant to use. Here that is the per-minion files directory, not the whole cache directory. Resolve the final destination and verify it lies inside that base using a path-aware containment helper such as clean_path, not a raw string prefix comparison. Reject the request if the check fails. Add a regression test that sends dot-dot components and confirms that a sensitive file in the parent cache directory is left unchanged.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the file receive handler only. Other code that builds paths from remote input needs the same base-directory containment check. This review relies on the diff alone and does not confirm affected or fixed release numbers.

fixtures.scenario: A Salt master accepts a file upload through recv_file. The caller supplies a destination name containing parent-directory references. The master joins it to its cache directory without checking the result, so the file lands outside the intended location.

A Salt master accepts a file upload through recv_file. It resolves the full destination path and verifies it is inside the master cache directory. A name containing parent-directory references resolves outside that directory, so the request is rejected and nothing is written.

citations.quote: Directory traversal vulnerability in recv_file method allows arbitrary files to be written to the master cache directory.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the file receive handler on the master so the base directory is the per-minion files directory instead of the whole cache directory. The old string-prefix check on the normalized path is replaced with the path-aware clean_path helper, which rejects dot-dot escapes. A new integration test sends a path that climbs to the master key file and confirms the request is refused and the file is unchanged.

patterns.title: Cross-site scripting in Roundup classhelper help template (CVE-2024-39124)
patterns.cause: In Roundup before 2.4.0, the classhelper templates (the generic help template, plus the calendar, help-list, help-submit and user help templates) built an inline script block from URL query parameters such as the form name and property name. They output those values unescaped, so a crafted link could close the script element and inject attacker-controlled script into the page (reflected XSS, CWE-79). Related hardening covered the CSRF failure message, which could echo a crafted Referer value, and files served for download, which could run script.
preconditions: The deployment runs a Roundup release older than 2.4.0.
The tracker uses the shipped or copied help, calendar or classhelper templates that place request parameters inside inline script content in raw output mode.
A victim follows an attacker-crafted URL that sets the form or property parameters of a help or calendar page.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Roundup 2.4.0 or later. In any customized or copied tracker templates, do not output request-derived values in raw mode inside script content. Let the template engine escape them, and keep any static JavaScript in a separate script block so that only fixed text is emitted raw. Also send a Content-Security-Policy header that disallows script on served user-uploaded files, and add error messages through the escaping message mechanism rather than storing raw text.
patterns.limitations: Upgrading the package does not rewrite templates already copied into an existing tracker, so those copies must be updated by hand. Escaping inside a script context is a partial defense. A strict script policy or nonces on the pages adds further protection. This analysis is based only on the shown commit and its tests.

fixtures.scenario: A Roundup tracker running a version earlier than 2.4.0 serves its classhelper popup through the _generic.help.html template, so the help page is exposed to cross-site scripting.
A Roundup tracker runs release 2.4.0 or later, and any custom copy of the help template has been compared against the updated release, so the classhelper page is not in the affected range.

citations.quote: In Roundup before 2.4.0, classhelpers (_generic.help.html) allow XSS.
In Roundup before 2.4.0, classhelpers (_generic.help.html) allow XSS.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes raw (unescaped) output of request-derived form and property values inside inline script content in the classhelper, calendar, help-list, help-submit and user help templates across all shipped templates. In help-submit, the static helper functions move into their own raw script block. It also routes the CSRF failure message through the escaping error-message mechanism, and sends a Content-Security-Policy header that blocks script on served files. The card covers all three changes.

patterns.title: Roundup XSS through a SCRIPT element in the HTTP Referer header
patterns.cause: Roundup before 2.4.0 allowed cross-site scripting when an HTTP Referer header contained a SCRIPT element. The header value is attacker-influenced input, and the affected versions did not neutralize it safely. The sources do not say which page or code path reflects the value.
preconditions: The deployment runs Roundup older than 2.4.0.
A request reaches Roundup with a Referer header containing a SCRIPT element.
A victim's browser loads the response that is affected by that header value.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Roundup to 2.4.0 or later, which is the version the advisories identify as no longer affected. In general, treat the Referer header like any other untrusted input. Do not place its raw value into HTML output. Encode it for the context where it appears, or avoid echoing it at all.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-line description. They do not name the vulnerable component, the output context, or how the fix works. They do not say whether other request headers were affected. The advice to encode untrusted header values is general guidance, not a description of the upstream change. Verify behavior on your own deployment after upgrading.

fixtures.scenario: A Roundup 2.3.x tracker receives a request whose Referer header holds a SCRIPT element, and the resulting page is delivered to a victim's browser.
The tracker runs Roundup 2.4.0 or later, and the same request with a SCRIPT element in the Referer header does not cause script content to be delivered to the browser.

citations.quote: Roundup before 2.4.0 allows XSS via a SCRIPT element in an HTTP Referer header.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes how a failed CSRF check reports its error. The error text, which can include the attacker-supplied Referer value, used to be stored raw. It now goes through the normal error-message function, which HTML-encodes it, and a new test confirms that a script tag in the Referer comes back encoded. The same commit also stops marking script-embedded template values as trusted markup in the helper pages, and adds a restrictive script policy header when serving uploaded files. The card's general advice to encode the Referer value or avoid echoing it matches this, even though it does not name the exact code path.

patterns.title: Script in PDF, XML, and SVG documents enables XSS in Roundup before 2.4.0
patterns.cause: Roundup before 2.4.0 allows cross-site scripting through JavaScript contained in PDF, XML, and SVG documents. These document types can carry script content, and affected versions let that script lead to XSS. The sources do not describe the exact code path.
preconditions: A Roundup version earlier than 2.4.0 is in use.
A PDF, XML, or SVG document that contains JavaScript reaches the application.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Roundup to version 2.4.0 or later, which the advisories identify as the first release not affected. In any similar application, treat PDF, XML, and SVG documents as able to carry script. Make sure script inside them cannot run in the context of the application's own pages.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-line description. They do not say how documents are uploaded, stored, or served, which headers or content types are involved, or what the upstream change does. The guidance on keeping script from running in the application's context is a general direction, not a confirmed description of the Roundup fix. Check the 2.4.0 release notes for specifics.

fixtures.scenario: A Roundup instance older than 2.4.0 handles an SVG document that contains JavaScript, and the script leads to cross-site scripting.
A Roundup instance at version 2.4.0 or later handles the same SVG, XML, or PDF document, and the embedded JavaScript does not result in cross-site scripting.

citations.quote: Roundup before 2.4.0 allows XSS via JavaScript in PDF, XML, and SVG documents.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes Roundup send a Content-Security-Policy header that disallows scripts whenever it serves an uploaded file, so script inside downloaded SVG or XML files cannot run in the tracker's origin. The same commit also stops the classic, devel, minimal, responsive and website templates from emitting request values unescaped inside script blocks, and it escapes the error message built from a bad referer. These extras are separate reflected-XSS hardening that the card does not mention.

patterns.title: Regular expression denial of service in Wagtail search query string parsing
patterns.cause: A bug in the parse_query_string function of Wagtail's search module made it take an unexpectedly large amount of time on crafted input. Sufficiently long strings of characters without a space triggered the slowdown, which allowed a denial of service.
preconditions: The application uses Wagtail's parse_query_string on user-supplied search text
The Wagtail version is unpatched, from 2.0 onwards and before 5.2.6, 6.0.6 or 6.1.3
An attacker can submit a long search term with no spaces, which in a default install means an authenticated admin user
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a patched Wagtail release (5.2.6, 6.0.6 or 6.1.3). If upgrading is not possible, cap the length of search terms before passing them to parse_query_string. The advisory reports that 1000 characters was still fairly fast and did not trigger the issue. In general, an implementation should bound the length of untrusted text and avoid patterns whose matching time grows sharply on long runs of characters without separators.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the faulty pattern or the exact change made in the patch. The 1000 character figure depends on the hosting environment. The advisory says no workaround is available for the Wagtail admin usage, so the length cap only protects custom code paths that call parse_query_string.

fixtures.scenario: A custom public search view passes the raw query to parse_query_string on an unpatched Wagtail. A very long string with no spaces ties up a worker for a long time.
The site runs a patched Wagtail release. A custom search view also truncates the query to a modest length, such as 1000 characters, before parsing it.

citations.quote: When used to parse sufficiently long strings of characters without a space, `parse_query_string` would take an unexpectedly large amount of time to process
Site owners who are unable to upgrade to a patched version can limit the length of search terms passed to `parse_query_string`.
Patched versions have been released as Wagtail 5.2.6, 6.0.6 and 6.1.3.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the filter-extraction pattern used when separating filters from the query so it is anchored at a word boundary and compiled once at module level. Before, a long run of word characters with no colon was rescanned from every start position, which made matching time grow sharply. With the anchor, matching begins only at word starts and stays fast, and the tests use very long inputs to confirm this. The card's cause (slow parsing of long space-free strings), its upgrade advice and its general advice to avoid patterns that degrade on long separator-free runs all agree with this.

patterns.title: NLTK data package download can lead to code execution through pickled content
patterns.cause: NLTK through 3.8.1 can be made to run attacker-chosen Python code when untrusted data packages contain pickled Python code and the integrated data package download functionality is used. Pickled data is treated as trusted input when it should be treated as untrusted. Affected examples named in the advisories are averaged_perceptron_tagger and punkt.
preconditions: NLTK version 3.8.1 or earlier is in use.
The integrated data package download functionality is used to obtain a package.
The downloaded package is untrusted and contains pickled Python code.
patterns.prevention: Treat every downloaded data package as untrusted input. Do not use the integrated download functionality to fetch packages from origins you do not control or trust. Do not deserialize pickled content from a package whose origin and integrity have not been established. Prefer resources you have vetted and stored in a controlled location. Review any data resource, such as a tagger or tokenizer model, as code-bearing content before it is loaded.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, the first patched version, or the exact download and loading code path. They do not say how packages become untrusted, for example through a tampered server or an interception of the download, so the guidance above is general. Only averaged_perceptron_tagger and punkt are named as examples, and the full list of affected packages is not given. Whether a newer NLTK release fully removes the risk is not stated in the sources and should be checked against the project's own release notes.

fixtures.scenario: An application on NLTK 3.8.1 uses the integrated download functionality to fetch the punkt package from a source an attacker can influence. The package contains pickled Python code, and loading it runs the attacker's code in the application process.

An application obtains NLTK data resources only from a trusted, vetted location under its own control. It does not run the integrated download against untrusted origins and does not load pickled content from unverified packages.

citations.quote: NLTK through 3.8.1 allows remote code execution if untrusted packages have pickled Python code, and the integrated data package download functionality is used.
This affects, for example, averaged_perceptron_tagger and punkt.

patterns.title: Malicious link injection during provider installation in Apache Airflow (CVE-2024-39863)
patterns.cause: The Airflow web UI Providers page converts reStructuredText-style link markup in a provider description into HTML anchors. The helper that builds these anchors did not check the URL scheme. A description containing a link with a javascript scheme became a clickable anchor, which gave stored cross-site scripting when a user clicked it. The text was HTML-escaped first, but the link target was still trusted.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version earlier than 2.9.3 is in use.
The attacker can supply a provider package whose description contains link markup with a non-http target, such as a javascript scheme.
A user opens the Providers page in the web UI and clicks the rendered link.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 2.9.3 or later. The fix parses each link target in the provider description and renders an anchor only for http or https schemes. Other links stay as escaped plain text. In general, validate URL schemes against an allowlist before putting any untrusted value into a link target, and install only trusted provider packages.
patterns.limitations: The fix only covers link rendering in provider descriptions. It does not address other places where untrusted metadata might be shown. Exploitation needs the ability to install a crafted provider and a user click on the link. The fix relies on scheme parsing of the link target, so any new link-building code needs the same check.

fixtures.scenario: An Apache Airflow 2.9.2 deployment lets an authenticated user install a provider. That user injects a malicious link during the installation, which is the condition the advisory describes for versions before 2.9.3.
The deployment runs Apache Airflow 2.9.3 or later, the release the advisory names as fixing the malicious link injection during provider installation.

citations.quote: Apache Airflow versions before 2.9.3 have a vulnerability that allows an authenticated attacker to inject a malicious link when installing a provider.
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.9.3, which fixes this issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the link-building helper in the Providers page description cleaner. It now parses each link target and renders an anchor only when the scheme is http or https. Any other link, such as one using a javascript scheme, is returned as escaped plain text. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Engine-specific SQL functions bypass query authorization in Apache Superset
patterns.cause: Superset's SQL authorization did not check certain engine-specific functions. Special elements in submitted SQL were not properly neutralized, so a user could call functions the authorization logic never inspected and thereby bypass the intended restrictions.
preconditions: The application accepts user-submitted SQL and relies on its own authorization check before running it against a database
The deployment runs Apache Superset earlier than 4.0.2
The backing database exposes engine-specific functions, such as the PostgreSQL ones named in the advisory, that the authorization check does not examine
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Superset 4.0.2 or later. That release introduces a configuration key named DISALLOWED_SQL_FUNCTIONS, which blocks the PostgreSQL functions version, query_to_xml, inet_server_addr, and inet_client_addr. An implementation should treat engine-specific functions as part of the authorization surface, keep a deny list of them per database engine, and extend that list with further functions where more protection is wanted.
patterns.limitations: The sources name only four PostgreSQL functions and do not describe how the bypass works in detail, nor whether other engines are affected. A deny list only covers the functions someone has listed, so it is not a complete guarantee. The sources do not describe the exact checks the fix performs or give advice beyond upgrading and extending the list.

fixtures.scenario: A Superset instance older than 4.0.2 backed by PostgreSQL lets a user submit a query that calls one of the engine-specific functions, such as query_to_xml. The authorization check does not examine the function, so the query is allowed through.

A Superset instance at 4.0.2 or later has DISALLOWED_SQL_FUNCTIONS configured with the default PostgreSQL entries plus any extra functions the operator chose to add, so queries calling those functions are rejected.

citations.quote: certain engine-specific functions are not checked, which allows attackers to bypass Apache Superset's SQL authorization.
This key disallows the use of the following PostgreSQL functions: version, query_to_xml, inet_server_addr, and inet_client_addr.
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 4.0.2, which fixes the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a per-engine deny list setting for SQL functions (PostgreSQL version, query_to_xml, inet_server_addr and inet_client_addr, plus entries for ClickHouse and MySQL). The base engine execute path parses the SQL, searches nested tokens for any listed function name, and raises an error if one is found. This matches the card's prevention of a per-engine deny list of functions the authorization check did not cover. The card's limitation that other engines are unclear is slightly off, since the diff also ships defaults for ClickHouse and MySQL, but the main point is the same.

patterns.title: Unescaped DataStore record data in a table preview view enables XSS
patterns.cause: The Datatables view plugin in CKAN did not properly escape record data coming from the DataStore before showing it, so markup inside a cell could be treated as active content by the browser.
preconditions: CKAN version 2.7.0 or later but earlier than the fixed releases 2.10.5 and 2.11.0
The datatables_view plugin is activated; it is part of CKAN core but not enabled by default
Tabular data containing attacker-controlled values is loaded into the DataStore, for example through DataPusher or XLoader
patterns.prevention: Treat every value read from the DataStore as untrusted text. Escape or encode each record value for the HTML context in which it is rendered, and insert it as plain text rather than markup. Upgrade to CKAN 2.10.5 or 2.11.0 or later. As a stopgap, avoid importing tabular files into the DataStore, especially files from untrusted publishers.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the exact rendering code path, the specific escaping routine used by the fix, or which HTML contexts were affected. The workaround of blocking imports reduces exposure but does not remove the flaw in the plugin. Sites that do not activate datatables_view are described as outside the stated impact.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs CKAN 2.9 with datatables_view active. A publisher uploads a spreadsheet whose cell holds script markup, and it is loaded into the DataStore. A viewer opens the preview and the cell is rendered unescaped.
A site runs CKAN 2.10.5 or later with datatables_view active. The same spreadsheet is imported, but the preview escapes the cell value, so the viewer sees it as literal text and nothing executes.

citations.quote: did not properly escape record data coming from the DataStore, leading to a potential XSS vector.
This vulnerability has been fixed in CKAN 2.10.5 and 2.11.0
Prevent importing of tabular files to the DataStore via DataPusher, XLoader,etc, at least those published from untrusted sources.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the datatables view AJAX endpoint so each record value is HTML-escaped (after conversion to text) before being returned as JSON to the table widget. A test confirms that special characters in a cell come back as entities. This matches the card's cause (unescaped DataStore values) and its prevention (escape values for the HTML context).

patterns.title: HTML injection in the redirect body built by Twisted redirectTo
patterns.cause: The twisted.web.util.redirectTo function builds an HTML body for its HTTP 302 response and inserts the destination URL into it without any output encoding. If an attacker controls all or part of the URL, for example through an open redirect, they can inject HTML into the response, which can lead to reflected cross-site scripting.
preconditions: Application code passes a URL that an attacker can fully or partly control to twisted.web.util.redirectTo
The Twisted version is older than 24.7.0rc1
A browser renders the HTML body of the redirect response; in the reported testing only Firefox did
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Twisted to 24.7.0rc1 or later, where the issue is fixed. Treat the redirect destination as untrusted input. Do not let request data choose the redirect target unless the application has checked it against what it expects. Any HTML that echoes a URL must be output-encoded for the context where the URL is placed, so that attacker-supplied characters stay data and cannot become markup.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so this card does not say how it encodes the URL. The advisory reports that only Firefox rendered the body in its tests, and says nothing about other browser versions. The sources do not say whether other Twisted code paths are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A Twisted web handler reads a url query parameter from the request and passes it unchanged to redirectTo on a version older than 24.7.0rc1. A crafted value ends the link attribute and adds markup that a browser renders in the redirect body.

The deployment runs Twisted 24.7.0rc1 or later, and the handler only redirects to destinations it has checked against what the application expects. Attacker-chosen URL text is never reflected into the redirect body as raw HTML.

citations.quote: The function reflects the destination URL in the HTML body without any output encoding.
All other tested browsers will display an error message to the user and will not render the HTML body.
This vulnerability is fixed in 24.7.0rc1.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes redirectTo HTML-escape the destination URL before placing it in the fallback response body, where it appears in both the meta refresh content and the anchor href. New tests confirm that a normal URL is unchanged and that quotes and angle brackets in a hostile URL become entities. This matches the card's cause (no output encoding of the URL) and its prevention (upgrade, and encode any URL echoed into HTML).

patterns.title: Provider documentation link XSS in Apache Airflow web UI
patterns.cause: Before version 2.10.0, Apache Airflow took the Documentation entry from an installed provider's package metadata (Project-URL) and used it as the provider documentation link in the web UI without checking the URL scheme. A malicious provider author could set this value to a javascript scheme URI, so clicking the link in the Providers page ran attacker-controlled script in the user's browser session.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version earlier than 2.10.0 is in use
A malicious or compromised provider package with a crafted Documentation Project-URL value is installed
A user opens the Providers page and clicks the documentation link
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 2.10.0 or later. When a link target comes from third-party package metadata, parse it and allow only an explicit list of schemes (http and https) with a non-empty host, and fall back to a safe default URL when validation fails. Output encoding alone does not stop script URIs in link targets, so scheme allowlisting is the key control. Also install providers only from trusted sources.
patterns.limitations: The check only covers the provider documentation link built from package metadata; other places that render externally supplied URLs need their own scheme validation. Exploitation requires a malicious provider on the web server and a user click, so the risk mainly applies where untrusted providers could be installed. An http or https link to an attacker-chosen site is still accepted, so this fix does not prevent phishing-style redirects.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 2.9 deployment has a third-party provider installed on the web server whose author supplied a hostile documentation link. A user opens the providers page and clicks the link, and the attacker's script runs in the user's browser session.
The deployment runs Airflow 2.10.0 or later, and only providers from trusted sources are installed. Clicking a provider documentation link does not execute injected script.

citations.quote: allows the developer of a malicious provider to execute a cross-site scripting attack when clicking on a provider documentation link
This would require the provider to be installed on the web server and the user to click the provider link.
Users should upgrade to 2.10.0 or later, which fixes this vulnerability.

patch_review.observation: The fix parses the Documentation Project-URL value taken from provider package metadata and only returns it if the scheme is http or https and a host is present. Otherwise the function falls through to the default documentation URL built from the provider name and version. A test confirms a javascript scheme value is replaced by the default link.

patterns.title: Denial of service in Django urlize, urlizetrunc and AdminURLFieldWidget via very large Unicode inputs
patterns.cause: The urlize and urlizetrunc filters ran URL and email matching, including regular expressions, on arbitrarily long words made of many short Unicode domain labels separated by dots. Matching and normalizing such input took disproportionate CPU time, so one crafted value could cause denial of service. AdminURLFieldWidget was also affected because it applied URL quoting to any non-empty value, even one it had already found to be an invalid URL.
preconditions: Django 5.0 before 5.0.8 or 4.2 before 4.2.15 is in use.
The application renders untrusted text through urlize or urlizetrunc, or shows untrusted values in AdminURLFieldWidget.
The attacker can supply a very long string of repeated Unicode domain labels, for example after an http prefix, a www prefix, or an at sign.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 5.0.8 or later, or 4.2.15 or later. The fix caps the length of a word that is considered for URL matching, rejects email domain parts longer than the 63-character label limit before further checks, and makes the admin widget quote its link only when the URL was validated. As defense in depth, bound the size of untrusted text before passing it to urlize-style helpers, and do not run expensive normalization on values already known to be invalid.
patterns.limitations: The length caps are fixed heuristics, so very long but legitimate URLs over the cap are no longer linkified. Other filters or custom code that run similar regexes on unbounded input are not covered by this change. Input size limits help as a mitigation but do not replace the upgrade.

fixtures.scenario: A site on Django 4.2.14 renders user comments through the urlize filter. An attacker submits a comment with a very large number of Unicode characters, and page rendering becomes a potential denial of service.
The same site runs Django 4.2.15, or a 5.0 deployment runs 5.0.8, so the same comment is handled by the patched urlize filter.

citations.quote: The urlize and urlizetrunc template filters, and the AdminURLFieldWidget widget, are subject to a potential denial-of-service attack
An issue was discovered in Django 5.0 before 5.0.8 and 4.2 before 4.2.15.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a 2048-character cap on a word before the two URL regular expressions are tried in urlize. It also rejects email domain parts longer than 63 characters in the simple email check. In the admin URL widget, the link is now quoted only when the URL was validated, rather than for any non-empty value. All three changes match the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Path traversal in Streamlit static file sharing on Windows
patterns.cause: The validation method of the static file handler in Streamlit before 1.37.0 acted on the attacker-supplied path before checking that it stayed inside the static directory. It resolved the path and queried the filesystem (directory check, size check) first, and only afterwards ran the base class root-containment check. On Windows, this early filesystem access to an attacker-chosen location outside the root, most likely a network share path, can make the host authenticate to a remote system and leak the password hash of the account running Streamlit.
preconditions: Streamlit open source version earlier than 1.37.0
The app runs on Windows
App static file serving is enabled
The app is reachable by an attacker over the network
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Streamlit 1.37.0 or later. The fix runs the base class containment check first, so any path that resolves outside the static root is rejected before the code touches the filesystem. In general, validate that a requested path is inside the allowed root before performing any operation on it, including existence, directory or size checks. Also reject absolute and network-style paths on Windows. Where an upgrade is not possible, disable app static serving.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows the ordering flaw and the fix, but not the exact path form used in the attack. The link to network share paths and hash leakage is inferred from the advisory impact. Restricting outbound SMB traffic or running Streamlit under a low-privilege account may reduce the impact, but this is not confirmed by the fix.

fixtures.scenario: A Streamlit app version 1.36 runs on a Windows server with static file sharing enabled and is exposed to remote users. An attacker sends a crafted request to the static file route to read files outside the static directory, and obtains the password hash of the Windows account running the app.
The same app runs Streamlit 1.37.0 or later on Windows, or runs on a host where static file sharing is not enabled. The crafted request does not expose files outside the intended static content.

citations.quote: Users of hosted Streamlit app(s) on Windows were vulnerable to a path traversal vulnerability when the static file sharing feature is enabled.
An attacker could utilize the vulnerability to leak the password hash of the Windows user running Streamlit.
We recommend all users upgrade to Version 1.37.0.
The vulnerability only affects Windows.

patch_review.observation: The fix moves the call to the base class containment check (validate_absolute_path in the parent handler) to the start of the static handler's validation, before the directory check and file size check. Paths outside the static root are now rejected with 403 before those filesystem queries run, and the tests were updated to expect 403 for outside paths and directories. This matches the card's cause (filesystem access before root containment) and its prevention (check containment first).

patterns.title: Command injection via unsanitized GitHub context values echoed in a CI workflow
patterns.cause: A functional test workflow echoed GitHub context information, namely the full name of the head repository, the head branch, and the workflow reference, in a command without adequate sanitization. Attacker-influenced values containing special elements could therefore be interpreted as part of the command.
preconditions: A CI workflow builds a command that includes GitHub context values such as the head repository full name, head branch, or workflow reference
Those values can be influenced by someone outside the maintainers, for example through a fork or a branch name
The special elements in those values are not neutralized before the command runs
The workflow runs with access to secrets such as GITHUB_TOKEN, COMMENT_TOKEN, or CHROMATIC_PROJECT_TOKEN
patterns.prevention: Treat every GitHub context value that a contributor can influence as untrusted data. Do not let such values be interpreted as command text. Either avoid echoing them in a command, or neutralize special elements first so they are handled strictly as plain data. Review all workflow steps that print or reuse the head repository name, head branch, and workflow reference.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream remediation, the specific trigger type, or which step was changed. They also do not say whether other workflows are affected. Only versions up to and including @gradio/video@0.6.12 are named as affected. The guidance here is general and not a verified description of the fix.

fixtures.scenario: A workflow step echoes the head repository full name, head branch, and workflow reference directly into a shell command. A contributor picks a branch name with shell special elements, and the runner executes them with secrets available.

The workflow treats the head repository name, head branch, and workflow reference as untrusted data. Special elements are neutralized so a hostile branch name is only printed as text and never executed.

citations.quote: where it echoes the full name of the head repository, the head branch, and the workflow reference without adequate sanitization
allowing for unauthorized modification of the base repository or secrets exfiltration

patch_review.observation: The fix deletes a step in the functional test workflow that echoed the head repository full name, head branch, and workflow reference by interpolating them straight into a shell command. Removing the step eliminates the injection path, which matches the card's cause and its option of not echoing untrusted context values in a command.

patterns.title: Gradio SSRF through unvalidated user-supplied URL fetched by the queue join endpoint
patterns.cause: In gradio 4.21.0, the queue/join endpoint accepts a path value from the user that is expected to be a URL. The save_url_to_cache function uses that value to make an HTTP request from the server without sufficient validation checks. The server therefore fetches whatever destination the client names.
preconditions: A gradio-app/gradio deployment at version 4.21.0, where the issue was discovered, exposes the queue/join endpoint to untrusted clients.
A path value supplied by the user and expected to be a URL reaches save_url_to_cache.
The server makes an HTTP request to that URL without sufficient validation checks.
The server host can reach the local network or the AWS metadata endpoint.
patterns.prevention: Treat every user-supplied URL as untrusted before the server requests it. Validate the destination first, and refuse to fetch anything that points at the local network or at a cloud metadata endpoint. Make the check on the destination the server will actually contact, and reject the request before any outbound connection is made. Upgrade to a gradio release that includes the upstream fix for this issue.
patterns.limitations: The advisories only say that validation checks were insufficient. They do not describe which checks the fix adds, how redirects or DNS resolution are handled, or which gradio versions other than 4.21.0 are affected.
