Add tests for traversal sequences in both the environment name and the file path.
patterns.limitations: The fix relies on the path containment check rather than an allowlist of environment names, so its strength depends on the clean_path logic and on symlink resolution. Other fileserver backends or code that still uses plain joins with client input are not covered by this change.

fixtures.scenario: An attacker-influenced tgt_env value reaches find_file in GitFS and is joined into a filesystem path with os.path.join without validation. The Master can then create directories or delete files outside the intended location, limited only by its own permissions.

The tgt_env value is validated before find_file uses it to build a path. A value that is not an acceptable environment name is rejected, so no path is built from it and no directory is created or file deleted.

citations.quote: In the find_file method of the GitFS class, a path is created using os.path.join using unvalidated input
This can be exploited by an attacker to delete any file on the Master's process has permissions to.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces plain path joins in the GitFS find_file method with the clean_join helper for the destination, hash glob, blob sha, and lock file paths. It also changes clean_join to join and validate one component at a time, each checked against the directory built so far, raising a validation error on escape. Tests cover traversal sequences in both the file path and the environment name.

patterns.title: Remote model checkpoints loaded with torch.load and default pickle settings allow code execution (CVE-2025-24357)
patterns.cause: Several vllm code paths loaded pickle-based .bin or .pt files with torch.load while leaving the weights_only option at its default of off, so the file was fully unpickled and a crafted checkpoint could run arbitrary code. The affected paths are the pt_weights_iterator and np_cache_weights_iterator functions and the bin-to-safetensors converter in model_loader/weight_utils.py, plus LoRA embedding loading, prompt adapter weight loading, and an image embedding asset helper.
preconditions: The application loads a model, adapter, or embedding file that comes from a source the operator does not fully control, such as a remote Hugging Face repository.
The file is in a pickle-based format (.bin or .pt) that goes through torch.load rather than the safetensors format.
torch.load is called without the restricted loading option, so unpickling is unrestricted.
The vllm version in use is older than v0.7.0.
patterns.prevention: Pass the restricted loading option to every torch.load call that reads externally supplied files, so only tensors and plain containers are unpickled and arbitrary objects are rejected. Prefer the safetensors format where possible. Only fetch weights and adapters from trusted repositories, and upgrade vllm to v0.7.0 or later, which applies the restricted option across the weight, LoRA, prompt adapter, and asset loading paths.
patterns.limitations: The restricted loading option blocks arbitrary object unpickling but can reject legacy checkpoints that store non-tensor objects, so some old files may fail to load. The fix covers the torch.load call sites shown in the diff; other code or third-party libraries that call torch.load with defaults are not addressed. It does not verify the provenance or integrity of downloaded files.

fixtures.scenario: A service downloads a model repository from a public hub that ships a pickle-based checkpoint. The loader opens it with torch.load using the default weights_only setting. A tampered checkpoint contains a payload that runs an operating system command on the host while the file is being unpickled.

The same service loads weights from a repository that provides safetensors files, or it loads pickle-based files only with the restricted loading option enabled and from a trusted source. It runs vllm v0.7.0 or later, so a tampered checkpoint does not get arbitrary code run during loading.

citations.quote: It use torch.load function and weights_only parameter is default value False.
when torch.load load a malicious pickle data it will execute arbitrary code during unpickling.
Note that most models now use the safetensors format, which is not vulnerable to this issue.
This vulnerability is fixed in v0.7.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds the restricted loading option to every torch.load call that reads externally supplied pickle files. These are the weight iterators and the bin-to-safetensors converter in weight_utils, LoRA embedding loading, prompt adapter weight loading, and the image embedding asset helper. This matches the card's cause (unrestricted unpickling of crafted checkpoints) and its prevention, and the listed call sites are the ones in the diff.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through user-uploaded images in CKAN group, organization and user profiles
patterns.cause: CKAN accepted user-supplied files for group, organization and user profile images. A specially crafted file could contain code that runs when the file is opened. The code could then send arbitrary requests to the server.
preconditions: CKAN version earlier than 2.10.7 (2.10 line) or 2.11.2 (2.11 line)
The attacker is a registered user of the site
File uploads for user or group images are enabled and the allowed types are not restricted
An administrator opens the crafted file
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to CKAN 2.10.7 or 2.11.2 or later. If an immediate upgrade is not possible, restrict the file types accepted for user and group uploads using the ckan.upload.user.mimetypes, ckan.upload.user.types, ckan.upload.group.mimetypes and ckan.upload.group.types options. Sites that do not need uploads can disable user uploads entirely by setting the user types option to none. In general, accept only the image types a profile or group image needs, and treat uploaded files as untrusted content that must not run code when opened.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code change in the fixed releases, which file types or formats carry the payload, or how uploaded files are served to the browser. The configuration restrictions are a workaround for older versions and are not shown to be equivalent to the patch. The sources do not say whether the workaround covers every upload path.

fixtures.scenario: A registered user uploads a specially crafted file as a group, organization or user profile image on CKAN older than 2.10.7 or 2.11.2. An administrator later opens it and the embedded code sends requests to the server.
The site runs CKAN 2.10.7 or 2.11.2 or later, or limits the allowed user and group upload types, or disables uploads, so the crafted file is not a usable attack vector.

citations.quote: Using a specially crafted file, a user could potentially upload a file containing code that when executed could send arbitrary requests to the server.
If that file was opened by an administrator, it could lead to escalation of privileges of the original submitter or other malicious actions.
This vulnerability has been fixed in CKAN 2.10.7 and 2.11.2
site maintainers can restrict the file types supported for uploading

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the upload check in the uploader stricter. Empty type and mimetype settings used to mean no restriction and now reject all uploads, and allowing everything needs an explicit star value in both options. It also checks the declared filename type and content type as well as the sniffed content type, and it rewrites the stored file extension to match the detected type, so script-capable files such as SVG are no longer accepted or served by default.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from unsanitized label config task data rendered on a GET example endpoint
patterns.cause: The view that builds example upload data from a label config accepted the config through a GET query parameter as well as POST. Because the config can carry inline task data with HTML or script, an attacker could put the payload in a link. When a victim opened that link, the response reflected the content and script ran in their browser. Allowing a state-free, link-shareable GET to feed untrusted markup into the response made the reflected XSS possible.
preconditions: An endpoint reads a label configuration from a GET query parameter
Inline task data in the config can contain HTML or script that ends up in the response
The victim can be persuaded to open an attacker-crafted URL
patterns.prevention: Do not accept untrusted, content-bearing input such as a label config through GET query parameters. Restrict the example-from-config endpoint to POST and read the config only from the request body, so a crafted link cannot trigger it. Also treat inline task data in a config as untrusted and escape or sanitize it wherever it is rendered, and enforce the Content Security Policy instead of using report-only mode as defense in depth.
patterns.limitations: The diff only removes the GET path. It does not show sanitization of task data, so POST requests that carry a malicious config may still need output escaping elsewhere. It does not change the Content Security Policy mode, and it does not show whether other endpoints render task data from request parameters. Existing clients that used GET for this endpoint will break.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens a link to the upload-example endpoint whose label_config query parameter holds an XML config with inline task data containing an image element with an error event handler. The page renders that HTML unsanitized, the handler runs, and attacker JavaScript executes in the victim's session.

The same link is opened, but inline task data from the label config is sanitized or escaped before rendering, and the Content Security Policy is enforced. The markup appears as inert content or is stripped, and no script runs.

citations.quote: the upload-example endpoint renders user-provided HTML content without proper sanitization on a GET request
Enable the Content Security Policy in enforcement mode instead of report-only mode to actively block unauthorized script execution
Deprecate the `GET` behavior at the `example-config` endpoint since it's not used
Version 1.16.0 contains a patch for the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix limits the example-upload-from-config view to POST only and reads the label config only from the POST body, not from the GET query string. This removes the link-shareable path through which an attacker could deliver a malicious config to a victim's browser. The card's cause and main prevention match this, and its extra advice on escaping and CSP is labeled as defense in depth, with the limitations noting the diff does not show it.

patterns.title: SSRF through user-supplied S3 endpoint URL in storage connections
patterns.cause: Users can set an arbitrary custom S3 endpoint, and the server makes requests to it with the boto3 SDK. When those requests failed, the raw exception text, which can include content returned by the target host, was shown to the user. This turned the server-side request into a channel for reading responses from internal or otherwise unintended hosts. The fix targets this disclosure: error details are now hidden unless the endpoint is on a trusted domain.
preconditions: The attacker is an authenticated user who can create or edit an S3 storage connection with a custom endpoint
The endpoint host is not checked against any allowlist before the server connects to it
A storage validation or sync is triggered so the server contacts the chosen host
Exceptions from failed requests are returned to the user with the underlying response details
patterns.prevention: Never surface raw exception messages or response bodies from storage backends to users when the custom endpoint is not on a known, trusted domain. Wrap the S3 storage operations so that errors for untrusted endpoint domains are logged only on the server, and the user receives a generic message with the original exception context suppressed. Determine the domain with a public-suffix-aware parser and compare it to an operator-configurable list of trusted storage domains. For stronger protection, also restrict the endpoint itself by scheme and destination, block private and link-local addresses, and limit outbound network access from the application server. Upgrade to version 1.16.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The fix only limits information disclosure. The server can still send requests to any endpoint host, so blind SSRF (probing reachability, timing, or side effects of internal services) remains possible. Trust is decided by the registered domain of the configured URL, with no checks on redirects or on what the hostname resolves to. Operators of self-hosted S3-compatible services must add their domain to the trusted list to get detailed errors.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user creates an S3 storage connection whose custom endpoint points at an internal web service over plain HTTP, then triggers sync. The server calls that host, and the resulting S3 parsing error echoes the internal response body.

The endpoint is checked against an allowlist of approved domains and protocols before use. An internal hostname is rejected when the connection is created, and sync failures return a generic message without any response body.

citations.quote: This endpoint URL is passed directly to the boto3 AWS SDK without proper validation or restrictions on the protocol or destination.
error messages from failed requests contain the full response body, allowing data exfiltration from internal services.
Add an allowlist of endpoint domains and protocols

patch_review.observation: The fix does not restrict where the server connects. It wraps the S3 storage methods so that when an exception occurs and the custom endpoint's registered domain is not in a configurable trusted list, the error is logged on the server and the user gets a generic message with the original exception context suppressed. The domain is extracted with a public-suffix-aware library, and the trusted list can be set through an environment variable. This matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Unsafe pickle deserialization of HTTP request payloads in BentoML serde
patterns.cause: In BentoML 1.4.2, the deserialization routine in serde.py passes payload bytes to pickle loading when the payload metadata has no buffer-lengths entry. The payload comes from an HTTP request the client fully controls, and nothing validates it first. Crafted serialized data therefore runs code on the server during deserialization, with no authentication needed.
preconditions: A BentoML service version 1.4.2 or earlier is reachable over HTTP by the attacker
The request body is turned into a payload object that the serde deserialization routine handles
The payload metadata lacks a buffer-lengths entry, so the pickle loading path is taken
The request declares the BentoML pickle content type
patterns.prevention: Never pass bytes taken from a network request to a pickle-style deserializer. Treat the request body and its declared content type as untrusted, and do not select a code-executing deserialization path based on client-supplied metadata. Accept only data-only formats with explicit validation on network-facing endpoints. Upgrade to BentoML 1.4.3 or later, where the vulnerability is reported fixed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how version 1.4.3 changes the code, so this card does not claim which formats or checks the fix uses. They also do not describe the code path taken when buffer-lengths metadata is present, nor other entry points that might reach deserialization. The proof of concept covers one API endpoint only.

fixtures.scenario: A BentoML 1.4.2 service listens on port 3000. An unauthenticated client posts a crafted pickle body with the BentoML pickle content type, and the server unpickles it, running attacker-chosen code.
The service runs BentoML 1.4.3 or later, and request bodies are never fed to a pickle loader. A crafted pickle body is rejected or parsed only as plain validated data, so no attacker code runs.

citations.quote: It allows any unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the server.
Due to the lack of validation in the code, maliciously crafted serialized data can execute harmful actions during deserialization.
This vulnerability is fixed in 1.4.3.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the public-facing main server reject requests that declare the BentoML pickle content type, returning an unsupported media type error before any deserialization happens. It also makes the internal proxy used for self-calls send JSON by default. This matches the card's cause (client-chosen pickle deserialization of request bodies) and its prevention (do not let client-supplied content type select a code-executing deserializer on network endpoints).

patterns.title: SSRF in langchain-community RequestsToolkit from unrestricted request destinations
patterns.cause: The langchain-community requests tools (GET, POST, PATCH, PUT, DELETE) and the RequestsToolkit and OpenAPIToolkit that wrap them could be created and handed to an agent with no explicit acknowledgment of risk. An agent steered by untrusted input could then ask the host to call internal or local-only servers. The tools had no safe-by-default gate, and load_tools registered the requests tools like harmless ones.
preconditions: The application builds an agent with the requests tools, RequestsToolkit, OpenAPIToolkit, or load_tools with a requests tool name, using langchain-community 0.0.27 or earlier as reported.
Untrusted users or content can influence the prompts or tool inputs that decide which URL the agent requests.
The host running the agent can reach internal services, local endpoints, or cloud metadata addresses that the user could not reach directly.
No proxy, sandbox, or network egress control sits between the agent and those internal targets.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a fixed langchain-community release (0.0.28 or later per the card) and the matching langchain release. The fix makes the dangerous behavior opt-in: each requests tool refuses to initialize unless the caller sets the allow-dangerous-requests option, both toolkits forward that option, and load_tools rejects the requests tools and terminal unless the allow-dangerous-tools option is set. Treat enabling these options as a conscious risk decision. Only enable them when inputs are trusted or the agent is sandboxed, and send requests through a proxy that blocks internal destinations. Enforce destination restrictions yourself, because the opt-in gate does not filter addresses.
patterns.limitations: The change is a consent gate, not a technical SSRF control. Once a caller sets the opt-in flags, the tools still request any address, including internal ones, and redirects and DNS rebinding are not addressed. Callers who pass the flag without understanding the risk stay exposed, and existing code breaks until it adds the flag. The diff covers only the requests tools, the two toolkits, and load_tools. Other tools that make outbound requests are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: An agent built with RequestsToolkit at version 0.0.27 is asked to fetch a URL chosen by an untrusted user. The URL points at a local service or a cloud instance metadata endpoint, and the toolkit sends the request and returns the response.
The same agent runs on langchain-community 0.0.28 or later. A request aimed at a local or internal address is refused, and only requests to intended remote internet addresses go through.

citations.quote: the toolkit does not enforce restrictions on requests to remote internet addresses, allowing it to also access local addresses.
an attacker could exploit this flaw to perform port scans, access local services, retrieve instance metadata from cloud environments
This issue has been fixed in version 0.0.28.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an opt-in gate. Each requests tool refuses to initialize unless the caller explicitly allows dangerous requests, RequestsToolkit and OpenAPIToolkit (including its from_llm constructor) forward that option, and load_tools moves the requests tools and terminal into a dangerous-tools set that needs an explicit allow flag. It adds no destination filtering, which matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Untrusted network bytes passed to pickle in the vLLM Mooncake KV transfer pipe
patterns.cause: When vLLM is configured to use Mooncake for disaggregated KV transfer, the receive path in the Mooncake pipe takes raw bytes from a ZMQ/TCP connection and hands them directly to pickle.loads(). Pickle deserialization can run attacker-chosen code, so whoever can deliver bytes to that path can execute code on the distributed host.
preconditions: vLLM is configured to use Mooncake to distribute KV across distributed hosts.
The Mooncake pipe receives data over ZMQ/TCP, which is exposed over the network by design to enable disaggregated prefilling.
The received bytes are deserialized with pickle without validation.
No network or authentication controls stop arbitrary senders from reaching the affected service.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade vLLM to version 0.8.0 or later, where the issue is fixed (see pull request 14228). More generally, an implementation should never pass bytes read from a network socket to pickle.loads(). Data arriving from other hosts must be treated as untrusted, even when the transport is intended only for cluster-internal use.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so this card does not prescribe a specific replacement format. The advisory also gives conflicting information on exposure: one passage is struck through (claiming the sockets listen on all interfaces), while the CVE text still says all network interfaces. The advisory says only the sender socket and the receiver ack socket are publicly accessible, and that the pickled data comes from the receive path using a locally configured decode host address. The sources do not say whether network restrictions alone would be adequate mitigation.

fixtures.scenario: A vLLM deployment on a version before 0.8.0 uses Mooncake for disaggregated prefilling across hosts. The receive routine reads raw bytes from the ZMQ/TCP link and deserializes them with pickle. A party who can send a crafted payload to the service gets code execution on the decode host.

A vLLM deployment runs version 0.8.0 or later, which contains the fix for this issue. Bytes received from other hosts are never passed to pickle.loads(), so a crafted payload cannot trigger code execution through the Mooncake pipe.

citations.quote: unsafe deserialization exposed directly over ZMQ/TCP on all network interfaces will allow attackers to execute remote code on distributed hosts
Additionally, it does not appear that there are any controls (network, authentication, etc) to prevent arbitrary users from sending this payload
This vulnerability is fixed in 0.8.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes pickle from the Mooncake pipe. The send path now serializes the tensor with safetensors, and the receive path parses the incoming network bytes with safetensors and moves the tensor to the local device. This closes the code execution risk from deserializing untrusted bytes, which is what the card describes.

patterns.title: Symlinks in an Obsidian vault let the reader open files outside the vault
patterns.cause: The ObsidianReader in LlamaIndex did not resolve symbolic links to their real paths and did not check whether the resolved paths were inside the intended vault directory. A symlink in the vault that pointed elsewhere was therefore treated as an ordinary Markdown file and read.
preconditions: The application uses the ObsidianReader from the LlamaIndex Obsidian reader integration. The sources name versions 0.12.23 to 0.12.28 of the repository and a fixed reader release of 0.5.1.
An attacker can place symbolic links inside the vault directory that is being read.
The symlinks point to files outside the vault directory, and the reader processes them as valid Markdown files.
patterns.prevention: Before reading any entry found while walking a vault, resolve it to its real path so symlinks are followed to their actual target. Then confirm that the resolved path lies within the resolved vault root, and skip or reject any entry that does not. Make this containment check on the resolved path rather than on the name as listed. Upgrade to a fixed release of the Obsidian reader integration (0.5.1 or later, per the advisory).
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the flaw and the affected versions but not how the upstream fix works, so this card gives only the general direction. They do not say whether other readers or loaders in the project have the same weakness. They do not cover platform-specific link types or how vault contents are stored. They do not discuss concurrent changes to the vault between the check and the read. The impact is described only as potentially exposing sensitive information.

fixtures.scenario: A vault directory contains a note whose name ends in the Markdown extension but is really a symbolic link to a sensitive file outside the vault. The reader lists the entry, does not resolve it, and loads the external file's contents as if it were a note.

The same vault is loaded, but each entry is resolved to its real path and compared against the real path of the vault root. The symlinked entry resolves outside the vault, so it is skipped or rejected and its contents are never loaded. Regular notes inside the vault are still read.

citations.quote: fails to resolve symlinks to their real paths and does not validate whether the resolved paths lie within the intended directory
This flaw enables attackers to place symlinks pointing to files outside the vault directory, which are then processed as valid Markdown files

patch_review.observation: The fix in the Obsidian reader resolves each Markdown file path to its real location and skips any file whose resolved path is not under the resolved vault directory, with a warning. It also stops the directory walk from following symlinked directories. This matches the card's cause and its prevention of resolving first, then checking containment against the resolved root. The version bump to 0.5.1 matches the card's fixed release.

patterns.title: Billion laughs XML entity expansion in the llama-index sitemap parser (CVE-2025-3225)
patterns.cause: Several llama-index reader integrations parsed externally supplied XML with the standard library ElementTree parser, which expands internal entities without limit. A crafted sitemap or API response with nested entity definitions (a billion laughs payload) makes the parser consume excessive memory and CPU, causing denial of service. The sitemap parsing in the web reader and the Stripe docs reader, and the PubMed response parsing in the papers reader, all used this unsafe parser.
preconditions: The application uses an affected reader package: llama-index-readers-web before 0.3.9, llama-index-readers-stripe-docs before 0.3.1, or llama-index-readers-papers before 0.3.2.
The application parses a sitemap or other XML through one of these readers with the standard library parser.
An attacker can supply or influence the XML document being parsed, for example by controlling a sitemap URL or a response the reader fetches.
patterns.prevention: Parse untrusted XML with the hardened defusedxml parser, which rejects entity declarations and expansion, instead of the standard library ElementTree parser. Upgrade to llama-index-readers-web 0.3.9, llama-index-readers-stripe-docs 0.3.1, and llama-index-readers-papers 0.3.2 or later, which declare defusedxml as a dependency. Review any custom code that parses XML from external sources and switch it to the safe parser as well.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the XML parsing calls in the sitemap, Stripe docs, and PubMed readers shown in this change. Other XML parsing code elsewhere in llama-index or in third-party readers is not shown and should be checked separately. The stated impact is denial of service through resource exhaustion, and advisory version ranges differ, so confirm your installed package versions against the advisory.

fixtures.scenario: A service built on an affected llama-index release loads a sitemap from a URL an outside party controls. The document is a billion laughs payload, so parsing exhausts system memory and may crash the host.

The same service runs Papers Loaders 0.3.2 or later, which ships with llama-index 0.12.29 or later. It loads the same hostile sitemap and does not suffer the memory exhaustion described in the advisories.

citations.quote: allows an attacker to supply a malicious Sitemap XML, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) by exhausting system memory
specifically affecting the Papers Loaders package before version 0.3.2 (in llama-index v0.10.0 and above through v0.12.29)
The issue is resolved in version 0.3.2 (in llama-index 0.12.29).

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the standard library ElementTree parsing of sitemap and PubMed XML with the defusedxml equivalent in the web sitemap reader, the Stripe docs reader, and the papers PubMed reader. It adds defusedxml as a dependency and bumps the three packages to 0.3.9, 0.3.1 and 0.3.2, which matches the card's cause, affected versions and prevention.

patterns.title: Pickle-based ZeroMQ receive on exposed sockets in vLLM Mooncake integration allows remote code execution
patterns.cause: The vLLM Mooncake integration exchanged data using pickle based serialization over unsecured ZeroMQ sockets. The advisory says the receive call recv_pyobj() contains an implicit pickle.loads(), so bytes from any peer that reaches the socket are deserialized as objects. The sockets were also set to listen on all network interfaces, which made them easier for an attacker to reach.
preconditions: vLLM version from 0.6.5 up to but not including 0.8.5
The Mooncake integration is in use; instances that do not use it are not vulnerable
The ZeroMQ sockets use pickle based serialization with no security on the channel
An attacker can reach the sockets over the network, which is more likely because they listen on all interfaces
patterns.prevention: Never deserialize network input with pickle. Do not use socket helpers that implicitly unpickle, such as recv_pyobj(), on any socket a peer outside the trust boundary could reach. Exchange data in a plain data-only format and validate it on receipt. Bind sockets only to the interface that is actually needed rather than all interfaces. Upgrade vLLM to 0.8.5 or later, or disable the Mooncake integration if it is not required.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, so they do not say which serialization format or binding policy replaced the old behavior. They do not say whether authentication or encryption was added to the sockets. They only confirm that version 0.8.5 patches the issue. Narrowing the bind interface reduces exposure but does not make unpickling untrusted data safe.

fixtures.scenario: A vLLM 0.8.4 deployment enables the Mooncake integration. Its ZeroMQ sockets listen on all interfaces and read incoming messages with recv_pyobj(). A host on the same network sends a crafted pickle payload, which is deserialized and runs attacker code.

A vLLM deployment runs 0.8.5 or later, or does not enable the Mooncake integration. Any socket that carries data between hosts accepts only a data-only format that is validated on receipt, and it is not bound to all interfaces.

citations.quote: vulnerable to remote code execution due to using pickle based serialization over unsecured ZeroMQ sockets.
The vulnerable sockets were set to listen on all network interfaces
vLLM instances that do not make use of the mooncake integration are not vulnerable.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops using the pickle-based send and receive helpers on the Mooncake ZeroMQ sockets. It now sends raw bytes and encodes the pointer and length as fixed-width network-order integers in a multipart message, which the receiver decodes with a struct unpack, so no object deserialization happens. It also changes the socket binds from the wildcard address to the configured host address, which narrows exposure.

patterns.title: ReDoS from backtracking-prone regular expression in transformers chat command
patterns.cause: The SETTING_RE pattern in transformers/commands/chat.py contains repetition groups and non-optimized quantifiers. Input that almost matches the pattern makes the regex engine backtrack exponentially, which consumes CPU time and can degrade or deny service.
preconditions: The deployment uses huggingface/transformers version 4.49.0, the version named in the advisories.
Input strings reach the SETTING_RE pattern in the chat command module.
An attacker can supply specially crafted strings that almost match the pattern.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade transformers to version 4.51.0 or later, where the issue is fixed. When writing or reviewing similar patterns, avoid repetition groups combined with non-optimized quantifiers, because these allow exponential backtracking on almost-matching input. Test such patterns against near-miss payloads, not only valid input, and treat any text from users as untrusted before it reaches a backtracking regex engine.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code change in the fix, the exact shape of the pattern, or how much input is needed to cause a noticeable slowdown. They also do not say how remote an attacker's access to the chat command is, or whether other patterns in the library are affected. Only version 4.49.0 is named as vulnerable, so the full range of affected versions is unclear.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs transformers 4.49.0 and passes user-supplied text to the chat command's settings parsing. A user sends a long string that almost matches the expected settings format. The regex engine backtracks exponentially and the process stalls on CPU, degrading the application for other users.
A service runs transformers 4.51.0 or later, which contains the fix. The same near-miss string is handled without exponential backtracking, and the application stays responsive.

citations.quote: The regex contains repetition groups and non-optimized quantifiers, leading to exponential backtracking when processing 'almost matching' payloads.
This can degrade application performance and potentially result in a denial-of-service (DoS) when handling specially crafted input strings.
The issue is fixed in version 4.51.0.

patterns.title: Catastrophic regex backtracking in Transformers get_configuration_file
patterns.cause: The get_configuration_file() function in transformers.configuration_utils uses a regular expression with an unbounded wildcard between a config prefix and a json suffix. Crafted input strings can force catastrophic backtracking and excessive CPU consumption.
preconditions: The application uses the Hugging Face Transformers library at version 4.49.0, the version named as affected.
The get_configuration_file() function in transformers.configuration_utils is reached during configuration lookup.
An attacker can influence the strings that this matching is applied to, though the sources do not say exactly which inputs are attacker-reachable.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Transformers to version 4.51.0 or later, where the issue is reported as resolved. When writing similar matching logic, avoid patterns that put an unbounded wildcard between fixed literal parts and run them on untrusted strings. Instead, use a narrow, explicit match for the expected file name shape, or non-regex string handling. Where inputs come from outside the trust boundary, also limit their length and treat unexpected names as invalid.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix changed the matching logic, so the exact replacement approach is not stated here. They also do not give the input lengths or shapes that trigger the worst case, or the routes by which untrusted strings reach the function. Only version 4.49.0 is named as affected, and versions before it are not addressed.

fixtures.scenario: A model serving application runs Transformers 4.49.0 and passes externally influenced file name strings through configuration lookup. A crafted string makes the matching consume excessive CPU, which raises latency and disrupts serving for other requests.
The same application runs Transformers 4.51.0 or later. Crafted configuration-related strings no longer cause catastrophic backtracking, so CPU use and latency stay normal.

citations.quote: The affected version is 4.49.0, and the issue is resolved in version 4.51.0.
can be exploited to cause excessive CPU consumption through crafted input strings, leading to catastrophic backtracking.
This can result in model serving disruption, resource exhaustion, and increased latency in applications using the library.

patterns.title: ReDoS in get_imports() when filtering try/except blocks from loaded module source
patterns.cause: The get_imports() function in dynamic_module_utils.py in Hugging Face Transformers used a regular expression to filter out try/except blocks from Python code. The pattern matches a try keyword and colon, then lazily consumes arbitrary text up to an except keyword and colon. Crafted input strings trigger catastrophic backtracking and excessive CPU consumption.
preconditions: Transformers version 4.49.0 is in use, which is the affected version named in the advisories
get_imports() processes Python source text that an attacker can influence, such as code for a remotely loaded model
The try/except filtering regular expression runs on that text without any bound on matching effort
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Transformers to version 4.51.0 or later, where the issue is fixed. In your own code, do not use regular expressions with lazy, unbounded wildcards to strip or detect structured constructs such as try/except blocks in untrusted text. Prefer a method whose running time grows linearly with input size. Treat dynamically loaded code as untrusted when it is analyzed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix changed the code, so this card does not say which replacement technique was used. They also do not give input sizes or timings that trigger the slowdown, or say whether versions before 4.49.0 are affected. Impact is described only in general terms.

fixtures.scenario: A service loads a model repository with custom code. Its import scanner applies a regex with lazy wildcards between try and except to a crafted file, backtracks catastrophically, and pins a CPU core.
The service runs Transformers 4.51.0 or later. Its import scanner handles the same crafted file in time proportional to its size, so loading finishes and the service stays responsive.

citations.quote: can be exploited to cause excessive CPU consumption through crafted input strings due to catastrophic backtracking.
This vulnerability affects versions 4.49.0 and is fixed in version 4.51.0.

patterns.title: Open redirect in Flask-AppBuilder via Host header manipulation
patterns.cause: Flask-AppBuilder versions before 4.6.2 let an unauthenticated actor trigger an open redirect by manipulating the Host header of an HTTP request. The Host value supplied by the client could therefore influence where the application redirected the user, and no explicit list of safe redirect domains was available to restrict it.
preconditions: The application runs a Flask-AppBuilder version earlier than 4.6.2.
An attacker can send HTTP requests with a manipulated Host header; no authentication is needed.
No reverse proxy or other layer enforces trusted Host header values in front of the application.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Flask-AppBuilder 4.6.2 or later. Then set the FAB_SAFE_REDIRECT_HOSTS configuration variable so that only domains the administrator explicitly lists, including subdomain patterns if needed, are accepted as redirect targets. As a workaround or defense in depth, put a reverse proxy in front of the application that enforces trusted Host header values and rejects requests carrying any other host. In general, never derive a redirect destination from a client-controlled Host header without checking it against an explicit allowlist.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which endpoints or login flows are affected, how the Host header reaches the redirect logic, or how the allowlist is matched internally. They also do not describe the behavior when the allowlist is left unset. The reverse proxy workaround is named without configuration detail. Check the vendor release notes and the fix commit for exact behavior before relying on this card.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs Flask-AppBuilder 4.5.x with no reverse proxy host filtering. An unauthenticated attacker sends a request with a Host header set to an attacker-controlled domain, and the application issues a redirect that sends the victim to that domain.

A deployment runs Flask-AppBuilder 4.6.2 or later with FAB_SAFE_REDIRECT_HOSTS limited to the organization's own domains, and a reverse proxy rejects unknown Host values. A request with a foreign Host header does not result in a redirect to that foreign domain.

citations.quote: Flask-AppBuilder prior to 4.6.2 would allow for a malicious unauthenticated actor to perform an open redirect by manipulating the Host header in HTTP requests.
which allows administrators to explicitly define which domains are considered safe for redirection.
Use a Reverse Proxy to Enforce Trusted Host Headers

patch_review.observation: The diff renames the configuration key read by the safe redirect check from SAFE_REDIRECT_HOSTS to a FAB_ prefixed name, and updates the tests that cover spoofed Host headers, an explicit allowlist and wildcard subdomain entries. This matches the card's advice to configure FAB_SAFE_REDIRECT_HOSTS with an explicit list of trusted domains, so the allowlist is the control that stops a spoofed Host header from steering redirects. The diff also shows that with no list configured, the check falls back to the host taken from the request, a detail the card leaves open.

patterns.title: ReDoS in DonutProcessor token2json via backtracking-prone regex
patterns.cause: The token2json() method of the DonutProcessor class in Hugging Face Transformers uses a regular expression with a lazy wildcard capture between an s_ prefix and a closing angle bracket. Crafted input strings trigger catastrophic backtracking in this pattern, which causes excessive CPU consumption.
preconditions: Transformers is at a vulnerable version (4.51.3 or earlier per the advisories; the CVE record says 4.50.3 or earlier).
The application calls DonutProcessor token2json() as part of Donut document processing.
An attacker can influence the string that reaches token2json().
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Transformers to version 4.52.1 or later, which the advisories list as the fixed release. Until the upgrade is done, treat strings that reach token2json() as untrusted. Avoid matching them with backtracking-prone patterns, and keep the processing of such strings away from latency-sensitive API workers.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the fix changes the code, so this card gives no fix details. They do not say which crafted inputs trigger the problem or how long inputs must be. The advisories disagree on the affected range: the GHSA and PYSEC entries say 4.51.3 and earlier, while the CVE record says 4.50.3 and earlier. All three agree the fix is in 4.52.1. The sources do not recommend interim mitigations such as input length limits or timeouts.

fixtures.scenario: A document-processing API runs a Transformers release at or below 4.51.3 and passes attacker-influenced text to DonutProcessor token2json(). A crafted string drives CPU use up through backtracking and degrades service for other requests.
The same API runs Transformers 4.52.1 or later, where the advisories report the issue as fixed, so crafted input to token2json() does not cause the excessive CPU consumption described.

citations.quote: A Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) vulnerability was discovered in the Hugging Face Transformers library
which can be exploited to cause excessive CPU consumption through crafted input strings due to catastrophic backtracking
This vulnerability affects versions 4.51.3 and earlier, and is fixed in version 4.52.1.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the single lazy-wildcard regular expression in token2json() with two simple steps. It first finds the start-tag prefix with a plain search, then locates the closing angle bracket with ordinary string operations and takes the key from the text between them. This removes the backtracking-prone pattern, which matches the card's cause and its advice to upgrade.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through uploaded HTML files served back for rendering in Open WebUI
patterns.cause: The file upload endpoint accepted HTML files containing JavaScript from low-privileged users. The file could then be opened in the browser through a content route that serves it as HTML. The browser ran the embedded script in the viewer's session, and the advisory's proof of concept used it to read the session token from browser local storage.
preconditions: A low-privileged user can upload files, including HTML files with script content, through the files API.
The uploaded file can be opened in a browser through an HTML content route using the returned file id.
A more privileged user, such as an admin, is lured into opening the link while signed in. Under default settings only admins and the uploader can view the file.
The application is a version before 0.6.6.
patterns.prevention: Make sure retrieving an uploaded file can never cause the browser to execute attacker-supplied script in a viewer's authenticated session. In practice, user-uploaded HTML should not be served back as a renderable page from the application. Do not rely on ad hoc content filtering: the advisory saw filtering reject a script-only upload but accept the same script when it was padded with other markup. Also keep session tokens out of reach of page scripts where possible. For Open WebUI, upgrade to version 0.6.6 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that version 0.6.6 contains a fix. They do not describe how the fix works, so the exact mechanism, such as changed response headers, blocked file types or sanitization, is unknown. The advisory describes only the HTML content route and uploaded HTML files, and says nothing about other file types or other routes. Its impact assessment is limited by the default rule that only admins and the uploader can view the file, and deployments that change that rule may differ.

fixtures.scenario: A low-privileged user uploads an HTML file that has some harmless markup plus a script, and receives a file id. They send the admin a link to the HTML content route for that id. The admin opens it while signed in, the browser runs the script, and the user's session token is exposed to the attacker.

A low-privileged user uploads the same HTML file. When the admin follows the link, the application does not deliver it as a renderable page in the application's session. The file is treated as inert data, so no script runs and no session token is exposed.

citations.quote: which can be used to open the file in the browser and trigger the JavaScript code in the user's browser.
will give the low-privileged user complete control over the admin's account, ultimately enabling RCE via functions
this file can only be viewed by admins and the user that uploaded it, but not by other low-privileged users
Version 0.6.6 contains a fix for the issue.

patch_review.observation: The change is in the HTML content route for uploaded files. It looks up the account that uploaded the file and adds a check tied to the uploader's role, so HTML served for rendering is meant to depend on who uploaded it rather than on any user's upload. The added check is written loosely and only rejects the request when the uploader record is missing, so it is a partial or awkward gate, but the direction matches the card's point that user-uploaded HTML should not be rendered back to other sessions.

patterns.title: Stored XSS from raw HTML rendering of chat markdown tokens in Open WebUI
patterns.cause: The markdown renderer checked whether an HTML token's text contained a prefix naming an iframe whose source pointed at the server's files API path. If it did, the whole token text was inserted with Svelte's raw HTML directive. The prefix check does not limit the rest of the tag, so an attacker could add an onload attribute that runs script. The script runs each time the chat transcript is opened.
preconditions: Chat message text controlled by an attacker is parsed into markdown HTML tokens in the browser.
A token whose text contains the expected iframe source prefix is passed to raw HTML insertion without escaping or sanitizing.
The victim opens the transcript, for example after the attacker shares it with users on the same server or through community sharing.
The access token is kept in browser localStorage, so injected script can read it.
patterns.prevention: Never insert message-derived text as raw HTML. Do not treat a substring or prefix match on the text as proof that the markup is safe, because the rest of the tag, including event handler attributes, stays attacker-controlled. Render untrusted HTML tokens as escaped text. If embedding files is needed, build the element from validated parts in trusted code instead of echoing the message text. Upgrade to version 0.6.6 or later, which contains the patch.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, so the exact patched behavior and any remaining allowed markup are not stated here. The advisory does not say whether other HTML token branches are affected. Keeping the token in localStorage is noted as what makes theft possible, but no change to token storage is described.

fixtures.scenario: A chat message holds an iframe tag whose source starts with the server's files API path and which also has an onload attribute. The renderer matches the prefix and inserts the text as raw HTML, so script runs when the chat is opened.
The same message is rendered so the iframe text is shown as inert escaped text, or the markup is removed. No event handler attribute is kept, and no script runs when the chat is opened or shared.

citations.quote: which is a dangerous Svelte functionality that allows text to be rendered as HTML code.
The JavaScript code will be executed in the user's browser every time that chat transcript is opened
This is possible because the access token is stored inside the user's localStorage, which is accessible by JavaScript.
Version 0.6.6 contains a patch for the issue.

patterns.title: Path traversal in setuptools PackageIndex download filename built from an untrusted URL
patterns.cause: The download routine derives a local file name from a URL and tries to sanitize it only by replacing double-dot sequences. It then joins the name to a temporary directory with os.path.join(). That function discards the base directory when the second argument begins with a slash or a drive letter, so a crafted URL can place the file outside the temporary directory.
preconditions: setuptools older than 78.1.1 is in use
PackageIndex download functionality is reached, for example through the deprecated easy_install or package_index code paths
The URL being downloaded is attacker-influenced, for example a malicious link on a package index page
The file name taken from the URL begins with a slash or drive letter
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to setuptools 78.1.1 or later. In any similar code, treat a file name derived from a URL as untrusted input. Do not rely on replacing dot sequences. Reject or reduce names that are absolute or contain drive letters or separators. Before writing, resolve the final path, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it is still inside the intended download directory.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how version 78.1.1 changed the code, so this card gives only a general fix direction. The advisory notes the exposed surface is reduced because easy_install and package_index are deprecated. Exact exploit conditions beyond malicious URLs on package index pages are not detailed. The sources say remote code execution is possible only depending on context.

fixtures.scenario: A package index page lists a link whose path component begins with a slash or drive letter. The downloader joins it to its temporary directory, the base is discarded, and the file is written to an arbitrary location.
The downloader reduces the link to a plain file name or rejects absolute or escaping names, then confirms the resolved path stays inside the temporary directory before writing.

citations.quote: if the second begins with a slash or drive letter
derived from a URL without sufficient sanitization
While there is some attempt to sanitize by replacing instances of '..' with '.', it is insufficient.
An attacker would be allowed to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem with the permissions of the process running the Python code

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the download filename resolver so that after joining the temporary directory with the name taken from the URL, it checks the result still lies under that directory and raises an error otherwise. The added test uses a URL with encoded slashes that decodes to an absolute path, which matches the card's cause of a join discarding the base directory when the name starts with a slash.

patterns.title: Unauthenticated pickle deserialization on the PyNcclPipe control channel exposed through an unbound TCPStore
patterns.cause: The PyNcclPipe control path receives objects from peers through StatelessProcessGroup recv_obj, which passes client-provided data to pickle.loads. The service was meant to be reachable only on the private network given by the kv-ip option. PyTorch's TCPStore listens on all interfaces regardless of the address supplied, and that address was only used client-side. Any host that could reach the port could therefore send a malicious serialized object and get remote code execution.
preconditions: vLLM versions 0.6.5 through 0.8.4 with the V0 engine
The PyNcclPipe KV cache transfer integration is in use
The TCPStore port is reachable from hosts outside the intended private network
The attacker can join the communication domain and send a serialized object to the receiving node
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to vLLM 0.8.5 or later, where the TCPStore socket is limited to the private interface that was configured. When building similar services, bind the listening socket explicitly to the intended private interface instead of treating the supplied IP address as a client-side hint, and confirm the real bind address. Keep the KV transfer port on a secured private network as the vLLM security documentation requires.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the fix as restricting the TCPStore socket to the configured interface. They do not say the deserialization of peer data was changed, so a peer that can reach the port may still be trusted to send serialized objects. Only the PyNcclPipe integration with the V0 engine is described as affected. PyTorch judged the all-interface listening behavior intentional. The sources give no further detail on the fix beyond the binding workaround.

fixtures.scenario: A node runs PyNcclPipe KV transfer on the V0 engine, vLLM 0.6.5 to 0.8.4, with kv-ip set to a private address. The TCPStore still listens on all interfaces, so any reachable host can send a serialized object that the node deserializes.

A node runs vLLM 0.8.5 or later, where the TCPStore socket is bound to the configured private interface, and the network is restricted per vLLM security guidance, so untrusted hosts cannot reach the control port.

citations.quote: Attackers can exploit this by sending malicious serialized data to gain server control privileges.
The intention was that this interface should only be exposed to a private network using the IP address specified by the
The IP address given was only used as a client-side address to use.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the group creator on rank 0 open its own listening socket bound to the configured host and port, then hands that socket to the TCPStore through a listen file descriptor. This replaces the default all-interface listening, so the store is reachable only on the intended private interface. The pickle-based receive path is left unchanged, which matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS via label_config in Label Studio upload-example endpoint
patterns.cause: The upload-example view accepted a POST without a login requirement, read the label_config form value, generated a sample task from it, and returned the serialized result through a plain HttpResponse that defaults to an HTML content type. Markup carried from label_config into the sample data was therefore rendered by the victim's browser as a page, giving reflected XSS. The upstream fix removes the view and its route entirely.
preconditions: Label Studio version prior to 1.18.0 is running with the upload-example route enabled.
The endpoint accepts cross-site form POSTs from the victim's browser, with no authentication or CSRF barrier stopping a crafted submission.
The attacker can lure the victim into submitting a crafted label_config value, for example through an auto-submitting form on another site.
Script content in label_config survives into the sample task data that is returned.
patterns.prevention: Remove endpoints that are unused or that merely echo request-derived content, as the upstream fix does by deleting the view, its URL entry, and its tests. If such an endpoint must remain, require authentication, return an explicitly typed JSON response such as Django's JsonResponse, add a no-sniff content type header, and avoid echoing raw user markup. Upgrade to 1.18.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows only removal of the endpoint, so it does not reveal which exact task data fields reflected the input. Other code paths that handle label_config are not covered by this change. Any client or tooling that relied on the upload-example feature loses it after the fix. The advisory notes that session cookies are http-only, which limits session theft even though other script-based impact remains possible.

fixtures.scenario: A page on an attacker site auto-submits a form to the upload-example endpoint with a label_config value holding script markup. The server reflects it in a response built from the sample task data, and the victim's browser runs it.

The same crafted label_config is submitted. The response is explicitly typed as JSON and values are encoded, so the browser never interprets the input as markup. The deployment runs release 1.18.0 or later.

citations.quote: The vulnerability is specifically located in line 57, where HttpResponse is used.
A vulnerability in versions prior to 1.18.0 allows an attacker to inject a malicious script into the context of a web page
Version 1.18.0 contains a patch for the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix deletes the unauthenticated upload-example view, which took a label_config form value, built a sample task from it and returned it as a default HTML HttpResponse. It also removes the URL route, the URL listing entry and the tests for that endpoint. The card's cause and its remove-the-endpoint prevention match this.

patterns.title: Internal-only upload form inputs let clients make the server move arbitrary host files
patterns.cause: The central file upload processor trusted form inputs meant only for internal use. A crafted HTTP request to an upload endpoint could supply them, so the server treated an arbitrary host file as a freshly uploaded temporary file and moved it into the upload folder, where it could be downloaded.
preconditions: Attacker holds an account with the FILE_UPLOAD permission
OctoPrint version 1.11.1 or earlier, or a third-party plugin upload endpoint built on the same upload processor
The target file is readable by the OctoPrint process
patterns.prevention: In the central upload processing component, strip every internal-only form input from incoming requests before any handler sees them, so only values the server itself generates can identify a temporary uploaded file. Do not let client-supplied fields decide which file on disk is moved. Upgrade to version 1.11.2 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how the internal form inputs are named or validated, so this card gives no detail on the fix mechanics. Third-party plugin endpoints might be affected, but the sources do not say which ones or how to check them. The sources also give no detail on how the moved file is later served.

fixtures.scenario: A user with FILE_UPLOAD sends a crafted multipart request to an upload endpoint with an internal-only field naming a config file path. The server moves that file into the upload folder, and the user downloads it.
The same crafted request is sent, but the upload processor first removes all internal-only form inputs. Only server-created temporary files are handled, and the named host file stays in place.

citations.quote: A specially crafted HTTP Request to an affected upload endpoint that contains some form inputs only supposed to be used internally
The fix removes any internal-only form inputs from incoming requests in the central file upload processor component.
allows an attacker with the FILE_UPLOAD permission to exfiltrate files from the host that OctoPrint has read access to

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the multipart upload handler in the Tornado utilities. When a request part finishes, any part whose name ends with one of the server's internal suffixes is thrown away, and its file handle is closed. Client-supplied fields can therefore no longer pose as server-generated temporary-file path entries, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Catastrophic backtracking in the vLLM pythonic tool call parser regex
patterns.cause: The pythonic tool parser matches model output against a complex pattern with nested quantifiers and optional groups using the standard library regular expression engine. Crafted near-matching input triggers catastrophic backtracking and burns CPU. The upstream change swaps that engine for the third-party regex package in the parser and across the codebase, which cuts the worst case from exponential to roughly quadratic but leaves the pattern itself unchanged.
preconditions: vLLM version 0.6.4 up to but excluding 0.9.0 is in use
The pythonic tool parser handles function call text from model output
An attacker can influence the text that reaches the tool call detection pattern
The pattern is evaluated by the standard library regular expression engine, which backtracks
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to vLLM 0.9.0 or later, where the parser modules use the regex package instead of the standard library module, and make sure that package is installed. For regexes applied to untrusted text, avoid nested unbounded repetitions over overlapping sub-patterns, so each part of the input can be consumed in only one way. Where possible, prefer a structural parser or a linear-time matcher, and cap input length. Also test with near-matching inputs of growing length and check that runtime stays low.
patterns.limitations: The commit is mainly an import swap, so it reduces backtracking cost without removing the ambiguity in the pattern. Quadratic behavior can remain on long crafted inputs. The diff adds no timeout, input length limit or pattern simplification. The same swap is applied to many unrelated modules, so it does not show which other patterns were actually exploitable.

fixtures.scenario: A server runs vLLM 0.8.x with the pythonic tool parser. A client sends model-bound text with many repeated, almost-valid call fragments. The nested-quantifier regex backtracks exponentially and one request pins a CPU.

A server runs vLLM 0.9.0 or later. The same crafted text is parsed with the patched pattern, which has far lower worst-case cost, and the team keeps testing long near-matching inputs because quadratic cost may remain.

citations.quote: The pattern contains multiple nested quantifiers, optional groups, and inner repetitions which make it vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking.
this regex may still be problematic. It has gone from exponential time complexity, O(2^N), to O(N^2).
the associated KV cache (used for model inference and typically stored in GPU memory) is not released in a timely manner.

patch_review.observation: The diff replaces the standard library regular expression module with the third-party regex package in the pythonic tool parser and many other modules, and adds regex as a build requirement. The pattern in the parser is not edited, and no timeout, length cap or pattern simplification is added, which matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: urllib3 redirect settings are ignored under Pyodide in browsers and Node.js
patterns.cause: When urllib3 runs in a Pyodide runtime, it uses the JavaScript Fetch API or XMLHttpRequest. The retries and redirect parameters are ignored there, and the runtime decides redirect behavior. Code that turns redirects off or limits them through urllib3 therefore gets no such control.
preconditions: urllib3 version 2.2.0 or later and before 2.5.0
Code runs in a Pyodide runtime, in a browser or in Node.js
The application relies on urllib3 retries or redirect settings to limit or disable redirects, for example to mitigate SSRF or open redirect
patterns.prevention: In Node.js, upgrade to a patched urllib3 release; the CVE record says 2.5.0 patched the issue. In browsers, urllib3 has no suitable way to control redirects, so do not treat its redirect or retries settings as a safeguard there. Expect the default browser redirect behavior and do not rely on disabled redirects as an SSRF or open redirect mitigation in that environment.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch works in Node.js, so this card does not either. Browsers have no remediation: XMLHttpRequest offers no redirect control, and the Fetch API returns opaque redirect responses without data when redirects are handled manually. The sources give no other mitigation for browser use. Environments outside Pyodide are not discussed.

fixtures.scenario: An app runs urllib3 2.4.0 under Pyodide and sets redirect to false to block redirects to internal hosts. The runtime ignores the setting and follows redirects itself, so the SSRF mitigation does not work.
An app in Node.js runs urllib3 2.5.0 or later. In browsers, it does not assume urllib3 settings stop redirects and accepts the default browser redirect behavior.

citations.quote: Starting in version 2.2.0 and prior to 2.5.0, urllib3 does not control redirects in browsers and Node.js.
the retries and redirect parameters are ignored with Pyodide; the runtime itself determines redirect behavior.
Redirects are often used to exploit SSRF vulnerabilities.
Expect default browser behavior for redirects.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a Node.js check in the Pyodide fetch code and, only there, sets the Fetch redirect mode to manual so urllib3 handles redirects itself. This makes the retries and redirect settings take effect in Node.js, and the new test confirms it. Browsers are left unchanged and the test skips them, which matches the card's cause, its upgrade advice for Node.js, and its warning about browsers.

patterns.title: Catastrophic regex backtracking in TensorFlow-to-PyTorch weight name conversion in Transformers
patterns.cause: The convert_tf_weight_name_to_pt_weight_name() function converts TensorFlow weight names to PyTorch format using a regular expression. The pattern matches a run of non-slash characters, then a triple underscore, then another run of non-slash characters. Crafted input strings can trigger catastrophic backtracking in this pattern and cause excessive CPU consumption.
preconditions: The application uses a Transformers version up to 4.51.3.
The application runs TensorFlow-to-PyTorch model conversion, which reaches the weight name conversion function.
An attacker can influence the weight name strings that the function processes.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Transformers to version 4.53.0 or later, which the advisories list as the fixed release. Until then, treat weight names from untrusted sources as potentially crafted. Avoid running TensorFlow-to-PyTorch conversion on such input inside a shared service where CPU exhaustion would cause service disruption. In general, name-parsing patterns should not allow backtracking blowup on attacker-controlled strings.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code change in the fix, the exact input shapes that trigger the slowdown, or how an attacker would deliver crafted names in practice. They also do not describe workarounds other than upgrading. The impact is described only as service disruption and resource exhaustion, with no further detail on exposed API surfaces.

fixtures.scenario: A service running Transformers 4.51.3 accepts uploaded TensorFlow checkpoints and converts them to PyTorch. An uploaded checkpoint contains a weight name crafted to cause catastrophic backtracking, so the conversion worker uses excessive CPU and other requests are delayed or fail.
The same service runs Transformers 4.53.0 or later. The same crafted weight name goes through the conversion step without catastrophic backtracking, and the worker stays responsive.

citations.quote: can be exploited to cause excessive CPU consumption through crafted input strings due to catastrophic backtracking
The vulnerability affects versions up to 4.51.3 and is fixed in version 4.53.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a guard in convert_tf_weight_name_to_pt_weight_name() before the regex substitution. It rejects names that are very long and contain the triple underscore separator, or that contain too many such separators, by raising a ValueError. This limits the input that could trigger catastrophic backtracking in the pattern, which matches the card's cause.

patterns.title: Unfiltered filter-error text in changedetection.io watch overview enables XSS
patterns.cause: The watch overview built error text from the last fetch or filter error, which can echo attacker-influenced content such as the configured include-filter string. That text was wrapped as trusted markup in the error-text builder and also marked safe in the overview template, so the template's automatic escaping was bypassed. A filter string containing HTML or script was therefore rendered as live markup (CWE-79).
preconditions: changedetection.io is running a version earlier than 0.50.4.
A watch has a filter value containing HTML or script that causes a filter error, so the stored last error echoes that value.
The watch overview page renders the error text for a user who views the list.
The error text is emitted as trusted HTML rather than being escaped.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to changedetection.io 0.50.4 or later. In your own code, do not mark error messages or other values derived from user-supplied configuration as safe markup. Let the template engine auto-escape them, or explicitly HTML-escape them in any code path that builds strings outside a template context. Only trusted, server-built fragments, such as a link you construct yourself, should be marked safe, and any user-influenced part inside them must be escaped first. Add a regression test that stores markup in a filter field and checks that the page shows it as escaped text.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the error text in the watch overview and the plain-text branch of the error builder. Other places that render stored errors or user-influenced strings as trusted HTML may need separate review. The escaped output now shows raw markup characters as text rather than formatting, which is the intended behavior.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment running a version before 0.50.4 has a watch whose filter fails. The resulting error text is shown in the watch overview without being filtered, so markup or script content in that text can run in the browser of the user viewing the overview.

A deployment runs version 0.50.4 or later. When a watch filter fails, the error text is filtered before it appears in the watch overview, so it is shown as inert text and does not run in the viewer's browser.

citations.quote: errors in filters from website page change detection watches were not being filtered resulting in a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability
XSS - Errors in filters from website page change detection watches were not being filtered.
This issue has been patched in version 0.50.4

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the safe marking from the error text in the watch overview template. It also changes the plain-text branch of the error builder in the watch model, which used to wrap the last fetch error and last notification error as trusted markup, so that both are fully HTML-escaped by a new helper in the safe rendering module. A regression test stores a script-bearing include filter and confirms the overview page shows it as escaped text.

patterns.title: SSRF through unvalidated gateway_path in MLflow gateway_proxy_handler
patterns.cause: In MLflow before 3.1.0, gateway_proxy_handler lacks gateway_path validation. The advisory classifies the result as server-side request forgery (CWE-918) via this handler.
preconditions: The deployment runs an MLflow version earlier than 3.1.0.
The gateway_proxy_handler code path is reachable.
A gateway_path value reaches the handler without being validated.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to MLflow 3.1.0 or later, which is the version the advisories give as the boundary for this flaw. In any similar proxy handler, treat gateway_path as untrusted input and validate it before it influences an outbound request. Prefer a strict allowlist of expected gateway paths and reject anything else.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that gateway_path validation is missing before 3.1.0. They do not say how the path is used to build the outbound request, what input forms are abusive, or what the upstream validation checks. They also do not say which deployments expose the handler or whether authentication is required. The allowlist approach is a general direction, not a description of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: An MLflow server older than 3.1.0 exposes gateway_proxy_handler. It accepts a caller-supplied gateway_path and applies no validation to it before handling the request.
An MLflow server at version 3.1.0 or later handles the request. Any custom proxy code of the same kind checks gateway_path against an allowlist of expected values and rejects everything else.

citations.quote: gateway_proxy_handler in MLflow before 3.1.0 lacks gateway_path validation.
gateway_proxy_handler in MLflow before 3.1.0 lacks gateway_path validation.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a validation step for the gateway path in the gateway proxy handler, run before the outbound request is built from the configured target address and the user-supplied path. For GET requests only the endpoints listing path is accepted. For POST requests only a path shaped like gateway, one name segment, then invocations is accepted. Anything else is rejected with an invalid-parameter error, and tests cover the rejected paths.

patterns.title: Unescaped user input rendered through NiceGUI ui.html() or HTML-mode ui.chat_message leads to XSS
patterns.cause: Before NiceGUI 3.0.0, ui.html() and ui.chat_message with HTML text enabled inserted their content into the page as raw markup, with no sanitization step and no requirement that the developer choose one. Untrusted text passed to these components could therefore carry script-executing markup, such as an image tag with an error handler, that ran in the victim's browser.
preconditions: The application runs NiceGUI 2.24.2 or earlier, or runs 3.x but explicitly disables sanitization for the component.
Untrusted input, for example from a ui.input() field or an AI/model response, reaches ui.html() or ui.chat_message with HTML text enabled.
No sanitizing function is applied to that content before it is rendered.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to NiceGUI 3.0.0 or later, where ui.html() and HTML-mode ui.chat_message require an explicit sanitize argument and raise an error if it is missing. For any content that may include user or model-generated input, pass a real sanitizing function (the project recommends the html-sanitizer package) so dangerous tags and event-handler attributes are stripped while safe markup is kept. Pass false for the sanitize option only for fully trusted static markup such as fixed SVG or documentation snippets. If markup is not needed, use a text-only component such as ui.label, or leave HTML mode off in chat messages, which escapes the text. In review, check every place sanitization is disabled and confirm its content is trusted.
patterns.limitations: Sanitization is opt-in per call: choosing false for the sanitize option reproduces the original vulnerability, and the quality of protection depends on the sanitizer the developer supplies. The fix covers ui.html() and HTML-mode ui.chat_message only. Other components that render raw markup, such as add_head_html or add_body_html, are not changed by this diff. Upgrading alone does not repair existing code that was updated mechanically by adding a false value to silence the new requirement.

fixtures.scenario: A page has a text input whose change handler takes the typed value and renders it with ui.html() as-is. A user types markup containing an image element with an error handler that runs script. The browser inserts it into the DOM and runs the script in the user's session.

The same page escapes the typed value as HTML text before giving it to ui.html(), or never passes the typed value to ui.html() at all. Markup typed by the user appears as visible characters and no script runs. The application is also upgraded to NiceGUI 3.0.0 or later.

citations.quote: Versions 2.24.2 and below are at risk for Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) when developers render unescaped user input into the DOM using ui.html().
Applications that do not pass untrusted input into ui.html() are not affected.
the library does not enforce any HTML or JavaScript sanitization
This issue is fixed in version 3.0.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the HTML element require a sanitize choice, either a sanitizing function or an explicit False, and applies it whenever content is set or changed. The chat message component raises a ValueError if HTML mode is on and no sanitize choice is given, and escapes text otherwise. Internal uses, examples and docs were updated to pass False or a real sanitizer, which matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Roundup XSS via URL and tracker template interaction (CVE-2025-53865)
patterns.cause: In Roundup before 2.5.0, several shipped tracker templates rendered user-controllable values without HTML escaping. These included item ids, titles, names, designators and the current username.
