They were output with the TAL replace statement, often inside translated page titles, headings and the edit-collision message, and the page header printed the username directly. A crafted value or a request URL that reaches these fields could inject markup or script into the page (CWE-79).
preconditions: The deployment runs Roundup older than 2.5.0.
The tracker is built from one of the affected shipped templates (devel, responsive, classic, minimal or the website issues tracker), or from a customized copy that kept the unescaped output pattern.
An attacker can influence a value that the template prints, such as an item title or name, a username, or a designator derived from the request URL, and a victim then views the page.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Roundup to 2.5.0 or later. In templates, output dynamic values with the TAL content statement or an explicitly escaping accessor instead of the replace statement that bypasses escaping, including inside translated blocks with named parts. Render the username in page headers with escaping enabled. Trackers with customized or copied templates must be audited and edited by hand, because the upgrade does not rewrite local template files.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows template-level escaping fixes only. It does not show whether other template constructs or custom tracker code still emit unescaped values, and the exact exploit URL is not described. The revised card relies on the diff, not on the advisory text.

fixtures.scenario: A tracker runs Roundup 2.4.x with the responsive template. An attacker sends a user a crafted link to the tracker, and the interaction between the URL and the template lets script run in the user's browser session.

The same tracker runs Roundup 2.5.0 or later with the updated devel or responsive template. Any customized template copies have been compared against the updated ones, so a crafted link does not lead to script execution.

citations.quote: In Roundup before 2.5.0, XSS can occur via interaction between URLs and issue tracker templates (devel and responsive).

patch_review.observation: The fix changes shipped tracker templates (classic, devel, responsive, minimal and the website issues tracker) so that item ids, titles, names, designators and the tracker name are printed with the TAL content statement instead of the replace statement, which skipped escaping. It also changes the username shown in the devel and responsive page headers to use an escaping plain accessor. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Unsafe dynamic evaluation of CAPTCHA responses in pyLoad web UI script
patterns.cause: The interactive CAPTCHA userscript in the pyLoad web interface runs script code delivered through a cross-window message using direct eval. Direct eval executes in the local scope of the message handler, so the executed code can reach handler internals such as the parsed request, the signature objects and other closure variables. The only gate is a signature check on the delivered code, so any flaw or bypass in how that code is supplied lets attacker-influenced script run with broad access in the page.
preconditions: A vulnerable pyLoad web interface version is deployed that serves the interactive CAPTCHA userscript using direct eval.
The userscript accepts message events and executes the script code carried in the message once its signature verifies.
An attacker can influence the script content or message that reaches the userscript, or can exploit the over-broad scope that the evaluated code runs in.
patterns.prevention: Do not use direct eval for code received at runtime. Run any such code through a Function constructor in strict mode, so it executes in global scope and sees only the parameters explicitly passed to it. Pass only the minimal objects the code needs. Keep the signature verification, and also check the origin of incoming messages and the message structure before acting. Where possible, avoid executing delivered script at all and use declarative data handled by fixed code.
patterns.limitations: The fix narrows the scope of the executed code but still performs dynamic code execution, so it depends on the signature check and on the trustworthiness of the signed script. It does not add origin checks or input validation. Strict-mode Function code can still use global objects such as the window and document, so it is not a sandbox.

fixtures.scenario: A CAPTCHA response field is submitted containing a short piece of script text that reads the page cookies. The client-side result handler passes the text straight to the JavaScript eval() function, so the script runs in the browser session with no check on its content.

The same response text is received, but the handler treats it only as an opaque string. It is checked against the expected CAPTCHA answer format, rejected when it does not match, and never passed to eval() or any other code execution facility, so the script text has no effect.

citations.quote: allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code in the client browser and potentially the backend server.
No sanitization or validation is performed on this input
Commit 909e5c97885237530d1264cfceb5555870eb9546, the patch for the issue, is included in version 0.5.0b3.dev89.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces direct eval of the signed CAPTCHA script code with a function built through the Function constructor in strict mode. The code now runs in global scope and receives only the request and the helper object as parameters, so it can no longer see the message handler's local variables such as the signature objects. The signature check stays, and no origin or structure validation is added. The rest of the diff is a version bump and a style cleanup that swaps var for let and const.

patterns.title: Path traversal through uploaded filename in pyLoad json/upload endpoint
patterns.cause: The /json/upload endpoint joins the configured storage folder with a prefix and the client-supplied filename of each uploaded file, then saves the file there. The filename is neither sanitized nor validated, so parent-directory sequences in it move the write location outside the intended upload directory.
preconditions: The attacker holds a valid authenticated session on the pyLoad web interface.
The attacker sends a multipart upload to the json/upload endpoint with a crafted filename containing parent-directory sequences.
The filename is appended to the storage folder path without validation before the file is saved.
The target location is writable by the pyLoad process.
patterns.prevention: Never treat a client-supplied filename as a trusted path component. Validate or sanitize the filename so it cannot contain directory separators or parent-directory sequences. Then resolve the final destination path, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it remains inside the intended storage folder before saving. Reject the upload if the check fails. Upgrade to pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev90 or later, where the issue is reported as fixed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so the validation approach above is general guidance rather than a statement of what the patch does. The CVE names version 0.5.0b3.dev89 as affected, while the advisory proof of concept refers to version 0.4.20, and the sources do not reconcile this. The sources give no information on other endpoints or on other ways filenames reach the filesystem.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user uploads a file whose multipart filename has several parent-directory sequences followed by a system path. The server joins it to the storage folder and saves it, writing outside the upload directory.

An authenticated user uploads a file with the same crafted filename. The server reduces it to a safe name or rejects it, and checks that the resolved path is inside the storage folder, so nothing is written elsewhere.

citations.quote: By manipulating the filename of an uploaded file, an attacker can traverse out of the intended upload directory
an authenticated path traversal vulnerability exists in the /json/upload endpoint of pyLoad.
This is fixed in version 0.5.0b3.dev90.

patch_review.observation: The fix passes the client-supplied upload filename through werkzeug's secure_filename before joining it with the storage folder and temporary prefix, so directory separators and parent-directory sequences can no longer move the write location. The card's cause (unsanitized filename joined into the storage path) and its prevention (sanitize the filename, then confirm the destination stays inside the storage folder) match this change. The patched code sits in the package-adding handler of the JSON blueprint rather than a function named for upload, but it is the same upload-saving logic.

patterns.title: SSRF via URL-based file upload fields in BentoML multipart and JSON handlers
patterns.cause: BentoML request deserializers automatically download files from user-supplied URLs for file-type parameters. The multipart path performs no validation. The JSON path checks only the URL scheme. Neither blocks internal network addresses, localhost, or cloud metadata endpoints, so an unauthenticated client can make the server issue arbitrary HTTP requests.
preconditions: BentoML 1.4.0 up to but not including 1.4.19
A service endpoint with a file-type parameter such as a filesystem path or image type
A client can send a multipart form field or JSON body containing a URL instead of file content
The server can reach internal services, localhost, or a cloud metadata endpoint
patterns.prevention: Treat every user-supplied URL as untrusted before the server fetches it. Apply the same validation in both the multipart and JSON paths. Go beyond a scheme check: use allowlist-style validation and reject targets in internal or private network ranges, localhost, and cloud metadata endpoints. Upgrade to 1.4.19 or later, which contains the patch.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch validates URLs. They do not say how redirects, DNS rebinding, or alternate IP encodings are handled, or whether the remote URL download feature can be disabled by configuration. Validate those cases separately.

fixtures.scenario: A service exposes an endpoint taking a file-type parameter. An unauthenticated client submits a multipart field whose value is a link-local cloud metadata URL. The server fetches it with no address validation.

The same endpoint checks the submitted URL against an allowlist and rejects internal, private, localhost, and metadata destinations in both the multipart and JSON paths. The server never issues the request.

citations.quote: neither path restricts access to internal networks, cloud metadata endpoints, or localhost services.
automatically download files from user-provided URLs without validating whether those URLs point to internal network addresses, cloud metadata endpoints, or other restricted resources.
should be enhanced to include allowlist validation rather than just scheme checking.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a new URL safety check that requires an http or https scheme, rejects localhost and the cloud metadata address, and resolves hostnames to reject private, loopback and link-local addresses. It is applied in both the body-URL download path and the multipart file-field helper, which previously had no validation. The card's cause and prevention match this, including the need to block internal ranges, localhost and metadata endpoints in both paths.

patterns.title: Stored XSS from insufficient sanitization in CKAN markdown_extract helper
patterns.cause: The helpers.markdown_extract() function did not sufficiently sanitize user-provided input before wrapping it in an HTML literal element. Markup in stored text, such as a resource description, could therefore reach rendered pages as active HTML.
preconditions: CKAN version prior to 2.10.9 (2.10 line) or prior to 2.11.4 (2.11 line)
User-provided data on dataset, resource, organization or group pages is rendered through markdown_extract
An extension page that uses the same helper also exposes the issue
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to CKAN 2.10.9, CKAN 2.11.4 or later. In custom code and extensions that call this helper, treat user-provided text as untrusted. Do not wrap it in an HTML literal (marked-safe) element until it has been sanitized or escaped.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact change made to the helper, any workaround short of upgrading, or what write access an attacker needs to store the malicious text. Only the pages named in the advisory are confirmed as affected.

fixtures.scenario: A user able to edit a resource stores a description containing HTML markup. A vulnerable CKAN version renders it through markdown_extract and wraps it as an HTML literal without sufficient sanitization, so the markup reaches other visitors.
The same description is rendered on CKAN 2.10.9 or 2.11.4 or later, where the helper sanitizes input before wrapping it, so the stored text does not become active markup on the page.

citations.quote: did not perform sufficient sanitization of input data before wrapping in an HTML literal element
This helper is used to render user-provided data on dataset, resource, organization or group pages
This vulnerability has been fixed in CKAN 2.10.9 and 2.11.4

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces a naive regular expression that stripped HTML tags from the markdown output in markdown_extract with a call to the bleach-based cleaner in strip mode. The same weak regex is also removed from render_markdown, which already used bleach. This confirms the cause was insufficient sanitization before the result was marked as a safe literal.

patterns.title: Path traversal in pyLoad CNL addcrypted endpoint via the package parameter
patterns.cause: The addcrypted endpoint of the CNL blueprint builds a file path from the request-supplied package value and writes the submitted content to it. The path is not reliably confined to the designated storage directory, so an unauthenticated caller can write arbitrary files outside it. The advisory shows only simple character stripping on the package value before the path is built.
preconditions: pyload-ng version 0.5.0b3.dev89 or below
The addcrypted endpoint is reachable by an unauthenticated attacker
The attacker-controlled package value is used to build the output file path
The pyLoad process can write to the target location, for example system files when running as root
patterns.prevention: Do not let a request value decide where a file is written. After building the output path, resolve it to its final absolute form, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it still lies inside the intended download directory before opening it. Reject the request otherwise. Do not rely on removing a few characters from the name. Upgrading to 0.5.0b3.dev90 or later addresses the issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the actual upstream fix, so this card gives only a general direction. They are also inconsistent: the quoted code strips slashes, backslashes and colons from the package value, yet the proof of concept uses dot-dot and slash sequences. The sources do not explain this gap, so the exact exploit mechanics are unclear. They do not describe authentication or deployment hardening.

fixtures.scenario: An unauthenticated client posts to the addcrypted endpoint with a package value meant to point at a cron directory and a crafted content field. The server joins the value to the download directory and writes the file outside it, which can lead to code execution as root.
The same request arrives. The server builds the target path, resolves it to a final absolute path, and sees that it is not inside the download directory. It rejects the request and writes no file.

citations.quote: suffers from an unsafe path construction vulnerability, allowing unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files outside the designated storage directory
overwrite critical system files, including cron jobs and systemd services
This issue is fixed in version 0.5.0b3.dev90.

patch_review.observation: The fix keeps the character stripping on the package name but then normalizes the joined path, makes it absolute, and checks that it lies under the configured storage folder, including the trailing separator. If the check fails, the endpoint returns a 400 error and never opens the file. This matches the card's cause (a request value controls the write location) and its prevention (confine the final path to the download directory and reject otherwise, not rely on stripping characters).

patterns.title: SQL injection through string-built IN clause in pyLoad link info update
patterns.cause: In pyLoad before 0.5.0b3.dev91, the add_links value submitted to the add_package JSON endpoint travels through the info thread and file manager to the database layer's link info update routine. That routine joins the submitted URLs into one string and inserts it directly into the text of a SELECT statement with an IN list. A quote character in a submitted link therefore ends the string literal and lets the attacker add their own SQL.
preconditions: Attacker-controlled text reaches the add_links parameter of the add_package endpoint (the published proof of concept sends it with session cookies).
The submitted link strings flow unchanged into the database layer's link info update routine.
That routine builds an IN list by joining the URL values into the SQL text instead of binding them as parameters.
patterns.prevention: Never place user-supplied values, including URLs, into SQL text by joining or formatting strings. Build the IN list from one bound-parameter placeholder per URL, and pass the URL values separately to the database driver's execute call. The same routine already binds its UPDATE statement values with question-mark placeholders, so the SELECT should follow the same pattern. Treat data that arrives through background threads and manager layers as untrusted, because it can originate from an HTTP request. Review other places that format SQL from lists of values.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say what privileges are needed to call the endpoint. The proof of concept only shows that a session cookie is sent. They do not name the database engine or say which injected statements run, so the full impact is unconfirmed beyond data modification or deletion. They also do not describe the upstream patch beyond the fixed version number, and this card does not assess other SQL construction sites in the project.

fixtures.scenario: A user submits a package whose add_links field contains a URL with an embedded single quote followed by extra SQL. The database layer joins the URLs into a quoted list inside the SELECT text, so the extra SQL is parsed as part of the statement instead of being treated as a URL.

A user submits the same package with the same quote-containing URL. The database layer builds a statement with one placeholder per URL and passes the URLs as separate bound values. The quote is treated as part of the URL text, no extra SQL runs, and the lookup simply finds no matching row.

citations.quote: the parameter add_links in API /json/add_package is vulnerable to SQL Injection.
statuses is constructed from data, and data is the value of the add_links parameter entered by the user through /json/add_packge.
data is list of tuples (name, size, status, url)

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the link info update routine in the file database. Instead of joining the URLs into the SELECT text, it builds one bound placeholder per URL and passes the URL list to the driver separately. This matches the card's cause (string-built IN clause) and its prevention (bound parameters, as the UPDATE statement already does).

patterns.title: Command injection through uploaded filenames used in OctoPrint system event handler commands
patterns.cause: OctoPrint event handlers of type system substituted placeholder values, such as the current file name, path, and event payload fields, directly into a command string and ran it through a shell by default. Uploaded filenames were not stripped of shell metacharacters, so a crafted name containing separators like a semicolon turned into extra commands when an event fired. The root flaw is unescaped untrusted placeholder values in a shell command, with unsanitized filenames as the delivery path.
preconditions: OctoPrint version 1.11.2 or earlier is running.
The attacker is authenticated and can upload a file with a chosen filename, or otherwise influence event payload values.
An event handler of type system is configured with a command that contains a filename-based or payload-based placeholder and runs through a shell.
The event tied to that handler is triggered after the upload.
patterns.prevention: Escape every placeholder value for the shell before substituting it into a system command, and prefer running commands without a shell so that values stay plain arguments. Also strip shell-significant characters (separators, pipes, ampersands, redirection, glob and variable characters, and control characters) from filenames during sanitization, in both the normal and the strict universal modes. Upgrade to version 1.11.3 or later. Until then, enable the option that enforces universally safe filenames or disable system event handlers that use filename placeholders, and review existing uploads for suspicious names.
patterns.limitations: Quoting only applies when the subscription uses a shell; with shell disabled, values are passed unescaped and safety depends on the command not interpreting its arguments. Existing files with hostile names are not renamed by the fix and still need manual review. Handlers that do not use placeholders are unaffected. Event handlers still run admin-configured commands, so a malicious configuration is outside this fix. Network exposure and access control are advisory mitigations only.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user uploads a file whose name contains a semicolon followed by a shell command. An administrator has an event handler that runs a system command with a filename placeholder, and the event fires after the upload. The attacker's command runs on the host.

The same upload is attempted on an instance that is upgraded to 1.11.3 or later, or that enforces safe filenames, or that has no enabled event handler passing filename placeholders to system commands. The crafted name is not interpreted as a command.

citations.quote: allows an authenticated attacker to upload a file under a specially crafted filename that will allow arbitrary command execution
If no event handlers executing system commands with uploaded filenames as parameters have been configured, this vulnerability does not have an impact.
then vet the existing uploads and make sure to delete any suspicious looking files
The vulnerability is patched in version 1.11.3.

patch_review.observation: The fix moves event handling into subscription classes. System subscriptions now quote every placeholder value for the shell when shell mode is on, and add a configurable shell option with a deprecation warning that the default will later become no shell. Filename sanitization now removes separators, pipes, ampersands, glob and redirection characters, the dollar sign, and control characters in both normal and strict modes. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Stored XSS from unsanitized blog post titles in the Mezzanine admin displayable links endpoint
patterns.cause: The displayable_links_js function in the Mezzanine admin includes blog post titles in JSON responses served from the admin displayable_links.js endpoint without properly sanitizing them. A script payload stored in a title is therefore delivered to an admin's browser and can execute there.
preconditions: Mezzanine version earlier than 6.1.1 is in use.
An authenticated admin user can create or edit a blog post and set a malicious JavaScript payload in the title field.
A second admin user is tricked into following a direct link to the admin displayable_links.js endpoint.
patterns.prevention: Treat every stored title as untrusted data when building the displayable links response. Sanitize or encode titles for the context in which the response is delivered, so that a title can never be interpreted as script by the browser. Apply this at the point where titles are placed into the response, not only when they are saved. Upgrade Mezzanine to version 6.1.1 or later, which is the first version not described as affected.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact escaping method, the response content type, or how the browser comes to execute the payload. They do not say whether content types other than blog posts, or fields other than the title, are affected. They do not describe the fix beyond the fixed version number. The attack needs an authenticated admin to plant the payload and another admin to follow the link, so the real-world impact depends on how many admin accounts exist and how far they are trusted.

fixtures.scenario: An admin creates a blog post whose title contains a script payload. A second admin opens a direct link to the admin displayable_links.js endpoint. The title is emitted into the response without proper sanitization, and the script runs in the second admin's browser session.

The same blog post title is stored, but the displayable links response neutralizes the title for its output context. When the second admin opens the direct link, the title is shown only as inert text and no script runs.

citations.quote: fails to properly sanitize blog post titles before including them in JSON responses served via
An authenticated admin user can create a blog post with a malicious JavaScript payload in the title field

patch_review.observation: The fix HTML-escapes each displayable's title inside the displayable_links_js view, at the point where titles are put into the links response. This matches the card's cause (unsanitized stored titles in that endpoint) and its prevention (encode titles when building the response, and upgrade).

patterns.title: ReDoS in Transformers EnglishNormalizer number normalization on long digit strings
patterns.cause: The number normalization method of the CLVP EnglishNormalizer applies several regular expressions to digit runs, and those patterns are ambiguous. In the pound and dollar patterns, a greedy repeated class of digits and separators is followed by another repeated digit. In the decimal and ordinal patterns, a plain digit run is followed by a suffix that often fails to match. A long digit string with no valid ending forces the engine to retry many ways of splitting the run, so CPU time grows polynomially with input length (CWE-1333).
preconditions: The application uses a Transformers release that predates the regex rewrite in the CLVP number normalizer.
Untrusted text reaches the normalizer's number normalization step, for example in text-to-speech preprocessing.
The attacker can submit a very long run of digits, possibly mixed with commas or periods, that fails to match the full pattern.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a Transformers release that contains the fix. The fix drops the redundant trailing digit quantifier in the pound and dollar patterns. It makes the leading digit runs in the decimal and ordinal patterns possessive, so a failed match gives up at once instead of backtracking. Because the standard re module supports this only from Python 3.11, the fix uses the regex package on older Python versions, so make sure that dependency is installed. When writing similar normalizers, avoid adjacent overlapping quantifiers over the same character class, and cap input length before regex processing as defense in depth.
patterns.limitations: The diff covers only the number normalization patterns in the CLVP normalizer. Other regular expressions elsewhere in the library are not reviewed here. The diff does not show the exact first fixed release, so the version boundary has to come from the advisory. The length limit is general hardening advice and is not part of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: A text-to-speech API runs Transformers 4.52.4 and passes user-submitted text to the normalize_numbers() method of the EnglishNormalizer class. A request containing a very long run of digits drives CPU usage up and delays or blocks other requests.
The same API runs Transformers 4.53.0 or later. A request with a very long run of digits is normalized without the excessive CPU consumption described for the affected versions.

citations.quote: crafted input strings containing long sequences of digits, leading to excessive CPU consumption
This vulnerability affects versions up to 4.52.4 and is fixed in version 4.53.0.
potentially causing service disruption, resource exhaustion, and API vulnerabilities

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the number normalization step in the CLVP English normalizer. It removes the redundant trailing digit quantifier in the pound and dollar patterns and makes the leading digit runs in the decimal and ordinal patterns possessive. It also imports the regex package on Python older than 3.11, since the standard re module only gains possessive quantifier support in 3.11. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from unvalidated parameters in pyLoad CNL and captcha endpoints
patterns.cause: Two input-trust gaps existed. The CNL addcrypted handler built a file path from the request-supplied package name, removing only a few separator characters, so a crafted name could affect the name and location of the written file. Separately, the interactive captcha userscript accepted cross-window messages from any origin, so any page that could message it could drive its script-activation logic.
preconditions: A vulnerable pyLoad version, earlier than 0.5.0b3.dev91, is running with the web UI or CNL endpoint reachable by the attacker.
An attacker can send a crafted package name to the CNL addcrypted endpoint.
For the captcha part, an attacker-controlled page can post messages to the window running the interactive captcha userscript.
patterns.prevention: Turn the package name into a safe filename with a vetted sanitizer, resolve the final path to an absolute form, and refuse any path that falls outside the intended storage directory. In the captcha userscript, check the origin of every incoming message against an explicit allowlist and ignore all others. Upgrade to 0.5.0b3.dev91 or later.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows only path sanitization and an origin allowlist, not a reflected output-encoding change, so the exact XSS or injection impact described in advisories is not confirmed by the code. The origin allowlist in the patch is a hard-coded placeholder list, which may break or weaken legitimate self-hosted setups. Other CNL handlers and the captcha endpoint on the server side are not shown to be changed.

fixtures.scenario: A CNL endpoint receives a query parameter containing script-like text and places it in the response unchanged. A victim who opens a crafted link runs the attacker's script inside the Web UI session.
The same endpoint checks the parameter against its expected format, rejects non-conforming input, and encodes any value placed in the response, so the text is never executed as script.

citations.quote: The application did not consistently enforce input validation or encoding, making it possible for an attacker to craft malicious requests.
user-supplied parameters from HTTP requests were not adequately validated or sanitized before being passed into the application logic and response generation.
Version 0.5.0b3.dev91 contains a patch for the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the manual character stripping of the package name in the CNL addcrypted handler with a standard filename sanitizer. It resolves the final path to an absolute form and rejects anything outside the storage folder. It also makes the interactive captcha userscript ignore cross-window messages whose origin is not in a trusted allowlist. The card describes both changes correctly and notes that no output-encoding change appears in the diff.

patterns.title: Hardlink-based path traversal in the llama-index ObsidianReader
patterns.cause: The load_data() method of ObsidianReader has path restrictions whose security checks fail to differentiate between real files and hardlinks. A hardlink inside the read location can therefore point to a sensitive file elsewhere on the system, and the check does not catch it.
preconditions: The application uses ObsidianReader from a vulnerable release, before llama-index-readers-obsidian 0.5.2 (reported against llama-index 0.12.27).
The application calls load_data() on a directory that an attacker can influence.
A hardlink in that directory refers to a sensitive file outside the intended location, such as /etc/passwd.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to llama-index-readers-obsidian 0.5.2 or later, where the issue is resolved. In your own file-reading code, do not assume a path check on the file name is enough, because a hardlink looks like a real file. Make the containment check treat hardlinks explicitly, and restrict what readers can access.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the fix works, so this card cannot say which check was added. They do not say whether other readers or other link types such as symlinks are affected. They give the fixed version as 0.5.2 but do not explain the version numbering between llama-index and the reader package.

fixtures.scenario: An application points ObsidianReader load_data() at a vault directory where an attacker placed a hardlink to /etc/passwd. The path check treats it as a normal vault file, and the contents of the sensitive file are read.
The application uses llama-index-readers-obsidian 0.5.2 or later, so the same hardlink placed in the vault is covered by the fixed release instead of being treated as an ordinary in-vault file.

citations.quote: allows for hardlink-based path traversal
the security checks fail to differentiate between real files and hardlinks
This issue is resolved in llama-index-readers-obsidian version 0.5.2.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that reads the file's link count and, inside load_data(), skips and warns about any file with more than one hard link before the existing path-prefix containment check runs. This matches the card's cause, that the resolved-path check cannot tell a hardlink from a real file, and its prevention, which is to handle hardlinks explicitly. The package version is bumped to 0.5.2, as the card states.

patterns.title: Unchecked sparse tensor loading from user prompt embeddings enables out-of-bounds write
patterns.cause: vLLM accepted user-supplied serialized tensors as prompt embeddings, and similar embedding inputs for multimodal data, by default and without any explicit operator opt-in. The prompt embeddings are deserialized with torch.load and densified. With sparse tensor integrity checks off by default in recent PyTorch, a crafted sparse tensor can cause an out-of-bounds write, leading to a crash or possibly code execution. Malformed embeddings could also crash the engine through bad shapes.
preconditions: A vulnerable vLLM release that accepts prompt embeddings or multimodal embedding inputs without a dedicated opt-in setting
The Completions endpoint or chat endpoint is reachable by untrusted users
PyTorch 2.8.0 or later, where sparse tensor invariant checks are off by default
patterns.prevention: Treat embedding inputs as a privileged feature that is disabled unless an operator explicitly enables it. Require the enable-prompt-embeds setting before loading prompt embeddings, and add a separate enable-mm-embeds setting that gates image embedding inputs in the chat parser and any embedding items in the multimodal processor. Return a clear client error when the feature is off. Enable these options only for trusted users, and upgrade to a release containing the patch. Validating sparse tensor invariants during loading is a useful additional layer, but it is not what this diff shows.
patterns.limitations: The gating only removes exposure when the options stay off. Deployments that enable embeddings for untrusted users remain exposed to malformed tensors and engine crashes from wrong shapes. The diff shown does not display any sparse invariant check, so it is unclear whether such a check was added elsewhere.

fixtures.scenario: A server on vLLM 0.10.2 with PyTorch 2.8.0 receives a base64 prompt embedding holding a crafted sparse tensor. It is loaded with torch.load(), passes the dtype check, and to_dense() performs an out-of-bounds write.

A server on vLLM 0.11.1 receives the same crafted sparse tensor. Sparse invariant validation is enforced before densifying, so the malformed tensor is rejected with an error and the process keeps running.

citations.quote: Due to a change introduced in PyTorch 2.8.0, sparse tensor integrity checks are disabled by default.
maliciously crafted tensors can bypass internal bounds checks and trigger an out-of-bounds memory write during the call to to_dense().
this needs to be enabled explicitly using the

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an opt-in gate: the prompt embeddings loader now rejects input unless the enable-prompt-embeds option is set. A new enable-mm-embeds option, off by default, is also enforced in the chat parser for image embeddings and in the multimodal processor for embedding items. Docs warn that wrong embedding shapes can crash the engine and that these flags are for trusted users only. The diff adds no sparse tensor invariant check, which the card correctly says.

patterns.title: Stored XSS via unvalidated watch URL scheme in the update API
patterns.cause: Watch URL validation was inconsistent and weak across entry points. The web form and the update API used a loose scheme-prefix check that stripped the source marker anywhere in the string and judged the raw text before template rendering. The API create and import routes only used a generic URL syntax validator with no scheme allow-list. A crafted URL could therefore be stored through the API, and when it was later rendered as a clickable link on the Preview page it could execute attacker script in the application origin.
preconditions: The application accepts watch URLs through several entry points, such as a UI form, a REST API and a bulk import endpoint.
Each entry point used its own validation logic, and some performed no scheme allow-list check or only a weak prefix check.
The attacker can call the API, for example with a valid API key.
A user views a page that renders the stored URL as a link and clicks it.
patterns.prevention: Use one shared URL safety routine for every path that creates or changes a watch URL, including form, API create, API update, import and datastore insertion. The routine should strip the source marker only as a leading prefix, render any template markup first and validate the final result, reject markup characters such as angle brackets, enforce a strict scheme allow-list with file access only when explicitly enabled, and finally run URL syntax validation. Apply the same check again when building the link shown in templates so stored legacy values are not emitted as links.
patterns.limitations: The diff does not show the Preview template itself, so it is unclear whether link targets are also escaped at render time. Previously stored malicious URLs are not cleaned up by this change, though the link property now refuses to emit unsafe ones. The new validator also rejects some formerly accepted inputs, such as URLs with unusual file scheme forms or template syntax in queries, which may break existing watches.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated API client updates an existing watch and sets its URL to a javascript: scheme value. The server stores it without any protocol check. A user later opens Preview and clicks the link, and the script runs in the application's origin.

The same update request is sent through the API, but the server applies the shared protocol check first. It rejects the javascript: URL with a validation error and leaves the stored URL unchanged. An ordinary http or https URL is accepted through both the UI and the API.

citations.quote: When instead the Watch API is used, this check is not performed resulting in unsafe URLs added as Watch.
Watch protocol is not permitted by SAFE_PROTOCOL_REGEX or incorrect URL format
When the user clicks on *Preview* and then on the malicious link, the JavaScript malicious code is executed.
Version 0.50.34 fixes the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the old loose scheme-prefix check with one shared validator that is used by the web form, API create, API update, import, datastore insertion, the link property and the template helper. The validator strips the source marker only at the start, renders template markup before checking, rejects angle brackets, allows file access only when explicitly enabled, and then runs URL syntax validation. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: HTML and script injection through printer-generated Action Command popups in OctoPrint
patterns.cause: Text sent by the printer for Action Command notification and prompt popups can contain arbitrary HTML and JavaScript. In OctoPrint 1.11.3 and earlier, this text is not neutralized before it appears in the web interface, so the markup is injected into the page.
preconditions: OctoPrint version 1.11.3 or earlier is in use
Action Command notification popups or prompt dialogs are enabled
A victim is convinced to print a specially crafted file that makes the printer emit the malicious text
The victim has an active OctoPrint session in the browser
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to OctoPrint 1.11.4 or later, where the issue is fixed. In your own code, treat any text that originates from the printer as untrusted data. Show it in popups as plain text and never as markup. If you cannot upgrade, an administrator can disable Action Command notification popups and set prompt dialog support to Never. Print only files from trusted sources, ideally sliced with your own slicer.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code change in 1.11.4, so the exact escaping or sanitizing approach is not covered here. Disabling popups is a workaround and does not remove the underlying flaw. Trusting file sources reduces exposure but is not a technical control. Other OctoPrint versions or output paths are not addressed by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A printer running a crafted file sends an action command notification whose text contains HTML and script markup. The web UI puts that text into the popup as markup, so the script runs in the logged-in user's session.
The same crafted file sends markup in the notification text. The UI shows it as literal text in the popup, so no script runs. The instance is also upgraded to 1.11.4 or later.

citations.quote: allows injection of arbitrary HTML and JavaScript into Action Command notification and prompt popups generated by the printer.
An attacker who successfully convinces a victim to print a specially crafted file could exploit this issue
It is also strongly recommended to ensure that files being printed originate from trusted sources
This issue is fixed in version 1.11.4.

patch_review.observation: The fix applies HTML escaping on the client side to printer-supplied text before it is shown. In the Action Command notification plugin it escapes the notification message. In the Action Command prompt plugin it escapes the prompt message and each button label. This matches the card's cause (printer text injected unescaped into the page) and its prevention (treat printer text as untrusted and show it as plain text).

patterns.title: Stored DOM XSS from unsanitised prompt body inserted as rich text via innerHTML
patterns.cause: When rich text insertion is enabled, the prompt body is converted by a markdown parser and assigned to the innerHTML property of a temporary element with no sanitisation. The markdown parser does not sanitise content, so attacker-supplied HTML and event handler attributes reach the DOM and run as script.
preconditions: The attacker has permission to create prompts, which low-privilege users do not have by default.
The victim has the Insert Prompt as Rich Text preference enabled; it is off by default.
The victim runs the slash command that inserts the attacker's prompt into the chat input.
Open WebUI is version 0.6.34 or below.
patterns.prevention: Treat the prompt body as untrusted. Sanitise the HTML produced from it with an HTML sanitiser such as DOMPurify before it is assigned to innerHTML or otherwise parsed into the DOM. Do not rely on the markdown parser or its character handling as a defence, because the advisory shows quote limits can be bypassed by building strings from character codes. Upgrade to version 0.6.35 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail, so this card does not claim which sanitiser settings it uses. They do not say whether other DOM sinks in the application are affected. The remediation text names DOMPurify only as a suggestion. Users with the rich text setting disabled are described as unaffected.

fixtures.scenario: A user with prompt-creation rights saves a prompt body containing an image tag with an error handler. A victim with rich text insertion enabled runs the slash command, and the body is assigned to innerHTML unsanitised, so script runs.

The same prompt body is passed through an HTML sanitiser such as DOMPurify before being assigned to innerHTML, so the event handler attribute is removed and no script runs when the victim inserts the prompt.

citations.quote: the prompt body is assigned to the DOM sink .innerHtml without sanitisation
Sanitise the user controlled HTML with DOMPurify before assigning it to
The setting is off by default. Users with this setting disabled are unaffected.
This issue is fixed in version 0.6.35.

patch_review.observation: The fix passes the HTML produced by the markdown parser through DOMPurify's sanitize step before it is placed into the temporary element in the rich text prompt insertion path. This removes attacker-supplied script-capable markup such as event handler attributes. It matches the card's cause (unsanitised parser output reaching innerHTML) and its prevention (sanitise with DOMPurify before parsing into the DOM).

patterns.title: Unvalidated user-supplied URL fetched by server-side web loader (SSRF)
patterns.cause: The web processing endpoint of Open WebUI passes the user-supplied URL straight to its content loaders, which fetch it from the server. No check is made on the destination, so any authenticated user can make the server send HTTP requests to arbitrary URLs and read the returned content.
preconditions: The attacker holds any valid authenticated account; no special role is needed
The server accepts a user-supplied URL and fetches it through a web loader
No validation of scheme, destination address, or domain is applied before the fetch
For credential theft, the server runs where an internal or cloud metadata endpoint is reachable
patterns.prevention: Treat every user-supplied URL as untrusted before any loader fetches it. Restrict the allowed protocols to the web schemes the feature needs, and reject file and other non-web schemes. Resolve the host and refuse loopback, private (RFC1918), link-local and cloud metadata addresses. Where practical, require the destination to match a domain allowlist. Apply these checks in the shared fetch path so every loader is covered, including the video loader. Upgrade to a release that contains the vendor fix, which the CVE record lists as 0.6.37.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the 0.6.37 fix works, so this card gives general direction only. They do not address redirects, DNS rebinding, or alternate IP encodings, and these need separate handling. They also do not say which of the listed checks the vendor applied.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user posts the cloud metadata endpoint URL to the web processing endpoint. The server fetches it and returns the content, exposing cloud credentials.

A user submits a web URL for retrieval. The server checks the scheme, rejects loopback, private and metadata addresses or requires an allowlisted domain, and only then fetches the page. A request for the metadata address is refused.

citations.quote: allows any authenticated user to force the server to make HTTP requests to arbitrary URLs
Both loaders fetch the user-supplied URL without validation
Cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254, fd00:ec2::254)
This vulnerability is fixed in 0.6.37.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes URL validation allow only http and https schemes, and adds a default blocklist of cloud metadata addresses and hostnames that can be extended through an environment setting. It applies the same filter logic to resolved IP addresses of search results, and raises an error when every supplied URL is blocked, so the loader never fetches unvetted destinations.

patterns.title: ReDoS in MarianTokenizer remove_language_code() via malformed language code patterns
patterns.cause: The remove_language_code() method of MarianTokenizer in the Hugging Face Transformers library relies on inefficient regex processing. Crafted input strings containing malformed language code patterns can make it consume excessive CPU, which can lead to denial of service.
preconditions: The application uses Hugging Face Transformers version 4.52.4, the version named as affected.
The application uses MarianTokenizer, and remove_language_code() runs on strings that an attacker can influence.
The attacker can supply input containing malformed language code patterns.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Transformers to version 4.53.0 or later, where the issue is reported as fixed. In any tokenizer or text-handling code, avoid inefficient regex processing of untrusted strings, especially when matching language code patterns. Prefer matching approaches whose running time does not blow up on malformed input.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the vulnerable regex, the exact trigger string, or how the fix changed the implementation, so no specific code-level remedy is given here. They name only 4.52.4 as affected and 4.53.0 as fixed, so the status of other earlier versions is not stated. They give no guidance on mitigations short of upgrading, such as input length limits or timeouts.

fixtures.scenario: A translation service runs Transformers 4.52.4 and passes user-submitted text through MarianTokenizer, where remove_language_code() handles it. An attacker sends strings with malformed language code patterns, and a worker spends excessive CPU on each request, degrading service for other users.

The same service runs Transformers 4.53.0 or later. The same crafted strings with malformed language code patterns no longer cause excessive CPU consumption in remove_language_code(), and request handling stays responsive.

citations.quote: This vulnerability is present in version 4.52.4 and has been fixed in version 4.53.0.
The issue arises from inefficient regex processing, which can be exploited by crafted input strings containing malformed language code patterns

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the regular expression used by the language code remover in MarianTokenizer, which could backtrack heavily on crafted input with a start marker but no matching end marker. It now uses plain string prefix and search operations to split off a leading language code, so the cost stays linear. The card's cause (inefficient regex handling of malformed language codes) and its direction of avoiding backtracking-prone matching agree with this.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS through style injection in NiceGUI add_css, add_scss and add_sass
patterns.cause: add_css placed caller-supplied text directly between style tags in the page head, and add_scss embedded it in an inline module script after JSON encoding but without escaping the less-than character. Input containing a closing style or script tag therefore ended the element early, and the remainder was parsed as HTML or script and executed in the victim browser.
preconditions: NiceGUI version 3.3.1 or earlier is in use
The application calls ui.add_css, ui.add_scss or ui.add_sass with text that is not fully trusted
Attacker-controlled input, such as a URL query parameter used for dynamic theming, reaches the style text
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NiceGUI to the fixed release (3.4.0 or later). The fix keeps style text out of raw markup: the content is JSON-encoded, the less-than character is escaped so no closing tag can appear in the inline script, and a helper defined in the page template creates the style element and assigns the text as plain text content. When injecting dynamic text into inline scripts or style blocks in your own code, use the same approach of encoding the data and applying it through DOM text properties instead of concatenating it into HTML. Until upgrading, do not pass untrusted input into these functions.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers add_css and add_scss, and add_sass shares the SCSS code path. It does not make the CSS content itself safe, so attacker-controlled CSS can still change page appearance or leak data through CSS features. Other APIs that add raw head or body HTML, such as ui.add_head_html, remain the caller's responsibility to sanitize.

fixtures.scenario: A NiceGUI 3.3.1 page takes a color from a URL query parameter and builds a style rule for ui.add_css. A value containing a closing style tag followed by markup runs script in the victim browser.
The app runs NiceGUI 3.4.0 or later and does not place unchecked untrusted values into style text, so a closing style tag in a request value does not break out of the style context.

citations.quote: Versions 3.3.1 and below are vulnerable to Reflected XSS through its ui.add_css, ui.add_scss, and ui.add_sass functions.
An attacker can break out of the intended <style> or <script> tags by injecting closing tags
This issue is fixed in version 3.4.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops style text from being placed as raw markup. In add_css, the content is now JSON-encoded with the less-than character escaped and passed to a small helper function. In add_scss, the same escaping is applied to the inline module script. The helper is defined in the page template and builds a style element, assigning the text as plain text content. This matches the card's cause (a closing style or script tag breaking out of the element) and its prevention.

patterns.title: Unsanitized SVG content in NiceGUI interactive_image enables XSS
patterns.cause: In NiceGUI 3.3.1 and earlier, the interactive image component and its layers render SVG content through Vue's v-html directive with no sanitization step. Attacker-controlled markup in the content property, for example a foreignObject element carrying HTML and script, is inserted into the page and runs in the viewer's browser.
preconditions: NiceGUI version 3.3.1 or earlier is in use, or a newer version is used without an explicit sanitizer configured.
User-controlled input can reach the content property of the interactive image or of one of its layers.
The content is rendered in a browser, for example on a multi-user page showing user-generated annotations.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to NiceGUI 3.4.0 or later, then pass an explicit sanitize function to the interactive image whenever content may include user input. The project recommends the html-sanitizer package's sanitize method, which must be installed separately. Layers created with add_layer inherit the same sanitizer. Only disable sanitization with a false value for fully trusted, developer-written content. Upgrading alone does not protect, because the default only logs a warning and leaves content unsanitized. Also avoid placing untrusted data in the content property.
patterns.limitations: The fix is opt-in: if no sanitizer is given, content is still passed through unchanged and only a warning is logged. Protection depends on the quality and configuration of the sanitizer the application chooses, and it requires an extra package. Existing apps that rely on unsanitized SVG must set the option explicitly. Other NiceGUI components that render HTML are not covered by this change.

fixtures.scenario: A multi-user dashboard on NiceGUI 3.3.1 lets users submit annotations that the app assigns to the content property of an interactive image. A foreignObject payload with embedded HTML then runs script in other viewers' browsers.
The app runs NiceGUI 3.4.0 or later, and user-submitted text is not passed into the content property of the interactive image.

citations.quote: The component renders SVG content using Vue's v-html directive without any sanitization.
This issue is fixed in version 3.4.0.
If an application allows user-controlled input to be passed to the content property of an interactive image

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an optional sanitize argument to the interactive image. When a function is given, content is passed through it before rendering, and layers created with add_layer inherit it. A false value turns sanitization off, and the default of none only logs a one-time warning and leaves content unchanged. This matches the card's cause, its opt-in prevention advice and its limitations.

patterns.title: Path traversal in NiceGUI add_media_files allows arbitrary file read
patterns.cause: The route for served media accepts a filename parameter that can contain full paths, including parent-directory sequences. The handler joins the configured local directory with the requested name and serves the result without checking that it still lies inside that directory. URL-encoded dots can be used to reach files outside it.
preconditions: The application calls app.add_media_files() to expose a local directory under a URL path
That URL path is reachable by an attacker, who needs no authentication
The server process has permission to read the targeted file
The NiceGUI version is 3.3.1 or earlier
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to NiceGUI 3.4.0 or later, where the issue is fixed. In custom file-serving code, resolve the combined path to its canonical form, for example with os.path.realpath() or Path.resolve(), and confirm it is still inside the canonical served directory before opening it. Reject requests that fall outside and return a not-found response.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how version 3.4.0 implements the fix, so the exact validation it uses is unknown. They do not cover symbolic links inside the media directory, other encodings beyond URL-encoded dots, or other NiceGUI file-serving functions. Only the add_media_files() path is documented as affected.

fixtures.scenario: An app serves a media folder at /media. A remote client requests /media with encoded parent-directory segments followed by etc/hosts, and the server returns that file from outside the folder.
The same app runs a fixed version. The same encoded request resolves outside the media folder, fails the boundary check, and gets a not-found response.

citations.quote: Versions 3.3.1 and below are vulnerable to directory traversal through the App.add_media_files() function, which allows a remote attacker to read arbitrary files
The code simply joins local_directory and filename without checking if the result is still inside the local_directory.
The `{filename:path}` parameter accepts full paths, including traversal sequences like `../`.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the media-file handler resolve both the configured directory and the requested path to canonical form. It returns a not-found response if the result is not inside the served directory or is not a regular file. A new test requests a URL-encoded parent-directory path and expects a 404 with no secret content.

patterns.title: Untrusted reason phrase in Tornado set_status and HTTPError enables header injection and XSS
patterns.cause: In Tornado 6.5.2 and below, the reason phrase given to RequestHandler.set_status or tornado.web.HTTPError is used unescaped in HTTP headers and in the HTML of the default error page. Untrusted data in that argument can therefore inject headers or script.
preconditions: The application runs Tornado 6.5.2 or earlier.
The application passes untrusted or attacker-influenced data as the reason argument to RequestHandler.set_status or tornado.web.HTTPError.
For the XSS case, the response is rendered by the default error page.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Tornado 6.5.3 or newer. Do not derive the reason argument from user input: use a fixed string literal, or omit it, since it is rarely required. For a general-purpose error message in HTTPError, use the log_message argument instead of reason.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the fix works internally or which characters are handled. They do not cover custom error pages. Only applications that explicitly reflect untrusted input into the reason argument are affected.

fixtures.scenario: On Tornado 6.5.2, a handler takes a query parameter and passes it as the reason argument to tornado.web.HTTPError. An attacker supplies markup or line breaks, and the default error page or response headers include it unescaped.
A handler raises HTTPError with a fixed string literal as the reason, or omits it, and puts any descriptive text in log_message. The application runs Tornado 6.5.3 or newer.

citations.quote: the supplied reason phrase is used unescaped in HTTP headers (where it could be used for header injection)
reason phrases are not used at all in HTTP/2
This issue is fixed in version 6.5.3.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes set_status check the reason phrase against the HTTP reason-phrase grammar and reject any value containing a less-than sign, replacing it with the generic text Unknown, which stops header injection through control characters. It also escapes the reason in the default write_error page to stop XSS, skips write_error for 304 responses, and updates the docs to say the reason is not a general-purpose error message. This matches the card's cause (unvalidated, unescaped reason in headers and the default error page) and its advice to upgrade and avoid untrusted reason values.

patterns.title: Static file path normalization in aiohttp can reveal which absolute path components exist
patterns.cause: In aiohttp 3.13.2 and below, the path normalization logic for static files is meant to prevent path traversal. It still lets an attacker ascertain whether absolute path components exist on the server. The advisories describe this as a brute-force leak of internal static file path components, so the traversal defense itself leaks information.
preconditions: The application uses web.static() to serve static files.
The installed aiohttp version is 3.13.2 or below.
An attacker can send requests to the static route and probe for path components.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade aiohttp to version 3.13.3 or later, where the issue is fixed. Avoid web.static() in production deployments, since the sources say it is not recommended there. More generally, an implementation that normalizes requested paths to block traversal should not let a client learn whether absolute path components exist on the server.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain how the probing works, which responses differ, or what the patch changes beyond a commit reference. They do not say whether other aiohttp features or versions are affected, or whether a mitigation exists short of upgrading or avoiding web.static(). The impact is limited to learning that path components exist; the sources do not describe file contents being read.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs aiohttp 3.13.2 and exposes a directory through web.static(). A remote client sends many crafted requests and uses the results to work out which absolute path components exist on the server.
The application runs aiohttp 3.13.3 or later, or does not use web.static() in production and serves static files by other means. Probing the static route does not reveal absolute path components.

citations.quote: Versions 3.13.2 and below enable an attacker to ascertain the existence of absolute path components through the path normalization logic for static files
If an application uses web.static() (not recommended for production deployments)
This issue is fixed in version 3.13.3.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the static resource resolver normalize the requested path before checking the route prefix, so requests that use dot-dot segments to climb out of the static root and re-enter via an absolute filesystem path no longer match the route. The old handler's explicit forbidden response for absolute-looking names is removed, so such probes now get a not-found result and the response no longer differs depending on whether the absolute path components exist. The tests were updated to expect not-found instead of forbidden.

patterns.title: XXE in EverNoteLoader via etree.iterparse() on untrusted XML
patterns.cause: The EverNoteLoader component of langchain-community parses XML with etree.iterparse() without disabling external entity references. A crafted XML file can therefore reference local files, which can lead to sensitive information disclosure.
preconditions: The application uses the EverNoteLoader component of langchain-community to load an XML file.
An attacker can supply or influence the XML content that the loader parses.
The installed langchain-community version is older than 0.3.27, the release the advisories name as the fix.
The parser still resolves external entity references.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade langchain-community to 0.3.27 or later. In any code that parses XML, configure the parser so external entity references are not resolved. Treat files handed to document loaders as untrusted input, and do not rely on the parser's default settings.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact parser settings used in the fix. They do not say whether other loaders are affected, or whether network-based entity resolution is possible; they mention only local files. The CVE text lists 0.3.63 as the affected version while the advisories say the fix is in 0.3.27, so verify the version range against the advisory before relying on it.

fixtures.scenario: A service accepts user-uploaded Evernote export files and passes them to EverNoteLoader on a langchain-community version older than 0.3.27. An uploaded file declares an external entity that points to /etc/passwd.

The same service runs langchain-community 0.3.27 or later, so the loader contains the fix. An uploaded file that declares an external entity pointing to a local file is not expected to expose that file's contents.

citations.quote: The vulnerability arises from the use of etree.iterparse() without disabling external entity references, which can lead to sensitive information disclosure.
This issue has been fixed in 0.3.27 of langchain-community.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the XML iterparse call in the EverNote loader so entities are no longer resolved and network access is blocked. It also turns off recovery from malformed XML and the huge-tree option to reduce entity-expansion and denial-of-service risk. This matches the card's cause (a parser that resolves external entities on untrusted ENEX input) and its prevention (stop resolving external entities).

patterns.title: Shell command injection via model_uri when serving MLflow models with MLServer enabled
patterns.cause: When a model is served with the MLServer option enabled, the model location string is embedded directly into a shell command run through bash -c without proper sanitization. Shell metacharacters in that string, such as command substitution syntax, are interpreted by the shell and run attacker-controlled commands.
preconditions: A model is served with the enable_mlserver option set to true
The model location string contains shell metacharacters such as command substitution syntax
The location value is influenced by an attacker, for example through a directory writable by lower-privileged users
The serving process runs with higher privileges than the attacker
patterns.prevention: Do not build a shell command string from the model location. Avoid invoking bash -c with interpolated values. Pass the location to the child process as a separate argument, without a shell, so metacharacters stay literal data. Also validate the location against the expected format before use. Serve models only from directories that lower-privileged users cannot write.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, the exact affected version range, or the exact code path. They state only that the latest version at disclosure was affected. The argument-separation and validation guidance is a general direction, not a confirmed description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A privileged service serves a model from a shared directory that a low-privileged user can write. The user names a model path containing command substitution syntax. The path goes into a bash -c command and the injected command runs with the service's privileges.

A privileged service serves models from a directory only it can write. The model location is validated and passed to the child process as a separate argument with no shell. A path containing metacharacters is treated as literal text and nothing is executed.

citations.quote: it allows for command substitution and execution of attacker-controlled commands.
can lead to privilege escalation if a higher-privileged service serves models from a directory writable by lower-privileged users.
Mlflow: Command Injection when serving models with enable_mlserver=True

patch_review.observation: The fix escapes the model location with the standard shell-quoting helper before it is placed into the mlserver start command string in get_cmd, so shell metacharacters such as command substitution are treated as literal text. The card correctly identifies the unsanitized model location reaching a shell as the cause. Its prevention advice to keep the value as literal data is compatible with the fix, though upstream kept the shell and added quoting rather than removing the shell or adding format validation.

patterns.title: Unvalidated user paths in nltk.util.filestring() allow arbitrary file read
patterns.cause: In nltk 3.9.2, filestring() in nltk.util opens a string argument as a file path with no containment check. An absolute path, a parent-directory traversal path, or a symlink pointing elsewhere therefore reaches the filesystem unchanged, so a caller who controls the path can read arbitrary files. The upstream change adds an opt-in sandbox directory option but leaves the default call unrestricted.
preconditions: The application uses an nltk release that still has the original filestring() in nltk.util, such as 3.9.2.
The application passes a string that a user or attacker can influence to filestring() as a file path.
The caller does not use the new allowed directory option, so no containment check is applied before the file is opened.
The function is reachable through a web API or similar interface that accepts user-supplied input.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to an nltk version that includes the fix, then pass the allowed directory option on every call that handles externally influenced paths. The fixed code resolves both the base directory and the requested path to their real locations, which collapses traversal sequences and follows symlinks. It then confirms the target lies inside the base using a common-path comparison, treats different Windows drives as outside, and raises a permission error otherwise. Because the default is unchanged, also validate user input in the application, avoid accepting raw paths where possible, and let users choose from a fixed set of known files. Prefer passing an already opened file-like object that the application itself controls.
patterns.limitations: The protection is opt-in, so upgrading alone does not protect callers that omit the allowed directory option, and calls without it behave as before. The check resolves the path before opening it, so a concurrent change to the filesystem between the check and the read can still race. The same change also alters file reading to use UTF-8 and ignore decoding errors, which is a behavior change unrelated to security. Applications must still choose the allowed directory carefully, since a too-broad base weakens the restriction.

fixtures.scenario: A web endpoint takes a file name from a request parameter and passes it straight to filestring() in nltk 3.9.2. A remote client sends an absolute path to a sensitive system file, or a traversal path, and the response contains that file's contents.

A web endpoint accepts only an identifier from a short allow-list of documents the application intends to serve, and maps it to a known path internally. Requests carrying absolute paths or traversal paths are rejected before filestring() is called, so no sensitive system file can be read.

citations.quote: The function directly opens files specified by user input without sanitization
allows arbitrary file read due to improper validation of input paths
particularly in scenarios where the function is used in web APIs or other interfaces that accept user-supplied input

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an optional allowed directory parameter to filestring(). When it is given, both the base and the requested path are resolved to real locations and compared with a common-path check, which blocks traversal and symlink escape. Different Windows drives count as outside and raise a permission error. When the parameter is omitted, the old unrestricted behavior is kept, and file reading now uses UTF-8 and ignores decoding errors.

patterns.title: Quadratic regex backtracking when PyJWT checks whether key bytes look like PEM
patterns.cause: Before PyJWT 2.14.0, the is_pem_format check used a lazy regular expression to find a PEM block. When the input has repeated BEGIN markers and no matching END marker, the engine scans toward the end of the input from each BEGIN marker, fails, and then retries from the next one. Total work grows roughly with the square of the input length, so a crafted input can consume a lot of CPU.
preconditions: PyJWT is a version earlier than 2.14.0.
An application passes attacker-controlled key or certificate bytes to PyJWT key preparation.
The input contains many repeated BEGIN markers and no matching END marker.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to PyJWT 2.14.0 or later, the first release containing the fix. When implementing PEM detection, do not run a lazy, backtracking pattern over untrusted bytes. Use a bounded scan for the BEGIN and END markers so that malformed input cannot trigger repeated rescans of the whole string. Do not hand key or certificate material from untrusted sources to key preparation in affected versions.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no absolute timings or input-size thresholds. They do not describe the lowest affected PyJWT version, only that versions before 2.14.0 are affected. They do not list every PyJWT entry point that reaches the check beyond key preparation. They describe no mitigations other than upgrading, such as input size limits. A later PEM-recognition report that shares the same implementation commit is described as a distinct finding and is not covered here.

fixtures.scenario: A service running a PyJWT version before 2.14.0 accepts a user-supplied certificate-like blob made of many repeated BEGIN CERTIFICATE lines with no END line and passes it to key preparation. Doubling the number of lines roughly quadruples the CPU time, which can make the service unresponsive.

The same service runs PyJWT 2.14.0 or later, or uses a bounded marker scan. The same malformed blob is rejected as not PEM without runtime growth like the earlier behavior, and ordinary valid PEM input is still recognized.

citations.quote: This occurs when a certificate-like input contains repeated BEGIN markers without a matching END marker.
doubling repeated BEGIN lines produced approximately fourfold runtime growth, while equal-sized ordinary input remained negligible.
The affected path is reached when an application passes attacker-controlled key or certificate bytes to PyJWT
PyJWT 2.14.0 is the first release containing the fix.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the lazy whole-block PEM regular expression, which rescanned the input from every BEGIN marker when no END marker existed. It now makes one linear pass that finds individual BEGIN and END markers and records the latest BEGIN position per label. It reports a match only when an END marker with the same label comes after a BEGIN marker. A test with many repeated incomplete BEGIN markers covers the attack input.

patterns.title: Prefix-only validation of a language pack plural header lets appended JavaScript run
patterns.cause: JupyterLab turns the Plural-Forms header of a language pack into a function with new Function. The regular expression meant to guard this was anchored at the start but not at the end. Any string that began with a valid plural rule was accepted, and everything after it was ignored. Text appended to the rule therefore became JavaScript that ran in the authenticated JupyterLab origin once a plural string was translated.
preconditions: JupyterLab 3.0.0 through 4.6.3, or an application that bundles it such as Notebook 7, or JupyterLite Core 0.8.3 and earlier
A third-party language pack that the user did not write is installed in the environment
That language is selected, so its catalogue is loaded and a plural string is translated
patterns.prevention: Before building any function from catalogue metadata, require the validation pattern to match the entire header from start to end, for example with a full-string match rather than a prefix match. Reject the header if anything follows a valid plural rule, and do not build a function from it. Treat catalogue metadata as untrusted input, because it travels through the translation pipeline and is reviewed as text rather than as code. Upgrade to JupyterLab 4.5.11 or 4.6.4, or JupyterLite Core 0.8.4. As a stopgap, use the default English locale, which loads no catalogue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not show the corrected pattern or the code changes, so this card cannot confirm how the full match is implemented. They do not say whether the patched code still builds a function from a header that passes the check. JupyterLab 3.x is end of life and gets no patch. Impact in JupyterLite is described as much more limited, but the sources do not detail which surfaces remain reachable. The English-locale workaround changes the interface language for everyone.

fixtures.scenario: A third-party language pack is installed and selected. Its plural header starts with a valid plural rule followed by extra script text. A prefix-only check accepts it, and translating one plural string runs the extra text in the user's session.
The same pack is selected, but the check must match the entire header. A header with anything after the plural rule is rejected and no function is built, so the extra text never runs.

citations.quote: The regex was anchored at the start but not at the end, so it accepted any string that began with a valid plural rule
