The check now has to match the whole header, so a plural rule followed by anything else is rejected
JupyterLab passes the accepted expression to new Function, so loading the catalogue and translating a plural string executes the appended code
The default English locale is unaffected because it does not load a translation catalogue.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an end-of-string anchor to the validation pattern for the plural forms header in the gettext code, in three branches. The whole header must now match the allowed plural rule grammar, so appended JavaScript fails validation and an error is raised before any function is built. A new test confirms that a header with trailing script is rejected and that the injected side effect never runs.

patterns.title: XSS via trusted metadata in notebook cells pasted from the system clipboard
patterns.cause: The system clipboard paste path parses clipboard text as cell JSON and inserts the cells without clearing metadata.trusted. A payload can therefore declare its own output trusted. JupyterLab does not sanitize trusted output and evaluates script elements in it, so the script runs in the JupyterLab origin on paste, without the user executing the cell.
preconditions: JupyterLab 4.5.0 through 4.6.3, or an application bundling it such as Notebook 7.5 or later
On 4.5.2 and later, useSystemClipboardForCells is enabled (off by default there; always on in 4.5.0 and 4.5.1)
The user runs a Paste Cells command while attacker-controlled text is in the clipboard
pasteCodeCellsWithoutOutput is off (the default), so pasted code cells keep their outputs
patterns.prevention: Do not honor a trust flag that arrives inside pasted data. When cells are read from the system clipboard and cannot be traced to the current window, remove the trusted marker before inserting them, so their outputs are sanitized like any other content of unknown origin. Upgrade to JupyterLab 4.5.11 or 4.6.4, Notebook 7.6.3, or JupyterLite Core 0.8.4. Interim measures: keep useSystemClipboardForCells off, or enable pasteCodeCellsWithoutOutput.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain how a cell is traced to the current window. The advisory says affected versions run through 4.6.3, while the CVE text gives a slightly different range. Disabling the system clipboard setting stops copying cells between tabs or windows. Pasting without outputs discards outputs on every paste. Only code cell output can run script this way; markdown and raw cells are always sanitized.

fixtures.scenario: JupyterLab 4.6.3 with system clipboard cells enabled. Clipboard text holds cell JSON marked trusted, with an HTML output containing a script element. The user runs Paste Cells and the script runs in the JupyterLab origin.
The same clipboard text is pasted into JupyterLab 4.6.4. The cell cannot be traced to the current window, so its trust marker is dropped, the HTML output is sanitized, and no script runs.

citations.quote: so pasting the cell runs attacker's JavaScript in the JupyterLab origin.
Cells read from the system clipboard that cannot be traced to the current window no longer carry
so their outputs are sanitized like any other content of unknown origin.
the system clipboard cell-paste path accepts attacker-controlled cell JSON without clearing metadata.trusted

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the system clipboard remember the last text this application wrote. On a system clipboard paste, if the pasted data does not match that last write, every cell is treated as foreign: code cells are forced to untrusted and other cells lose any trusted flag. Cells copied from within the same application keep their trust, and tests cover scripted HTML outputs, missing metadata and stripped outputs. This matches the card's cause (an attacker-supplied trust flag honored on paste) and its prevention (drop trust for cells that cannot be traced to the current window).

patterns.title: Mako TemplateLookup path traversal via drive-letter URI on Windows
patterns.cause: Template resolution uses posixpath, while the traversal check in Template.__init__ uses os.path, which is ntpath on Windows. For a URI that begins with a drive designator, ntpath absorbs the dot-dot segments before the leading dot-dot check runs. posixpath treats the drive as an ordinary component, so the same URI can still escape the configured template directory.
preconditions: The application runs on Windows.
The Mako version is older than 1.4.2.
Attacker-controlled template names or include paths reach TemplateLookup.get_template().
The URI survives to Mako, for example through query strings, form or JSON bodies, route parameters, or dynamic include expressions.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Mako 1.4.2 or later. An implementation should normalize the URI for the confinement check with the same path module used for resolution. Then the drive designator stays an ordinary component and the dot-dot segments remain visible to the check. The advisory's remediation direction also converts backslashes to forward slashes and strips leading slashes before the check. Avoid passing untrusted input as template names or include paths.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the issue as Windows-only; on POSIX the same URIs are refused. Raw URL paths are generally normalized before reaching this form, so exposure depends on how the application handles input. The sources do not say whether other differences between the two path modules exist beyond the separator and drive cases already described. If the targeted file contains template syntax, it may also be parsed and executed.

fixtures.scenario: A Windows application passes a template name from a query string to TemplateLookup.get_template(). The name starts with a drive letter and colon, followed by many parent-directory segments, so a file outside the template directory on the same volume is loaded.

The check uses the same path module as resolution, so the drive letter is an ordinary component and the parent segments stay visible. The request is refused with a lookup exception, or Mako 1.4.2 or later is in use.

citations.quote: A URI beginning with a drive designator causes ntpath to absorb the traversal segments before the leading dot-dot check
Normalize both sides with the same module.
The issue is Windows-only.
This issue is fixed in version 1.4.2.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the traversal check in the Template constructor to normalize the URI with the posix path module instead of the platform path module. This is the same module the lookup uses to resolve the file, so a drive-prefixed URI keeps its dot-dot segments and is refused. The new tests cover plain, extra-slash, backslash and drive-letter spellings under both posix and Windows path behavior, and confirm that traversal which cancels out inside the root is still accepted.

patterns.title: Unescaped IMAP LIST/LSUB wildcard patterns enable regex backtracking DoS in Twisted
patterns.cause: The wildcardToRegexp() function in twisted/mail/imap4.py translates only the IMAP asterisk and percent wildcards. It passes every other character of a client-supplied LIST or LSUB pattern to re.compile() unchanged, so the client controls regular expression syntax. Nested or otherwise expensive constructs then cause catastrophic backtracking when matched against mailbox names.
preconditions: Twisted 25.5.0 or earlier with the IMAP server in twisted/mail/imap4.py
The attacker is an authenticated IMAP client able to send LIST or LSUB patterns
The pattern is converted with wildcardToRegexp() and matched against mailbox names
The server runs on the cooperative single-threaded reactor, so one slow match blocks all connections
patterns.prevention: Treat the client pattern as literal text except for the two IMAP wildcards. Before compiling, escape every character that is not the asterisk or percent wildcard, for example with re.escape(), and substitute only the wildcard tokens with their intended regex equivalents. Never let client input contribute grouping, quantifiers or alternation to a compiled expression.
patterns.limitations: The sources state that no fixed release was available at review time and name 25.5.0 and earlier as affected. They do not describe the contents of the upstream fix or say whether other code paths compile client-controlled patterns. Timing figures come from one proof of concept on Twisted 25.5.0 and vary by hardware.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated IMAP client sends a LIST pattern with nested quantifier syntax. The server compiles it verbatim as a regular expression, and matching it against a long mailbox name stalls the reactor.

The server escapes all non-wildcard characters in the LIST pattern before compiling. Parentheses and plus signs match literally, so the same pattern returns quickly and the reactor keeps serving other clients.

citations.quote: passes all other characters from an authenticated client's LIST or LSUB pattern directly to re.compile()
the blocking match suspends all server input and output for the duration of the match
No fixed release is available as of this review.

patch_review.observation: The fix rewrites wildcardToRegexp so the client pattern is split on the two IMAP wildcards, the asterisk and the percent sign. Each wildcard becomes its fixed non-greedy regex piece, and all other text is escaped so it matches literally. A new LSUB test checks that a dot in the pattern is literal. This matches the card's cause (unescaped client text compiled as a regex) and its prevention (escape everything except the wildcards).

patterns.title: Ghostscript argument injection through unsanitized EPS filename in Pillow
patterns.cause: When Pillow renders an EPS image, EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript builds the Ghostscript command line and places the input file name after the file flag without converting it to a safe absolute path. Ghostscript treats a leading hyphen as an option and a leading at-sign as an argument-file token, so an attacker-influenced file name can inject Ghostscript arguments. The default safer-mode setting does not stop this.
preconditions: Pillow from 2.6.0 up to but not including 13.0.0 is used to open and render EPS input
The file name passed to Image.open reaches Ghostscript and is attacker-influenced, for example a stored upload name derived from user input
For arbitrary command execution, the name must start with an at-sign and the attacker must also control the referenced text file holding extra Ghostscript arguments
patterns.prevention: Make sure a file name can never be read by Ghostscript as an option or an argument-file token. Convert the input path to a safe absolute path before building the command line, for example with os.path.abspath(), so it cannot begin with a hyphen or at-sign. Upgrade to Pillow 13.0.0 or later, where the issue is fixed. Applications should also avoid keeping attacker-chosen file names for files that Pillow opens by path.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream change in detail, so the exact normalization it applies is not confirmed here. The advisory reports testing on Pillow 12.3.0 while the CVE text gives 13.0.0 as the fixed version, and the sources do not reconcile this. They do not say whether other Ghostscript options or callers are affected. Blocking untrusted EPS input is a separate risk and is not covered by this card.

fixtures.scenario: An upload service keeps the user-supplied name, such as one starting with a hyphen or at-sign, and opens the stored EPS by path with Pillow. Rendering passes that name unchanged to Ghostscript after the file flag.
The same service resolves the stored name to an absolute path before Ghostscript is called, so a leading hyphen or at-sign cannot be parsed as an option or an argument file.

citations.quote: EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript passes a caller-controlled input filename after -f without converting it to a safe absolute path
Arbitrary command execution specifically requires a leading @ argument-file filename and control of the referenced text file containing additional Ghostscript arguments
This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the Ghostscript helper in the EPS plugin so that an existing file's name is converted to an absolute path before it goes onto the Ghostscript command line. A name starting with a hyphen or at-sign can then no longer be read as an option or an argument-file token. A regression test opens a file named like a help option and checks that it still renders.

patterns.title: Catastrophic backtracking in Pillow XBM header regex during Image.open()
patterns.cause: The XBM plugin matched its header with one regular expression over the first 512 bytes of any stream that passed a loose format check. Adjacent quantified parts could match the same characters: whitespace runs overlapped with the identifier wildcard, and runs of line terminators overlapped with the trailing match-anything part. When the final bits marker was malformed, the backtracking engine tried every split and rescanned the buffer, so cost grew polynomially with run length. This ran before the format was confirmed, so size and decompression-bomb limits never applied.
preconditions: The application opens attacker-supplied bytes with Image open or the incremental parser, using the default plugin set
The Pillow version is earlier than 13.0.0
No formats allowlist excluding XBM is passed when opening the image
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Pillow 13.0.0 or later. The fix replaces the single backtracking regex with a bounded line-by-line parser: it reads at most 75 bytes per line, checks fixed prefixes and suffixes, and takes numeric values from split fields, so work stays linear. It also narrows the sniffing check to a direct prefix test instead of stripping leading whitespace. When parsing untrusted headers, prefer bounded line reads and simple string checks over regexes with adjacent overlapping quantifiers, and add a worst-case regression test with a short timeout. Interim: pass a formats allowlist that excludes XBM.
patterns.limitations: The new parser is stricter and line-oriented. Header lines longer than 75 bytes, unusual layouts, or files with extra leading whitespace may now be rejected as not XBM. Other plugins and regexes were not assessed. Timings in the original report come from one environment and vary by machine.

fixtures.scenario: An upload service calls Image.open() with defaults on a 512-byte file: define lines with long space runs, many carriage returns, then a bits marker without the bracket pair. A worker stalls for minutes.
The same service runs Pillow 13.0.0 or later, or passes a formats allowlist excluding XBM. The crafted file is rejected immediately and a well-formed XBM still opens normally.

citations.quote: Several adjacent parts of the pattern can match the same characters.
Because this happens before any format is identified, none of Pillow's size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb limits apply
This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the header regex in the XBM plugin and replaces it with a loop that reads lines of at most 75 bytes, checks fixed prefixes and suffixes, and takes numbers from split fields. It also tightens the format sniffing check to a direct prefix test with no leading whitespace stripping, and adds a regression test with long runs of spaces and carriage returns under a short timeout. This matches the card's cause (overlapping quantifiers causing backtracking) and its prevention.

patterns.title: Argument injection through role dependency src field in ansible-galaxy role install
patterns.cause: When ansible-galaxy installs a role from a git source, it builds a git clone command from the src and name values in the role's dependency or requirements data and appends them with no end-of-options marker. A value beginning with a dash is therefore parsed by git as an option rather than as a repository location or directory name. A malicious role author can use this to inject git configuration, such as a custom ssh command, which leads to arbitrary command execution on the installing user's machine.
preconditions: A user runs ansible-galaxy to install a role, or its dependencies, from a source that is not trusted.
The role's dependency data supplies a src or name value that starts with a dash and carries git configuration content.
The value is appended to the git clone command line without a preceding end-of-options marker.
patterns.prevention: When building the git clone command, put an end-of-options marker (a double dash) before the repository location and destination name, so every value from role requirements is a positional argument and never an option. Apply this to all externally supplied values in the command, not only src. Upgrade ansible-core to a release that includes the fix. Until then, install only roles from trusted sources and review requirements files for entries whose src or name begins with a dash.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the git clone invocation in the role install path. The diff does not show whether other source control types or other commands that build external command lines have the same weakness. The first fixed ansible-core version is not stated in the diff.

fixtures.scenario: A user installs a third-party role. Its meta/requirements.yml lists a dependency whose src field carries extra text that git treats as configuration flags. ansible-galaxy role install passes that text to git, and code runs on the user's machine.

A user installs a role whose dependency src values are checked first. A value that could be read as a git flag is rejected, or it is kept strictly as a repository location. Git never receives attacker-supplied configuration flags, and no unexpected code runs.

citations.quote: The ansible-galaxy role install command processes dependency specifications from a role's meta/requirements.yml file.
Due to improper neutralization of argument delimiters, a malicious role author can inject arbitrary git configuration flags through the src field.
This allows arbitrary code execution on the machine of a user who installs the role via ansible-galaxy role install.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the clone command built in the galaxy utility so an end-of-options marker comes before the src and name values. Both are then treated as positional arguments (repository and destination) and cannot be read as git options such as a configuration override for the ssh command. The added integration test uses dash-prefixed src and name values and checks that no injected command runs.

patterns.title: Path traversal in nbconvert cell output filenames allows arbitrary file write
patterns.cause: ExtractOutputPreprocessor joins the filename value from cell output metadata, which the notebook author controls, to the output files directory. It performs no canonicalization check, so a value with parent-directory segments resolves outside the intended directory and the output data is written there.
preconditions: The victim converts an untrusted or attacker-supplied notebook with nbconvert
The exporter is markdown, LaTeX, reStructuredText or AsciiDoc, which use output extraction
A cell output carries a metadata filename containing parent-directory traversal segments
The nbconvert version is 5.4.0 up to before 7.17.2
patterns.prevention: Treat the output metadata filename as untrusted. After joining it to the output directory, canonicalize the result and confirm it stays inside that directory, for example by resolving both paths and comparing them. Reject or neutralize any name that escapes. Upgrade to 7.17.2 or later, and avoid converting untrusted notebooks with privileged accounts.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail, so this card does not say how 7.17.2 validates names. They also do not cover platform-specific path forms such as absolute paths or Windows drive and separator handling, or other metadata fields. Re-running a cell replaces the malicious metadata, but converting the notebook alone does not.

fixtures.scenario: A notebook has an image output whose metadata filename climbs several parent directories toward a sensitive location. The user converts it to markdown, and the exporter writes the image bytes outside the output directory.

The same notebook is converted by a fixed nbconvert or an implementation that resolves the final path and checks it is inside the output directory. The escaping name is rejected and nothing is written outside it.

citations.quote: joins the attacker-controlled cell output metadata filename to output_files_dir without limiting the result to the intended directory
If a victim runs nbconvert on a malicious ipynb file, it can create some files with arbitrary data in arbitrary locations

patch_review.observation: The fix in the output extraction preprocessor stops trusting the filename in output metadata. It keeps only the final path component, so parent-directory segments, absolute paths and subdirectories can no longer move the write location. If nothing is left after this, it skips that output, and it logs a warning whenever a name is altered. This matches the card's cause (an attacker-controlled name joined to the output directory without validation) and its prevention (treat the name as untrusted and neutralize names that escape).

patterns.title: Loopback HTTP exemption bypass via userinfo in Authlib transport-security check
patterns.cause: The transport-security check in authlib.common.security.is_secure_transport() decides whether a URL is acceptable by comparing the start of the raw URL string with https:// and loopback http:// prefixes. In a URL, text before an at-sign is userinfo, not the host. A URL whose userinfo starts with a loopback name and a colon therefore matches a loopback prefix even though its real host is an external system and its scheme is plain http.
preconditions: The application relies on is_secure_transport(), directly or through Authlib validators, to reject cleartext non-loopback URLs.
An external party can supply a URL to a consuming call site, such as OIDC RP-Initiated Logout dynamic client registration or authorization-server metadata validation.
The installed Authlib version is in the affected range, from 0.13 until the 1.8.0 fix.
patterns.prevention: Do not judge transport security by matching the start of the URL string. Parse the URI into its components and evaluate the real host and scheme. Accept https, or http only when the parsed host is a loopback address. Reject URIs that carry a userinfo component at these validation sites. Upgrade Authlib to 1.8.0 or later, where this issue is fixed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the internals of the 1.8.0 change, so this card does not verify how it parses URIs. The issue is rated low severity. It does not bypass redirect URI exact matching and does not forge tokens or authenticate users. Exploiting metadata validation requires influence over the metadata document. The sources also show an environment-variable override that makes the check always pass; that is separate from this flaw.

fixtures.scenario: A provider with dynamic registration and RP-Initiated Logout accepts a public client's post-logout redirect entry that starts with http://localhost:80@ followed by an external host. The browser is later redirected over plain HTTP to that external host.
The provider parses the registered URI, sees an external host over http or any userinfo component, and rejects it. Only https URIs, or http URIs whose parsed host is loopback, are accepted.

citations.quote: uses a textual prefix comparison for loopback HTTP exemptions, so a URL whose userinfo begins with a loopback host can be accepted
The issue does not bypass redirect URI exact matching and does not by itself forge tokens or authenticate users.
This is a defense-in-depth / spec-conformance failure; severity is low.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the string-prefix check in is_secure_transport with proper URL parsing. It requires a host, accepts https, and accepts http only when the parsed host is localhost or a loopback IP address. Lookalikes such as a loopback name in the userinfo or fragment are now rejected, and malformed authorities return false instead of raising an error.

patterns.title: SSRF via unvalidated request_uri passed to the JAR fetch hook in Authlib
patterns.cause: The RFC 9101 extension passed the unauthenticated, client-controlled request_uri straight to the get_request_object hook with no approval step, and the documentation example fetched any URL. An attacker could make the authorization server send requests to internal or otherwise attacker-chosen destinations.
preconditions: Authlib older than the fixed 1.9.0 release with the JWT-secured authorization request extension and request_uri support enabled.
The integrator implements get_request_object as an outbound network fetch, as the old documentation showed.
The attacker can send authorization requests with a known client identifier; no other authentication is needed.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to the fixed release. It calls a new validate_request_uri hook before get_request_object, and the default rejects every URI, so applications must implement an explicit allow policy. Accept only exact pre-registered URIs or locally stored references owned by the requesting client. For network fetches require HTTPS, block private and resolved addresses and DNS rebinding, refuse redirects, and limit size, time and media type. For OIDC registration checks use the new OpenID subclass and implement get_client_request_uris.
patterns.limitations: The primitive is blind because the response is consumed as a JWT and not reflected. Safety still depends on the integrator's validation policy and fetch code enforcing network restrictions. The default-deny behavior breaks existing request_uri setups until a policy is written. The same change also hardens nonce and signature-requirement handling, which is separate from the SSRF fix.

fixtures.scenario: An authorization server on an affected Authlib version implements the fetch hook as a plain HTTP GET of the given request_uri. An unauthenticated request with a known client_id and a link-local metadata URL as request_uri makes the server fetch it.

The fetch hook first checks request_uri against an approved allowlist of registered locations and rejects anything else. It also applies a timeout, a media type check and no recursive fetching. A link-local metadata URL is rejected with no outbound request.

citations.quote: passes the unauthenticated, client-controlled request_uri parameter to the abstract get_request_object() hook before applying a destination or registration policy
Deployments whose custom hook already applies a secure allowlist, destination controls, and retrieval limits are not affected.
Deployments following the documented pattern get an unauthenticated SSRF primitive.
This issue is fixed in version 1.9.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an approval step, a validate_request_uri hook that runs before get_request_object and rejects every URI by default. It also rewrites the documentation example, which fetched any URL, to require HTTPS, block private and resolved addresses, refuse redirects, and limit size, time and media type. An OpenID subclass now handles request URI registration through get_client_request_uris. The same commits also stop token claims from disabling nonce checks and keep the signature requirement from being weakened by the algorithm list, which the card correctly calls separate.

patterns.title: Path traversal and unescaped output in the Mistune Include directive
patterns.cause: The Include directive resolves the include path without checking that the resolved file stays within the source directory, so ../ sequences can reach arbitrary files. Error messages and included file contents are also rendered without HTML escaping, which allows XSS even when the escape option is on.
preconditions: Mistune version before 3.3.0 is in use
The Include plugin is explicitly enabled through the plugins parameter
An attacker can influence the include path in the Markdown that is processed
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Mistune 3.3.0 or later. After resolving an include path, confirm that the final location is still inside the intended source directory, for example by comparing canonical paths from os.path.realpath(), and reject anything outside it. HTML-escape error messages and included file contents before they reach the output. Do not enable the Include plugin for untrusted Markdown.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream fix, how symlinks are handled, or whether any other directives are affected. They name only the Include directive, its path resolution, block_error() and render_html_include(). The only version detail is that releases before 3.3.0 are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A service renders user-submitted Markdown with the Include plugin enabled and escaping turned on. A document includes a path with ../ sequences, and a file outside the source directory is read and shown with its contents unescaped.
The service runs Mistune 3.3.0 or later, or leaves the Include plugin off for untrusted input. A ../ path that resolves outside the source directory is rejected, and any error text is HTML-escaped.

citations.quote: does not validate that the resolved file path stays within the source directory
Mistune before 3.3.0 contains a path traversal vulnerability in the Include directive
The Include plugin must be explicitly enabled via the plugins parameter.

patch_review.observation: The fix resolves both the source file and the include target to real paths, rejects absolute include paths and any target outside the source directory, and returns a block error instead. It also escapes included text in the include renderer when HTML escaping is enabled, and adds circular-include detection as a side hardening. This matches the card's traversal and unescaped-output cause and its prevention.

patterns.title: SSRF through attacker-chosen constructor arguments in MLflow third-party scorer deserialization
patterns.cause: The scorer invoke, register, and GenAI evaluate endpoints accept serialized third-party scorer data. Scorer.model_validate_json checks only the module path against an allowlist. It does not constrain the selected class or its constructor arguments, so the request controls what the scorer is built with. With the trulens module, a model URI outside the native provider registry routes to the LiteLLM fallback, which forwards request-supplied endpoint and key arguments to the outbound client. The invoke endpoint needs no authentication, and the deserialization runs before any tracking-store lookup or job submission.
preconditions: MLflow version from 3.12.0rc0 up to but not including 3.17.0
Optional trulens and trulens-providers-litellm packages installed in the server environment
Scorer invoke, register, or GenAI evaluate endpoint reachable by the attacker; invoke needs no authentication
Request names the trulens scorer module and a model URI outside MLflow's native provider registry
patterns.prevention: Do not let request data choose constructor arguments for reflectively built objects. Validate the selected class and each constructor argument against an explicit per-class allowlist, not just the module path. Reject or ignore network-destination and credential arguments such as a custom API base or key when they come from a request payload, and take such values only from trusted server-side configuration. Apply this check at every entry point that deserializes scorers, including invoke, register, and evaluate, before any object is instantiated. Upgrade to MLflow 3.17.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream change in detail, so the exact set of arguments or classes it restricts is unknown. They describe the exploit path only through the trulens scorer and the LiteLLM fallback, and do not say whether other third-party scorer modules are exposed in the same way. They give no guidance on authentication or network egress controls for the server.

fixtures.scenario: A tracking server on an affected version has trulens and the LiteLLM provider package installed. An anonymous request to the scorer invoke endpoint names the trulens module, a non-native model URI, and a custom endpoint and key; the server then calls the attacker host.

The server runs 3.17.0 or later, or the scorer payload is checked so only approved classes and constructor arguments are accepted and endpoint or credential arguments from the request are rejected before instantiation.

citations.quote: accept serialized third-party scorer data that Scorer.model_validate_json resolves using a module-path allowlist without constraining the selected class or its constructor arguments.
choose a model URI outside MLflow's native provider registry so execution uses the LiteLLM fallback
an unauthenticated attacker can force the server to make an outbound HTTP request to an arbitrary host of their choosing

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a shared server-side check that walks the serialized scorer, including scorers nested in ensembles and memory-augmented judges. It rejects third-party scorer kwargs that name network destinations, such as an API base or base URL, at any nesting depth, and rejects kwargs that are not a JSON object. The check runs in the register, invoke, and GenAI evaluate handlers, for both inline payloads and scorers fetched from the store, before deserialization or job submission.

patterns.title: Forged shared-memory handles in the multimodal cache reach worker pickle.loads()
patterns.cause: The shared-memory multimodal cache treats an address and monotonic id pair supplied inside public multimodal feature data as authority to read shared memory in the worker. Nothing authenticated that pair, so an authenticated caller could forge a handle pointing at attacker-staged bytes in the ring buffer, and the shared-memory deserializer would then run pickle loading on those bytes. This worked even with insecure serialization disabled.
preconditions: vLLM version earlier than 0.32.0
Multimodal processor cache type set to shm in a scale-out deployment
Attacker is an authenticated caller who can submit multimodal feature data through the public token-in token-out route
Attacker can get chosen bytes written into the shared-memory ring buffer through ordinary requests
patterns.prevention: Never trust a caller-supplied address and monotonic id pair. Have the server issue an unforgeable signature (a keyed HMAC) for each handle, bound to the cache key, address and monotonic id, with the secret held in the shared memory segment and never sent to clients. Verify it at the public boundary before engine handoff, requiring on the writer side that the handle is still the current entry for that key, and verify it again on the worker reader side in both read and touch paths before dereferencing the address. Strictly validate handle field types, ranges and signature length, and reject missing or invalid signatures. Keep monotonic ids increasing across cache clears so stale handles fail the id check once their chunk is reused. Upgrade to vLLM 0.32.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The fix authenticates handles but the shared-memory deserializer still uses pickle for stored byte objects, so the protection depends on the secret staying private to the server processes. Anyone who can read the shared memory segment can recover the signing secret. Other cache types and other deserialization paths are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A server runs with the shm multimodal cache. An authenticated caller sends a generate request whose features.kwargs_data carries a made-up address and monotonic_id aimed at bytes staged earlier. The worker reads those bytes and unpickles them.

The server accepts a shared-memory handle only with a server-issued capability tied to cache key, address and monotonic id. A forged handle lacks it and is rejected at the public boundary and again in the worker before any read.

citations.quote: treats that pair as authority to dereference shared memory in the worker.
workers trust those values and pass attacker-selected bytes to pickle.loads(), allowing arbitrary Python execution even when insecure serialization is disabled.
Authenticate every SHM carrier with a server-issued capability bound to the cache key, address, and monotonic id

patch_review.observation: The fix stops clients from supplying their own shared-memory handles. It adds a random 32-byte secret at the start of the segment and has the server sign each handle with a keyed hash over the cache key, address and monotonic id. The signature is checked at the public token-in token-out entry (the writer also requires the handle to be the key's current entry) and again in the worker's get and touch paths before the address is read. Handle fields get strict type, range and length checks, and monotonic ids now keep increasing across cache clears.

patterns.title: Open redirect through substitutions in RedirectHandler URL templates
patterns.cause: In Tornado before 6.6, RedirectHandler builds its target by inserting parts of the request path, taken from regex capture groups, into a URL template. If a substitution sits at the start of the path, directly after a fixed host, or at the start of the template, a crafted request path can change the scheme or host of the redirect. Protocol-relative, absolute, backslash, encoded, host-extension and user-info variants are all interpreted by browsers as attacker-controlled destinations.
preconditions: The application uses RedirectHandler with a URL template that contains regex-capture substitutions.
A substitution is placed where it can influence the scheme or host: at the start of a path, directly after a fixed host, or at the beginning of the template.
The Tornado version is older than 6.6.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Tornado 6.6 or later. There, RedirectHandler returns a 400 error when substituted values would change the scheme or host that the template specifies. Substitutions can no longer be used in the scheme or host part of a template. Also design templates so every substitution follows a fixed prefix ending in a slash, or constrain capture-group patterns so they cannot match slash, backslash, at-sign, dot or colon where they could affect the host. Alternatively, use a custom handler that validates the target before redirecting. Applications that pass user-controlled input to RequestHandler.redirect() should validate it themselves.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation logic in the fix, and do not give a full list of encoded or whitespace variants. They only say the similar StaticFileHandler check was hardened against backslash and whitespace variants. Other uses of RequestHandler.redirect() are outside this advisory, so the sources give no guidance on them beyond advising the application to validate input. Any impact beyond phishing is not described.

fixtures.scenario: A route maps a path regex with a capture group to a redirect template that begins with the captured text. A request whose captured part starts with two slashes and an outside hostname redirects the browser to that outside host.

A route maps a path regex to a template with a fixed host and a slash before the captured text, on Tornado 6.6 or later. A request that tries to alter the host gets a 400 error or stays on the fixed host.

citations.quote: now returns a 400 error if the substituted values would change the scheme or host of the redirect from what the template specifies.
Affected placements include substitutions at the start of a path, directly after a fixed host, or at the beginning of the template
Static templates and substitutions after a fixed host followed by a slash are not affected.

patch_review.observation: The fix first adds a check for a leading double slash, then widens it to browser-style normalization (backslashes, tabs, newlines, leading control characters). The final version formats the template with a harmless placeholder to learn the expected scheme and netloc. It returns a 400 error if the real redirect target differs, which covers substitutions at the template start, after a fixed host, and host-extension or user-info variants. The card describes this cause and fix direction accurately.

patterns.title: Prompt model version source bypasses path validation and enables arbitrary file read
patterns.cause: The model version creation handler has a special branch for prompt requests. That branch rejects file URIs and absolute paths, but runs relative-path validation only when the source has a URL scheme. A schemeless source such as a relative traversal, a dot, a percent-encoded path or a Windows drive-letter path is stored unchanged as the artifact location. The prompt branch was also chosen by the presence of the prompt tag rather than its value, so a false value still selected the weaker branch. The model version artifact endpoint later reads files from that stored location with the server process privileges.
preconditions: The tracking server exposes the model registry endpoints and is reachable by the attacker; the default server has no authentication.
The caller can create a registered model and a model version, which any authenticated user can do under basic-auth.
The request carries the prompt tag and a schemeless local source, so the weaker prompt branch is used.
The artifact download endpoint trusts the stored source and serves the resulting local file.
patterns.prevention: Do not let a client-supplied source choose a server-local directory. For prompt model versions, accept only the application's own placeholder sources and reject every other value, including schemeless relative paths, dots, percent-encoded paths and drive-letter paths. Decide the prompt branch from the tag value being true, not from the tag merely being present. Apply the same source validation as ordinary model versions, or stricter, on every branch that stores a source. Treat the stored artifact location as untrusted when serving downloads, and run the server with minimal filesystem privileges and with authentication enabled.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact format of the placeholder sources, so the allow-list shape is not specified here. They do not say whether other handlers or artifact repositories store client-supplied sources without the same checks. They do not assess how robust the existing path check on the download parameter is. Affected versions are reported as 3.10.0 up to 3.17.0, and the sources give no detail on other deployment hardening.

fixtures.scenario: An unauthenticated server gets a request to create a model version with the prompt tag and a schemeless relative source that climbs out of the artifact root. The source is stored, and the get-artifact endpoint then serves a file from the server.

A prompt model version request supplies a schemeless relative source, or a prompt tag whose value is not true. The server rejects it, because only MLflow's own placeholder sources are accepted for prompt versions and the tag value must be true.

citations.quote: runs path validation only when the source carries a URL scheme
mlflow.prompt.is_prompt is interpreted by tag presence rather than a true value
A remote caller can store a server-local path as the model version artifact location

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the weak prompt-source check with a validator that allows only two known placeholder sources for schemeless or file-scheme values, and still applies relative-path checks to other schemes. It also makes the prompt branch depend on the prompt tag's value being true, with the last duplicate tag winning, instead of the tag merely being present. This matches the card's cause (schemeless sources stored unchanged, branch chosen by tag presence) and its prevention (allow-list of placeholders, decide by tag value).

patterns.title: SQL injection via band index in RasterField lookups on PostGIS
patterns.cause: When PostGIS raster lookups on RasterField are compiled, the band index for the left or right operand is placed directly into the SQL template text. Nothing checks that it is an integer. Normal left-hand usage converts the value to an integer, but the right-hand band value in a lookup tuple was passed through unchecked. A string supplied as a band index therefore became part of the SQL statement.
preconditions: Django version is in an affected series: 6.0 before 6.0.2, 5.2 before 5.2.11, or 4.2 before 4.2.28
The project uses RasterField with raster lookups on PostGIS
A band index in a raster lookup (especially the band value paired with a raster in the right-hand tuple) can be influenced by an attacker and is not forced to an integer by the application
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 6.0.2, 5.2.11, or 4.2.28 or later. The fix makes the raster check reject any band index that is not an integer, on both sides of the lookup, with a TypeError. Until upgrading, convert any externally supplied band index to an integer yourself before building the lookup, and never pass request data as a band value unchanged.
patterns.limitations: The fix is a type check on band indices in the PostGIS raster operator code only. Custom lookups or transforms that bypass the standard integer conversion were the reason for the added defense-in-depth check on the left side. Unsupported series such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x were not evaluated and may also be affected. Other backends are not relevant because raster lookups are implemented only on PostGIS.

fixtures.scenario: A PostGIS-backed Django 5.2.10 app filters a RasterField with a raster lookup. The band index comes straight from a query string parameter supplied by a remote user.
The app runs Django 5.2.11 or later, or 6.0.2 or 4.2.28 on those series. Band indexes for raster lookups are chosen by the developer, not taken from request data.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject SQL via the band index parameter.
An issue was discovered in 6.0 before 6.0.2, 5.2 before 5.2.11, and 4.2 before 4.2.28.
Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a type check in the PostGIS raster operator code (check_raster) so that a band index on either side of a raster lookup must be an integer. Anything else raises a TypeError before the value reaches the SQL template. The tests cover a string band on the right-hand side and a custom lookup that evades the integer conversion on the left-hand side, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: NLTK URL validation misses RFC 6598 shared address space (SSRF)
patterns.cause: The network URL validation function nltk.pathsec.validate_network_url() is meant to reject internal network addresses. It fails to reject IPs in the RFC 6598 shared address space, 100.64.0.0/10. Python's ipaddress module classifies such addresses as neither private nor global, and the guard only checks the private category plus a few explicit categories, so these addresses pass validation.
preconditions: The application uses nltk version 3.9.4 or the current develop branch at the time of the report.
The application relies on NLTK strict-mode network URL validation to block internal destinations.
An attacker can influence a URL passed to NLTK's network-loading helpers.
Hosts in 100.64.0.0/10 are reachable from the application host.
patterns.prevention: Do not treat a failed private-address check as proof that a destination is public. An address range that the ipaddress module marks as neither private nor global slips through a guard built on the private flag. Make the guard cover the shared address space explicitly, or accept only destinations positively classified as global. Apply the check to the address the request will actually use. Upgrade to an NLTK release that includes the upstream fix once available. As defense in depth, restrict egress from the application host to non-public infrastructure at the network level.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream change, a fixed release number, or how hostnames are resolved and checked. They do not say how redirects or DNS rebinding are handled. They only say that the guard fails to reject 100.64.0.0/10 and that impact is limited to SSRF-style confidentiality exposure, with no code execution claimed. Other address ranges that the ipaddress module leaves unclassified are not covered by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A service in strict mode accepts a user-supplied URL whose host is an address inside 100.64.0.0/10 and passes it to an NLTK network-loading helper. Validation approves the URL, and the service sends a request to a non-public host reachable from its network.

The same service receives a URL whose host is inside 100.64.0.0/10. The validation explicitly covers the shared address space, or allows only globally routable addresses, so the URL is rejected before any request is sent.

citations.quote: fails to reject IPs in the RFC 6598 shared address space
module does not classify such addresses as
and the current guard only checks
An attacker who can influence a URL passed to NLTK's network-loading helpers can exploit this vulnerability

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the explicit loopback, link-local, multicast and private checks with a policy that forbids any address that is not globally routable. This covers the 100.64.0.0/10 shared space, and it also unwraps IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses before checking them. It also pins the connection to the already-validated numeric address, so a second DNS lookup at connect time cannot reach an internal host. This matches the card's cause and its advice to accept only global destinations and check the address actually used.

patterns.title: SQL injection through crafted column alias names in FilteredRelation keyword expansion in Django
patterns.cause: FilteredRelation is subject to SQL injection in column aliases. Control characters in alias names can trigger it when a crafted dictionary is expanded into keyword arguments for QuerySet methods. Those methods are annotate, aggregate, extra, values, values_list and alias. The sources do not describe the internal mechanism beyond this.
preconditions: The application runs Django 6.0 before 6.0.2, 5.2 before 5.2.11, or 4.2 before 4.2.28. Older unsupported series were not evaluated and may also be affected.
Application code expands a dictionary into keyword arguments for annotate, aggregate, extra, values, values_list or alias.
The dictionary keys, which become column aliases, can be influenced by an attacker and can contain control characters.
FilteredRelation is involved in the affected query path.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 6.0.2, 5.2.11, or 4.2.28 or later. Until then, do not build the dictionary that is expanded into keyword arguments for the listed QuerySet methods from untrusted input. In particular, do not let external input choose the alias names. Take alias names from a fixed server-side set of known-good names, and reject any candidate name that contains control characters before it reaches the ORM. Treat user input as values, never as alias or keyword names.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which control characters are dangerous, which database backends are affected, or how the upstream fix works, so the name-allowlist and control-character rejection advice is a defensive direction and not a confirmed complete mitigation. Series older than 4.2 were not evaluated, so their status is unknown. Only upgrading to a fixed release is confirmed as the remedy.

fixtures.scenario: A reporting endpoint on Django 5.2.10 accepts a JSON object from the client and expands it into keyword arguments for annotate or values. The client-chosen keys become column aliases, so a key containing control characters can alter the generated SQL.

The same endpoint runs on Django 5.2.11 or later. It also maps each client-requested field to an alias from a fixed server-side list and rejects any name outside that list or containing control characters, so no client-supplied text becomes an alias.

citations.quote: An issue was discovered in 6.0 before 6.0.2, 5.2 before 5.2.11, and 4.2 before 4.2.28.
is subject to SQL injection in column aliases via control characters, using a suitably crafted dictionary, with dictionary expansion
Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected.

patch_review.observation: The fix widens the forbidden-alias check in the query's alias validation so that ASCII control characters and the C1 control range are rejected, with the error message updated to match. Tests cover annotate, alias, aggregate, extra and values, including FilteredRelation aliases, so the weakness is control characters in alias names reaching SQL generation. This matches the card's cause and its advice to upgrade and reject control characters in alias names.

patterns.title: Django order_by() SQL injection via dotted aliases reused in FilteredRelation
patterns.cause: The SQL compiler's ordering logic assumed that any order_by name containing a period came from extra() ordering. It split the name into a table and a column and passed it through verbatim instead of resolving it as an annotation. A crafted annotation alias with a period, created through FilteredRelation by expanding a dictionary of keyword arguments, was therefore emitted as raw table-qualified SQL in ORDER BY. This let an attacker alter the generated SQL. FilteredRelation also accepted aliases containing periods without validation.
preconditions: Django 6.0 before 6.0.2, 5.2 before 5.2.11, or 4.2 before 4.2.28 is in use
The application builds annotation or FilteredRelation aliases from untrusted input, for example by expanding a dictionary whose keys an attacker controls
The attacker-chosen alias contains a period
The same alias is then passed to QuerySet.order_by()
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 6.0.2, 5.2.11, or 4.2.28 or later. The fix restricts the verbatim table-and-column ordering path to names registered through extra() ordering, and it makes FilteredRelation raise an error for aliases containing a period. Until upgrading, never take annotation or FilteredRelation alias names from untrusted input. Accept them only from a fixed, application-defined set and reject any name containing a period.
patterns.limitations: The patch targets dotted aliases reaching the ordering code, mainly through FilteredRelation. Names passed to extra(order_by) are still emitted as raw SQL by design, so they must never come from untrusted input. Only the stated version ranges are confirmed, and older unsupported Django series were not evaluated.

fixtures.scenario: A search endpoint builds a dictionary from request parameters and expands it into FilteredRelation annotations. A client-chosen alias containing a period is also used as an order_by() key on an affected Django version.
The endpoint maps client choices to a fixed set of alias names without periods and builds FilteredRelation arguments only from those names. The project runs Django 5.2.11 or later.

citations.quote: An issue was discovered in 6.0 before 6.0.2, 5.2 before 5.2.11, and 4.2 before 4.2.28.
is subject to SQL injection in column aliases containing periods when the same alias is, using a suitably crafted dictionary, with dictionary expansion,
Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected.

patch_review.observation: One commit changes the ORDER BY compiler so a name containing a period is passed through verbatim only when it was registered through extra() ordering, so a dotted annotation alias is no longer mistaken for a table-qualified column. The other commit makes the FilteredRelation alias path raise a ValueError for aliases with periods. This matches the card's cause, its prevention and its note that extra(order_by) stays raw by design.

patterns.title: Doubly-encoded package URLs from an index can place downloaded files outside the target location in pip
patterns.cause: pip handled doubly-encoded package URLs from a package index incorrectly. A malicious index could use this to make files be installed to arbitrary locations on disk, even when the package is a wheel.
preconditions: The user downloads or installs a package from a malicious package index; a malicious package alone cannot exploit this.
The index supplies a package URL that is doubly-encoded.
The impact is material mainly for pip download with the only-binary option, because installing source distributions from an untrusted index already executes code.
patterns.prevention: Treat any location derived from an index-supplied URL as untrusted input. Decode URL data in one well-defined, consistent way rather than leaving a second layer of encoding to be interpreted later. Before writing anything, confirm that the final destination stays inside the intended directory. Avoid using indexes you do not trust for download or install operations.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact decoding steps, the affected pip versions, or the fix. They do not say which characters or sequences are dangerous, or how the file path is built from the URL. The prevention direction above is general guidance, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A user runs pip download with the only-binary option against a malicious index. The index lists a wheel whose URL is doubly-encoded, and the downloaded file ends up at a location outside the directory the user chose.
The same download runs against the same malicious index, but the doubly-encoded URL is handled so the file is written only inside the user-chosen directory, or the download is rejected.

citations.quote: pip would incorrectly handle doubly-encoded package URLs from indexes allowing for files to be installed to arbitrary locations on disk even when installing wheels.
This vulnerability requires downloading or installing a package from a malicious package index to succeed
installing source distributions from an untrusted index is already an unsafe operation that executes code during install time.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the second percent-decoding of the file name taken from the link path, so a doubly-encoded separator stays a literal part of the name instead of becoming a path separator. It also reduces the name to a single path component, rejecting empty, current-directory and parent-directory results, and routes all download-directory joins through a helper that accepts only such validated components.

patterns.title: Command injection through the cmd argument of async_run_command in OpenLLM 0.6.30
patterns.cause: In bentoml OpenLLM 0.6.30, the function async_run_command in src/openllm/common.py, part of the Model Repository Directory Name Handler component, can be given a manipulated cmd argument. This results in command injection, so attacker-influenced content is treated as part of a command instead of as plain data.
preconditions: OpenLLM 0.6.30 is in use.
The attacker has local access, since the advisory says attacking locally is a requirement.
The attacker can influence the value that reaches the cmd argument of async_run_command, for example through the model repository directory name handling.
patterns.prevention: Do not build a command from untrusted values such as repository or directory names. Where possible, pass the program and each of its arguments as separate items to a process-launching API that does not go through a shell, so that metacharacters have no special meaning. Validate externally supplied names against a strict allowlist of expected characters and reject anything else before it reaches any command-running helper. Treat every caller of the command-running helper as a trust boundary, not only the directory name handler.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief. They do not say how a directory name reaches the cmd argument, whether a shell is involved, which versions other than 0.6.30 are affected, or which release fixes the issue. They also say the project had not responded when the advisory was written. The prevention steps are general hardening guidance for this vulnerability class, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A local user creates or selects a model repository directory whose name contains command-separator characters. The name is placed into the cmd argument of async_run_command, and the extra text is run as a separate command.

The same directory name is validated against an allowlist and rejected if it contains unexpected characters. Any accepted name is passed as one discrete argument to a launcher that does not use a shell, so it is never interpreted as a command.

citations.quote: This affects the function async_run_command of the file src/openllm/common.py of the component Model Repository Directory Name Handler.
Performing a manipulation of the argument cmd results in command injection.
Attacking locally is a requirement.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes async_run_command so it no longer joins the command items into one string for a shell. It now launches the program directly with the arguments as a separate list, so shell metacharacters in values such as names derived from cloned repository directories are no longer interpreted. This matches the card's cause (untrusted content treated as command syntax) and its main prevention (separate arguments, no shell).

patterns.title: Wheel extraction can write files outside the installation directory
patterns.cause: The helper that decides whether an extraction target lies within the destination directory compared the two absolute paths by their longest shared string prefix, not by path components. A crafted archive entry that resolves to a sibling path whose name begins with the destination directory name plus extra characters therefore passed the check, and the file was written outside the intended directory.
preconditions: pip is unpacking a crafted wheel or other archive
An entry name resolves to a path outside the destination directory whose text begins with the destination directory path
The containment check relies on a character-level prefix comparison instead of a path-component comparison
patterns.prevention: When verifying that an extraction target is inside the destination, normalize both paths to absolute form and compare them by whole path components, for example with a common-path function that respects separators, or by requiring a separator boundary after the destination directory. Never use a plain string prefix comparison for containment. Add tests for sibling directories that share a name prefix with the destination, alongside tests for parent-relative segments.
patterns.limitations: Impact is bounded because the escape only reaches sibling paths that share a name prefix with the installation directory, and it does not typically allow overwriting executable files. This card describes only the prefix-comparison flaw; it does not cover other traversal vectors such as symlinks or link entries in archives, and it does not name the affected or fixed pip versions.

fixtures.scenario: A user installs a wheel from an untrusted source. One archive entry is crafted so that its extracted location lands outside the installation directory, and the extractor writes it there without confirming the destination is inside the target.

A user installs a wheel with the same crafted entry. The extractor determines the entry's final destination, finds it is outside the installation directory, and rejects the entry, so no file is written outside the target.

citations.quote: When pip is installing and extracting a maliciously crafted wheel archive, files may be extracted outside the installation directory.
The path traversal is limited to prefixes of the installation directory, thus isn't able to inject or overwrite executable files in typical situations.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the containment helper in pip's unpacking utilities to use a path-component-aware common path function instead of a character-level common prefix, so a sibling path like a directory name plus extra characters is no longer treated as inside the destination. A test was added for a target whose name merely extends the parent name.

patterns.title: Unsafe torch.load of RNG state checkpoint in Transformers Trainer enables code execution
patterns.cause: The Trainer class method that restores RNG state (_load_rng_state() in trainer.py) loads a checkpoint file such as rng_state.pth through torch.load() without requesting weights-only loading. Pickle-based deserialization of an attacker-supplied checkpoint can therefore run arbitrary code. The safe_globals() context manager gives no protection on PyTorch versions below 2.6.
preconditions: Application uses the Trainer class from a Transformers version before v5.0.0rc3 that supports torch>=2.2
PyTorch version in use is below 2.6
Training is resumed from a checkpoint directory that an attacker can influence, containing a malicious rng_state.pth
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Transformers to v5.0.0rc3 or later, where the issue is resolved. Only resume training from checkpoints produced by trusted sources, and treat checkpoint directories from outside parties as untrusted input. When deserializing with torch.load(), request weights-only loading so that arbitrary objects are not unpickled, and do not rely on safe_globals() alone on PyTorch versions below 2.6.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, nor whether other loading paths in the library are affected. They also do not state how PyTorch 2.6 or later behaves beyond noting that the safe_globals() protection is absent below 2.6. Mitigation guidance beyond upgrading is inferred from the described cause.

fixtures.scenario: A training script resumes from a downloaded checkpoint folder. The folder holds a crafted rng_state.pth, and the environment runs PyTorch below 2.6, so loading it executes attacker code.
A training script resumes only from a checkpoint it produced itself, runs a fixed Transformers release (v5.0.0rc3 or later), and loads RNG state with weights-only loading.

citations.quote: calls `torch.load()` without the `weights_only=True` parameter
as the `safe_globals()` context manager provides no protection in these versions
An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by supplying a malicious checkpoint file, such as `rng_state.pth`, which can execute arbitrary code when loaded.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the Trainer method that restores RNG state so the checkpoint file is loaded in weights-only mode instead of through a full pickle load. It also adds a call to the library's torch load safety check before loading, which guards against unsafe PyTorch versions. This matches the card's cause (unrestricted torch.load of rng_state.pth) and its prevention (request weights-only loading).

patterns.title: Unvalidated artifact file paths in MLflow Tracking Server allow directory traversal and code execution
patterns.cause: The file store's run lookup treats any directory containing a run metadata file and matching the requested run id as a run. A user can upload a forged metadata file into an artifacts folder, for example when an experiment's artifact location overlaps the store root. Requesting a run id equal to that folder name then loads the forged metadata, and its attacker-chosen artifact location is trusted. Later artifact reads and writes go to arbitrary locations outside the intended storage, which can lead to code execution.
preconditions: The tracking server uses the file-based store for run metadata.
A user can create an experiment whose artifact location overlaps the store root, or otherwise write files into a run's artifacts folder.
The run lookup does not check that a matching directory has the structure of a real run.
Metadata fields such as the artifact location are trusted without checking them against the directory they came from.
patterns.prevention: Do not trust a metadata file just because it sits under the store tree. When resolving a run id, accept only directories that have the expected run layout (metrics, params and artifacts subfolders) and are not nested inside an artifacts folder. Also check that the run id recorded in the metadata equals the directory name, and treat a mismatch as invalid state. Keep user-writable artifact areas separate from metadata areas, and refuse artifact locations that overlap the store root. Cleanup paths that run after artifacts are deleted may need a relaxed check, but only for run ids already validated.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the file-based store only. Database-backed stores and artifact path checks in the HTTP handlers are not changed by this diff. The diff does not show the exact network endpoint or whether authentication is needed, and the code-execution step is not described. Adding the layout and run id checks reduces this attack but does not replace general validation of artifact paths and locations.

fixtures.scenario: A remote, unauthenticated client sends a request to the MLflow Tracking Server artifact handler with a crafted artifact file path. The server uses the path in a file operation without validating it, so the operation can reach files outside the intended artifact area.

The same request reaches a server that validates the user-supplied artifact path before any file operation. The path would resolve outside the intended artifact area, so the server rejects the request and performs no file operation.

citations.quote: The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied path prior to using it in file operations.
Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.
An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the service account.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the file store's run lookup so a directory is accepted as a run only if it has the real run layout (metrics, params and artifacts subfolders) and is not nested inside an artifacts folder. It also makes run info loading reject metadata whose recorded run id differs from the directory name. The permanent-delete path skips the layout check because artifacts may already be gone, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Chainlit SSRF through user-controlled element url in the SQLAlchemy data layer
patterns.cause: The element update endpoint turned the client-supplied element dictionary directly into a server-side element object. Fields that should be server-controlled, such as the url, a local file path, the object key and the chainlit key, came straight from the request. When the element was created and persisted, the server fetched the url over HTTP, or read the path from disk, and stored the result. This gave an authenticated user server-side request forgery and, through the path field, arbitrary local file read. The delete endpoint similarly trusted client-supplied storage keys and url.
preconditions: Chainlit version is prior to the release containing the fix (2.9.4 or later is fixed).
The attacker is an authenticated user with a valid websocket session who can call the element update endpoint.
A data layer persists elements and processes the url or path when creating the element, such as the SQLAlchemy data layer with a storage provider.
The server can reach internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or sensitive local files.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Chainlit to 2.9.4 or later. In general, never build a server-side object from a client-supplied dictionary wholesale. For custom elements, rebuild the object from an explicit allowlist of harmless fields (identifier, owning step, thread, name, props, display mode) and discard fields that drive server-side fetching, file access or storage lookup, such as url, path, object key and storage key. Apply the same sanitizing step to both the update and delete endpoints, and keep the ownership check on the rebuilt element.
patterns.limitations: The fix removes the client-controlled fields only for custom elements on the update and delete endpoints. Other element types are already rejected by the type check. It does not add general address filtering for server-initiated fetches, so other code paths that fetch user-supplied URLs would need separate review.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated client sends an element update with a url pointing at an internal service or a cloud metadata endpoint. A Chainlit server before 2.9.4 using the SQLAlchemy data layer fetches it and stores the response.
The deployment runs Chainlit 2.9.4 or later, and an element update carrying a client-chosen internal url does not cause the server to make an outbound request to that destination.

citations.quote: Chainlit versions prior to 2.9.4 contain a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in the /project/element update flow
An authenticated client can provide a user-controlled url value in an Element, which is fetched by the SQLAlchemy element creation logic
make arbitrary HTTP requests from the Chainlit server to internal network services or cloud metadata endpoints

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that rebuilds a custom element from an explicit allowlist of fields (id, owning step, thread, name, props, display). It drops url, path, object key and chainlit key. The helper replaces the wholesale dictionary-to-object conversion in the update endpoint and the partial trust of client keys in the delete endpoint. The type check and ownership check are kept, and the tests cover both URL forgery and local file read.

patterns.title: MLflow webhook URL accepted without validation allows server-side request forgery
patterns.cause: In MLflow versions before 3.9.0, the webhook URL validator only checked basic shape and the URL scheme. It never looked at where the hostname actually resolves. An authenticated user could register a webhook whose host points at loopback, private network ranges, or a cloud metadata address, and the delivery routine (_send_webhook_request) would send server-side HTTP POST requests there. Stored URLs were also not re-checked at delivery time.
preconditions: MLflow tracking server older than 3.9.0 with the webhook feature in use.
The attacker can create or update a webhook with a URL of their choosing, or can make a hostname resolve to an internal address.
The server host can reach internal services or cloud metadata endpoints that the attacker cannot reach directly.
patterns.prevention: Resolve the webhook hostname and reject the URL if any returned address is not a publicly routable address, covering loopback, private, link-local, carrier-grade NAT, and the IPv6 equivalents. Also reject URLs with no hostname or a hostname that cannot be resolved. Run the same validation both when a webhook is created or updated and immediately before each delivery, so a stored URL or a changed DNS record is not trusted. Keep any opt-out for private addresses off by default and limit it to local development. Upgrade to MLflow 3.9.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The check resolves the name separately from the actual outbound request, so a DNS rebinding attacker could still return a different address between validation and connection. The diff does not show handling of HTTP redirects to internal addresses. The opt-out setting disables the protection entirely when enabled. Other code paths that fetch user-supplied URLs are not covered by this change.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user creates a webhook whose URL points to a cloud metadata endpoint or an internal service. The server accepts it without validation. When the webhook event fires, the MLflow backend sends an HTTP POST to that internal address on the attacker's behalf.

An authenticated user tries to create a webhook with a URL using a disallowed scheme or an internal or metadata destination. The server rejects it at creation because it fails scheme filtering and allowlist validation. No outbound request is sent to that address.

citations.quote: This allows an authenticated attacker to force the MLflow backend to send HTTP requests to internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or arbitrary external servers.
The lack of input sanitization, URL scheme filtering, or allowlist validation on the webhook URL enables exploitation

patch_review.observation: The fix extends the webhook URL validator to require a hostname, resolve it, and reject the URL if any resolved address is not globally routable (loopback, private, link-local, carrier-grade NAT, IPv6 equivalents). It also unresolvable names are rejected, and the same validator is now called at the start of the webhook delivery routine, so stored URLs are re-checked at send time. A private-address opt-out environment variable is added, off by default, and only the end-to-end tests enable it.

patterns.title: Post-extraction permission changes must not use unsanitized archive member names (wheel unpack)
patterns.cause: The wheel unpack command extracts each archive member, then applies the permission bits stored in the archive to a path built from the raw filename in the archive header. Extraction may sanitize the path, but the permission step does not. A name containing parent-directory segments can therefore point the permission change at a file outside the destination directory.
preconditions: wheel versions 0.40.0 through 0.46.1 are in use (fixed in 0.46.2).
The unpack function is run on an untrusted or attacker-crafted wheel file.
A member name in the archive contains parent-directory segments that resolve outside the destination directory.
The user running unpack has permission to change the mode of the targeted file.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade wheel to 0.46.2 or later. Downstream projects that vendor wheel, such as setuptools, should also take a fixed copy. In your own archive-handling code, never build a path from the raw member name for any step after extraction. Apply permission changes only to the path that the extraction routine reports it actually wrote. Skip the permission step when nothing was written. Also reject or normalize member names that resolve outside the destination before any file operation, and confirm that the resolved path stays inside the destination directory.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the unsafe pattern and the fix direction, but not how the released fix is implemented. They do not say whether other wheel commands or other archive formats are affected. They state the issue is fixed in 0.46.2 but do not list versions before 0.40.0. The proof of concept shows an extraction error being ignored while the permission change still took effect. The sources do not explain that behavior further.

fixtures.scenario: A wheel lists a member named with two parent-directory segments followed by a read-only file name and stores world-writable mode bits. Unpack extracts safely, then applies those bits to the raw joined path, so the file outside the destination becomes world-writable.

The same wheel is unpacked with wheel 0.46.2 or later, or with code that applies modes only to the path the extraction step reports. The outside file keeps its original read-only mode, and only files inside the destination are changed.

citations.quote: blindly trusts the filename from the archive header for the chmod operation
