The unpack function must not use zinfo.filename for post-extraction operations.
This issue has been fixed in version 0.46.2.

patch_review.observation: The unpack command used to extract each member and then change its mode on a path built from the raw member name in the archive, so a name with parent-directory segments could change the mode of a file outside the destination. The fix applies the mode change to the path that the extract call reports it actually wrote, which is sanitized and stays inside the destination. A new test confirms that an outside file keeps its content and mode.

patterns.title: Bentofile path fields can copy arbitrary host files into a bento
patterns.cause: BentoML resolves user-supplied file paths from the build configuration (description, docker setup script, docker Dockerfile template, conda environment file) without validating that they stay inside the build context directory. The description field joins the path with pathlib directly. The other fields go through a resolver that expands the tilde and environment variables and returns the real path with no containment check.
preconditions: A victim builds a bento from a bentofile.yaml that an attacker wrote or modified, for example one cloned from a malicious repository.

A file path field in the bentofile refers to a location outside the build context, using an absolute path, relative parent-directory segments, a tilde, an environment variable, or a process filesystem path.
The built bento is later pushed to a registry or BentoCloud, exported, or containerized, which exposes the copied content.
patterns.prevention: Treat every file path field in the build configuration as untrusted. For each one, resolve the path against the build context, canonicalize it (for example with os.path.realpath()), and confirm the result is still inside the canonical build context before reading or copying. Reject absolute paths, parent-directory escapes, and paths that only point outside after tilde or environment variable expansion. Apply the same check to all four fields, including description, which bypasses the shared resolver. Upgrade to version 1.4.34 or later, which contains a patch.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how version 1.4.34 implements its fix, so the exact rejection rules are unknown. Symlinks inside the build context and error handling are not discussed. The sources mention only the four listed fields, so other path-accepting settings are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A cloned project has a bentofile whose description refers to an absolute system file or the process environment listing. Building copies that file into the bento readme, and pushing the bento exposes its contents.

The bentofile references a readme inside the project directory. The real path is checked to lie within the build context before copying, and a path outside it, such as a home directory key, is rejected.

citations.quote: The vulnerability exists in how BentoML resolves user-provided file paths without validating that they remain within the build context directory.
The exfiltrated contents are embedded in the bento archive and will be included in any push, export, or containerization of the bento.
Version 1.4.34 contains a patch for the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a secure mode, on by default, to the shared path resolver. It rejects absolute paths and any resolved path outside the current working directory, which is now set to the build context. It also blocks hidden files and the /etc and /proc trees. The description field now goes through this resolver instead of a direct join. Trusted callers such as the bentofile argument, deployment config and secret files opt out of the check.

patterns.title: Absolute client filename escapes upload directory in python-multipart when original filenames are kept
patterns.cause: When an upload directory is configured and the option to keep the original filename is enabled, the library builds the destination by joining the upload directory with the client-supplied filename using os.path.join(). That function discards every earlier path component when the second argument begins with a slash. An attacker can therefore supply a filename that starts with a slash and make the file land at an arbitrary location instead of inside the upload directory.
preconditions: The upload directory option (UPLOAD_DIR) is set.
The option to keep the original filename (UPLOAD_KEEP_FILENAME) is set to true, which is not the default.
The uploaded file is larger than the in-memory size limit (MAX_MEMORY_FILE_SIZE), so it is flushed to disk.
The attacker controls the filename in the multipart request.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade python-multipart to version 0.0.22 or later. If an upgrade is not possible, do not enable the keep-original-filename option, which is the workaround the advisory gives. In application code that joins a base directory with a client-supplied name, never let the untrusted name act as a path that can replace the base. Treat it as a single leaf name, and check that the final destination is still inside the intended upload directory before writing.
patterns.limitations: The sources only describe the leading-slash case with os.path.join() and do not describe how the upstream patch works. The leaf-name and containment checks above are a general design direction, not a statement of the upstream change. The sources do not say whether other traversal forms, such as parent-directory segments, are affected or fixed. The default configuration is stated to be not vulnerable, and the sources say nothing about versions after 0.0.22 beyond the patch.

fixtures.scenario: A service configures an upload directory and enables keeping original filenames. A client uploads a file larger than the in-memory limit with a filename that begins with a slash and names a sensitive system location. The server flushes the file to that location instead of the upload directory.

A service uses python-multipart 0.0.22 or later, or leaves the keep-original-filename option disabled. The same oversized upload with a slash-prefixed filename is stored only inside the configured upload directory and no file appears at the attacker-chosen location.

citations.quote: An attacker can write uploaded files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem by crafting a malicious filename.
all preceding path components are discarded
The default configuration is not vulnerable.
Users should upgrade to version 0.0.22 to receive a patch

patch_review.observation: The fix reduces the client-supplied filename to its final path component before splitting off the extension. A name with a leading slash can then no longer replace the upload directory when the destination path is built. The added test checks that a file with an absolute-path name lands inside the upload directory under its leaf name.

patterns.title: SSRF allowlist bypass in vLLM MediaConnector through URL parser differences over backslashes
patterns.cause: MediaConnector checks the allowed host using the urlparse function from Python's urllib, but the request is sent through the requests library, which relies on urllib3 parse_url. The two parsers handle backslashes differently, so a URL can pass the host restriction yet be fetched from a different host.
preconditions: The server fetches media (images, audio, video) from URLs supplied by users through the multimodal feature
Host restriction is enforced by parsing the URL with one library, while the HTTP request is made with a different library
The attacker can submit a URL containing backslashes
The vLLM version is earlier than 0.14.1
patterns.prevention: Make validation and fetching agree on one interpretation of the URL. Take the host that will actually be contacted from the same parser that the HTTP client uses, or parse once and reuse that result for both the check and the request. Consider rejecting URLs with backslashes or other ambiguous characters. Upgrade vLLM to 0.14.1 or later, which contains a patch. Also restrict outbound network access from the serving pod to internal resources.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream patch changes the code, so the exact fix is not covered here. They also do not say whether redirect handling or other URL characters matter beyond backslashes. The preventive measures beyond upgrading are general direction, not confirmed vendor guidance.

fixtures.scenario: A user submits an image URL with a backslash in the authority part. The allowlist check parses it with urllib and sees an allowed host, but the requests library reads a different host and the server fetches an internal endpoint.

The same URL is submitted, but the host is taken from the parser the HTTP client uses, or the URL is rejected for containing a backslash. The allowlist check and the contacted host agree, so the internal request is refused.

citations.quote: These two parsing libraries have different interpretations of backslashes, which allows the host name restriction to be bypassed.
This allows an attacker to coerce the vLLM server into making arbitrary requests to internal network resources.
Version 0.14.1 contains a patch for the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the standard library URL parser with the urllib3 parser, the same one the requests library uses, in the media loader, the HTTP connection URL validation, and a few other helpers. The allowed-domain check and the actual fetch now read the same host from a URL with backslashes. Small adjustments handle the different result type, such as missing scheme or path values and data URL media type prefixes.

patterns.title: Static route group segment allows parent-directory traversal to application source files
patterns.cause: The static file route took a group segment from the URL and only stripped characters outside word characters, dots and hyphens. Because dots survive that filtering, a group made of two dots passes validation. The value is then used to build the base directory handed to the static file sender, so the base directory moves up one level into the application package directory. The route needs no authentication, so any client can read files there.
preconditions: A route builds a base directory for a file-sending helper from a user-supplied URL segment.
The sanitization permits dot characters, so a parent-directory segment is not rejected.
The route is reachable without authentication.
The running version is earlier than 0.53.2.
patterns.prevention: Do not let a user-supplied segment choose or alter the base directory of a file-sending helper. Treat a segment made only of dots as invalid, and do not rely on a character filter that allows dots. Before serving, resolve the final directory (for example with os.path.realpath()) and confirm it is still inside the intended static root, rejecting the request otherwise. Keep the set of valid group names to a known list where possible.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, so the checks above are general directions rather than a statement of what version 0.53.2 changed. The advisory says the route rejects slashes in the filename, so reads are limited to the application package directory and do not reach arbitrary system paths. The advisory rates the impact as low-severity information disclosure.

fixtures.scenario: An unauthenticated client requests the static route with a group of two dots and the name of an application source file. The filter keeps the dots, the base directory moves up to the application package directory, and the source file is returned.

The same request is made, but the group is rejected because it is not an expected group name or because the resolved directory falls outside the static root. The server returns an error and no source file content.

citations.quote: sanitization allows dots, so
Anyone with network access (no authentication required)
It is limited to files inside the application package directory.
Version 0.53.2 fixes the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix tightens the sanitization in the static content route for both the group and filename segments so that only lowercase letters, digits and underscores survive. Dots are therefore removed, which blocks a parent-directory group segment. It also returns a not-found response when either segment ends up empty after filtering. This matches the card's cause (a filter that keeps dots) and its prevention (do not allow dots, reject dot-only segments).

patterns.title: Crafted XCom payloads can lead to code execution in the Airflow webserver
patterns.cause: The operator link lookup for XCom-backed extra links read the stored XCom value and passed it through the generic XCom deserializer. A Dag Author could store a payload that looks like a serialized object, with a class name, version and data fields, in the link XCom. When the API server or webserver served the extra-links request, it instantiated the named class from that untrusted data, which allowed code execution in a context that should not run Dag Author code.
preconditions: The deployment runs an Apache Airflow version earlier than 3.2.0.
A user with Dag Author privileges can write a crafted value into an operator link XCom key.
Someone requests the extra links of that task instance through the API or UI, so the server reads the XCom value and deserializes it.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade apache-airflow to 3.2.0 or later. In the code, never rebuild objects from XCom values read in the API server or webserver. Treat the link value as data: parse it as plain JSON and convert it to a string, or return the raw value when the type is not supported. Keep Dag Author access limited to trusted people.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the operator link path only. Other code that deserializes XCom values in server components needs separate review. Severity is rated Low because Dag Authors are already highly trusted. Links whose XCom holds a serialized object now come back as text rather than a rebuilt object, which may change the output for unusual link types.

fixtures.scenario: A Dag Author stores a specially crafted XCom payload. A pre-3.2.0 webserver later handles that payload and executes arbitrary code in the webserver context.
The deployment runs Airflow 3.2.0 or later. A crafted XCom payload from a Dag Author does not lead to code execution in the webserver.

citations.quote: could craft XCom payload causing the webserver to execute arbitrary code
Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Airflow 3.2.0, which fixes the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the call to the generic XCom value deserializer in the XCom-backed operator link lookup with plain JSON parsing followed by conversion to a string. If the type is not supported for stringifying, the raw value is returned as text. This stops a crafted payload with class name, version and data fields from being used to instantiate arbitrary classes in the API server, and a test confirms such a payload now comes back as a string with a 200 status.

patterns.title: SSRF allowlist bypass from URL parser mismatch between validator and HTTP client
patterns.cause: The hostname check used urllib3 to parse user-supplied URLs, but the request was sent with aiohttp, which parses URLs with yarl. The two parsers treat a backslash differently. urllib3 keeps the allowed host and treats the rest as path, while yarl reads the text before the at sign as userinfo and takes the host after it. A URL can therefore pass validation for one host and be fetched from another.
preconditions: The server fetches user-provided URLs and validates the hostname with a different URL parser than the one the HTTP client uses
The attacker can supply a URL with a backslash before an at sign after an allowed host name
The check relies on a hostname allowlist or similar host-based restriction
patterns.prevention: Make validation and request use the same interpretation of the URL. Derive the host to check from the parser the HTTP client actually uses, and send the request to that parsed result, not to the raw string. Treat any disagreement between parsers as a rejection. Rejecting URLs that contain backslashes or userinfo is a stricter option, but the sources do not say what the upstream fix did.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail, so the exact change is unknown. The affected version range is vague: the CVE text mentions an earlier fix in 0.15.1 and a vulnerability in 0.17.0. Only the backslash difference is documented. Other parser differences, redirects and DNS behavior are not covered by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A service checks the host of a submitted URL with one parser, sees an allowed host, then fetches the raw string with a client using another parser. The URL has a backslash before an at sign, so the client connects to the host after the at sign.

A service parses the submitted URL once with the same parser its HTTP client uses, checks that parsed host against the allowlist, and rejects the URL if parsers disagree. The URL with a backslash before an at sign is refused.

citations.quote: Bypass the hostname allowlist check
load_from_url_async uses aiohttp for making the actual HTTP requests, and aiohttp internally uses the yarl library for URL parsing

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the synchronous and asynchronous load paths in the media connector to pass the URL as normalized by the validating parser (urllib3) to the HTTP client, instead of the raw user string. The client then connects to the same host the allowlist check approved, so a backslash before an at sign no longer lets yarl pick a different host. Tests cover the backslash bypass and the case where the allowlist still rejects a disallowed host.

patterns.title: Client-supplied prompt tag bypasses model version source validation and enables arbitrary file read in MLflow
patterns.cause: The model version creation handler skips source path validation when a request carries the mlflow.prompt.is_prompt tag. An attacker can therefore store an arbitrary local filesystem path as the model version source. The artifact-serving handler later uses that source to serve files without verifying the model version's prompt status.
preconditions: MLflow server version 3.9.0 or earlier is reachable by the attacker
The attacker can send a CreateModelVersion request, and no authentication is required
The request includes the prompt tag, which causes source path validation to be bypassed
The artifact download handler serves files from the stored source without checking prompt status
patterns.prevention: Do not let a client-controlled tag switch off validation of a filesystem-bearing field. Validate the model version source on every creation path, whatever tags the request carries. Make the artifact-serving handler independently confirm that the model version's source and prompt status permit serving before it reads any file. Upgrade to MLflow 3.10.0 or later, where the issue is fixed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation rules, the content of the upstream fix, or workarounds for versions before 3.10.0. They also do not say whether deployments with an authentication layer in front of the server are affected differently.

fixtures.scenario: An unauthenticated client sends a CreateModelVersion request with the prompt tag and a local filesystem path as the source. The server stores it without validation, and a later artifact request returns the contents of that file.

A client sends the same request with the prompt tag and a local path as the source. The server validates the source regardless of the tag and rejects the request, so the artifact handler never serves an arbitrary local file.

citations.quote: allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to read arbitrary files from the server's filesystem
This enables an attacker to store an arbitrary local filesystem path as the model version source.
later uses this source to serve files without verifying the model version's prompt status

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the model version creation handler so that requests carrying the prompt tag are no longer exempt from source checks. For prompts, it now rejects file-scheme URIs and absolute local paths, and it runs the relative-path traversal check on sources that have a URL scheme. Schemeless placeholder sources are still allowed. The artifact-serving handler is not changed in this diff.

patterns.title: Client-side method name executed via eval fallback allows XSS in NiceGUI
patterns.cause: The JavaScript-side runMethod() function fell back to eval() when a method name was not found on the element. User-controlled text passed as a method name could therefore run as arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser. Element.run_method() and Element.get_computed_prop() also built the name by plain string interpolation instead of JSON string encoding, so quote characters could break out of the intended string.
preconditions: The application passes user-controlled input, such as a URL query parameter, as the method or property name to an element method-execution API like Element.run_method(), AgGrid.run_grid_method() or EChart.run_chart_method().
The NiceGUI version is older than 3.8.0.
A victim opens an attacker-crafted link, and the payload is sent to their browser over the WebSocket.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NiceGUI to 3.8.0 or later. Never take method or property names for these APIs from user input; keep them fixed by the developer. An implementation should encode method and property names as proper JSON strings when building client-side calls. The client-side runtime should not evaluate unknown names as JavaScript and should raise an error instead. Code that relied on passing JavaScript functions as method names should move to ui.run_javascript() with developer-authored script.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the affected APIs and the general fix direction only. They do not say whether other NiceGUI APIs that accept user text, such as ui.run_javascript() called with untrusted input, are safe. They do not recommend an allow-list of method names, so that is an extra hardening step rather than a documented fix. Exploitation also depends on application code that forwards untrusted input.

fixtures.scenario: A page reads a query parameter from the URL and passes it unchanged as the method name to an element method-execution API. A crafted link makes the victim's browser run attacker JavaScript.
Method names are fixed by the developer and never taken from user input. On NiceGUI 3.8.0 or later, an unknown method name raises an error instead of being evaluated.

citations.quote: When user-controlled input is passed as the method name, an attacker can inject arbitrary JavaScript that executes in the victim's browser.
method names that are not found on the element now raise an error instead of being evaluated as arbitrary JavaScript
allowing quote injection to break out of the intended string context.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the eval fallback in the client-side method runner, so an unknown method name now logs and emits a 'not found' error instead of running as JavaScript. It also encodes the method name in run_method and the property name in get_computed_prop as JSON strings, so quote characters can no longer break out of the string. The docs and tests are changed to use ui.run_javascript() for arbitrary script, and new tests check that injected payloads do not execute.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from an unescaped UUID path parameter in the changedetection.io RSS single-watch error responses
patterns.cause: The RSS single-watch endpoint builds its not-found and not-enough-history error messages by placing the UUID path parameter directly into the response body without HTML escaping. Flask sends plain string responses as text/html by default, so the browser parses any markup in the UUID and runs injected JavaScript in the victim's session.
preconditions: The endpoint echoes a user-controlled URL path segment into an error message body without HTML escaping.
The response is served with the default text/html content type, so the browser interprets the reflected text as markup.
The attacker has a valid RSS access token. The report says it appears in a link tag on the homepage, visible without authentication on instances that do not require a login.
A victim with an active session on the instance opens the crafted link.
patterns.prevention: Treat the UUID path segment as untrusted data in every response. Either do not echo it back, or HTML-escape it before it goes into any text/html response, including error responses. Review all error branches of the endpoint, not only the first one. Where a response is not meant to be a page, consider whether a non-HTML content type is appropriate. Also consider setting the HttpOnly flag on session cookies, since the report says cookie theft leads to account takeover when that flag is missing.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code change in version 0.54.1, so the exact fix and its completeness are unknown. The advisory says three vulnerabilities were found but describes only this one in detail. The sources do not say whether other endpoints reflect input in the same way. The effect of the token on exploitability is described only for instances without authentication.

fixtures.scenario: A request to the RSS single-watch path supplies a UUID segment that contains URL-encoded HTML markup with an event handler, plus a valid token. No watch matches, and the server returns a 404 text/html body with the segment inserted verbatim. A victim's browser renders the markup and runs the script.

The same request is made with a markup-bearing UUID segment and a valid token. The 404 or 400 response either omits the segment or HTML-escapes it, so the browser shows it as inert text and no script runs.

citations.quote: the RSS single-watch endpoint reflects the UUID path parameter directly in the HTTP response body without HTML escaping.
Since Flask returns text/html by default for plain string responses, the browser parses and executes injected JavaScript.
The attack requires a valid RSS access token, which is a 32-character hex string exposed in the HTML

patch_review.observation: The fix stops the reflected markup in two ways. The single-watch RSS error responses for a missing watch and for too little history are now sent as plain text instead of the default HTML type. A strict UUID route converter now rejects path segments that are not canonical UUIDs (apart from one sentinel value), and it is applied to this endpoint and to many other watch, tag, API and UI routes.

patterns.title: SSRF through watch URLs that are never checked against internal address ranges
patterns.cause: The URL validator for watch URLs checked only the protocol and URL format and never looked at the address the hostname resolves to. The fetcher also did no address check of its own and followed HTTP redirects automatically. A user could therefore add an internal, loopback or cloud metadata URL, or a public URL that redirects or later resolves to one. The server fetched it, stored the response and showed it in the web UI, so this was not a blind SSRF.
preconditions: changedetection.io version earlier than 0.54.1
A user can add watch URLs, either authenticated or with no password set, which is the default
The server can reach internal services, loopback addresses or a cloud metadata address
Fetched content is stored and viewable through the web UI or the API
patterns.prevention: Resolve the hostname of every user-supplied URL and reject it if any resolved address is private, loopback, link-local or otherwise reserved, and treat names that cannot be resolved as unsafe. Do this in the shared validator so all add paths benefit. Because validation results can be cached and DNS answers can change, repeat the check with a fresh lookup in the fetcher immediately before each request. Disable automatic redirect following and validate each redirect target the same way, with a cap on the number of hops, so an open redirect on a public host cannot reach internal addresses. Offer an explicit opt-in setting for operators who need to watch internal services, off by default. Upgrade to 0.54.1 or later.
patterns.limitations: The check relies on a name lookup performed by the validator or fetcher, and the connection may do its own lookup afterwards, so a small timing gap for DNS rebinding can remain. Only the plain requests fetcher is shown doing the fetch-time and redirect checks; browser-based fetchers are not covered by the diff. Setting the opt-in option to allow restricted addresses removes the protection entirely. A password only limits who can add watches and does not stop an authenticated user.

fixtures.scenario: On a default instance with no password, a user adds a watch for the link-local cloud metadata address. The validator accepts it because the protocol and format are fine. The server fetches the address periodically, stores the response, and shows it in the preview page.

The same submission is rejected at validation time because the resolved address is in a link-local range. The same happens for loopback and private addresses. No fetch is made, and no internal content is stored or shown.

citations.quote: does not validate the resolved IP address of watch URLs against private, loopback, or link-local address ranges
The application fetches these URLs server-side, stores the response content, and makes it viewable through the web UI
By default, no password is set - the web UI is accessible without authentication
Version 0.54.1 contains a fix for the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a hostname resolution check that rejects private, loopback, link-local and reserved addresses and treats unresolvable names as blocked. It runs in the URL validator at add time and again, uncached, in the requests fetcher before each fetch. The fetcher also stops following redirects automatically and checks each redirect target with a hop limit. An environment opt-in setting, off by default, allows restricted addresses.

patterns.title: Symlink target not validated in tar extraction allows arbitrary file write in BentoML
patterns.cause: The safe_extract_tarfile() function checks that each tar member's own path lies inside the destination directory. For symlink members it never checks where the link points. A symlink aimed outside the destination is created. A later regular file entry that writes through that link is opened with a call that follows symlinks, so the data lands outside the extraction directory. The path check uses os.path.abspath(), which does not resolve symlinks, so it passes on the string alone.
preconditions: BentoML earlier than 1.4.36 extracts an untrusted bento or model tar archive
The archive contains a symlink member whose target is outside the extraction directory
A later regular file member is written under the symlink's name, so the write follows the link
The user pulls or imports the archive, for example from a shared bento or BentoCloud
patterns.prevention: Validate the target of every symlink member before creating it. Resolve the link target relative to the directory that holds the link, normalize it, and skip or reject the member if the result is outside the destination directory. Checking only the member name is not enough. On Python 3.12 or later, the tarfile data extraction filter can be used instead of hand-written checks. Upgrade BentoML to 1.4.36 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail, only a suggested remediation and the fixed version. They do not discuss hard links, chained symlinks, or race conditions. They do not say whether the suggested target check alone covers every escape path, so treat it as a minimum.

fixtures.scenario: A shared bento archive has a symlink entry pointing to a directory outside the extraction folder, followed by a file entry under the symlink's name. Extraction creates the link, then writes the file through it into the outside directory.

The extractor resolves each symlink target relative to the link's directory and rejects any target outside the destination. The malicious link is skipped, so the later file entry cannot write outside the extraction folder.

citations.quote: for symlink members it only validates the symlink's own path, not the symlink's target
A malicious bento can overwrite any writable file:
Validate symlink targets:
This vulnerability is fixed in 1.4.36.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes safe_extract_tarfile() resolve the destination to its real path. It rejects any symlink member whose target, resolved relative to the link's own directory and normalized, falls outside the destination. As a second layer, it resolves the real path of each regular file before writing and skips the file if it lands outside the destination. This matches the card's cause (symlink target never checked, so a later write follows the link out) and its prevention (validate the link target relative to the link's directory, then normalize).

patterns.title: Root-relative paths bypass absolute-path checks in Gradio on Windows with Python 3.13+
patterns.cause: Python 3.13+ changed os.path.isabs so that root-relative paths on Windows, such as one starting with a single slash and naming a system file, are no longer treated as absolute. Gradio's logic for joining paths safely relied on that definition, so a crafted request path could escape the intended directory and read arbitrary files.
preconditions: Gradio version earlier than 6.7
Server runs on Windows
Python 3.13 or later
Attacker can send HTTP requests to the app; authentication does not stop the attack
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on os.path.isabs alone to decide whether untrusted input is safe to join to a base directory, because its result depends on the Python version and platform. Treat any request-supplied path as untrusted, resolve the final joined path (for example with os.path.realpath()), and confirm it stays inside the intended base directory before opening it. Upgrade Gradio to 6.7 or later, which the advisories say fixes the issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact code change in the fix, other affected platforms or Python versions, or which Gradio routes beyond the static file route are reachable. The advice on resolving and containing paths is general hardening direction and is not confirmed as the upstream approach.

fixtures.scenario: A Gradio app older than 6.7 runs on Windows with Python 3.13+. An unauthenticated client requests a static file path whose remainder starts with a slash and names a system file. The join logic sees it as relative and the file is served.
The app runs Gradio 6.7 or later, or the file-serving code resolves the joined path and rejects any target outside the allowed directory. The same request for a system file is refused.

citations.quote: Gradio apps running on Window with Python 3.13+ are vulnerable to an absolute path traversal issue
resulting in a vulnerability in Gradio's logic for joining paths safely
This can be exploited by unauthenticated attackers to read arbitrary files from the Gradio server, even when Gradio is set up with authentication.
Version 6.7 fixes the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the safe_join helper in gradio/utils.py so it also rejects any user-supplied path that begins with a forward slash, in addition to the existing os.path.isabs test. This closes the gap where Python 3.13+ on Windows no longer treats root-relative paths as absolute, which let them slip past the check. The card's cause (isabs semantics changed) and its prevention (do not rely on isabs alone, validate untrusted paths, upgrade) agree with this.

patterns.title: Open redirect through unvalidated target URL parameter in Gradio OAuth logout and login callback
patterns.cause: The redirect helper in Gradio's OAuth flow takes the _target_url query parameter from the request and redirects to it without validation. A crafted link on a trusted domain can therefore send users to any external site after logout or login callback.
preconditions: Gradio version earlier than 6.6.0
OAuth enabled on the app, for example a Hugging Face Space using the login button component
The /logout or /login/callback endpoint is reachable by the victim
The victim follows an attacker-crafted link carrying an external _target_url value
patterns.prevention: Treat the post-login or post-logout destination as untrusted input. Reduce it to a local destination made of only a path, query, and fragment, and discard any scheme or host so the redirect always stays on the app's own origin. Upgrade to Gradio 6.6.0 or later, which sanitizes the parameter this way. In custom redirect helpers, apply the same normalization before building the redirect response.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe only the open redirect and its phishing impact, and say no direct data exposure or server-side impact. They do not explain the other listed weakness categories (information exposure, access control, weak randomness). They also do not detail how edge-case inputs such as scheme-relative or malformed URLs are handled, so those cases should be tested directly.

fixtures.scenario: A Gradio app earlier than 6.6.0 with OAuth enabled receives a request to its logout endpoint whose _target_url value names an external attacker site. The app redirects the user there, and the link looks trustworthy because it starts with the app's own domain.

A Gradio app at version 6.6.0 or later receives the same logout request with an external _target_url. Only the path, query, and fragment are kept and the scheme and host are dropped, so the user stays on the app's own origin.

citations.quote: accepts an unvalidated _target_url query parameter, allowing redirection to arbitrary external URLs
Starting in version 6.6.0, the _target_url parameter is sanitized to only use the path, query, and fragment, stripping any scheme or host.
Because the URL originates from a trusted hf.space domain, users are more likely to trust the link.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the redirect helper so the _target_url value is parsed and rebuilt from only its path, query, and fragment, dropping any scheme and host. Redirects therefore stay on the app's own origin, as the card says. The same commit also replaces the real token in the mocked local OAuth info with a dummy value, which is a separate information exposure fix that the card does not claim to cover.

patterns.title: SSRF through a remote Space proxy_url trusted by gr.load() in Gradio
patterns.cause: When gr.load() loads a remote Space, the config is fetched and processed by Blocks.from_config(). The proxy_url value from that untrusted config is added directly to the app's set of trusted proxy URLs. The built-in proxy route then validates a requested URL only by comparing its host with the hosts of those trusted entries. An attacker who controls the Space can therefore name any internal host, such as a cloud metadata address, and the victim's server will fetch from it.
preconditions: The application uses gr.load() to load a Space that an attacker controls or can modify.
The loaded config contains a proxy_url value chosen by the attacker.
The application exposes the built-in proxy route, which every Gradio app provides automatically.
The attacker can send HTTP requests to the victim's Gradio server.
patterns.prevention: Treat the config of a loaded Space as untrusted data. Do not let a value supplied by a remote config add hosts to the allowlist that the proxy route uses to decide which URLs the server may fetch. Build that allowlist only from origins the operator has chosen. Upgrade Gradio to version 6.6.0 or later, which the advisories state fixes the issue. Avoid loading Spaces you do not control into applications that can reach internal networks or cloud metadata endpoints.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how version 6.6.0 changes the validation, so the exact fixed behavior is not covered here. They do not say whether other config fields or other code paths are affected. They name no workaround besides upgrading and avoiding untrusted Spaces. They give no guidance on network-level egress controls.

fixtures.scenario: A Gradio app calls gr.load() on a third-party Space whose config sets proxy_url to the cloud metadata address. The app is launched on all interfaces, and a remote user requests the built-in proxy route to read internal credentials.

A Gradio app runs version 6.6.0 or later, or loads only Spaces the operator controls, so remote config cannot add hosts to the proxy allowlist and a proxy request for an internal address is not honored.

citations.quote: The validation only checks if the URL's host matches any trusted
allows an attacker to make arbitrary HTTP requests from a victim's server by hosting a malicious Gradio Space
Version 6.6.0 fixes the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops untrusted proxy_url values from a loaded Space config from becoming trusted proxy targets. The config-loading code now adds a proxy URL to the trusted set only if its host ends with the Hugging Face Space domain. The proxy route also rejects any requested host outside that domain, even if it is in the trusted set, and new tests confirm that cloud metadata and internal hosts are blocked.

patterns.title: Unsanitised upload filename and verbose error leak server path in transcription endpoint
patterns.cause: The speech-to-text endpoint took the file extension from the raw multipart filename by splitting on dots, with no path sanitisation. The result went into a filesystem path passed to open(). A filename with a slash after the last dot made open() fail, and the exception text, including the absolute data directory path, was returned verbatim in the HTTP 400 body. The MIME check looked only at the Content-Type field, so it did not constrain the filename.
preconditions: The caller is any authenticated non-admin user, the lowest privilege tier allowed on the route
The extension is derived from the client-supplied filename without reducing it to a base name
The upload passes the MIME-type guard because that guard checks Content-Type, not the filename
Exception messages are returned to the client in the HTTP error response
patterns.prevention: Reduce the client-supplied filename to its final path component before deriving the extension, as the sibling upload handlers do with os.path.basename(), and use a safe default extension when none remains. Treat the filename as untrusted even when the MIME type looks valid. Do not return raw exception text to clients. Log the detail server-side and return a generic failure message. The vendor patched the issue in version 0.8.6.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the impact as information disclosure only. The write primitive is reported as blocked in practice by a fresh UUID path segment. They do not show the exact upstream patch, only a recommended direction. They do not say whether other endpoints return raw exception text. Whether the 0.8.6 patch covers every error path is not stated.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated non-admin user uploads audio with Content-Type audio/wav and a filename containing a slash after the last dot. The handler builds a path from it, open fails, and the 400 body shows the absolute data directory path.
The same upload has its filename reduced to a final component before the extension is taken. Any failure returns a generic message such as Transcription failed, while details go only to server logs.

citations.quote: An unsanitised filename field in the speech-to-text transcription endpoint allows any authenticated non-admin user to trigger a
Filesystem structure can be enumerated by varying traversal depth and observing which error messages change.
Both sibling handlers apply it explicitly:
Version 0.8.6 patches the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix reduces the uploaded filename to its base name before taking the extension, and it replaces both error responses in the transcription handler with a fixed generic message, so exception text and server paths no longer reach the client. This matches the card's prevention of sanitising the filename and not returning raw exceptions. The pre-patch code already stripped some slash characters from the extension, so the card's claim of no sanitisation is slightly overstated, but the main cause and fix direction agree.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from unescaped path parameter in RSS tag not-found response
patterns.cause: The RSS tag endpoint accepted any string as its tag identifier path parameter and echoed it unescaped into the not-found response body. Flask serves plain string responses as text/html, so markup in the path was parsed by the browser. The route should only have accepted well-formed UUID values, since tag identifiers are always UUIDs.
preconditions: The attacker can craft a URL for the RSS tag endpoint whose path segment contains HTML or script and does not match an existing tag.
The attacker has a valid RSS access token, which the advisory says can be read from the unauthenticated homepage.
The not-found message is returned as a plain string, so the default text/html content type applies.
A victim opens the crafted link in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Constrain identifier path parameters to their expected format at the routing layer, here by using a UUID-only route converter for the tag identifier so that any non-UUID value gets a routing 404 and never reaches handler code or the error message. As defense in depth, also HTML-escape any request-derived value included in a response, or return error text with a plain-text content type. When one endpoint is fixed for this pattern, check sibling endpoints for the same loosely typed route and unescaped message. Upgrade to a release containing the fix, 0.54.4 or later per the CVE records.
patterns.limitations: Route-level validation protects only endpoints that use the strict converter; other routes that accept free-form strings and echo them remain exposed. A strict UUID check does not help where legitimate values may contain arbitrary characters, so escaping is still needed there. Real-world impact such as session theft depends on deployment details like cookie flags.

fixtures.scenario: A request to the tag RSS endpoint with a valid token and a path value containing HTML markup, for a tag that does not exist, gets a 404 body that echoes the markup as text/html, so the browser runs the script.
The same request, but the handler escapes the path value or returns the not-found message as plain text, so the browser shows the markup as literal text and runs nothing.

citations.quote: The tag_uuid path parameter is reflected directly in the HTTP response body without HTML escaping.
Since Flask returns text/html by default for plain string responses, the browser parses and executes injected JavaScript.
but did not address the identical pattern in the tag RSS endpoint.
This issue has been patched in version 0.54.4.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the RSS tag feed route so the tag identifier uses a UUID-only route converter instead of a free-form string converter. Non-UUID path values now get a routing 404 before reaching the handler, so they are never echoed into the not-found response. The diff does not add output escaping, but the card names that only as defense in depth.

patterns.title: Zip Slip path traversal in changedetection.io backup restore
patterns.cause: The backup restore function extracts an uploaded ZIP archive into the datastore directory using zipfile.extractall() without validating entry paths. Entries containing parent-directory sequences keep their relative paths and are written outside the intended extraction directory.
preconditions: The application accepts a ZIP archive upload through the backup restore feature
Archive extraction uses a bulk extraction call that preserves entry paths from the archive
Entry paths are not checked against the extraction directory before files are written
patterns.prevention: Before writing any archive entry, resolve its full destination path, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it remains inside the intended extraction directory. Reject the whole archive if any entry would land outside. Do not rely on bulk extraction of untrusted archives without this check. The advisory states the issue is patched in version 0.54.4, so upgrade to that version or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the missing validation and the patched version but not the exact upstream fix. They do not discuss other archive risks such as symbolic links, absolute paths, or oversized archives, and do not say which of those the patch covers. The advisory does not state whether authentication is required to reach the restore endpoint.

fixtures.scenario: A user uploads a ZIP to the backup restore endpoint with an entry whose path climbs out of the datastore directory toward the Flask secret key file. Bulk extraction writes the attacker content outside the directory.

The same ZIP is uploaded, but each entry's resolved destination is checked against the datastore directory before extraction. The escaping entry causes the restore to be rejected and nothing is written outside the directory.

citations.quote: The application uses zipfile.extractall() without validating entry paths, allowing ../ sequences to escape the extraction directory.
Prior to version 0.54.4, a Zip Slip vulnerability in the backup restore functionality allows arbitrary file overwrite via path traversal in uploaded ZIP archives.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the bulk extraction in the restore import routine with a per-entry loop. Each entry's destination is resolved to a real path and the whole archive is rejected with an error if any entry falls outside the extraction directory. This matches the card's cause and prevention. The patch also adds hardening the card does not mention: an uncompressed-size limit, an upload-size limit, UUID-only top-level directories, removal of the session secret file from backups, and a stricter download path check.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS in NLTK WordNet Browser lookup route from unescaped word
patterns.cause: In nltk.app.wordnet_app, the lookup_ route decodes URL state into a word value and, when no results are found, inserts that word directly into the HTML body. The search route escapes its input, but the lookup_ route does not, so a crafted URL injects HTML or JavaScript into the response page.
preconditions: The nltk.app.wordnet_app WordNet Browser server is running (versions 3.9.3 and prior).
A request to a lookup_ URL carries an attacker-chosen word, which the URL state decoder accepts.
The word is placed into the HTML response without escaping, as on the not-found message path.
A user opens the attacker-supplied link in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Treat every value decoded from the URL as untrusted. Apply HTML escaping, for example html.escape(), to the word at the point where it is written into the page, on every route and branch. Do not rely on one route escaping while another does not. Prefer one shared output-encoding step for all user-derived text, and re-check the decoded value rather than trusting its origin.
patterns.limitations: The sources name the not-found message as the confirmed sink and do not list other places where the word may be rendered. They do not describe the exact upstream change, nor how the pickle-based URL state decoding should be hardened. The fix is stated only to be in a commit. The sources also note that the server listens on all interfaces by default, but give no guidance on changing that.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens a lookup_ link whose encoded word is a script tag. The word has no dictionary match, so the not-found message embeds the raw word and the browser runs the script.
The same lookup_ link is opened, but the word is HTML-escaped before the not-found message is built. The browser shows the tag as plain text and runs no script.

citations.quote: This impacts users running the local WordNet Browser server and can lead to script execution in the browser origin of that application.
accepts attacker-controlled base64-encoded pickle data for the URL state.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the not-found branch of the page_from_reference function so the word decoded from the URL is HTML-escaped before it is placed in the response body. This matches the card's cause (an unescaped word in the not-found message on the lookup route) and its prevention (escape the decoded value where it is written into the page).

patterns.title: NLTK downloader path traversal via unvalidated index subdir and id
patterns.cause: The NLTK downloader builds local file and directory paths from the subdir and id attributes of a remote XML index without validating them. A malicious index can supply values with parent-directory sequences such as ../, so the path escapes the download directory.
preconditions: NLTK version 3.9.3 or earlier is in use
The downloader is pointed at a remote XML index server that an attacker controls
A download is requested for a package whose index entry carries malicious subdir or id values
patterns.prevention: Treat the subdir and id values from a remote index as untrusted input. Reject absolute paths and parent-directory sequences. Before creating any directory or opening any file for writing, resolve the final target path and confirm it stays inside the configured download directory. Apply the same check to both directory creation and file writing.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream commit implements its fix, so this card gives only the general direction. They do not say whether other index attributes, symlinks, or archive extraction need extra checks. Only versions 3.9.3 and prior are named as affected.

fixtures.scenario: A downloader uses an attacker-controlled index. A package entry has a subdir with many ../ segments pointing to a system temp location. Downloading it creates directories and writes a file outside the download directory.

The downloader resolves the target path for each index entry and checks it lies inside the download directory. An entry whose subdir contains ../ and escapes the directory is rejected before any directory or file is created.

citations.quote: which can lead to arbitrary directory creation, arbitrary file creation, and arbitrary file overwrite.
Can create arbitrary directories outside the download directory
Create directories at arbitrary locations in the file system

patch_review.observation: The fix rejects package subdir values that are absolute or contain parent-directory components, and rejects id values containing path separators or parent-directory sequences, when a package object is built from the remote index. It also adds a containment check in the package download routine that resolves the final target path and aborts with an error if it falls outside the download directory. This matches the card's cause (unvalidated index values) and its prevention (reject traversal input and confirm the resolved path stays inside the download directory).

patterns.title: Unrestricted class import when deserializing serialized DAGs in Airflow
patterns.cause: The deserialize method of BaseSerialization allowed unrestricted use of the import_string helper on class paths taken from the serialized DAG. A DAG author controls that data, so a class path they embedded was imported and used by the Scheduler or API Server. This is unsafe deserialization (CWE-502).
preconditions: The Scheduler or API Server loads a serialized DAG that contains attacker-controlled class paths.
The attacker can author or submit DAGs, for example by embedding a malicious trigger in a DAG.
The deployment runs a version of apache-airflow older than 3.3.0.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade apache-airflow to 3.3.0 or later. Do not let class paths read from serialized data be imported without an explicit check. Resolve them only against a fixed allowlist of expected classes. Where DAG-author trust is limited, set the allowed_deserialization_classes option in the core configuration section to a narrow allowlist. Keep DAG-author code out of the Scheduler and API Server processes, since the security boundary requires that it never run there.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which versions before 3.3.0 are affected, which serialized fields or trigger types carry the class path, or how the upstream change works. They describe the allowlist configuration only as defense-in-depth, not as a full fix. They do not say whether other deserialization paths need the same protection.

fixtures.scenario: A DAG author submits a DAG whose serialized form embeds a trigger with an attacker-chosen class path. The Scheduler or API Server loads it, the class path is imported without restriction, and the attacker gains remote code execution in that process.

The deployment runs apache-airflow 3.3.0 or later, and the allowed_deserialization_classes option holds a narrow allowlist. A serialized DAG that names a class outside the allowlist is not turned into an imported class in the Scheduler or API Server.

citations.quote: a DAG author could embed a malicious trigger into a DAG to gain remote code execution on the API Server / Scheduler process
crossing the Airflow security boundary that DAG-author code must never execute in those processes.
3.3.0 or later. As a defense-in-depth mitigation, deployments where DAG-author trust is limited can restrict the

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the base-trigger type from BaseSerialization, so its deserialize method no longer imports a class by path and instantiates it with kwargs taken from serialized data. It also stops decoding trigger kwargs and next-method kwargs when a serialized DAG is loaded, keeping them as raw encoded data. The scheduler then stringifies the encoding keys when it stores them. This matches the card's cause of unrestricted class import from DAG-author-controlled serialized data.

patterns.title: Validate request paths before resolving them to avoid UNC-based SSRF on Windows
patterns.cause: Attacker-supplied filesystem paths were resolved with os.path.realpath() or Path.resolve() before sufficient validation, including in the ComponentRequestHandler. On Windows, a UNC path made this resolution start an outbound SMB connection, which could send NTLMv2 credentials of the account running the Streamlit process.
preconditions: Streamlit Open Source version earlier than 1.54.0
The server runs on a Windows host
Component endpoints are reachable by untrusted parties, with no authentication needed
The server can open outbound SMB connections on port 445
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Streamlit 1.54.0 or later. In your own code that handles request-derived paths, validate the untrusted path before passing it to any resolving call such as os.path.realpath() or Path.resolve(), and reject values that point to remote network locations. As defense in depth, restrict NTLM, disable outbound NTLM authentication, require SMB signing, or block NTLM authentication to remote servers.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the exact validation rules used in the fix, so this card does not specify them. They state only that the issue affects Windows. NTLM hardening reduces the impact of credential relay or hash exposure but does not remove the unvalidated path handling. Residual risk depends on the organization's authentication configuration and network posture.

fixtures.scenario: A Streamlit server older than 1.54.0 on Windows exposes component endpoints to an untrusted network. A GET request appends an attacker-controlled SMB host to the URI path, and the server resolves it as a filesystem path before validating it.

The server runs Streamlit 1.54.0 or later. Any request-derived path is validated and rejected if it targets a remote network location before os.path.realpath() or Path.resolve() is called, so no outbound SMB connection starts.

citations.quote: The vulnerability arises from improper validation of attacker-supplied filesystem paths.
can cause the Streamlit server to initiate outbound SMB connections over port 445
Streamlit Open Source versions prior to 1.54.0 running on Windows hosts.
Organizations that enforce NTLM restrictions, disable outbound NTLM authentication, require SMB signing, or block NTLM authentication to remote servers

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a shared check, run before any call that resolves a path, that rejects UNC paths, drive-qualified paths, rooted or absolute paths, traversal segments and null bytes. It is applied in the safe-path builder used by the component handlers, in the app static file handler, in the static routes, and in a new Starlette middleware. Rejected requests now get a 400 response. This matches the card's cause (resolving untrusted paths before validation, which lets Windows open an SMB connection) and its prevention (validate first, reject remote locations).

patterns.title: Unsafe deserialization of XCom values through legacy serialization keys in the Airflow webserver
patterns.cause: The public XCom creation API accepted arbitrary user-supplied values without checking for the reserved serialization metadata keys that Airflow's deserializer treats as instructions to rebuild objects. This covers the current format keys (class name, version, data, schema id, cache) and the legacy type, source and var keys. A Dag Author could store a crafted nested value that looked like serialized output, and the webserver could later reconstruct an attacker-chosen object while handling it, leading to code execution.
preconditions: The attacker can create XCom entries through the API, for example a Dag Author or any user allowed to post XCom values.
The stored value contains a dictionary, possibly nested inside other dictionaries or lists, that uses reserved serialization keys in either the current or the legacy format.
The value is later deserialized in the webserver context, and the deployment runs an Airflow release before 3.2.0 that lacks the creation-time check.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 3.2.0 or later, which rejects XCom create requests whose value contains reserved serialization keys at any nesting depth, returning a validation error. More generally, validate untrusted data at the point where it enters storage and refuse any value that imitates internal serialization markers, for both current and legacy formats. Keep a single shared list of reserved markers so the deserializer and the input check cannot drift apart.
patterns.limitations: The diff only shows the check on the XCom create request body. Values written by other paths, such as task code through the execution API, or existing stored entries are not shown as covered. The deserializer's handling of legacy keys is not changed, so safety depends on the input check being applied wherever untrusted values enter. Severity is rated Low because Dag Authors are already trusted.

fixtures.scenario: A Dag Author on a pre-3.2.0 deployment stores an XCom value that uses the legacy serialization keys. When the webserver's XCom API handles that value, it deserializes it in the webserver process and arbitrary code runs there.
The deployment runs Apache Airflow 3.2.0 or later. The same crafted XCom value with legacy serialization keys does not lead to code execution in the webserver context.

citations.quote: Unsafe Deserialization via Legacy Serialization Keys (__type/__var) Bypass in XCom API
could craft XCom payload causing the webserver to execute arbitrary code
Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Airflow 3.2.0, which resolves this issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a validator on the XCom create request body. It walks the submitted value through nested dictionaries, lists and tuples and rejects it with a validation error if any reserved serialization key appears. The reserved set covers the five current-format keys and the three legacy keys (type, source, var). The constants move into a new shared serialization package so the deserializer and the check use one list. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Stored XSS from unsafely parsed MLmodel YAML artifacts shown in the MLflow web UI
patterns.cause: The MLflow web UI parses MLmodel YAML artifacts with the js-yaml load function, which uses the full schema. That schema can build non-plain values, such as functions, from special tags in untrusted YAML. A user who uploads a crafted MLmodel file can therefore get script to run in the browser of anyone who opens the artifact in the logged model view or triggers signature validation. The weakness is unsafe deserialization at parse time, not missing escaping at render time.
preconditions: The attacker can log or upload a model with a crafted MLmodel artifact to a tracking server.
Another user opens that logged model artifact view, or the UI runs logged model signature validation on it.
The MLflow version is 3.10.1 or earlier, where the front end uses the unrestricted YAML load function.
patterns.prevention: Parse all YAML read from artifacts in the front end with the safe-schema loader, which accepts only plain data types such as strings, numbers, lists and maps and rejects executable or custom tags. Apply this to every place the UI reads MLmodel or other artifact YAML, and check for any remaining uses of the unrestricted load function. Treat parsed values as plain data, and upgrade to a MLflow release that includes the fix.
patterns.limitations: The fix covers the two call sites shown in the diff. Other front-end code paths that parse artifact YAML would need their own review. Safe parsing also does not remove the need to escape or sanitize parsed strings that are later rendered as markup. The exact payload and exploit chain are not described in the diff.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user uploads an MLmodel file whose YAML content carries a script payload. A second user opens the artifact in the MLflow UI, and the payload runs in that user's browser session.
The same MLmodel file is uploaded, but the UI shows its parsed content only as plain text. Opening the artifact does not execute anything in the viewer's browser.

citations.quote: MLflow is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) caused by unsafe parsing of YAML-based MLmodel artifacts in its web interface
An authenticated attacker can upload a malicious MLmodel file containing a payload that executes when another user views the artifact in the UI.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the unrestricted YAML load call with the safe-schema loader at two front-end call sites: the logged model artifact view and the logged model signature validation hook. This stops crafted MLmodel YAML from building non-plain values such as functions during parsing, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: SSRF through unvalidated download link submission in pyload-ng
patterns.cause: The package submission endpoint passes user-supplied links straight to the download engine. The engine accepts any URL scheme and requests arbitrary destinations, including internal addresses and cloud metadata endpoints, without validating the destination.
preconditions: The attacker holds a valid pyLoad account of any role, ADMIN or USER.
The application fetches user-supplied URLs through its download engine with no destination validation.
The host can reach internal network services or a cloud metadata endpoint such as 169.254.169.254.
patterns.prevention: Validate every submitted link before the download engine starts a request. Allow only the http and https schemes. Check the destination host and reject private address ranges (RFC 1918), link-local addresses, and known cloud metadata endpoints. Enforce this check in the download path, not only in the web endpoint, so all entry points are covered.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no detail on the actual patch in version 0.5.0b3.dev97, so its exact behavior is unknown. They do not discuss redirects, DNS resolution tricks, or IPv6 and alternate address encodings. The remediation list is advisory, and a name-based blocklist alone may be incomplete. Affected versions beyond 0.5.0 are described only as potentially earlier.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user submits a package whose link points to the link-local cloud metadata address on a cloud-hosted pyLoad server. The download engine fetches it and saves the metadata, including keys, as a downloadable file.
The same submission is rejected before any request is made, because the destination is link-local. A link to a public http or https host is accepted. A link using a non-http scheme is also rejected.

citations.quote: PyLoad's download engine accepts arbitrary URLs without validation, enabling Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks.
Block requests to private IP ranges (RFC 1918, link-local addresses)
Whitelist allowed URL schemes (http/https only)

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the downloader plugin base download method. It parses the hostname from the download URL, resolves it to IP addresses, and fails the download if any address is not globally routable, which blocks private, loopback, link-local and metadata destinations. This is the same destination validation in the download path that the card recommends. The diff does not show scheme restriction or redirect handling, but the card's main cause and prevention still match.

patterns.title: SSRF through unvalidated file URLs in the vLLM batch runner
patterns.cause: The batch runner's download_bytes_from_url function fetched any http or https URL taken from the file_url field of batch transcription and translation requests, with no host check. The media allowlist used elsewhere was never applied here, and redirects were followed freely. Whoever controls the batch input can therefore make the server connect to internal or metadata endpoints. Any host check must also use the same URL parse that the HTTP client uses, because parser differences such as backslash-before-@ confusion let a crafted URL pass the check while the client connects elsewhere.
preconditions: vLLM version from 0.16.0 up to but not including 0.19.0
An actor can control the batch input JSON read by the batch runner
Batch requests use the audio transcription or translation endpoints, which take a file_url field
Internal services such as cloud metadata endpoints or internal HTTP APIs are reachable from the vLLM host, and no allowed media domains list is configured
patterns.prevention: Pass the configured allowed media domains into the batch download path and reject any http or https URL whose hostname is not on the list. Normalize the URL with the same parser before checking and reuse the normalized form for the actual request, so the checker and the HTTP client agree on the host. Do not follow redirects unless the operator has explicitly enabled that, since a redirect can leave the allowed domain. Treat an empty list as deny-all. Operators must configure the allowlist, because leaving it unset still permits all hosts for backward compatibility. Upgrade to vLLM 0.19.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: Protection only applies when an allowed media domains list is configured; with it unset the batch runner still fetches any host. The check matches hostnames only, so it does not block private IP ranges or DNS names that resolve to internal addresses, and it does not guard against DNS rebinding. If redirects are enabled through the media redirect setting, redirect targets are not re-checked against the allowlist. Data URLs are intentionally exempt from the restriction.

fixtures.scenario: A batch input line sets the file_url of a transcription request to an internal metadata address. The batch runner fetches that URL from the server and returns or reports the result, with no host check.

The batch runner checks the file_url host against a configured allowlist, including redirect targets, before fetching. A line pointing at an internal address is rejected, and an approved audio host is fetched.

citations.quote: allows any actor who can control batch input JSON to make the vLLM batch runner issue arbitrary HTTP/HTTPS requests from the server
This is a classic SSRF pattern: a server-side component makes arbitrary HTTP requests to a URL string taken from untrusted input.
does not reuse this allowlist or any equivalent validation, even though it also fetches user-provided URLs.
This vulnerability is fixed in 0.19.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix passes the configured allowed media domains into the batch download function used by the transcription and translation wrappers. For http and https URLs it checks the hostname against the list, treats an empty list as deny-all, and fetches the URL in the normalized form from the urllib3 parser to close the backslash-before-@ parser mismatch with aiohttp. It also makes redirect following depend on the media redirect environment setting. When no list is configured, behavior is unchanged, and data URLs are exempt.

patterns.title: Arbitrary code execution from loading untrusted files with aiohttp CookieJar.load()
patterns.cause: In aiohttp releases before 3.14.0, the cookie jar's save and load methods stored cookies in Python's pickle format, and load passed the file to the unrestricted pickle loader. Pickle can import and call arbitrary callables while rebuilding objects, so a crafted cookie file runs attacker-chosen code at load time (CWE-502). The fix stores cookies as JSON, which is pure data, and makes the legacy pickle fallback use an unpickler that rejects any class outside a small cookie-related allow-list.
preconditions: The application uses an aiohttp release prior to 3.14.0.
The application calls the cookie jar's load method on a file path.
An attacker can control, replace or supply the content of that file.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade aiohttp to 3.14.0 or later. After the upgrade, save writes JSON, load reads JSON first, and any old pickle file is read through a restricted unpickler that raises an error for non-cookie classes. Also load only cookie files the application itself wrote for the same user, never uploaded or downloaded ones. Re-save existing cookie files in the JSON format so the legacy pickle path is no longer needed. As a general rule, avoid pickle for persistent data and use a data-only format such as JSON, or restrict which globals the unpickler may resolve.
patterns.limitations: The allow-list approach still leaves a legacy pickle code path, which is safer but not as strong as dropping pickle entirely. Files saved by older aiohttp versions are pickle, so they only become safe to load after upgrading. The JSON loader assumes a well-formed structure and may raise errors on malformed but harmless input. Only the cookie jar's load method is affected; other aiohttp APIs are not covered by this fix.

fixtures.scenario: A service running an aiohttp version older than 3.14.0 lets users upload a cookie file and passes the uploaded file to CookieJar.load(), so an attacker can supply a crafted file.
A service running aiohttp 3.14.0 or later loads with CookieJar.load() only a cookie file that the same application previously saved for the same user, and does not accept cookie files from outside.

citations.quote: AIOHTTP is Vulnerable to Deserialization of Untrusted Data
Version 3.14.0 patches the issue.
a workaround on older releases would be to sanitize the files before loading.
Most applications using this function will be doing so with the user's own data, so this is unlikely to affect many applications.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the cookie jar's save method to write JSON and its load method to try JSON first, which is pure data. If the file is not valid JSON, load falls back to a restricted unpickler that raises an error for any class outside a small cookie-related allow-list. This matches the card's cause (unrestricted pickle loading) and its prevention. The 3.14.0 version number is not visible in the diff, but nothing in the diff contradicts it.

patterns.title: SSRF filter bypass through automatic HTTP redirects in a download manager
patterns.cause: The SSRF check validated only the hostname of the initial download URL. The HTTP client was configured to follow redirects automatically, up to 10 hops, so redirect targets were never checked against the filter. An attacker-controlled public server could therefore redirect the client to an internal address.
preconditions: The application checks that a user-supplied URL resolves to a global address, but only for the initial URL.
The HTTP client (pycurl here) follows redirects automatically, with no per-hop validation.
An authenticated user with ADD permission can submit a URL that points to a server they control.
patterns.prevention: Apply the same address validation to every redirect hop, not only the first URL. One direction is to turn off automatic redirect following and follow redirects manually, validating each target before the next request. Another is to restrict the allowed redirect protocols to HTTP and HTTPS and add a callback that checks the destination IPs before the client follows. Treat loopback, private and link-local addresses, including cloud metadata endpoints, as blocked at every hop.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, so the two directions above come from the advisory's suggestions and are not confirmed as what was shipped. They do not discuss DNS rebinding between the check and the connection, or how redirect hostnames should be resolved. The reported affected range is 0.5.0b3.dev96 and earlier.

fixtures.scenario: A user with ADD permission submits a link on a public attacker host. The host passes the address check, then answers with a redirect to a cloud metadata address. The client follows it without validation and saves the response to storage.

The same link is submitted. The public host passes the check and answers with a redirect to a metadata address. The redirect target is validated before it is followed, is rejected as non-global, and no request reaches the internal address.

citations.quote: Redirect targets are never validated against the SSRF filter.
An authenticated user with ADD permission can bypass the SSRF fix by submitting a URL that redirects to an internal address.
Disable automatic redirect following and validate each redirect target

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the one-time hostname check on the initial download URL. In its place it registers a pre-request callback on the HTTP client that checks the actual connected IP address before every request, including each redirect hop, and aborts the transfer if that address is not global. A failed check is reported as a refusal to download from an internal host.

patterns.title: Admin-only guard skipped for plugin config lets non-admin users set an executable path
patterns.cause: The admin-only check for security-critical settings is applied only to core config options, not to plugin config options. The AntiVirus plugin stores an executable path in its config and passes it directly to a process-spawning call, so a non-admin user with SETTINGS permission can change it and gain code execution.
preconditions: The attacker is an authenticated non-admin user with SETTINGS permission
Plugin config values can be written through the settings API without an admin check
