fixtures.scenario: An administrator enables the sample MySQLBrowserProvider on an anonymous read share. A GET to a path under /db/users/ whose key contains a single quote and an extra condition breaks out of the literal, and the status code reveals whether the condition matched.

The same request with a quote in the key is handled with the key kept as plain data, separate from the SQL text, so it only fails to match a record and returns 404. Deployments on 4.3.5 or later, or without the sample provider, are also not affected.

citations.quote: the record key from the request URL goes straight into the WHERE clause with no escaping
The table name is validated against the real table list, but the key is dropped directly into the query.
This issue is fixed in version 4.3.5.

patch_review.observation: The fix passes the record key to the database driver as a bound parameter instead of concatenating it into the query, which closes the injection through the URL key. It also adds a helper that escapes identifiers (database, table and field names) and removes the numeric versus string branching that built unquoted or quoted literals by hand. The card's cause and its parameter-binding prevention match this.

patterns.title: Unbounded regex compilation for structured outputs lets one request hang an inference worker
patterns.cause: The structured_outputs.regex request parameter passes a user-supplied regular expression straight to the grammar compiler backends with no compilation timeout. The xgrammar backend has no guard at all. The outlines backend only rejects structural issues such as lookarounds and backreferences and does no complexity analysis, so nested quantifier patterns pass and cause exponential state-space expansion.
preconditions: The server accepts the structured_outputs.regex parameter from untrusted clients
The xgrammar or outlines backend compiles the supplied pattern
The vLLM version is earlier than 0.24.0
No compilation deadline or pattern complexity check is applied before compilation
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to vLLM 0.24.0 or later. In an implementation, run grammar compilation for user-supplied patterns under a hard deadline of a few seconds so a slow compile fails the request instead of occupying the worker. Also add a complexity check before compilation that rejects nested quantifier patterns, because structural validation alone does not detect exponential blow-up. Treat both the xgrammar and outlines paths as needing these controls.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail, so the exact timeout value, the complexity rules and whether a timed-out compilation is actually cancelled are not established here. The advisory suggests a thread with a deadline, which may bound the request without necessarily freeing the underlying work. A complexity check aimed at nested quantifiers may not cover every pattern that causes state-space growth. Other backends or parameters are not discussed.

fixtures.scenario: A client sends a completion request whose structured_outputs.regex value is a pattern with nested quantifiers. The server hands it to the grammar compiler with no deadline and no complexity check, and the worker stays busy compiling.

The same request is checked for nested quantifier patterns before compilation and is rejected. Any pattern that is accepted is compiled under a short deadline, so a slow compile fails that one request and the worker stays available.

citations.quote: a single request containing an adversarial regex to hang an inference worker indefinitely and deny service
performs no complexity analysis, so a pattern with nested quantifiers passes all checks
provides zero protection against exponential DFA state-space explosion

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that runs regex compilation in a worker thread and fails the request with a value error if it exceeds a configurable deadline, with a default of 5 seconds and 0 to disable. It is applied to the xgrammar compile and validation paths and to the outlines index build. The diff adds no pattern complexity check, and a timed-out thread is only abandoned, not truly stopped, so the card's main cause and timeout-based prevention match, and its complexity check is extra advice beyond the fix.

patterns.title: Windows image viewer command injection through an unescaped file path in Pillow
patterns.cause: In Pillow before 12.3.0, the Windows viewer's get_command() built a cmd.exe command string by embedding a file path directly, with no escaping. The string was then run through subprocess.Popen with shell mode enabled. Shell metacharacters in the path, such as a double quote that closes the wrapping quotes followed by an ampersand, let an attacker append arbitrary cmd.exe commands. The macOS and Linux viewers quote the same path, so only the Windows path was exposed.
preconditions: Pillow earlier than 12.3.0 is running on Windows and uses the Windows viewer class
An attacker can influence the file path passed to the viewer command builder
The path is embedded in a command string that cmd.exe interprets through a shell
patterns.prevention: Do not build a shell command string from a file path. Pass the viewer program and the path as separate arguments without a shell, or apply correct cmd.exe-aware escaping to every place the path is embedded. A quoting helper written for POSIX shells does not automatically fit cmd.exe. Treat any path that contains quote or command-separator characters as untrusted. Upgrade Pillow to 12.3.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, so this card cannot say which escaping or argument-passing approach it uses. They also do not say how an attacker gets a hostile path into normal Pillow use. The proof of concept calls get_command() directly with a crafted path, so real exposure depends on how the application chooses file names. Only the Windows viewer is described as affected.

fixtures.scenario: On Windows with Pillow before 12.3.0, an app passes a user-influenced file name containing a double quote and an ampersand to the Windows viewer command builder. The command string is run with shell mode enabled, so cmd.exe runs the injected command.

On Windows with Pillow 12.3.0 or later, or a wrapper that launches the viewer without a shell, the same hostile file name stays a single path. The metacharacters are not interpreted, and no extra command runs.

citations.quote: WindowsViewer.get_command() constructed a cmd.exe shell command by directly embedding a file path into an f-string without escaping
allowing shell metacharacters in the file path to inject arbitrary cmd.exe commands.
This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

patch_review.observation: The upstream changes make the Windows viewer's command builder reject file names containing a double quote and escape percent signs so cmd.exe cannot expand them. The viewer's show_file method also stops running a shell command and opens the file with the OS file-open call, then removes the temporary file later through a shared helper. This matches the card's cause (an unescaped path inside a shell command string) and its prevention (avoid the shell or escape for cmd.exe). The card does not mention percent-sign expansion, but that is a secondary detail.

patterns.title: Missing sparse tensor validation in vLLM prompt embeddings enables DoS and memory corruption
patterns.cause: PyTorch disables sparse tensor invariant checks by default. vLLM did not validate sparse tensors in multimodal embeddings processing, so crafted embedding requests with negative or out-of-bounds indices were accepted. The earlier fix for CVE-2025-62164 only disabled prompt embeds by default and left this root cause in place.
preconditions: vLLM version at or above 0.10.2 and below 0.13.0
The prompt-embeds feature is enabled
An attacker can submit embedding requests containing sparse tensors
patterns.prevention: Validate every client-supplied sparse tensor before use. Confirm that indices are valid, non-negative and within the bounds of the declared shape, and do not rely on PyTorch to check them, since its invariant checks are off by default. Reject malformed input with an error. Treat turning the feature off by default as a mitigation only, not a fix. Run a release that includes the validation change.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no proof of concept and do not name the exact validation calls. They do not describe the performance cost of the checks. They describe the fix only as a pending change, so they do not confirm which release first contains it beyond the stated affected range. The memory corruption outcome is described only as a potential.

fixtures.scenario: An affected vLLM server has prompt embeds enabled and accepts an embedding request whose sparse tensor holds negative or out-of-range indices. No invariant check runs, so the process crashes or exhausts resources.
The server checks that sparse tensor indices are non-negative and within the declared bounds before using the tensor. It rejects a malformed embedding request with an error instead of processing it.

citations.quote: Because PyTorch disables sparse tensor invariant checks by default, an attacker can submit crafted embedding requests with malformed (negative or out-of-bounds) tensor indices
vLLM is adding the sparse tensor validation to ensure indices are valid, non-negative, and within bounds.
The fix only disables prompt embeds by default rather than addressing the root cause

patch_review.observation: The fix turns on PyTorch's sparse tensor invariant checking around loading and densifying client-supplied tensors in the prompt embeds loader and the image and audio embedding loaders. Malicious sparse tensors with out-of-bounds or negative indices are now rejected with an error instead of causing out-of-bounds writes during conversion to dense form. This matches the card's cause (checks off by default, no validation) and its prevention (validate sparse tensors and reject malformed input).

patterns.title: Default WebDataset decoder deserializes pickle and torch payloads from untrusted tar archives
patterns.cause: The default decoder of the WebDataset reader in Ray routes tar members by file extension. Members ending in pkl or pickle are passed to pickle.loads(), and members ending in pt or pth are passed to torch.load() with weights_only set to False. Both calls deserialize attacker-controlled bytes without validation. The reader enables this decoder by default, so a crafted archive runs code in the Ray process that reads it.
preconditions: Ray version earlier than 2.56.0 is in use
read_webdataset() is called with the default decoder setting
An attacker can supply or modify the tar archive, for example via a shared bucket, an HTTP URL, or a public hub
The archive contains members with pkl, pickle, pt, or pth extensions
patterns.prevention: Do not deserialize archive members with general-purpose object loaders by default. Make pickle and unrestricted torch loading an explicit opt-in that is documented as safe only for trusted sources, or remove those branches from the default decoder so callers supply their own decoder. Until upgraded, pass no decoder or a custom decoder that handles only known-safe formats and rejects pickle-style members. Only read archives from sources you trust. Upgrade Ray to 2.56.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact change shipped in 2.56.0. The two patch options come from the reporter's suggestion, not a confirmed fix. A custom decoder is only as safe as its own logic. The sources do not say whether other Ray readers have similar behavior.

fixtures.scenario: A pipeline calls the WebDataset reader with the default decoder on a tar shard from a shared bucket. One member has a pkl extension and holds a crafted payload, which runs inside the Ray worker that decodes the sample.
The pipeline passes no decoder, or a custom decoder that handles only text and image members and rejects pkl and pt members. The same shard is read, but its crafted payload is never deserialized.

citations.quote: The _default_decoder() function in webdataset_datasource.py unconditionally calls pickle.loads() on tar entries with .pkl/.pickle extensions
No flags, no opt-in, no environment variable.
and require callers to provide their own decoder when working with .pkl/.pt samples.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the default WebDataset decoder refuse pickle and pt/pth members, raising an error that tells the caller to supply a custom decoder or explicitly opt in through an environment variable meant for trusted sources. A custom decoder bypasses the guard. This matches the card's cause (unrestricted object deserialization of attacker-controlled tar members by default) and its opt-in prevention. The card's limitations note about the exact shipped change is outdated, but that does not affect the cause or prevention.

patterns.title: Unrestricted class import when deserializing exception nodes in Airflow serialized Dags
patterns.cause: The deserializer rebuilt exception nodes by importing a class name taken from the serialized blob, for both the Airflow exception node and the builtin exception node, and then called the result with arguments from the same blob. Nothing limited which module or attribute could be named, so a Dag author could make the deserializer import an arbitrary module and call an arbitrary callable, including builtin functions.
preconditions: A Dag author can place a crafted value in serialized Dag data, such as an operator executor_config, that is decoded as an exception node.
The Scheduler or API server deserializes that Dag, which happens in the normal Scheduler loop and on authenticated reads of Dag details.
The deployment runs a version where exception nodes are still resolved with a generic import. No non-default configuration is needed.
patterns.prevention: Never import a name chosen by a serialized blob. For Airflow exception nodes, split the stored name into module and attribute, look the module up only among modules already loaded, read the attribute from the module namespace directly so that lazy deprecation hooks cannot trigger an import, and accept it only if it is a class deriving from AirflowException; otherwise raise a deserialization error. For builtin exception nodes, map the name through a small fixed allow-list of the exceptions the encoder actually emits (KeyError and AttributeError) and reject everything else. Upgrade to a release that contains this change. Deployments that only fixed the earlier trigger-branch issue (CVE-2026-33264) must upgrade again, because the exception branch is a separate sink in the same deserializer.
patterns.limitations: Exception classes defined in modules that are not yet loaded in the process will no longer resolve, and user-defined subclasses of builtin exceptions will not round-trip. Constructors of legitimate AirflowException subclasses still run with arguments from the blob, so side effects in such constructors remain possible. The diff covers only the exception-node branches, so other deserializer branches are not shown to be covered.

fixtures.scenario: A Dag author sets an executor_config value whose exception node names a process-running or eval-style callable. When the Scheduler or API server reconstructs the Dag, it imports and calls that callable with attacker-chosen arguments.

The same executor_config value is rejected at deserialization because the imported object is not a subclass of BaseException. A genuine exception class name still deserializes normally, and the Scheduler and API server run no Dag-author code.

citations.quote: so a Dag author could place a value there that causes an arbitrary callable to be imported and invoked
with no restriction on what could be imported.
deployments that upgraded in response to that advisory are still affected through the exception branch and must upgrade again
Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the generic import of a class name taken from the serialized blob in the exception-node branch. Airflow exception nodes are now resolved only from modules already loaded, by reading the module namespace directly, and are accepted only if the result is an AirflowException subclass, otherwise a deserialization error is raised. Builtin exception nodes are mapped through a fixed allow-list of KeyError and AttributeError, and everything else is rejected.

patterns.title: Overlapping quantifiers in skill-mention regexes cause quadratic backtracking
patterns.cause: Open WebUI parsed skill-mention tags (a dollar-prefixed id with an optional pipe-separated label inside angle brackets) with two regular expressions whose id and label parts could match the same characters. When the input had the opener but no closing angle bracket, the engine retried every split point between the two parts, so work grew quadratically with input length. The patterns ran synchronously on the asyncio event loop for every chat completion, with no feature gate.
preconditions: Open WebUI version 0.9.2 up to, but not including, 0.10.0
Text reaches the mention-parsing code containing the mention opener followed by a long run with no closing angle bracket
The deployment runs a single worker, which is the default, so a blocked event loop stalls all users
patterns.prevention: Write mention patterns so adjacent quantified parts cannot match the same characters. Make the optional label a single optional group that starts with its own delimiter, so the id part and label part are unambiguous and matching stays linear. Check any pattern with consecutive quantifiers for overlapping character classes. Test patterns against long inputs that start a tag but never close it, and confirm that well-formed mentions still produce the same captures and output.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe only these two patterns and the 0.10.0 fix. They give no guidance on input size limits, running regex work off the event loop, or auditing other patterns in the codebase. Exploit cost varies by version: 0.9.2 to 0.9.5 needed a large input, while 0.9.6 needed only a small one.

fixtures.scenario: A chat message or retrieved RAG chunk contains the two-character mention opener followed by tens of thousands of characters and no closing angle bracket, on a single-worker instance running version 0.9.2 to 0.9.6.

The same oversized input is scanned by a mention pattern whose optional label part cannot overlap the id part, so the scan stays linear and returns quickly, and well-formed mentions still yield the same captures.

citations.quote: parsed <$skillId|label> skill mentions with overlapping quantifiers, allowing an authenticated chat message containing <$ without a closing > to trigger quadratic backtracking
Polynomial, not exponential, but more than enough to hang a single worker on a ~100 KB input.
Both patterns become linear; captures and substituted output are unchanged on well-formed

patch_review.observation: The fix rewrites both skill-mention regexes (the detection pattern and the stripping pattern in the strip function) so the optional label becomes one optional group that begins with the pipe delimiter. Before, the id part and the label part could both match non-pipe characters, so an unclosed tag forced the engine to try every split point. Now the split is unambiguous and matching stays linear, which is what the card describes.

patterns.title: Reserved-key guard skipped for JSON string literals in Airflow XCom deserialization
patterns.cause: The reserved-key validator applied when XCom values are created or updated through the API only walked dicts and lists and ignored strings. A value submitted as a JSON string literal containing reserved serialization keys was stored verbatim, and a later read with deserialization enabled re-parsed it into a dict, so the reserved keys reached the deserializer and could cause instantiation of arbitrary classes (CWE-502). The gap was in write-time validation, not in the read endpoint.
preconditions: Attacker is an authenticated API user allowed to create or patch XCom entries and to read them
The submitted XCom value is a string that decodes as JSON to an object or list carrying reserved serialization keys
The XCom entry is later read with the deserialize option enabled
Running an Airflow version earlier than the release containing the fix (3.3.1)
patterns.prevention: Upgrade apache-airflow to the fixed release (3.3.1 or later). In the validator for untrusted XCom data, decode string values that parse as JSON and check the resulting dicts and lists, including nested ones, for reserved keys, on both create and update paths. Do not rely on a check that sees only the outer shape of the payload. Also restrict XCom write access to trusted users and avoid server-side deserialization of values that untrusted principals can write.
patterns.limitations: The fix only blocks reserved keys at submission time through the create and update endpoints. It does not re-validate values already stored, or values written through other paths such as task execution, so existing malicious entries are not cleaned up. Strings that are not valid JSON, or that decode to scalars, are still accepted. The sources do not list every affected version before 3.3.1.

fixtures.scenario: A user with XCom write and read access stores a JSON string literal containing reserved serialization keys, then requests that entry with the deserialize option on. The server skips the reserved-key guard and instantiates an airflow class.

The same user stores the same string literal on a patched server. The reserved-key check runs on string literals too, so the read with deserialization is rejected and no class is instantiated on the API server.

citations.quote: An authenticated user who can write an XCom value and then read it back with
Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later, which rejects reserved XCom serialization keys submitted as JSON string literals.

patch_review.observation: The fix extends the reserved-key check used on XCom create and update requests so that string values are parsed as JSON. If a string decodes to an object or list, that structure is checked recursively for reserved serialization keys. Strings that are not valid JSON or that decode to scalars are still accepted, and the added tests cover both the create and patch paths.

patterns.title: Request-supplied OIDC file references in LiteLLM connection tests allow local file read
patterns.cause: The /health/test_connection endpoint passed request-supplied litellm_params through the secret resolver, which expanded environment references. The OIDC file provider in that resolver opened whatever path it was given, with no restriction on location. A caller could therefore make the proxy read arbitrary local files. Per-request callback parameters had the same unsafe resolution.
preconditions: LiteLLM proxy runs a version earlier than 1.83.10-stable
The caller can reach the /health/test_connection endpoint, which needs administrator or similar permission to test model connections
The request body carries litellm_params with an environment reference that resolves to an OIDC file source pointing at an arbitrary path
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to 1.83.10-stable or later. Never resolve environment or secret references that arrive in request bodies; reject or drop them and keep such values in server-side configuration. Confine the OIDC file provider to an allowlist of credential directories: require absolute paths, resolve symlinks and dot segments first, then check containment. Operators who store tokens elsewhere should extend the allowlist deliberately. Limit access to the connection-test endpoint to trusted administrators as defense in depth.
patterns.limitations: The patch does not remove OIDC file reads for server-side configuration; it only limits them to allowed directories, and the default allowlist or an operator-widened one still permits files in those locations. Other secret sources and providers are not changed by this fix. The issue needs privileged access, so its practical impact is limited.

fixtures.scenario: An administrator-level caller sends a connection-test request to a proxy older than 1.83.10-stable. The model parameters include an oidc/file/ reference pointing at a local file, and the proxy resolves the reference and reads that file from its own filesystem.

The proxy runs 1.83.10-stable or later, and access to the connection-test endpoint is restricted to trusted administrators. A request carrying an oidc/file/ reference in its parameters does not cause the proxy to read an arbitrary local file.

citations.quote: Because exploitation requires privileged proxy access, this is treated as a defense-in-depth issue rather than a cross-tenant privilege bypass.
Prior to 1.83.10-stable, LiteLLM's /health/test_connection endpoint resolved request-supplied environment and OIDC file references in litellm_params
read files from the local filesystem via an oidc/file/ reference

patch_review.observation: The fix stops request-supplied environment references from being resolved. The connection-test endpoint now rejects them with a 400 error, and per-request callback parameters drop them with a warning. It also confines the OIDC file provider to an allowlist of credential directories: paths must be absolute, symlinks and dot segments are resolved first, and a containment check follows. The default directories are the standard container secret mounts, and operators can extend the list through an environment setting.

patterns.title: Path traversal in LiteLLM Skills ZIP archive extraction
patterns.cause: Skills archive extraction did not sufficiently validate file paths from uploaded skill ZIP archives. Entries with path traversal sequences could therefore be written outside the intended extraction or staging directory.
preconditions: LiteLLM is running a version earlier than 1.83.7-stable.
The caller is authenticated and can reach the Skills upload route, for example through LLM API routes or a key whose allowed_routes includes /v1/skills, anthropic_routes, or llm_api_routes.
The caller uploads a crafted skill ZIP archive containing path traversal entries.
The skill is processed for execution, which triggers extraction of the entries.
patterns.prevention: Validate every entry path from an uploaded archive so that each extracted file stays inside the intended extraction or staging directory, and reject any entry that would land outside it. Upgrade to 1.83.7-stable or later. If upgrading is not possible, block POST /v1/skills at the reverse proxy or API gateway and restrict Skills API access to trusted users only.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation the fix applies, nor which entry forms (such as dot-dot sequences, absolute paths or symlinks) were exploited. Impact beyond arbitrary file write, including code execution, depends on deployment configuration and writable paths. The workarounds reduce exposure but do not fix the extraction logic.

fixtures.scenario: A key allowed to call /v1/skills uploads a skill ZIP whose entries use traversal sequences. When the skill is processed on a LiteLLM version before 1.83.7-stable, a file is written outside the staging directory.
The same upload is handled on 1.83.7-stable or later, or POST /v1/skills is blocked at the gateway, so no entry is written outside the intended extraction directory.

citations.quote: did not sufficiently validate file paths from uploaded skill ZIP archives
those entries could be written outside the intended extraction/staging directory.
This issue is fixed in version 1.83.7-stable.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds path checks in two places. When skill files are read from the ZIP, extract_all_files normalizes each entry path and skips any that start with a parent-directory component or are absolute. When the sandbox executor stages files into a temporary directory, it resolves each target path and skips any that fall outside that directory. This matches the card's cause (unvalidated archive entry paths written outside the staging directory) and its prevention (confine every entry to the intended directory and reject the rest).

patterns.title: SSRF in LiteLLM Proxy via api_base nested in user_config
patterns.cause: The request body guard is_request_body_safe rejected top-level api_base and base_url but did not inspect or reject user_config. Because user_config is used to build the outbound router, a caller could nest a destination there and bypass the check.
preconditions: LiteLLM Proxy version 1.83.8 or earlier is running
The caller holds a valid virtual key
The caller can send a user_config object in the request body
The proxy can reach internal or external hosts the caller cannot reach directly
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to LiteLLM 1.83.9 or later. In general, apply destination-parameter checks to every request field that can feed outbound routing, including nested objects such as user_config, not only the top-level keys. Do not let caller-supplied configuration choose the host the server contacts.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch works internally. They do not say whether other nested fields can carry a destination, nor whether host allowlisting or network egress controls are in place. Exploitation requires a valid virtual key, so unauthenticated callers are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated caller sends a request whose user_config object contains an api_base pointing at an internal host. The guard checks only top-level keys, so the proxy contacts that host for the caller.
The same request is rejected because the nested api_base inside user_config is inspected like a top-level one, or the proxy runs version 1.83.9 or later.

citations.quote: user_config constructs the outbound router, the nested destination redirects a server-side request to an internal or external host selected by the caller
which blocks top-level api_base and base_url but previously did not inspect or reject user_config
Exploitation requires a valid virtual key.

patch_review.observation: The relevant change extends the banned parameter list in the request body safety check (is_request_body_safe) so that user_config is rejected from caller-supplied bodies, alongside api_base and base_url. This closes the bypass where a destination was nested inside user_config. The rest of the diff (an internal-call context variable, stripping internal keys and spoofable auth metadata, formatting) is related hardening and does not change the SSRF fix.

patterns.title: Quadratic-time scanning in mistune strikethrough, mark and insert plugins
patterns.cause: In the mistune formatting plugin, the strikethrough, mark and insert parsers look for the closing marker with a forward regex search from each opening marker. The close pattern rejected any marker pair followed by another marker character, so in a long run of adjacent closed pairs almost every candidate close was refused and the search ran to the end of the input. Because this repeated from every opening marker, the total work grew quadratically with input length.
preconditions: The application renders user-supplied Markdown with mistune earlier than 3.3.0.
The strikethrough, mark, or insert plugin is enabled; the default configuration does not enable them.
An attacker can submit a payload of several kilobytes made of repeated closed marker pairs placed back to back.
No input size limit or per-request CPU time limit applies to the rendering step.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to 3.3.0 or later. The upstream fix finds the closing marker with plain string search and accepts a close that is followed by another full marker pair, so the scan ends at the first valid close instead of running to the end of the input. Where upgrading is not possible, disable these plugins for untrusted input, and cap the size of untrusted Markdown and the rendering time. When writing similar inline parsers, avoid close conditions that reject nearby candidates in a way that forces a full-length rescan from every opening marker.
patterns.limitations: The fix mainly shortens the scan for the repeated-pair payload. It does not remember failed start positions, so other marker layouts that never produce a valid close may still cost a forward scan per opener. A delimiter stack or a cap on tracked markers would be a stronger structural defense, but the diff does not add either. Timings depend on the machine and Python version, and the sources give no safe input size limits.

fixtures.scenario: A comment service renders untrusted Markdown with mistune before 3.3.0 and the strikethrough plugin on. An anonymous user posts about 40 KB of closed tilde pairs around one letter, and one request keeps a worker busy for seconds.
The same service runs mistune 3.3.0 or later, or caps input size and render time. The same repeated-marker payload is rejected or parsed in time roughly proportional to its length.

citations.quote: a run of closed tilde, equals-sign, or caret marker pairs around a character causes quadratic work in src/mistune/plugins/formatting.py
This issue is fixed in version 3.3.0.
The minimal fix is to cap the number of simultaneously-tracked unmatched markers, treating extras as literal text.
The bounded regex on each individual scan does not bound the parser-level repetition.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the close-marker regexes, which rejected a close followed by another marker character and so scanned to the end of the input from each opener. It adds a helper that uses plain string search and accepts a close followed by a full marker pair. It also keeps the checks for the preceding character and for escaping, so repeated closed pairs now end at the first valid close. A regression test covers the repeated-pair payload for all three plugins.

patterns.title: Percent-encoded javascript scheme bypasses Mistune safe_url() link filtering
patterns.cause: HTMLRenderer.safe_url() checks the lowercased URL prefix against harmful protocols without first URL-decoding the input. A scheme written with a percent-encoded colon is therefore not recognized as javascript. The browser later decodes the URL, so script runs when the user interacts with the link.
preconditions: The application renders attacker-controlled Markdown to HTML with a Mistune version before 3.3.0.
The application relies on the built-in safe_url() protection and adds no separate URL sanitization.
A victim opens the rendered HTML in a browser and interacts with the link.
patterns.prevention: Evaluate the URL scheme on the decoded form of the URL, so percent-encoded characters in the scheme cannot hide a harmful protocol from the check. Upgrade to Mistune 3.3.0 or later, which is reported as fixed. Until then, add application-level URL sanitization that decodes before checking.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how version 3.3.0 changes the check. They do not say whether other encodings, such as double encoding or entity encoding, are handled. They also do not state whether image URLs and link URLs are covered identically beyond a brief mention of both.

fixtures.scenario: A comment system renders user Markdown with Mistune 3.2.0. An attacker posts a link whose target starts with the word javascript followed by a percent-encoded colon. The filter misses it, and a viewer who clicks it runs script.
The same system runs Mistune 3.3.0 or later. The same link target is neutralized, or the check decodes the URL before testing the scheme, so clicking the link does not run script.

citations.quote: However, the input URL is not URL-decoded before this check.
When rendered in a browser, the URL is decoded, resulting in execution of arbitrary JavaScript upon user interaction.
Prior to 3.3.0, HTMLRenderer.safe_url() does not block percent-encoded javascript URIs, allowing attacker-supplied Markdown links or images to bypass URL protections

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the safe URL check percent-decode the URL, repeating up to three times to catch double encoding, before lowercasing and comparing it against the harmful protocol list. It also adds several more blocked schemes, and tests cover encoded javascript and data schemes for links, reference definitions and images. This matches the card's cause (no decoding before the scheme check) and its prevention (check the decoded form).

patterns.title: Path traversal in mistune Include directive when reading markdown files
patterns.cause: In versions before 3.3.0, Include.parse() joins a user-supplied include path to the directory of the source markdown file and normalizes it. It never checks that the result stays inside an intended directory. Traversal sequences such as parent-directory segments can therefore point at files outside that location.
preconditions: The application uses mistune before version 3.3.0.
The Include directive is enabled, for example through the RST directive plugin.
Markdown files are processed with md.read(), so include paths are resolved relative to the source file.
The markdown content, and therefore the include path, can be influenced by an untrusted party.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to mistune 3.3.0 or later. In any code that resolves include paths, convert the final path to its resolved form, for example with os.path.realpath(). Compare it against a trusted base directory and refuse to open it if it falls outside. Do this check before opening the file. If untrusted markdown is processed, consider leaving the Include directive disabled.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream fix or how it treats symbolic links. They do not say which base directory the fix enforces, or whether other directives or code paths are affected. Impact depends on how the feature is used and which files the process can read.

fixtures.scenario: A markdown file contains an include directive whose path climbs several parent directories to reach a file outside the content folder. It is processed with md.read() on mistune before 3.3.0, and the outside file is read.

The same markdown file is processed on a version with the fix, or with path validation. The resolved include path falls outside the allowed directory, so the request is rejected and the file is not opened.

citations.quote: Include.parse() joins and normalizes user-supplied include paths without verifying that the result remains within the intended markdown directory
Validate the resolved path and ensure it remains within an allowed directory before opening the file.
This issue is fixed in version 3.3.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix resolves both the source file and the include target to their real paths, rejects absolute include paths, and refuses any target that is not under the source file's directory, returning an error block instead. It also adds circular-include detection and escapes included text on output, which are secondary hardening. The card's cause (no containment check after joining and normalizing) and its prevention (resolve the path, compare to a trusted base directory, refuse before opening) match the main fix.

patterns.title: Quadratic emphasis parsing in mistune inline parser on long runs of strong-emphasis pairs
patterns.cause: The inline parser treats every opening run of one to three asterisks as a possible start and scans forward for a matching close marker from each one. Each scan is bounded per call, but the scan is repeated from every potential start position. A long input of many well-formed double-asterisk or triple-asterisk pairs therefore costs quadratic work, even in the default configuration with no plugins.
preconditions: The application uses a mistune version prior to 3.3.0 to render markdown.
The markdown comes from an untrusted party, such as a network user who needs no authentication.
The input contains a long sequence of well-formed double-asterisk or triple-asterisk emphasis pairs around a character.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to 3.3.0 or later, which the advisories list as the fixed version. When writing or reviewing an inline parser, do not rescan forward to the end of the input from every opening marker. Process delimiters in a single pass with a delimiter stack, as CommonMark reference implementations do, so each marker is handled a bounded number of times. The advisory also suggests, as a weaker alternative, capping how many unmatched opening markers are tracked at once and treating the rest as literal text. Add a regression test that renders a very large run of emphasis pairs and checks that it finishes quickly.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe what the 3.3.0 change actually does, so this card does not claim a specific upstream approach. The cap on open markers is only a suggestion in the advisory, and its effect on rendering of real documents is not verified here. The reported timings come from one PoC on one machine and version, and the sources give no safe input size limit. Related bracket and formatting-plugin denial-of-service reports are mentioned but not detailed.

fixtures.scenario: A comment service renders user markdown with default mistune before 3.3.0. An attacker posts about 40 KB made of thousands of short strong-emphasis pairs, and one request keeps a worker busy for several seconds.
The service runs mistune 3.3.0 or later. The same large input of repeated emphasis pairs renders in time roughly proportional to its size, and a regression test guards this.

citations.quote: long sequences of well-formed double-asterisk or triple-asterisk emphasis pairs around a character cause quadratic work
Each scan is bounded per call, but the parser invokes the scan from every potential start position.
The CommonMark reference parser handles emphasis in linear time using a delimiter-stack algorithm

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the per-opener forward regex search for a closing marker. The emphasis rule now only emits the marker as plain text, and a finalize step at the end of inline parsing resolves emphasis in one pass over a delimiter list, using a lower-bound table for openers as in the CommonMark reference algorithm. The same commit also reworks link bracket matching, link href and title parsing, and block-level parsing, but the emphasis change matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Attribute injection XSS via unescaped class option in mistune Admonition directive
patterns.cause: The render_admonition() function in the Admonition directive concatenates the user-supplied class option directly into the HTML class attribute without escaping. The option comes from raw user input, so it can break out of the attribute and inject new attributes or script.
preconditions: The application uses a mistune version prior to 3.2.1
The Admonition directive is enabled in the Markdown renderer
Untrusted users can author Markdown containing the class option on an admonition
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to version 3.2.1 or later. In an implementation, treat the class option as untrusted input and escape it for the HTML attribute context before placing it in the class attribute, or validate it against a strict allowlist of class names. Do not assume that enabling escape mode on the HTML renderer covers directive options, because it does not.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact fix, the full set of directives or options that may be affected, or which characters are accepted in the class option. They state only that the directive name is validated against a whitelist. Whether other directives handle options safely is not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A site renders user Markdown with an old mistune and the Admonition directive. An author supplies a class option containing a quote that closes the attribute and adds an event handler, and it appears in the output HTML despite escape mode.

The site runs mistune 3.2.1 or later, so the class option is escaped before it enters the class attribute. A quote in the option cannot close the attribute, and no injected attribute or script reaches the page.

citations.quote: concatenates the `:class:` option directly into the HTML class attribute without escaping
This allows attribute injection and XSS even when `HTMLRenderer(escape=True)` is used.
This issue is fixed in version 3.2.1.

patch_review.observation: The fix escapes the user-supplied class option in the admonition renderer before it is added to the HTML class attribute, which matches the card's cause and prevention. The same commit also escapes the figure directive's class and width options and the error block text, so the weakness reaches beyond the admonition directive. The card's limitations note already leaves other directives open.

patterns.title: Quadratic parse time from many reference-link definitions in mistune
patterns.cause: For each reference-link definition, the block parser searched the rest of the document for the next blank line to bound the optional title. In a document made of many consecutive definitions with no blank lines, every search scanned to the end of the input, so total work grew with the square of the number of definitions. The cost came from this repeated forward regex scan, not from the definition dictionary or from revisiting stored definitions.
preconditions: The application uses a mistune version before 3.3.0.
The application renders attacker-supplied Markdown with the default configuration, with no special plugins needed.
The attacker can submit a document with thousands of reference-link definitions placed back to back without blank lines between them.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to 3.3.0 or later. The fix scans the source once for blank-line positions, caches that sorted list for the current source text, and answers each next-blank-line query with a binary search. In general, avoid running an unbounded forward regex search from every candidate position. Precompute the boundaries once, or bound each search to the current block.
patterns.limitations: The cache is keyed on the identity of the source string, so the benefit depends on the parser environment persisting across definitions within one parse. Other potentially superlinear paths in the parser are not addressed by this change. Input size limits and timeouts remain useful additional defenses for untrusted Markdown.

fixtures.scenario: An application renders attacker-supplied Markdown with default mistune create_markdown() on a version before 3.3.0. A document of thousands of short repeated reference definitions followed by one reference link pegs the CPU for seconds.

The same application runs mistune 3.3.0 or later. The same document of repeated definitions is parsed in time that grows linearly with the number of definitions, so doubling the input roughly doubles the time.

citations.quote: Prior to 3.3.0, a Markdown document containing many repeated or distinct reference-link definitions causes quadratic work
Doubling input quadruples time.
The patched build (with the surrounding parser amortised to O(N)) keeps the time linear.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the per-definition forward regex search for the next blank line in parse_ref_link with a helper, _find_next_blank_line. The helper scans the source once for all blank-line positions, caches the list in the parser environment keyed on the identity of the source string, and answers each query with a binary search. This removes the quadratic rescanning the card describes, and the added test uses thousands of back-to-back definitions.

patterns.title: Mistune safe_url denylist lets legacy and chained URL schemes reach href and src
patterns.cause: The URL safety check in the mistune HTML renderer compared the lowercased raw target against a short prefix denylist of four schemes. There were two gaps. Legacy or wrapper schemes such as feed, jar, livescript, mocha, ms-its, mk, res and view-source were not listed. The check also never percent-decoded the target, so a harmful scheme written with an encoded colon, or encoded twice, did not match any denylist prefix and reached href and src unchanged. Decoding by a later component could then turn it into a live harmful URL.
preconditions: The application renders attacker-influenced Markdown with a mistune version earlier than 3.3.0.

The link or image target uses an unlisted legacy or chained scheme, or a listed scheme with a percent-encoded colon or other encoded characters, through a direct link, reference link, autolink or image.
A user agent or downstream component honours the scheme, or decodes the percent-encoded target before use.
The caller has not disabled filtering or allowed harmful protocols, and no other control rewrites or rejects the URL.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to mistune 3.3.0 or later. That release blocks the additional legacy and wrapper schemes and repeatedly percent-decodes the target, with a small bounded number of passes, before checking it, so encoded forms are replaced with the inert placeholder. Harmless image data types stay allowed. For custom URL handling, decode the target to a stable form and normalise case and whitespace before any scheme comparison. Apply the same check to direct links, reference links, autolinks and image sources. Prefer an allowlist of needed schemes over a denylist where possible, and require explicit opt-in for any extra protocol.
patterns.limitations: The upstream fix is still denylist-based, so a scheme that is not listed can still pass. Decoding is limited to a few passes, so deeper nesting is not normalised. Exploitability depends on the user agent, since modern mainstream browsers ignore most of these schemes and treat encoded forms as relative paths. Callers who opt in to harmful protocols re-open the risk. This card covers URL scheme filtering only and does not address other XSS vectors.

fixtures.scenario: An application renders user-submitted Markdown with mistune before 3.3.0 using default settings. A link whose target begins with feed: followed by javascript: is emitted unchanged into an anchor href, so a legacy browser may run script on click.

The application uses mistune 3.3.0 or later, or a URL check that accepts only listed schemes. The same feed: chained link is not emitted as a live link, while ordinary http, https and mailto links still render normally.

citations.quote: the safe_url filter in src/mistune/renderers/html.py blocks only javascript:, vbscript:, file:, and data: schemes
Switch from denylist to allowlist. The set of schemes a markdown renderer needs to allow is small and well-known
This issue is fixed in version 3.3.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds eight legacy and wrapper schemes (feed, jar, livescript, mocha, ms-its, mk, res, view-source) to the harmful-protocol denylist. It also makes the URL safety check percent-decode the target, up to three passes, and lowercase it before the prefix comparison. The new tests show that encoded-colon and double-encoded forms are replaced with the harmful-link placeholder, while an encoded harmless image data URL is still allowed.

patterns.title: Symlink in corpus root bypasses path validation in IPIPANCorpusReader
patterns.cause: Several public reader methods pass fileids to an internal routine that opens the file with the builtin open() on a plain string. A string replace on the path pointer discards the PathPointer wrapper, so nltk.pathsec validation is skipped. A symlink with a plain name, with no separators or parent references, is then opened directly.
preconditions: nltk version before 3.10.2 with IPIPANCorpusReader in use
An attacker can place a symlink inside the corpus root directory, for example in a shared or tampered corpus
The application calls channels(), domains(), categories() or fileids(channels=...) with the symlink filename
The target file is readable by the process
patterns.prevention: Do not hand a plain string derived from a path pointer to the builtin open(). Route file access through nltk.pathsec.validate_path() with the corpus root as the required root, or through CorpusReader.open(), so the symlink target is checked before reading. Avoid string operations on path pointers before validation, since they drop the wrapper. Use nltk 3.10.2 or later, as earlier versions are listed as affected.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how validate_path() evaluates symlinks internally, nor the exact upstream change. Literal parent-directory traversal in a fileid is reported as already blocked, so this is only the symlink case. Impact is read-only, and local symlink placement is required. Other readers are not assessed here beyond the two mentioned as fixed earlier.

fixtures.scenario: A shared corpus directory holds a file named evil_link.xml that is a symlink to a file outside the root. An application on an nltk version before 3.10.2 calls channels() on the IPIPAN reader with that fileid, and the outside file content is returned.

The same directory and symlink exist, but file access goes through validated path handling with the corpus root as the required root, so the symlink pointing outside the root is rejected instead of being read.

citations.quote: Attackers can place a symlink in the corpus root directory and read arbitrary files accessible to the process
Symlink-based arbitrary file read in IPIPANCorpusReader, bypasses nltk.pathsec entirely

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a containment check in the internal tag-reading routine of the IPIPAN reader. It calls the pathsec validation function with the corpus root as the required root before the file is opened. This closes the gap where a string replace turned the path pointer into a plain string, which let a symlink with a harmless name escape the root. The new tests cover channels, domains, categories and fileids by channel, and they confirm that legitimate in-root files still work.

patterns.title: Symlink inside FrameNet corpus subdirectory escapes the corpus root in NLTK
patterns.cause: FramenetCorpusReader checks caller- or corpus-supplied names only for literal separators, parent-directory markers and drive prefixes. It then builds the path with a plain lexical join and opens it without a root-scoped, symlink-resolving check. A symlink with a separator-free name passes the name check and is followed to a file outside the corpus root.
preconditions: An attacker can place a symlink inside the frame, lu or fulltext subdirectory of a FrameNet corpus directory, for example a shared or tampered corpus.
The application calls frame_by_name(), _lu_file() or doc() with a name that matches the symlink.
The NLTK version is earlier than 3.10.2.
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on name filtering alone. Resolve the final path, including symlinks, and confirm it stays inside the corpus root before opening it. Open corpus files through the reader's scoped open routine, which does this check, rather than a lexical join followed by a raw pointer open. Upgrade NLTK to 3.10.2 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the fix direction only in general terms. They do not say how the patched release handles symlinks that point to files inside the corpus root, or how it behaves when strict sandbox enforcement is off. The read target is described as XML files, and the sources do not say whether other file types are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A shared FrameNet corpus directory has a symlink in its frame subdirectory pointing to an XML file outside the corpus root. The symlink name has no separators. A routine frame lookup by that name returns the outside file's content.

The same corpus and lookup, but the reader resolves symlinks and checks the result against the corpus root before opening. The lookup is refused because the target lies outside the root, and no outside content is returned.

citations.quote: NLTK versions before 3.10.2 contain a symlink-based sandbox bypass in FramenetCorpusReader that allows attackers to read arbitrary XML files outside the corpus root.
It never resolves symlinks.
A symlink placed inside the corpus's own subdirectory, with a name containing no separators at all, passes the guard cleanly

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that calls the shared symlink-resolving path validator with the corpus root as the required root. It runs in doc, frame_by_name and _lu_file right after the path is built and before the XML is opened. This closes the gap where the existing name check never resolved symlinks, and the new tests cover a separator-free symlink in each subdirectory pointing outside the root.

patterns.title: Corpus-root escape in NLTK FrameNet and NKJP readers via unsafe selectors or index state
patterns.cause: The FrameNet and NKJP corpus readers build XML filenames from caller-controlled selectors (frame names, document filenames, LU ids, NKJP file identifiers) or from index state without keeping the resulting path inside the corpus root. The reader then parses XML located outside the root and returns its content through normal public calls.
preconditions: The application uses an NLTK release before 3.10.0 (version 3.9.4 was reproduced).
The application exposes FramenetCorpusReader frame_by_name, doc or lu, or NKJPCorpusReader header, and relies on NLTK to keep parsing inside the corpus root.
An attacker can influence the selector values or the index state those readers use to build filenames.
An attacker-chosen XML file exists outside the corpus root and is readable by the application.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.0 or later. An implementation avoids the problem by keeping these reader paths on the same root-confinement model as the generic corpus file-opening path, and by rejecting unsafe path components before it builds any filename from a frame name, document filename, LU id or NKJP file identifier. Values read from index files should be treated as untrusted in the same way as caller-supplied selectors, and a rejected value should produce an explicit path-safety error instead of a parse.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not list which path components or patterns the patched release rejects, so this card cannot say how complete that rejection is. Only 3.9.4 was reproduced; the CVE text says versions before 3.10.0 are affected without naming the earliest one. The sources describe only parsing of XML files outside the root and do not discuss other file types. They give no interim mitigation for applications that cannot upgrade.

fixtures.scenario: An application on NLTK 3.9.4 passes a user-supplied frame name containing parent-directory segments to the FrameNet frame_by_name method. An XML file placed outside the corpus root is parsed and its definition text is returned to the caller.
The same application runs NLTK 3.10.0 or later. The same frame name, or a poisoned LU id or NKJP file identifier, is rejected with an explicit path-safety error and no outside-root file is parsed.

citations.quote: allows attackers to parse XML files outside the corpus root by supplying unsafe selectors or poisoned index state.
Stable reader paths still construct raw XML filenames from unsafe selectors, poisoned index state, or unsafe file identifiers.
Reject unsafe path components before constructing filenames from frame names, document filenames, LU ids, or NKJP file identifiers.

patch_review.observation: The FrameNet fix rejects frame names, document filenames taken from the index, and LU ids that contain separators, parent references, or drive prefixes. It then resolves the file through the reader's root-confined path method instead of a bare string path. The NKJP fix makes the root-adding helper validate the resulting path against the corpus root, resolving symlinks, and raise an error when it escapes. This matches the card's cause and its prevention of root confinement plus explicit rejection.

patterns.title: SSRF URL validation fails open when DNS resolution fails
patterns.cause: The SSRF pre-check in nltk/pathsec.py resolves the hostname through a cached helper that swallows resolution errors and returns an empty list, so the validator passes silently. The actual connection is then made by the standard HTTP stack, which resolves the hostname again on its own, so the address that was checked is not the address that is used. A hostname that fails or looks public during the check can resolve to an internal address at connect time (DNS rebinding). The address policy was also an incomplete denylist and missed ranges such as carrier-grade NAT and unspecified addresses, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 forms could slip past.
preconditions: NLTK 3.9.4 or earlier (before 3.10.0) is in use
Network fetches go through the secure urlopen wrapper with no proxy in effect, so NLTK itself resolves and connects
An attacker can influence the requested URL or control DNS answers for a hostname in it
The target host resolves to an internal, loopback, link-local or otherwise non-global address at connect time, or only fails to resolve during the pre-check
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on a separate pre-check resolution. Resolve the host once at connect time, validate every returned address, and connect only to those validated numeric addresses so no second name lookup can be redirected. Fail closed with an error when no validated address is available, and never fall back to connecting by raw hostname. Allow only globally routable addresses rather than a denylist of known bad ranges, and evaluate IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses as their embedded IPv4 address. Keep certificate and SNI checks tied to the original hostname. Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: Connect-time pinning is applied only when no proxy is in effect. When an explicit or environment proxy is configured, the proxy performs resolution and tunneling, so only the early pre-check protects that path, and it still passes when resolution returns nothing. Redirect handling and non-HTTP schemes are outside this change.

fixtures.scenario: The DNS lookup for the host of a user-supplied URL raises an error, the helper returns an empty list, and the validator returns normally. The request to a cloud metadata address such as 169.254.169.254 then goes ahead unchecked.
When the lookup yields no addresses, the validator raises an error and the URL is rejected before any request is made. Only URLs whose resolved addresses were all checked are fetched.

citations.quote: when DNS resolution fails, the validation loop executes no IP checks and the function fails open
The correct behavior is fail-closed: if DNS resolution fails, the URL should be REJECTED (not allowed).
Never allow a URL request to proceed when IP validation was impossible.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops relying on the early pre-check lookup. It adds connection classes that resolve the host once at connect time, validate every returned address, connect only to those numeric addresses, and fail closed with a resolution error when nothing validated is available. It also replaces the denylist with an allow-only-global-addresses policy that treats IPv4-mapped IPv6 as the embedded IPv4, and it skips pinning when a proxy is in effect.

patterns.title: NLTK StreamBackedCorpusView skips pathsec.ENFORCE path validation
patterns.cause: StreamBackedCorpusView opens and stats string file paths directly with the builtin open and os.stat calls. It never goes through the pathsec validation wrapper. Setting pathsec.ENFORCE to true therefore does not restrict reads made through this class. XMLCorpusView and corpus reader subclasses that pass a raw string fileid to it are also affected.
preconditions: NLTK version earlier than 3.10.0 is in use
An attacker can influence the fileid string passed to StreamBackedCorpusView or a corpus reader built on it
The operator relies on pathsec.ENFORCE as the control that limits file access to allowed NLTK data directories
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NLTK to 3.10.0 or later. In custom code, do not pass untrusted strings as fileid to corpus views or readers. Map user input to a fixed allowlist of known corpus file identifiers instead. Any code path that opens or stats a user-influenced path should go through the same pathsec validation as other NLTK file access, and should not call the builtin open directly. Do not treat pathsec.ENFORCE as a guarantee for corpus readers on affected versions.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change or list every reader class affected beyond XMLCorpusView and subclasses that pass a raw string fileid. They do not say whether non-string fileids are safe. Check the vendor release notes for 3.10.0 before relying on this card for full coverage.

fixtures.scenario: A web service sets pathsec.ENFORCE to true, then builds a StreamBackedCorpusView from a file name taken from a JSON request body. A client submits a system password file path and the service returns its first line, despite enforcement being enabled.

A service runs NLTK 3.10.0 or later. It accepts only a short corpus name from a fixed allowlist and resolves it to a known file inside the NLTK data directory. A request naming a system password file is rejected before any file is opened.

citations.quote: NLTK before 3.10.0 contains an arbitrary local file read vulnerability in StreamBackedCorpusView that bypasses pathsec.ENFORCE
Attackers who control the fileid argument can read arbitrary local files regardless of the ENFORCE setting

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the stream-backed corpus view open string file paths through the pathsec secure open wrapper instead of the builtin open, so path validation now applies to these reads. A regression test confirms that a string fileid outside the allowed roots is rejected. The same change also stops the corpus fileid search from descending into symlinked directories that resolve outside the corpus root, which the card does not mention. The diff does not touch any stat call, so the card's claim about stat is not confirmed by it.

patterns.title: Webhook delivery SSRF via unvalidated redirects and unpinned DNS resolution
patterns.cause: The webhook URL guard resolved the hostname and rejected non-public addresses, but only for the original URL. Delivery then followed HTTP redirects and re-resolved the hostname without pinning the validated address, so redirect targets and rebinding answers were never checked. The test endpoint returned the upstream status and body to the caller.
preconditions: The server exposes the webhook API without authentication; the sources say webhook authorization lives only in an optional auth plugin that is not loaded by default
The URL check runs only on the original webhook URL, before the request is sent
Delivery follows redirects and resolves the hostname again at connect time without reusing the validated address
The attacker can host a public HTTPS endpoint that passes the check and redirects to an internal target
patterns.prevention: Validate the address a connection actually reaches, not just the result of an earlier name lookup. Check the peer IP of every established connection against public-address rules right after connect and before any TLS or HTTP exchange. Route redirect hops through the same protected connections so each new target is checked. Otherwise stop following redirects, or re-validate every hop. Normalize IPv6 forms that embed an IPv4 address (IPv4-mapped, 6to4, NAT64) before classifying an address as public. Do not return upstream response bodies to unauthenticated callers.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the full fix internals. The CVE record says affected versions start at 3.3.0 and are fixed in 3.15.0, while the advisory says the guard shipped in 3.10.0; this mismatch is unresolved. The advisory also reports later IPv6-transition bypasses of the first fix, fixed in 3.16.0, so 3.15.0 alone may not cover IPv6 or NAT64 networks. Redirects with status 307 or 308 allow blind POST writes to internal endpoints as well as reads.

fixtures.scenario: A default no-auth tracking server accepts a webhook whose URL is an attacker public HTTPS host. At delivery that host redirects to a link-local metadata address, the server follows it, and the test endpoint returns the body.

Delivery checks the peer IP of every established connection, including each redirect hop, against public-address rules before sending any request, so a redirect to a metadata or loopback address is refused.

citations.quote: follows redirects and re-resolves the hostname without pinning the validated address
the peer IP of each connected socket is validated against public-IP rules immediately after
each redirect opens a new connection through the protected pool
The original is_global classifier did not decode IPv6 addresses embedding an IPv4 address

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a webhook-only HTTP adapter whose connections check the peer IP of the connected socket right after connect, before TLS or any HTTP data, and fail closed on non-public addresses. Because the whole session uses this adapter, redirect hops and re-resolved hostnames are checked too. It also turns off environment proxy handling so a proxy cannot become the validated peer, and an env setting can allow private addresses.

patterns.title: Scheduler deserializes human-in-the-loop next_kwargs without an allow-list
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow 3.3.0 the scheduler sweep for awaiting_input human-in-the-loop tasks calls the shared event-submit function, which decodes the task instance's stored next_kwargs. That value is controllable by a Dag author through the task execution API. The decode and re-encode steps had no error handling and no check that the result is a dict, so an unusable or hostile payload raised out of the function and aborted the whole sweep and the scheduler job, and it could stall other waiting tasks.
preconditions: Apache Airflow 3.3.0 is deployed (the fix is in 3.3.1)
Human-in-the-loop tasks use the awaiting_input state, whose timeouts the scheduler sweeps
The attacker is a Dag author who can set next_kwargs through the task execution API
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later. The fix decodes next_kwargs in one helper that verifies the result is a dict, and wraps both decoding and re-encoding with the event payload in error handling. On failure the task is logged, requeued with the special fail method so a worker fails it normally, and the loop moves on. In general, code in a privileged loop process such as the scheduler must treat stored author-controlled payloads as untrusted, catch decode errors per item, and fail the one item instead of the whole batch.
patterns.limitations: The change makes the sweep resilient but does not itself add or change an allow-list of deserializable classes. A human-in-the-loop response whose parameters cannot be encoded is now recorded and discarded instead of rejected, and the submitter cannot retry it; write-side validation is left as follow-up work. The sources do not describe any workaround short of upgrading.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 3.3.0 deployment runs a human-in-the-loop task in the awaiting_input state. A Dag author sets next_kwargs through the task execution API, and the scheduler sweep deserializes it with no allow-list.

An Airflow 3.3.1 or later deployment runs the same human-in-the-loop task. The scheduler sweep no longer deserializes author-supplied next_kwargs without an allow-list, so arbitrary imports are not triggered.

citations.quote: can cause an arbitrary module import and object instantiation inside the scheduler process, or terminate the scheduler job.
No non-default configuration is required: the sweep runs unconditionally every 15 seconds
Versions before 3.3.0 are not affected, because human-in-the-loop tasks deferred onto the triggerer instead.
Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later.

patch_review.observation: The fix moves decoding of the stored next_kwargs into a helper that checks the result is a dict. It wraps both decoding and re-encoding with the event payload in error handling, and a task instance that fails either step is requeued with the special fail method instead of raising. The scheduler timeout sweep therefore finishes its batch and counts such tasks separately. The diff adds no deserialization allow-list, which matches the card's limitations section.

patterns.title: GitPython option injection via keyword arguments and dash-leading revisions
patterns.cause: The unsafe-option check that blocks upload-pack and exec style options is only called from fetch, pull, push and clone_from. Repo.archive() and git.ls_remote() turn caller keyword arguments into Git options without it, so attacker-chosen options can run commands. Repo.iter_commits() and Repo.blame() place the revision before the separator and do not reject a leading dash, so a revision can act as an option that makes Git open and truncate a file.
preconditions: An application passes attacker-controlled keyword arguments or option dictionaries to Repo.archive() or git.ls_remote().
An application passes attacker-controlled revision strings to Repo.iter_commits() or Repo.blame().
GitPython is a version before 3.1.51.
patterns.prevention: Never forward untrusted dictionaries as keyword arguments to Repo.archive(), git.ls_remote() or dynamic git command calls. Accept only a fixed allowlist of option names and values you define, and reject command-selecting options such as exec and upload-pack. Reject any revision that starts with a dash before it reaches Repo.iter_commits() or Repo.blame(), and validate it as a real ref or object name. Upgrade to 3.1.51 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so it is unclear which other Git subcommands reached through the dynamic command interface are covered. The advisory text says the dynamic surface never got the earlier fix. Allowlisting remains the application's job.

fixtures.scenario: A web service exports repository archives and forwards a user-supplied options dictionary to Repo.archive(). The user adds a remote option and an exec option naming a command, and the server runs it.
The service builds archive options itself from a fixed allowlist of format and prefix values, ignores other user keys, rejects revisions starting with a dash, and runs GitPython 3.1.51 or later.

citations.quote: GitPython before 3.1.51 fails to guard against dangerous Git options passed as keyword arguments in Repo.archive() and git.ls_remote()
Repo.iter_commits() and Repo.blame() do not check for leading-dash revision arguments
Exploitation requires an application that passes attacker-controlled arguments to these methods.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds unsafe-option checks to the ls_remote, archive, iter_commits, iter_items and blame paths. These block upload-pack, exec and output style options, whether they arrive as keyword arguments or as a dash-leading revision. It also makes the shared option check recognise abbreviated spellings and checks the archive remote for unsafe protocols. This matches the card's cause and prevention, and the new allow_unsafe_options flag is the opt-out.

patterns.title: Option blocklist bypass through git long-option prefix abbreviation in GitPython
patterns.cause: The unsafe-options guard normalizes option names only by converting underscores to hyphens, then does an exact-match lookup against a blocklist. Git accepts any unambiguous prefix of a long option, so an abbreviated key misses the blocklist but is still resolved by git to the blocked option, such as upload-pack, and executes an attacker-chosen command.
preconditions: The host application passes attacker-controlled keyword argument keys into a GitPython clone, fetch, pull or push call.
The allow_unsafe_options setting is left at its default of false, so the blocklist is the only defense.
The installed GitPython version carries the blocklist fix but is older than 3.1.51.
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on exact-match blocklists when the downstream parser accepts a wider grammar than the guard models. Treat any option name that is a prefix of a blocked long option as blocked, after the same normalization that is used when building the command line. Better, use an allowlist of permitted option names for security-sensitive subcommands, or invoke git so that long-option abbreviation is disabled. Also validate keyword keys against a fixed, developer-chosen set before they reach the library, and upgrade GitPython to 3.1.51 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which approach the released fix uses; the remediation options come from the report's suggestions. Abbreviations of the config option bypass the blocklist, but the report says weaponizing them through an ext:: URL is separately blocked by the protocol allowlist. Exploitation requires the host to forward attacker-controlled keys, so applications that use only fixed keys are not reachable. The sources do not discuss other git subcommands beyond clone, fetch, pull and push.

fixtures.scenario: A web service forwards user-supplied option names and values into a repository clone call with default safety settings. The user supplies an abbreviated upload-pack option name and a program path, and git runs that program.
The service accepts only a fixed set of option names chosen by the developer and rejects any abbreviated or unknown name before it reaches git.

citations.quote: Git accepts any unambiguous prefix of a long option
It does not account for git's unambiguous long-option prefix abbreviation.
Where the host passes only fixed/validated keys, this is not reachable
GitPython before 3.1.51 contains an incomplete command injection blocklist that fails to account for git's long-option prefix abbreviation feature.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the unsafe-option check reject abbreviated long options, such as a short prefix of upload-pack, receive-pack, exec or config, which matches the card's cause and prevention. It also blocks unsafe short options with attached values, including after clustered flags, and avoids treating bare option values in the multi-option list as abbreviations. These extras go beyond the card, but the card's main point about the abbreviation bypass is correct.

patterns.title: Callback deserialization imports attacker-named modules in the Airflow scheduler
patterns.cause: The Task SDK rebuilt a Callback object from serialized data by re-running its constructor. That constructor imports the module named by the stored callback path. SyncCallback is an Airflow class, so it passes the default allowed_deserialization_classes allow-list, and the allow-list does not stop the import. A Dag author controls a task instance's next_kwargs through the task execution API, so that author can choose the module path. The scheduler deserializes the value during its awaiting_input timeout sweep, and the chosen module is then imported inside the scheduler process.
preconditions: apache-airflow at version 3.3.0 or later but before 3.3.1 (versions before 3.3.0 lack the scheduler sweep that reaches the class)
An attacker can act as a Dag author and set a task instance's next_kwargs through the task execution API
The scheduler's awaiting_input timeout sweep deserializes that stored value, which runs unconditionally with default configuration
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later. In general, do not rebuild objects from stored data by running constructors that import a module or class named inside that data.
