Treat values that task code can write, such as next_kwargs, as untrusted input in privileged processes like the scheduler. Check any stored import path against a fixed set of expected targets before importing, and do not rely on a class-name allow-list alone when the allowed class itself triggers imports.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream change in detail, so the exact validation it adds is not covered here. They do not say what an imported module can do beyond being imported in the scheduler process. They do not state whether 3.3.0 itself is affected beyond saying only earlier versions are not. Tightening allowed_deserialization_classes is stated not to help. Fixes for CVE-2026-58076 and CVE-2026-67260 are stated not to cover this path.

fixtures.scenario: A Dag author submits a next_kwargs value containing a serialized SyncCallback whose stored callback path names an arbitrary module. When the scheduler's awaiting_input timeout sweep deserializes it, the constructor imports that module inside the scheduler process, even with a tightened allow-list.

A deployment runs apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later. The same crafted next_kwargs value is deserialized by the sweep, and no arbitrary module named in the stored data is imported into the scheduler process.

citations.quote: can therefore cause an arbitrary module to be imported inside the scheduler process, when the scheduler's
so tightening that setting does not help.
No non-default configuration is required; the sweep runs unconditionally.
Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later.

patch_review.observation: The fix marks a callback path read back from stored data with a private string subclass during deserialization. The path lookup step then returns it as-is instead of importing the named module. Stored values that are not shaped like a dot path are still rejected, and creating a callback from user-supplied input still imports and checks the path.

patterns.title: SSRF through unvalidated sub-resource requests in a browser-based web loader
patterns.cause: The Playwright web loader in Open WebUI checked the destination address only for the top-level document request. The request interceptor returned early for every other resource type. Once the validated page loaded, its own scripts could issue further requests to blocked internal addresses, and the loader returned the final page DOM to the user, so data read from those addresses appeared in web-search or RAG output.
preconditions: The Playwright web loader engine is selected instead of the default loader, on a version from 0.9.6 up to but not including 0.11.0.
A Playwright browser is reachable, either local or through a remote websocket endpoint.
An authenticated user, with no administrator role needed, can submit a URL for ingestion or trigger a web search.
The browser process has a network route to something worth reading, such as cloud instance metadata, other containers or internal APIs.
patterns.prevention: Apply address validation to every request a headless browser makes, not just top-level navigation. Fetch each intercepted request with automatic redirects disabled, re-validate the destination on every redirect hop, and fulfill the request only if the address is global. Also close the paths that bypass request interception: block service-worker requests and handle WebSocket connections so they never connect upstream. Upgrading to 0.11.0 resolves the issue without configuration changes.
patterns.limitations: The sources say the flaw gives read access only, with no write or availability impact, and only within the browser's existing network position. They do not describe how the address check resolves hostnames or handles DNS rebinding, so those points are not covered here. Deployments on the default loader are reported as unaffected. The proof of concept exercised the interceptor with stand-in objects rather than a full browser.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment on version 0.10.2 uses the Playwright loader. An authenticated user submits a page whose script requests a cloud metadata address, and the response is returned in the page DOM in search or RAG output.

Every browser request, including scripts, redirects, service workers and WebSockets, must resolve to a global address. The same page's metadata request is blocked and no internal data appears in the output.

citations.quote: the Playwright web loader validates only the top-level page request and lets sub-resource requests pass unvalidated
Every intercepted request is now validated, fetched with redirects disabled, re-validated on each redirect hop and then fulfilled
The same change blocks the two paths that never reached the interceptor at all

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the early exit that let every non-document request bypass validation, so each request the browser makes is now checked before it is fetched. Redirects are followed manually with a hop limit, and each hop is re-validated. Pages are also opened with service workers blocked and WebSocket connections closed, which closes the paths that bypass request interception.

patterns.title: Client-side SSRF through the default Vega loader in chat chart rendering
patterns.cause: The chart renderer treated a chart spec as trusted authored content rather than untrusted chat text, so it accepted Vega's default loader. That loader fetches data url and topojson or geo sources at view construction. It also lets image mark URLs into the output SVG, where the browser fetches them on display.
preconditions: Vega or vega-lite fenced blocks in chat content are rendered in the viewer's browser with the default loader.
An attacker can place a block where another user will see it, such as a shared chat, a channel message, or model, RAG or tool output the attacker can influence.
The victim must open the message, so exploitation is not zero-click.
patterns.prevention: Treat chart specs from chat text as untrusted. Build the Vega view with a restricted loader whose load operation always fails and whose sanitize step resolves each URI with the browser's own URL parser and permits only data: and same-origin results. Cover both exits: data and geo sources fetched at view construction, and image mark URLs written into the SVG as href and fetched on display. Charts then work only with inline data values. Downstream SVG sanitization alone is not enough, because the URL is a legitimate attribute value. For Open WebUI, upgrading to 0.11.0 is sufficient.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the fix only at a high level and do not list every Vega feature that could load resources. Requests are GET only and no server-side data is exposed directly. Impact depends on what the victim's browser can reach. The CVE record gives the affected range as 0.6.34 up to 0.11.0.

fixtures.scenario: A user posts a vega-lite block in a shared chat whose data section uses a url pointing at an attacker or internal host. When the victim opens it, the victim's browser fetches that URL at view construction.
The same block is rendered with a loader that always fails loading and permits only data: and same-origin URIs. No outbound request is made, and charts with inline data values still render.

citations.quote: Any user who can place such a block where another user will see it can make that user's browser issue attacker-chosen outbound GET requests
The renderer treated a chart spec as trusted authored content rather than as untrusted chat text, so it accepted Vega's default loader.
The second path survives downstream SVG sanitization because the URL is a legitimate attribute value, not markup.

patch_review.observation: The fix builds the Vega view in renderVegaVisualization with a custom loader instead of the default one. The loader's load operation always throws, which blocks data and geo fetches at view construction. Its sanitize step resolves each URI with the browser URL parser and permits only data: and same-origin results, which covers image mark URLs written into the SVG. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: SSRF filter bypass via IPv4 addresses embedded in NAT64 IPv6 literals
patterns.cause: The server decided whether a user-supplied URL destination was allowed by applying the ipaddress is_global test to the literal IPv6 address, without looking at the IPv4 address embedded inside it. The NAT64 well-known prefix is a global prefix that can carry any IPv4 destination, so an internal or cloud-metadata target wrapped in it passed the check. The same test backed the pre-fetch URL validation and the connect-time re-checks, so no later layer caught it.
preconditions: The attacker has any verified user account; no admin role is needed.
The deployment network provides NAT64 translation for the well-known 64:ff9b::/96 prefix.
The application fetches user-supplied URLs server-side (RAG URL ingestion, URL-to-markdown conversion, web-search content retrieval) and returns the response body to the caller.
The default local-fetch setting is off and the default hostname blocklist is in place; neither stops the attack because the blocklist matches hostname strings.
patterns.prevention: Do not judge a destination by the literal IPv6 address alone. Before deciding whether an address is global, unwrap the IPv4 address embedded in IPv6 transition encodings and classify that embedded address. Cover every standardized transition encoding, not just the NAT64 prefix, since the same reasoning error applies to each. Apply the same classification at every checkpoint: the pre-fetch URL check and each connect-time re-check that guards against DNS rebinding. Public destinations wrapped in these encodings should still be allowed, to avoid over-blocking.
patterns.limitations: The sources only demonstrate the NAT64 well-known prefix; they do not list the other transition encodings the fix covers. The proof of concept modelled NAT64 by binding translated addresses locally, not through a real gateway. Impact is described only for GET responses. Deployments without NAT64 translation are reported as unaffected. The sources do not describe other SSRF vectors or other filter weaknesses.

fixtures.scenario: A verified user submits a URL whose host is an IPv6 literal in the NAT64 well-known prefix wrapping a cloud metadata IPv4 address, on a network with a NAT64 gateway. The filter accepts it and the internal response body is returned.
The same URL is rejected because the embedded IPv4 address is unwrapped and classified as non-global, while a NAT64-wrapped public address is still allowed to be fetched.

citations.quote: Open WebUI checked whether a user-supplied URL destination was globally routable by applying ipaddress.is_global to the literal IPv6 address
Address classification now unwraps the IPv4 embedded in IPv6 transition encodings before deciding whether a destination is global
Deployments on IPv4-only networks, or on any network without a NAT64 gateway, are not affected: the address has nowhere to route.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that first applies the standard global-address test, then, for IPv6 addresses, extracts any embedded IPv4 address from the transition encodings (mapped, 6to4, Teredo, IPv4-compatible, the NAT64 well-known prefix, and the local-use NAT64 prefix) and requires that address to be global as well. The helper replaces the plain global check in the pre-fetch URL validation and in both connect-time re-checks (the urllib3-style connection and the aiohttp resolver). This matches the card's cause and prevention, including that public wrapped addresses stay allowed.

patterns.title: Sandboxed preview iframe must not combine script execution with same-origin access for files served from the app origin
patterns.cause: In Open WebUI 0.9.0 through 0.10.2, the terminal file-preview branch that loads HTML from a served URL used a fixed iframe sandbox that always granted both allow-scripts and allow-same-origin. The terminal proxy is mounted under the application's own origin, and the response carries no Content-Security-Policy unless the operator configured one. The sandbox was therefore the only isolation boundary, and it granted the permission that removed that isolation. The other preview path, which uses inline document content, already made same-origin access opt-in and injected a policy. The served-URL branch ignored that setting.
preconditions: An admin has configured at least one terminal server that the victim can reach. Deployments with none are not affected.
The attacker has a normal authenticated account with access to that terminal server and needs no admin rights.
No restrictive Content-Security-Policy is applied through the terminal proxy header setting, which is unset by default.
A malicious HTML file gets written and displayed. A display_file tool call opens the preview automatically, but producing the file needs a prompt injection or a social step.
patterns.prevention: Do not hardcode allow-same-origin in the sandbox of any iframe that renders HTML from a user- or tool-controlled source. Build the sandbox value from the same opt-in user setting for every preview path, so the default is an opaque origin that cannot reach the parent window or its stored session token. Keep the two preview paths consistent so a hardened path cannot be bypassed through a newer one. Where operators can set response headers on proxied content, a restrictive Content-Security-Policy adds a second layer.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the opt-in setting behaves when users enable it. They do not say whether serving previews from a separate origin was considered. They do not give a default Content-Security-Policy for the proxy. With the setting turned on, the same exposure presumably returns, though the sources do not state this. The advisory notes that no global policy is set and that the file reaches the app only through a prompt injection or a social step.

fixtures.scenario: A user with terminal access has a tool write an HTML file that reads the parent window's stored session token. The chat auto-opens it in an iframe with scripts and same-origin both allowed, so the script runs at the app origin and leaks the token.
The same file opens in an iframe whose sandbox omits same-origin access unless the user opted in. The page loads at an opaque origin, cannot reach the parent window, and cannot read the token.

citations.quote: the terminal file-preview serveUrl iframe branch always granted allow-same-origin together with allow-scripts for HTML files served from the application origin.
the sandbox was the only isolation boundary left, and it was granting precisely the permission that dissolved it.
so by default the preview loads at an opaque origin and cannot reach the parent context.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the file-preview iframe that loads HTML from a served URL so it no longer always grants same-origin access alongside script execution. Same-origin access is now added only when the user has turned on the matching opt-in sandbox setting, which defaults to off. This is what the card describes as cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Unbounded recurrence walk from a fixed far-past anchor stalls the event loop
patterns.cause: Recurrence parsing for sub-daily rules used the fixed date 2000-01-01 as the start of enumeration. A near-present anchor was only used on a narrow fast path: a plain single-line rule with a few simple fields and a known current time. Any other input fell back to the far-past anchor, so finding the next run meant stepping through about a quarter-century of occurrences synchronously on the event loop. A caller-supplied start-date line in the rule text could also push enumeration far into the past. Since the scheduler recomputes the next run for stored automations, the cost repeated and grew with real time.
preconditions: The attacker can create or update an automation, which is admin-only by default but may be open to ordinary users where the automations feature was granted.
The recurrence rule is a sub-daily frequency, mainly minutely, and falls outside the fast path, for example by carrying extra fields, multiple lines, a start-date line or different letter case.
The deployment runs a single worker, so the stalled event loop blocks scheduler, HTTP and WebSocket traffic.
The automation is stored, so the scheduler repeats the expensive next-run computation on each poll.
patterns.prevention: Never enumerate sub-daily rules from a fixed far-past date. Always compute the anchor from the current time, snapped down to a multiple of the interval from the epoch so clock-aligned phases such as :00, :05 and :10 are kept, and enumeration starts near the present. Apply this to every input shape, not only a simple fast path, and include the seconds frequency. Discard any start-date line supplied inside the rule text so a caller cannot choose the starting point. Parse the rule keyword and field names case-insensitively so variants cannot slip past the safe path. Treat the cost of next-run computation as bounded work, because the scheduler repeats it for every stored automation.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows only the parsing change in the automation utility. It does not show whether the computation was moved off the event loop or whether any explicit cap on occurrences or on the interval was added. A very small interval combined with other rule fields may still do more work than a plain rule. Only this fix is described, and no other mitigation is documented.

fixtures.scenario: A user permitted to create automations submits a minutely recurrence rule with no start date or one far in the past. The parser walks from a fixed year-2000 anchor on the event loop, and the scheduler repeats the walk on every poll.

The same minutely rule is anchored to the current clock, so the next run is found at once. A supplied start date is used only when the occurrences it implies stay under a fixed bound; otherwise the clock anchor replaces it.

citations.quote: Nothing bounds the walk, and nothing moves it off the loop.
Sub-daily rules are now anchored to the current clock instead of the year-2000 date, so the walk starts at the next occurrence
This causes availability impact for every other user of the instance.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the narrow fast path and always anchors sub-daily rules (now including the seconds frequency) near the current time, snapped down to a multiple of the interval from the 2000 epoch. It also drops any start-date line from the rule text and parses the rule keyword and field names case-insensitively, so unusual input shapes no longer fall back to the far-past anchor.

patterns.title: Escape KaTeX fallback output so failed math renders as text, not HTML
patterns.cause: In Open WebUI 0.10.0 up to 0.11.0, the KaTeX renderer component caught any rendering failure and fell back to showing the original math source. It put that untouched source into the page through the HTML insertion directive. Deeply nested math input makes KaTeX fail with a stack overflow rather than a parse error, so the fallback runs. The Markdown math tokenizer keeps everything between the delimiters verbatim, including complete tags, so the author of a message controls the inserted string exactly. Script in it runs in the viewer's browser.
preconditions: The application renders user-supplied math with KaTeX and has an error fallback that shows the original source.
The fallback inserts that source as HTML, not as text.
An attacker can store a message with deeply nested math, using a normal user account, and a victim opens it in a chat, shared chat, or channel.
patterns.prevention: Treat the original math source on the error path as untrusted text. HTML-escape it before it reaches the DOM, or insert it as plain text, so a failed render shows the formula as text and never as markup. Do not assume the renderer's option for suppressing parse errors covers every failure. Stack overflows from deeply nested input surface as a different exception class, so the catch branch must be safe for any failure. Upgrading to 0.11.0 resolves the issue and needs no configuration change.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe only the escaping of the fallback source in this one component. They do not say whether other renderers or the successful KaTeX output were reviewed, and they do not describe any input depth or size limit. Affected versions are 0.10.0 through 0.10.2, per the advisory. Exploitation needs the victim to open the content, but no interaction with the message itself.

fixtures.scenario: A user posts a message with one inline math block: nested opening braces, an image tag with an error handler, then matching closing braces. KaTeX overflows the stack, and the fallback inserts the raw source as HTML, so the handler runs in the viewer's session.
The same message is posted, KaTeX still fails, but the fallback HTML-escapes the source first. The viewer sees the formula and tag as literal text, and no script runs.

citations.quote: the renderer falls back to inserting the original math source into the page as HTML rather than as text
The error path now HTML-escapes the math source before it reaches the DOM
makes KaTeX fail with a stack overflow instead of a parse error

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the catch branch of the KaTeX renderer component so the fallback no longer puts the raw math source into the HTML-rendered output. It now escapes ampersands and angle brackets first, so a failed render shows text instead of markup. The added comment explains that the option to suppress errors covers only parse errors, while a range error from deep nesting still reaches the catch branch. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Unbounded backtracking regex in knowledge file search stalls the worker
patterns.cause: The knowledge search tool let a chat participant choose the pattern used to grep knowledge files. Any pattern containing regex metacharacters was compiled with a backtracking regex engine and run over every line of every reachable file. Nothing limited matching time. Existing caps on results returned and files scanned did not bound the time one line could take. Because the search ran synchronously inside the event loop, one slow match blocked the whole worker.
preconditions: The knowledge builtin tool group is enabled, which is the default, and the model is given the grep-style knowledge file tool
The attacker is any authenticated user who can read at least one file, such as their own upload, so both the pattern and the searched text are attacker-controlled
A model is willing to call the tool with the attacker's literal pattern, which the advisory says is reliable in practice but not guaranteed on every turn
The affected versions run from 0.9.6 up to but not including 0.11.0
patterns.prevention: Do not run user-influenced patterns through a regex engine that has no time limit. Use an engine that supports a per-search timeout and give each tool call one overall matching budget. When the budget is exhausted, stop and return an error instead of continuing to match. Do not rely on capping pattern length, line length, match count or file count, because backtracking cost grows exponentially with the length of the matched text rather than with the pattern. Treat any pattern with regex metacharacters as untrusted input to the matcher.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say whether other code paths accept user-chosen patterns. They do not say whether the search still runs inside the event loop after the fix, so a timeout may still hold the worker for up to the budget. The advisory states only that upgrading to 0.11.0 is sufficient and does not describe any other mitigation for older versions.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user uploads a file with one short line of repeated characters. They ask the model to call the knowledge grep tool with a nested-alternation pattern that cannot match. The worker spins at full CPU and other users on it get no responses.

The same request runs under a timeout-capable engine and a roughly 2 second matching budget for the whole tool call. The search aborts and the tool returns an error, so the worker stays responsive to other users.

citations.quote: Cost scales exponentially with the length of the matching text
neither of which bounds the time a single line can consume
Backtracking cost is exponential in the length of the matched text rather than in the pattern
every tool call now runs its searches under a single 2 second matching budget

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the standard backtracking regex module with the third-party regex package in the knowledge file matcher, and passes a timeout to each search. It also adds one shared matching-time budget of about two seconds per tool call, covering every search in a command. When the budget runs out, the search stops and reports an error. This matches the card's cause and prevention, including the point that capping pattern or line length does not bound backtracking cost.

patterns.title: Gateway secret api_base stored and fetched without SSRF validation
patterns.cause: The AI Gateway stores the auth_config.api_base value of a gateway secret verbatim, with no check of scheme, host, or IP range. The gateway proxy endpoint later sends an HTTP request to that stored base plus a caller-supplied path and returns the full response body. The existing SSRF guard for webhook URLs is never called on this path.
preconditions: The attacker can authenticate to the MLflow server, and read-only accounts are enough
The attacker can create a gateway secret with a chosen api_base, since that action needs only basic authentication and no specific scope
The attacker can reach the gateway proxy endpoint, which requests the stored api_base plus a caller-chosen path
An internal address such as a cloud metadata service is reachable from the MLflow server
patterns.prevention: Validate any user-supplied api_base before it is stored and before the proxy uses it. Check the scheme, host, and resolved IP range, and reject non-global and metadata addresses. Reuse the existing webhook URL guard on the gateway secret and proxy code path instead of leaving it uncalled. Also give the secret-creation action an explicit permission check so that basic authentication alone is not enough.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail. They do not say how redirects, DNS rebinding, or later changes to a stored value are handled, or which permission scope is required. Applying the existing guard at both save time and request time is a reasonable direction, but the sources do not confirm it. Related issue CVE-2026-4035 concerns a separate mechanism and is not covered here.

fixtures.scenario: A read-only user creates a gateway secret whose api_base points at an internal metadata address. The server saves it unchecked. The user then calls the proxy endpoint with a chosen path and receives the internal response body.

A user submits a secret with an internal or metadata api_base. The server validates scheme, host, and IP range with the existing SSRF guard and rejects it. Nothing is stored, so the proxy never contacts the internal address.

citations.quote: MLflow's AI Gateway accepts an auth_config.api_base value when creating a gateway secret (mlflow/server/handlers.py, _create_gateway_secret) with no validation of scheme, host, or IP range
MLflow's existing SSRF guard, _validate_webhook_url (which blocks non-global and metadata IPs), is never invoked anywhere in this gateway secret/proxy code path.
subsequently issues an HTTP request to that stored api_base plus a caller-supplied path and returns the full response body

patterns.title: Dotted-name bypass in NLTK AllowlistUnpickler enables code execution via untrusted parser models
patterns.cause: The allowlist unpickler checked only the pickle module string and not the global name. A dotted global name could then be resolved by attribute traversal to a callable outside the allowlisted namespace, so a crafted model file could run arbitrary commands when loaded.
preconditions: NLTK version earlier than 3.10.3 is in use
The application loads a transition-parser model through allowlisted_pickle_load, for example via TransitionParser.parse
The model file comes from an untrusted or attacker-influenced source
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NLTK to 3.10.3 or later. When writing an allowlist for deserialization, validate both the module and the global name together, and do not let dotted names resolve through attribute traversal to objects outside the approved set. Treat model files from untrusted sources as unsafe to load.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change or how names are checked after the fix. They do not say whether other loaders in NLTK are affected. Only the transition-parser model loading path is named as an attack route.

fixtures.scenario: A service downloads a transition-parser model from a third party and calls TransitionParser.parse on it with NLTK 3.10.2. The model file holds a dotted global name that escapes the allowlist and runs a command.
The service runs NLTK 3.10.3 or later and loads only models from trusted, verified origins. The loader checks the full global name against the allowlist, so the dotted-name trick is rejected.

citations.quote: validates only the pickle module string and not the global name, allowing attackers to resolve dotted names by attribute traversal
Attackers can craft untrusted transition-parser models that execute arbitrary commands when TransitionParser.parse loads the model through allowlisted_pickle_load.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the allowlist unpickler reject any global whose name contains a dot, which closes the attribute-traversal route to os.system through an allowed module such as sklearn. It also rejects dunder names and denied modules, checks the resolved object after lookup, and replaces broad namespace allowlists in the parser and Punkt loaders with exact global lists. The card's cause and prevention match the dotted-name part of the fix. The extra hardening against in-namespace gadgets is not mentioned, but that does not change the main point.

patterns.title: Absolute path in Crubadan table.txt escapes the corpus root in NLTK
patterns.cause: In NLTK 3.9.4 through 3.10.2, CrubadanCorpusReader joins the corpus root with the column-0 value read from the table.txt mapping file. When that value is absolute, os.path.join discards the root. The file is then opened with the builtin open() instead of the pathsec-validated opener, so the containment check that nltk.pathsec applies when ENFORCE is set never runs.
preconditions: The application loads a corpus package whose contents an attacker controls.
The table.txt mapping file has an absolute path as its column-0 value.
The language n-gram file is opened with the builtin open() rather than the pathsec-validated opener.
The target file name ends in -3grams.txt and its contents parse as token count lines.
patterns.prevention: Treat the column-0 value from table.txt as untrusted input. Open corpus files through the pathsec-validated opener so the containment check is applied, not through the builtin open(). Reject absolute values and confirm that the resolved path stays inside the corpus root before reading. Do not load corpus packages from untrusted sources.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name a patched release or describe the upstream fix. They do not say whether ENFORCE is on by default. They also do not cover other corpus readers. Disclosure is limited to paths ending in -3grams.txt whose contents parse as token count lines, so other file types are outside what the sources describe.

fixtures.scenario: A corpus package ships a table.txt whose first column holds an absolute path ending in -3grams.txt outside the corpus directory. Calling lang_freq on that language reads the outside file and returns its parsed contents.
The same table.txt entry is rejected or confined to the corpus root by the validated opener, so lang_freq cannot read any file outside the corpus directory.

citations.quote: os.path.join discards the root when that value is absolute and the read escapes the corpus directory
opens the result with the builtin open() rather than the pathsec-validated opener
limited to paths ending in -3grams.txt whose contents parse as token count lines

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the Crubadan reader open both the language mapping file and the per-language n-gram file through the pathsec opener, passing the corpus root as the required root. The n-gram path is built from the untrusted first column of the mapping file, so an absolute value used to escape the root. The same commit also hardens the pathsec opener for read modes (no symlink following, hardlink refusal, and a check of the opened descriptor's real path) and applies it to several other corpus readers.

patterns.title: Catastrophic regex backtracking in NLTK TweetTokenizer naked-domain URL matching
patterns.cause: Several regular expressions in nltk/tokenize/casual.py, compiled into the TweetTokenizer word pattern, repeat groups without any upper bound, so a crafted string can be divided among them in exponentially or polynomially many ways. The affected parts are the domain prefix that precedes a slash, the naked-domain label repetition, the balanced-parentheses alternatives in the URL body and ending, and the email domain part. Each needs a suffix that the crafted input never supplies, such as a top-level domain, a slash, a closing parenthesis or an at sign, so the engine tries every split and fails at each offset. A short input of repeated dots, dot-hyphen pairs or open parentheses can then hang the tokenizer.
preconditions: The application runs a version of nltk that does not include the upstream bounding fix.
The application calls TweetTokenizer.tokenize or casual_tokenize.
The text being tokenized comes from untrusted users, such as submitted social-media text.
The input holds long runs of dots, label separators or open parentheses that nearly match a URL or email but lack the required ending.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade nltk to a release that includes the fix, which caps the repetition counts in the URL and email patterns at limits taken from DNS and email length rules, such as about 255 characters for a domain prefix and at most 126 extra labels. When writing or reviewing similar tokenizer patterns, give every repeated group a realistic upper bound, avoid pieces that can be split in more than one way, and test against long near-miss inputs that lack the required ending. Keep a regression test that runs such inputs in a separate process with a hard timeout.
patterns.limitations: The bounds are tied to protocol length limits, so unusually long but legitimate URLs or emails may now tokenize differently. Other patterns in the tokenizer that were not changed were not shown to be safe or unsafe. Exact input sizes and timings that trigger the hang vary by environment, and applications that cannot upgrade still need input size limits or timeouts.

fixtures.scenario: A web service passes user-submitted text to casual_tokenize on an nltk version older than 3.10.1. A request of a few kilobytes made of alternating label separators with no top-level domain ties up one CPU for seconds to minutes.

The service runs nltk 3.10.1 or later, where the label repetition is bounded. The same separator-heavy input is rejected by the pattern quickly and tokenization completes without stalling the request.

citations.quote: Input consisting of many alternating label separators can be partitioned in exponentially many ways
A few kilobytes of input therefore consumes seconds to minutes of single-threaded CPU
Version 3.10.1 bounds the label repetition.

patch_review.observation: The fix puts upper bounds on the unbounded repeats in the TweetTokenizer URL and email patterns: the domain prefix before a slash, the balanced-parentheses alternatives in the URL body and ending, the naked-domain label repetition, and the email local and domain parts. It also adds a regression test that runs long near-miss inputs in a separate process with a hard timeout. This matches the card's cause, its prevention advice, and the bounds it cites.

patterns.title: Image viewer blob URL lifetime allows same-origin script from crafted SVG in JupyterLab
patterns.cause: The JupyterLab image viewer builds a blob URL for text-format images such as SVG and keeps it valid for the whole life of the viewer. Because the URL is revoked too late rather than too early, a user can open the displayed image in a new browser tab. The browser then loads the blob as a top-level document in the JupyterLab origin, so script inside a crafted SVG runs with same-origin privileges. This is cross-site scripting (CWE-79) and can lead to code execution through the JupyterLab server.
preconditions: JupyterLab earlier than 4.5.10 (4.5 line) or earlier than 4.6.2 (4.6 line).
The image viewer is enabled and used to open a text-format image such as SVG.
The SVG file contains attacker-controlled script content.
The user opens the displayed image in a new browser tab while the blob URL is still valid.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to JupyterLab 4.5.10 or 4.6.2. The patched viewer tracks the active blob URL and revokes it as soon as the image has loaded or failed, and again when the content changes or the viewer is disposed, so the image can no longer be reopened from that URL in a new tab. For similar code, never keep blob URLs for untrusted SVG alive longer than the load needs. Treat SVG from untrusted sources as active content, and prefer rendering it in a way that cannot become a same-origin top-level document, such as a sandboxed context or a separate origin. If upgrading is not possible, disable the image viewer plugin.
patterns.limitations: The upstream commits also bundle unrelated hardening: plugin lock handling, case and separator canonicalization of extension listing names, and safer injection of the side-by-side margin style. Those changes are not part of this weakness. The patch narrows the window in which the blob URL is valid rather than sanitizing the SVG, so other paths that expose untrusted SVG at the same origin are not addressed by it.

fixtures.scenario: A user of a JupyterLab 4.5.9 server opens a crafted SVG file in the image viewer and then opens the image in a new browser tab. The blob URL has already been revoked, the image retains a same-origin executable context, and its script runs against the JupyterLab server.

The same crafted SVG is opened in JupyterLab 4.5.10 or 4.6.2, or on a server where the image viewer plugin is disabled. Opening it in a new tab does not give the image an executable same-origin context.

citations.quote: JupyterLab's ImageViewer uses URL.createObjectURL for a specially crafted SVG image and revokes the blob URL too early
allowing the image to retain an executable same-origin context when it is opened through the image viewer
This XSS issue can be used to cause remote code execution (RCE) on the JupyterLab server.
This issue is fixed in versions 4.5.10 and 4.6.2.

patch_review.observation: The image viewer fix tracks the active blob URL for text-format images such as SVG and revokes it as soon as the image loads or errors, when the content is replaced, and when the viewer is disposed. Previously the URL stayed valid for the viewer's lifetime, so it could be opened in a new tab as a same-origin document. The patch also adds a custom context menu for SVG viewers, and the commits carry unrelated hardening (plugin locks, listing name canonicalization, side-by-side margin style injection), which the card correctly sets aside.

patterns.title: Unvalidated notebook margin settings from overrides.json allow script injection through style content in JupyterLab
patterns.cause: The sideBySideLeftMarginOverride and sideBySideRightMarginOverride notebook settings were not properly validated before being inserted into style content. A crafted overrides.json could therefore carry instructions that run as code in the JupyterLab page instead of only changing a display preference.
preconditions: JupyterLab version in the affected range (the CVE record says from 3.3.0 until 4.5.10 and 4.6.2)
A crafted overrides.json is applied, either imported by the user with the Import button in the Settings Editor or loaded automatically from a settings location
For the automatic path, the attacker can write to a directory JupyterLab loads settings from, such as on a shared or multi-tenant file system
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to JupyterLab 4.5.10 or 4.6.2 or later, as no workaround is listed. When implementing similar features, treat every setting value as untrusted data. Validate it strictly against the narrow form it is meant to have before it is placed into style content, and do not rely on a settings file being limited to display preferences. Operationally, restrict write permissions on the application settings directory and other Jupyter configuration paths on shared file systems. Distribute configuration through a trusted process instead of ad-hoc importing of shared files.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation rules or the code change in the fix. They do not give the exact payload form either. They are inconsistent on the first affected version: the advisory says 4.5+ while the CVE record says 3.3.0. Directory permissions only reduce cross-user planting and do not fix the flaw, and the user-import path still needs a patched version.

fixtures.scenario: A user imports a shared overrides.json through the Settings Editor Import button. Its left margin override holds crafted text instead of a plain margin value, and the unvalidated text goes into style content and runs as code with the user's access.

The same import on a patched JupyterLab (4.5.10 or 4.6.2 or later) is checked first, so margin overrides that are not valid display values do not reach style content. Settings directories are also not writable by other users.

citations.quote: the sideBySideLeftMarginOverride and sideBySideRightMarginOverride settings are not properly validated before being inserted into style content
a crafted settings file to contain instructions that execute as code instead of only changing display preferences
restrict write permissions on the application settings directory and other Jupyter configuration paths

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a strict unit-based pattern to the left and right side-by-side margin settings in the notebook settings schema. It also stops building the style element from an HTML string and instead creates the element and sets its text content, and it repairs the missing closing brace in the generated rule. The rest of the diff (plugin lock rules, PyPI listing canonicalization, image viewer) is bundled but unrelated to this CVE.

patterns.title: Unbounded regex compile in vLLM lm-format-enforcer backend enables ReDoS
patterns.cause: The lm-format-enforcer structured-output backend passes the user-supplied regex to lmformatenforcer.RegexParser, which builds an interegular FSM synchronously. No timeout or buildability check applies, and request validation returns immediately when a regex is present. The sibling xgrammar and outlines backends had already been guarded by compile_regex_with_timeout. A catastrophic pattern therefore pegs a CPU core and stalls the engine path.
preconditions: vLLM version earlier than 0.26.0 is running.
The operator selected the lm-format-enforcer backend through the structured outputs configuration; the default auto setting resolves to xgrammar.
A client can send a structured_outputs.regex value in a completions request; vLLM has no authentication by default.
patterns.prevention: Treat every user-supplied regex as untrusted input to an expensive compile step. Run the lm-format-enforcer regex compile under a bounded timeout, as the xgrammar and outlines backends do with compile_regex_with_timeout. Also validate the pattern at request-validation time, rejecting un-buildable or oversized patterns before they reach the engine. Return a clean error instead of blocking the structured-output path. Apply the same guard to every backend that compiles user regexes, so none is left as a missed sibling. Upgrading to 0.26.0 or later also resolves this issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the timeout value, the size limits, or the buildability rules. They do not say whether a timed-out compile is cancelled or merely abandoned. The reproduction covers one nested bounded-repetition pattern and does not characterize all patterns that trigger the hang. The upstream fix is not described in the sources beyond the version in which it landed.

fixtures.scenario: A vLLM server older than 0.26.0 uses the lm-format-enforcer backend. An unauthenticated completions request sets a structured output regex made of deeply nested bounded repetitions. The compile never finishes, one core is pegged, and other requests stall.

The same deployment compiles the regex under a timeout, and request validation rejects un-buildable or oversized patterns. The nested-repetition request returns a clean error quickly, and other requests continue to be served.

citations.quote: it compiles the attacker-supplied regex with no timeout and no buildability check.
One request pegs a CPU core and blocks the structured-output engine path.
This issue is fixed in version 0.26.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix wraps the lm-format-enforcer regex parser construction in the shared timeout-bounded compile helper, both when the grammar is compiled and during request validation. In validation, any failure or timeout is converted into a clean value error, so a catastrophic pattern is rejected before reaching the engine.

patterns.title: Model processor fetches user media strings directly, bypassing the media connector's SSRF and local-file checks
patterns.cause: The MiMoV2Omni multimodal processor in vLLM passed attacker-controlled image and audio strings to a direct HTTP GET call and to a local image-open call instead of the shared MediaConnector. Earlier hardening lived only in MediaConnector, so this later-added code path skipped the domain allowlist, the local-path allowlist and the size caps. The result was server-side requests and reads of any file the vLLM process can access.
preconditions: vLLM version earlier than 0.26.0 serving the MiMoV2OmniForCausalLM architecture
An attacker controls a string value supplied as image or audio multimodal input
The string reaches the model processor directly, for example through library use or batch processing, rather than only through the protected chat path
The vLLM host can reach internal services or cloud metadata endpoints, or holds sensitive readable files
patterns.prevention: Send every externally sourced media string through one hardened loader that enforces a URL scheme and domain allowlist, a local-path allowlist and size limits before any network request or file open. Model-specific processors should not make their own HTTP or file calls on user strings. Alternatively, keep string inputs from reaching processors at all and require all media fetching to happen in the shared loader first. Upgrading to version 0.26.0 or later applies the vendor fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, so this card does not say how the fix is implemented. They do not say how redirects or DNS rebinding are handled inside the shared loader. Only this model's processor is described as affected; other processors would need their own review. The advisory text suggests the audio loader was affected in the same way, but the fixed-version statement is the only confirmation given.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment serves MiMoV2OmniForCausalLM and passes a user-supplied image string, such as an internal metadata URL or a local file path, straight into multimodal input; the processor fetches or opens it with no allowlist.
The same deployment, on version 0.26.0 or later, has every user-supplied image or audio string fetched through the shared media connector, so disallowed domains and local paths are rejected.

citations.quote: bypassing allowed_media_domains and allowed_local_media_path protections and allowing server-side requests and reads of arbitrary files accessible to the vLLM process
route every external resource fetch through
This issue is fixed in version 0.26.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix deletes the processor's own fetching code: the direct HTTP GET and the local file and data-URI image opening, plus the audio equivalents that also fetched URLs and paths. The processor now accepts only already-decoded images and (waveform, sample rate) tuples, and rejects strings or bytes, leaving resolution to the shared media pipeline. This matches the card's cause (a model-specific processor bypassing the shared loader's checks) and its prevention (no processor-level fetching, with all media loading going through the hardened loader).

patterns.title: Stored XSS in django CMS edit-mode plugin exception heading
patterns.cause: In django CMS 5.0.8 until 5.0.9, when plugin rendering fails in edit mode, the exception renderer builds a cms-rendering-exception heading from the exception message, placeholder, placeholder source and plugin short description. These values are interpolated without escaping, and the output is returned as safe markup. Stored HTML therefore runs in the editor's browser.
preconditions: An editor can store HTML in data used by a plugin's get_short_description(), or in other values interpolated into the exception message.
A plugin raises an exception during edit-mode rendering and placeholder rendering catches it.
The custom heading is returned as safe markup, so Django template autoescaping does not apply.
patterns.prevention: Escape every value placed into the custom exception heading before the placeholder output is marked safe, for example by building the heading with Django's format_html helper so the message is escaped. Keep Django's traceback HTML separate from the custom heading, because its escaping does not cover extra markup assembled by django CMS. Upgrade to 5.0.9 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources give 5.0.8 until 5.0.9 as the affected range and say only that older code was affected, so earlier releases are not clearly covered. Restricting plugin editing to fully trusted staff is only a partial mitigation. Setting DEBUG to false does not help. The sources do not describe other rendering paths.

fixtures.scenario: An editor saves HTML markup in a plugin field used by its short description. The plugin then raises during edit-mode rendering, and the exception heading includes that text unescaped, so a script runs in another staff user's browser.
The same plugin fails in edit mode, but the heading is built with escaping. The stored markup appears as plain text in the error block and no script runs in the staff user's browser.

citations.quote: Values from get_short_description(), the exception message, the placeholder, or placeholder.source are interpolated into a cms-rendering-exception heading and later returned through mark_safe.
Escape the custom exception heading before returning it as safe placeholder markup.
does not mitigate the issue: it only controls whether Django's traceback HTML is appended.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the edit-mode exception heading in the plugin renderer so the message is built with Django's HTML-escaping helper instead of plain string interpolation. The new test stores an HTML payload in the page title, which feeds the placeholder source in the message, and checks that it comes out escaped. The same commit also makes the clipboard-clearing admin endpoint require POST, which is a separate CSRF hardening the card does not cover but which does not change the XSS cause or prevention.

patterns.title: GitPython rm and checkout forward pathspec file options, letting callers read arbitrary files via error text
patterns.cause: IndexFile.remove() and Head.checkout() pass caller-supplied keyword arguments straight into git rm and git checkout with no option guard. If a caller supplies a pathspec-from-file option together with the NUL-delimited pathspec option, Git treats the whole named file as one pathspec. When nothing matches, Git's error message quotes that pathspec, and GitPython returns it in GitCommandError.stderr. The full contents of the file are therefore disclosed to the caller.
preconditions: Application code calls IndexFile.remove() or Head.checkout() with keyword arguments that an untrusted party can influence
The GitPython version is older than 3.1.58
The chosen file is readable by the process running GitPython
The caller can see the error output, for example GitCommandError.stderr
patterns.prevention: Do not forward untrusted keyword arguments into git rm or git checkout. Validate options before the command runs, and reject the pathspec-from-file option and the NUL-delimited pathspec option, preferably with an allowlist of expected options. Upgrade to GitPython 3.1.58 or later. Where the application builds these calls itself, keep file-reading options out of any caller-controlled input, and do not show raw Git error output to untrusted users.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail, so the exact set of rejected options is unknown. The report says git reset and git mv did not disclose file contents in testing, and that git status and the guarded checkout-index did not either. Whether other call sites or Git versions behave differently is not covered. The disclosure relies on how Git quotes unmatched pathspecs in its error text.

fixtures.scenario: A web service lets users pass extra options to a wrapper around IndexFile.remove(). A user sends a pathspec-from-file option naming a sensitive file plus the NUL pathspec option, and the error text returned in the response contains the whole file.

The wrapper accepts only a fixed set of known options and rejects pathspec-related options before calling IndexFile.remove() or Head.checkout(). The same request is refused and no file content appears in any error.

citations.quote: GitPython versions before 3.1.58 fail to validate options passed to git rm and git checkout commands in IndexFile.remove() and Head.checkout()
makes Git treat the whole file as a single NUL-delimited pathspec, and the unmatched-pathspec error quotes it verbatim.
to read arbitrary files accessible to the process, with full file contents returned in GitCommandError.stderr.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a denylist containing only the pathspec-from-file option and checks caller keyword arguments against it in IndexFile.remove, Head.checkout and Head.reset. The check is skipped only when the caller sets the allow_unsafe_options flag. It also makes the option-candidate helper count falsey non-boolean values such as 0, so those cannot slip past the check. This matches the card's cause (unguarded kwargs reaching git rm and git checkout so a pathspec file leaks through error text) and its direction of rejecting that option before the command runs.

patterns.title: Unguarded option forwarding in GitPython Repo.init allows hook planting via template
patterns.cause: Repo.init forwards its keyword arguments verbatim to git init, with no unsafe-option check and no allow_unsafe_options parameter. The git init template option copies the hooks directory of the template into the new repository's hooks directory. An attacker-controlled template value therefore plants an executable hook that runs on a later git operation, such as a commit.
preconditions: The application passes externally influenced keyword arguments, in particular a template value, into Repo.init.
The attacker can stage an executable hooks directory at a path known to the host process.
The GitPython version is earlier than 3.1.58; the advisory lists 3.1.57 and earlier as affected.
A later git operation, such as a commit, runs in the newly initialized repository.
patterns.prevention: Never forward untrusted option names or values to Repo.init. Build the init options inside the application from a fixed allowlist, and reject template and separate-git-dir. Any option check should run before git is invoked and should cover path-taking and hook-installing options. Upgrade to GitPython 3.1.58 or later, which the CVE text implies is the first non-vulnerable release.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix itself, so its exact behavior is unconfirmed. The denylist in the advisory is only a suggestion and names just template and separate-git-dir; the full set of dangerous git init options is not given. The separate-git-dir option is described only as a redirect vector with value control. The sources do not say how the hook directory gets staged on the host.

fixtures.scenario: A service accepts a caller-supplied options mapping and passes it to Repo.init. The caller sets template to a directory holding an executable post-commit hook, and the next commit in the new repository runs it.
The service ignores caller-supplied option names and builds init options from a fixed allowlist that excludes template and separate-git-dir, so no hook is copied from an outside directory.

citations.quote: GitPython before 3.1.58 contains a remote code execution vulnerability in Repo.init that forwards unsafe git options without validation.
Arbitrary code execution (hook fires on next git op) at the privileges of the host process.
path-taking / hook-installing options

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a list of unsafe git init options (template and separate-git-dir) and an allow_unsafe_options parameter to Repo.init. Unless the caller opts in, the kwargs are checked before git runs and an unsafe option raises an error, with prefix abbreviations such as templa also caught. This matches the card's cause (unguarded forwarding that lets a template plant hooks) and its prevention (reject those options before invoking git).

patterns.title: Option injection into git read-tree via treeish arguments in GitPython IndexFile methods
patterns.cause: IndexFile.from_tree, IndexFile.reset (which delegates to from_tree) and IndexFile.merge_tree pass caller-influenced treeish strings positionally to git read-tree. They apply no unsafe-option check and add no argument separator. A treeish that looks like the path-taking index-output option is therefore read as an option, and because the last occurrence wins, it overrides the method's own temporary output path.
preconditions: The application passes attacker-influenced treeish values to IndexFile.from_tree, IndexFile.reset or IndexFile.merge_tree
GitPython is a version before 3.1.58
The host process can write to the attacker-chosen target path
patterns.prevention: Do not let untrusted text reach the treeish positions unchecked. Reject values that start with a dash, or validate them as real revisions before use. Put an argument separator before positional treeish values where git allows it, and block the path-taking index-output option on this call. Upgrade GitPython to 3.1.58 or later. The advisory suggests an unsafe-option guard with an opt-in parameter, a separator before the positional arguments, or both.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the fix only as a suggestion and do not detail the upstream change. Only the index-output option is shown to be exploitable. They do not say whether other read-tree options are dangerous here, so a broad dash-prefix rejection is a conservative choice, not a documented requirement. The written content is a git-index blob the attacker does not choose, so the impact is file overwrite or destruction, not code execution. The advisory text names the affected versions inconsistently (up to 3.1.57 versus before 3.1.58).

fixtures.scenario: A web service takes a revision string from a request and passes it to IndexFile.from_tree. A caller supplies a string naming the index-output option with a path to an existing config file, and that file is replaced by a git-index blob.
The service checks that the revision string does not begin with a dash and resolves to a real commit before calling IndexFile.from_tree. An option-shaped string is rejected and no file is touched.

citations.quote: Attackers can inject the --index-output option to overwrite arbitrary files with a valid git-index blob
append caller-influenced treeish strings to git read-tree without option validation or argument separation
Arbitrary file overwrite / destruction at the privileges of the host process.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a class-level list of unsafe read-tree options naming the index-output option. from_tree and merge_tree now check their treeish arguments (and extra keyword options for from_tree) against that list and raise an unsafe-option error unless the caller opts in with a new allow_unsafe_options parameter. reset forwards that opt-in to from_tree. No argument separator is added, so the card's guard-based cause and prevention match the change, and the separator is only an extra suggestion.

patterns.title: GitPython unsafe-option guard bypass through joined short-option token when single-char splitting is disabled
patterns.cause: The check_unsafe_options guard checks a candidate list of option names built from the kwargs. When split_single_char_options is False, that list holds only the single-character key and omits the value-derived option. The argv builder still emits a joined token of the short flag plus its value. Git clusters short flags and reads the tail of that token as the upload-pack option, so the guard never sees what git executes. This is an incomplete fix for an earlier bypass that handled only the split case.
preconditions: The application forwards a user-controlled kwargs dictionary to a guarded GitPython method such as clone_from, fetch, pull, push, ls_remote, iter_commits, blame or archive.
The attacker can include the split_single_char_options switch set to False together with a single-character key whose value carries the payload.
GitPython is older than 3.1.58, with unsafe options left disallowed by default.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to GitPython 3.1.58 or later. When building or reviewing such a guard, make it judge the same tokens git will receive. Either derive candidate options from the joined short-option form as well as the split form, or run the unsafe-option check over the fully transformed argument list instead of a reconstructed name-only list. Do not forward untrusted kwargs dictionaries to these methods without reviewing them.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change in 3.1.58 or confirm which approach it uses. They do not say whether other short options besides the upload-pack one are reachable the same way. The impact depends on the application forwarding attacker-controlled kwargs, and the report gives no guidance on filtering such input.

fixtures.scenario: A web service passes a client-supplied options dictionary straight into a clone call. The client sets the single-character-splitting switch to False and adds a one-letter option whose value starts with a short flag for upload-pack followed by a shell command. The guard passes and the command runs.
The service runs GitPython 3.1.58 or later, and the unsafe-option check sees the joined token that git will parse. The upload-pack option is detected and the call is rejected before any command runs.

citations.quote: Attackers can supply a crafted kwargs dictionary to guarded methods like clone_from to emit a joined token parsed as --upload-pack
git clusters value-less short flags then parses
The guard's candidate list omits the smuggled option
Precondition: the app forwards a user-controlled kwargs dict containing

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the candidate-option builder so that, when single-character splitting is disabled, it emits the joined short-flag-plus-value token (for example the flag followed directly by its value). It no longer emits only the bare flag. The unsafe-option check therefore sees the same joined token that git receives, and the new tests confirm this. This matches the card's cause and its advice to check the joined short-option form.

patterns.title: Untrusted .gitmodules include directive leaks local file content through GitPython submodule enumeration
patterns.cause: The parser used to read .gitmodules for submodule enumeration inherits the default behavior of merging include directives. A .gitmodules file shipped in a cloned repository can therefore name any local file in an include section. The include resolver follows absolute paths and unchecked relative paths, and its only gate is a readability check. When the target is not valid git-config syntax, the parser raises MissingSectionHeaderError, whose message embeds the file's first line verbatim. Submodule enumeration does not catch this error type, so the text reaches the caller, logs or error pages.
preconditions: The application opens a repository whose .gitmodules file is controlled by an untrusted party, such as a cloned third-party repository.
The application uses a GitPython version before 3.1.59 and accesses the repository submodules list, a read-only operation.
The target file is readable by the process and its first line is not a valid git-config section header.
Exception text from GitPython is visible to the attacker, for example through CI logs, error pages, or exception trackers.
patterns.prevention: Never let content from an untrusted repository pull in other files through include or includeIf directives. When parsing .gitmodules, construct the submodule config parser with include merging disabled, as the config writer path already does. Upgrade GitPython to 3.1.59 or later. As defense in depth, reject resolved include paths that fall outside the repository tree, and avoid echoing raw file content in parse errors for files the caller did not explicitly choose to open. Treat parser exceptions from submodule enumeration as untrusted-input failures and do not forward their text to users.
patterns.limitations: Only the first line of the target file leaks, because parsing aborts at the first error, but the same behavior works as a file-existence oracle. The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, so the path containment and error message hardening are advisory suggestions rather than confirmed parts of the fix. Include conditions (includeIf) are only followed when a repository is supplied to the parser, and the sources do not say whether other callers are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A service clones an untrusted repository whose .gitmodules adds an include section pointing at a local credentials file, then lists the repository submodules. The resulting parse error text, containing the file's first line, is written to a shared log.
The same service lists submodules with include merging disabled for .gitmodules, so the include section is ignored, no foreign file is opened, and no file content appears in any error message.

citations.quote: GitPython before 3.1.59 fails to disable merge_includes when parsing .gitmodules, allowing attackers to disclose local file content by including arbitrary file paths via [include] directives.
when repo.submodules is accessed, GitConfigParser raises MissingSectionHeaderError embedding the target file's first line verbatim in the exception message
a readability check, not a path restriction.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the submodule config parser factory so the parser for .gitmodules is built with include merging disabled. A regression test shows that an include section pointing at a non-config file is no longer followed. This matches the card's cause (untrusted .gitmodules includes being resolved) and its main prevention. The extra config writer escaping in the pull request is a separate hardening change that does not affect this card.

patterns.title: GitPython clone_from allows --separate-git-dir to place git metadata outside the destination
patterns.cause: The clone denylist, unsafe_git_clone_options, does not list --separate-git-dir, although the init denylist does and the clone docstring says allow_unsafe_options should gate it. The check only compares option names against the denylist and does not validate the path value. A separate_git_dir keyword therefore reaches the real git clone command with allow_unsafe_options at its default of False. Git then writes the full repository metadata tree to the given path and leaves a gitlink file at the intended destination.
preconditions: The host application forwards a caller-influenced value as the separate_git_dir keyword of Repo.clone_from() or Repo.clone(), or as a raw --separate-git-dir token in multi_options.
The application does not validate or reject that value and does not intentionally set allow_unsafe_options to True.
The process has permission to create directories at the attacker-chosen path.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to GitPython 3.1.59 or later. Do not pass untrusted keyword arguments or multi_options entries into clone calls, and keep allow_unsafe_options at False. An implementation should treat --separate-git-dir as unsafe on the clone path, as the init path already does, so that the same option-name guard used for --template, --upload-pack and --config also rejects it. Applications should also reject any caller-supplied repository-metadata location themselves.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change or its handling of option aliases. The guard inspects option names only, so it does not validate path values. Hook execution needs a later git operation on the redirected or colliding directory. Impact is bounded by the filesystem permissions of the process running GitPython.

fixtures.scenario: A service forwards a client-supplied separate_git_dir value into Repo.clone_from() with allow_unsafe_options left at its default. No error is raised, and git writes the repository metadata outside the clone destination.

The service never forwards client-controlled separate_git_dir values and runs GitPython 3.1.59 or later. Clone options come from a fixed set, so repository metadata stays inside the intended destination.

citations.quote: GitPython before 3.1.59 omits --separate-git-dir from unsafe_git_clone_options, allowing attackers to create arbitrary git directories outside the intended clone destination.
Parity gap between two sibling denylists that guard the same underlying primitive (arbitrary redirection of git metadata storage)
redirect repository metadata to an attacker-controlled filesystem path, enabling arbitrary directory creation and potential hook execution.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds the separate-git-dir option to the clone unsafe-option denylist in the Repo class, so clone and clone_from now raise an unsafe-option error for it unless allow_unsafe_options is set. Submodule cloning sets this option internally, so the submodule clone path now first checks the caller-supplied keyword and multi_options against the denylist and only then enables unsafe options for its own use. Tests cover both the keyword and raw-token forms.

patterns.title: SSRF bypass in NLTK pathsec when an HTTP proxy is configured
patterns.cause: The URL helper validates the requested hostname locally. When proxy handlers are inherited, the safe HTTP and HTTPS handlers that pin the validated destination are disabled. The proxy then performs the real fetch against a destination that is never re-validated, so the validated hostname no longer matches the actual egress target.
preconditions: NLTK version before 3.10.3 using nltk.pathsec.urlopen or its callers (nltk.data.load, Downloader.index, Downloader.download)
An HTTP proxy is configured in the runtime
The application relies on pathsec as its SSRF barrier
An attacker can choose a public URL that the proxy forwards to an internal loopback-only service
patterns.prevention: Do not treat local hostname validation as sufficient when a proxy performs the fetch. Either validate the destination the proxy will actually reach, or fail closed and refuse the request when it would fall back to an unpinned proxied path. Apply this to every kind of proxy, including environment-configured proxies and explicitly added proxy handlers. Allow proxied fetches only through a deliberate operator opt-in for a proxy that is trusted. Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.3 or later. Add regression tests covering pathsec.urlopen, nltk.data.load and downloader fetches with a proxy configured.
patterns.limitations: The sources conflict on patch status: the advisory text says not yet patched, while the CVE record says versions before 3.10.3 are affected. The sources do not describe the exact commit contents. The operator opt-in restores the exposure, so the proxy's own network controls then decide what can be reached. Direct, non-proxied fetches were described as still protected by destination pinning. Published 3.9.4 did not reproduce the issue.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs an affected NLTK with an HTTP proxy configured and loads a public URL that passes hostname validation. The proxy forwards it to a loopback-only internal service, and the internal content is returned to the caller.

The same service runs a patched NLTK with a proxy configured and enforcement on. The proxied fetch is refused unless operators deliberately opted in to trust the proxy, so the internal service is not reached.

citations.quote: proxy-handler inheritance disables the safe HTTP/HTTPS handlers so the actual fetch is performed by the proxy against a destination that is never re-validated
NLTK cannot pin the egress through a proxy, so it stops pretending to
NLTK before 3.10.3 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability

patch_review.observation: The fix makes pathsec.urlopen fail closed when a proxy is configured, because the proxy resolves the host and performs the egress, so NLTK cannot pin the validated address. The request is refused with a permission error under enforcement unless the operator opts in through a module setting or an environment variable that asserts the proxy is trusted. Tests cover the default refusal, the opt-in path, and an end-to-end case where the proxy points at a loopback service.

patterns.title: Unrestricted pickle loading of NLTK TransitionParser model files allows code execution
patterns.cause: In NLTK 3.9.4 and earlier, TransitionParser.parse() loads a model file through the library's pickle_load() helper with its restricted option left at the default of off. That routes the data through WarningUnpickler, which only warns and does not override find_class(). Any class or function named in the file can therefore be resolved during unpickling, so a crafted model file runs arbitrary Python code. NLTK ships a RestrictedUnpickler that blocks this, but the sources say no production code path uses it. The same default is reported at call sites in the chart parser application.
preconditions: The application runs NLTK 3.9.4 or earlier (fixed in 3.10.0).
The application calls TransitionParser.parse() with a model file path.
An attacker can supply or replace the model file that gets loaded.
The pickle loading helper is used without its restricted option turned on.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.0 or later, where the same malicious file is rejected because its global is not in a pickle allowlist. Treat every model file as executable content: load only files from trusted, integrity-controlled locations and never from user-supplied or world-writable paths. In code that calls the pickle loading helper, choose the restricted deserialization mode so unpickling resolves only allowlisted globals. Where stricter control is needed, prefer an allowlist of permitted modules over trusting file names or paths.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe exactly what 3.10.0 changed or what its allowlist contains. They note that restricted loading may break older sklearn-based models and that a module allowlist would be more robust. Chart parser application call sites are listed as using the same unsafe default, but the sources do not say whether 3.10.0 changes them. The sources do not cover other NLTK loaders or verification of model file provenance.

fixtures.scenario: A data pipeline on NLTK 3.9.4 accepts a model file path from an upload form and passes it to TransitionParser.parse(). An attacker uploads a pickle whose reduce hook invokes a system command. Unpickling runs it with the privileges of the pipeline user.

The pipeline runs NLTK 3.10.0 or later and loads models only from a read-only directory controlled by the operator. A crafted pickle naming a system call is rejected with an error saying the global is not in the allowlist, and no command runs.

citations.quote: WarningUnpickler, which does not override find_class() and therefore permits arbitrary class resolution.
NLTK provides a RestrictedUnpickler for safe deserialization, but it is not used by production code paths.
embedded pickle gadget chains execute arbitrary Python code with the privileges of the user running the application.
A more robust approach would implement a module allowlist in `RestrictedUnpickler.find_class()`.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the warn-only unpickling of TransitionParser model files in parse() with a new allowlisting unpickler. It overrides class lookup so that only globals from numpy, scipy and sklearn can be rebuilt, and anything else, such as os.system, raises an unpickling error. This matches the card's cause (unrestricted class resolution in the default loader) and its main prevention (an allowlist of permitted modules).

patterns.title: Allowlisted pickle loaders that trust whole module namespaces allow code execution
patterns.cause: The allowlisted pickle loaders in NLTK trusted entire module namespaces instead of exact safe callables. A crafted pickle can use the REDUCE opcode to call dangerous functions inside an allowed namespace, such as the REPP tokenizer execute method or a numpy f2py helper that evaluates attacker-controlled input. The code runs during unpickling.
preconditions: The application loads a tokenizer or model artifact from an untrusted source.
The artifact is loaded through an allowlisted loader such as the punkt loader or the transition parser parse method.
The loader's allowlist permits a whole module or namespace prefix rather than exact names.
patterns.prevention: Allow only exact pairs of module and qualified name for the few classes or functions that are genuinely needed. Never allow whole namespaces such as the tokenize package or numpy. Reject dotted attribute names during class lookup. Deny dangerous modules (os, subprocess, sys, builtins, numpy.f2py, the REPP tokenizer module) as a backstop even when a broad allowlist exists. Name safe primitives such as int individually. Treat post-load type checks as a secondary defense only, because code runs before they happen. Upgrade NLTK to 3.10.3 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the full 3.10.3 fix. The GHSA text says not yet patched, while the CVE text says versions before 3.10.3 are affected. The transition parser still allows numpy, scipy and sklearn because array unpickling needs their submodules, so it relies on the deny guards. A denylist is only a backstop. Some other loaders read user-selected files and rely on warnings.
